summary: Don’t work for Onyx if you’re a designer
advice:
Listen to the feedback you have received from the designers who have left this team. There are so many amazing design leaders in the world who could protect the physiological safety of their teams, pick one of them and stop this happening again.

I am surprised and ashamed that this guy is still allowed to work there.
pros: Training was good, as this mostly came from the umbrella UX group, there was one opportunity to learn story mapping from Jeff Patton too, that was very cool
cons:
This review is for Onyx at JPM, not JPM as a whole.

The design manager for Onyx comes across as insightful and supportive in your interview. When you are finally hired, it begins to shift in to a really weird and often very psychologically damaging dynamic. 


My time at Onyx saw me coming in to work with a huge amount of anxiety, not from the workload, which was heavy but could have been alright with better leadership, but from the way the design manager conducts himself. I have never experience manipulation in the way I have working under this person. The worst part is, I don’t think he will ever be aware of what he is doing wrong, it is a topic that was brought up by the team on multiple occasions. We even had team workshops to try to fix the behaviour. We felt like we had to do this workshop anonymously for fear of him singling out any one of us and punishing us. He heard all of this feedback being brought up and didn’t once make the link back to himself, he thought it was the design team sorting things out between ourselves as opposed to giving him feedback. I raised concerns to JPM design management, then reports, then complaints, then ultimately after one of the worst years in my career for mental health, I left the role and the company. 

If you are a designer and you are all about career and want to move up and up and up a corporate ladder and are willing to do anything to get where you want to be, go for it. 

Please listen to this feedback designers-
Anxiety
Manipulation
Fear
Punish

JPM design is a great team in general to work for, the problem is with the design manager specifically for Onyx.

pros: Internal Moves are surprisingly straightforward and easy. Even moves into roles above your Job Grade (though you won't move into that Job Grade and probably won't have any change of comp) with internal moves being plentiful and the ability to work all over the world. Good schemes for Graduates. Working hours during the week are flexible usually and I haven't been made to work past my allocated hours unless for major production issues. Pay is fairly good when entering the company and for similar roles. The Grad schemes have a very good pay structure. Depending on the team the work isn't that demanding most of the time Managers are more lenient than they should be with poor-quality or slowly delivered work than they should be. This is either a pro or con depending on your situation The interview process isn't a 4 stage ordeal like some other higher prestige tech companies and doesn't revolve solving leetcode questions nor making long presentations depending on the role. This could be a con because some inferior employees sometimes slip through the cracks There are a lot of helpful internal tools. Free Coffee? I don't drink Coffee so I don't care about this one but if you do like Coffee it's a plus. Though I hear it isn't good so people go to Pret/Starbucks anyway. Depending on the LOB there are plenty of Social Events for networking. You will work with talented people usually.
cons: 3 Days a Week in the Office is just stupid when every other Bank has at most 2 days in the office. Though managers are increasingly taking a more liberal view of this policy The 3 days in the office have caused a lot of very talented people to leave and talented developers are not joining. Manager Russian Roulette. Some Managers are really good and some are terrible. A lot of time your team leaders are too busy (too many meetings) to do tasks such as 1-2-1s, and other support. A Mid-Year review basically boiled down to me saying I thought I was doing a good job and that was it. You'll be in a lot of meetings due to most teams being distributed. This can pose difficulties when the same team is spread over time zones. I've been in teams with members in Houston and Mumbai who never overlap in working hours. You will get a lot of emails. A lot of which will have no impact on your job. If you stay in a team long enough it will be moved around organizationally. A lot of managers do not know the HR policy well at all. This results in some minor levels of exploitation as I was not made aware that covering support work for a week constituted a payment. This went on with my team for years and took 6 months from finding out about this system to be back paid for these activities. Working on Weekends is sometimes expected depending on the team for certain activities. Salary Ranges are deliberately obscured and discussion between employees is taboo. So I imagine a lot of people are underpaid. You're working in a bank so there are a lot of processes to get access to tools to do your job Onboarding documentation is done on a team-to-team basis so you're at the mercy of that team's documentation Periods of benching in certain teams/roles. End-of-Year pay rises and Bonuses have been curbed due to COVID even though the bank has made record profits. From my understanding, you will only get minor rises in pay unless you come with an offer from another company. Furthermore, if you move teams during the team your bonus budget will be shared between both teams. This results in a lot of people getting a cut bonus and has caused at least one person to leave shortly after this. A lot of Cognizant consultants are used and they are at times very bad (though some are really good) I don't understand why it's cheaper to get to 2 consultants when one full-time developer would be better long-term. Internal Job Grade promotions take a very long time to materialize. I would advise that it is easier to leave and get a promotion than move internally. I would estimate it takes about 5 years to move between each Officer Title Assoc -> VP -> ED -> MD. Though I would add that these job titles are tangibly worthless, outside of not getting overtime once you hit VP, and if you want more responsibility/money the best course of action would be to move around. You're not going to be working on "fun" greenfields tech or activities. Developers roles will mostly be around writing boilerplate Java. Or if you're in the business/project management side combing through Jira or Excel, to plan for said boilerplate Java tasks. One Senior ex-colleague said once he was made redundant that he was happy he didn't need to go into "The Most Boring Office in the World" anymore. Take of that what you will I've been here for over 5 years I think the lifelessness has a certain charm to it. I don't know if this is just the people I work with or me. Still, I find a lot of people to lack emotional or situational intelligence with meetings being cancelled last minute or just not attending a meeting that was created for them in mind. Certain decision-making can be obscured and lengthened in certain LOBs because of the amount of middle management in it i.e. Too Many Cooks in the Kitchen If you need stuff done you're better off doing it yourself. A lot of time people will not perform tasks or actions for you unless you have a superior job title to them or bring someone with a superior job title into the conversation. Even people you're meant to be in the same team with. Like many businesses, there is a ton of butt-kissing which at times verges on the embarrassing. Too many talented people, who have better things to do, do not get rewarded properly because of this and leave There is a lot of Regulatory training for financial stuff even if you're in tech. This is almost always half-arsed by every employee. Been in positions where a line manager is responsible for multiple disparate teams within the same organization which don't really collaborate with each other. Which causes the line manager to become extremely stretched and causes issues to slip through the cracks. In some teams, it has been unclear what the exact role of the team is and due to this a team does much disparate Management uses terms such as Agile, DevOps, and SRE but doesn't actually do such tasks. Many Development Teams will be expected to be responsible for the entire SDLC. So you will have to do all the development work, DevOps work and them support the application fully in production. So many Project Managers I've encountered call themselves Agile but don't do Agile properly or at all

advice:
Yeah right I don't think so. Here's another one for my banker friends out there. Your branch manager's bonus is based on peer groups. This means he/she can make pretty good money despite being in a bad branch so long as he/she whips enough productivity out of you. Not the same for bankers. The incentive plan is the same for all bankers whether they are on Main St or Park Ave. Nothing changed about me, my skill set, or my work ethic when I moved to a wealthy demographic. I just started making way more money. 

TLDR: Only pursue the RB/PCB position at Chase so long as the branch assignment is in a wealthy area. Don't let them sell you on starting anywhere else. Once they realize you're good at your job they'll try to keep you there as long as possible. 2 years in my case...not worth the hassle believe me.
pros:
- Health, retirement, and PTO benefits are fine
- In my experience most of my colleagues were smart, competent, and fun to work with day to day
- If you are in the right place at the right time there is opportunity for upward mobility
- Great resume builder
- You get your licenses paid for by the Firm, time to study, and a fair amount of money while you're building your pipeline
- The money can be pretty good depending on where you are at
- Free suckers
cons:
- It's all about what branch you are in plain and simple. That is to say, your success, happiness, and INCOME are dependent on what branch you reside in. There's not a lot of middle ground here. If your branch is in an affluent demographic you will have plenty of non-licensed staff to deal with the non-opportunity walk in traffic (i.e. broke people with bad credit but all the time in the world to talk). The people who schedule time with you will, generally speaking, have more money, better credit, and some kind of opportunity beyond the scope of the meeting. Your Business Relationship Manager, Private Client Advisor, and Home Lending Advisor will actually be there with you in the branch as a resource. And finally, your book of business will be filled with lots and lots of clients that can yield big time $$$
- Take it from a guy who started in a bad branch (i.e. the hood). I learned over a long period of time I was making tens of thousands of dollars less yet working twice as hard than bankers in better branches. When I finally demanded/worked my way into an affluent branch suddenly I was the man. I doubled my commissions within a year. For the record, my stress level was also severely reduced in that branch. It is impossible to impart upon you, dear reader, how much better my life was in my last branch.
- I had to work real hard to get out of the bad branch. It felt like prison time. Gaslit the whole way about adjusting behaviors or digging deeper blah blah blah. But I got out. I would be leaving a 5 star review across the board had I just started out in a place like my last branch.

Prioritize transparency in job descriptions and interviews to ensure alignment of expectations and responsibilities.

summary: "Detail-Oriented Business Analyst Specializing in Data-Driven Solutions and Strategic Insights"
advice:
Here’s some key advice for senior management:

1. **Lead by Example**: Your actions set the tone for the organization. Demonstrate the behavior, ethics, and work ethic you want to see in your team.

2. **Foster Open Communication**: Encourage transparency and create a culture where employees feel comfortable sharing ideas and concerns.

3. **Empower Your Team**: Delegate effectively, trusting your team to make decisions and take ownership of projects. Support their growth through mentorship.

4. **Stay Adaptable**: Business landscapes change rapidly. Be open to new technologies, strategies, and ideas to stay competitive and innovative.

5. **Focus on Long-Term Vision**: Don’t get bogged down in day-to-day operations. Keep the company’s mission and long-term objectives in sight, driving strategic decisions.

6. **Prioritize Employee Well-being**: A happy, motivated workforce is productive. Invest in their development, mental health, and work-life balance.

7. **Embrace Diversity**: Encourage diverse perspectives and create an inclusive environment. It enhances problem-solving and innovation.

8. **Measure Success with Data**: Base decisions on analytics and performance metrics, ensuring actions align with business goals.

9. **Be Decisive but Thoughtful**: While timely decision-making is key, consider all angles and potential impacts before making significant choices.

10. **Keep Learning**: Stay updated on industry trends, leadership strategies, and management tools to continually improve your effectiveness.
pros:
Here are some key pros of being a Business Analyst:

1. **Problem-Solving Opportunities**: Business analysts tackle complex business problems, helping companies improve processes, reduce costs, and make strategic decisions.

2. **High Demand**: The role is in demand across various industries like finance, healthcare, and technology, offering solid job security.

3. **Diverse Career Paths**: BAs can specialize in areas like data analysis, process improvement, or project management, allowing for career flexibility and growth.

4. **Collaboration and Networking**: BAs work closely with stakeholders, developers, and other teams, building strong communication and networking skills.

5. **Impactful Role**: Business analysts play a crucial role in driving efficiency and innovation within an organization, leading to tangible, measurable improvements.
cons:
Here are some cons of being a Business Analyst:

1. **High Expectations**: BAs are often expected to deliver solutions quickly and efficiently, which can lead to stress and pressure, especially with tight deadlines.

2. **Ambiguity**: The role often involves working with incomplete or unclear requirements, which can be frustrating and require a lot of problem-solving.

3. **Constant Learning**: Technology and business processes are constantly evolving, meaning BAs need to stay updated, which can be time-consuming.

4. **Stakeholder Conflicts**: Balancing the needs of various stakeholders can be challenging, especially when their goals and expectations don’t align.

5. **Limited Technical Involvement**: While BAs work closely with IT teams, they often don’t have hands-on involvement in the technical aspects, which might be unsatisfying for those interested in tech-heavy roles.

summary: Global Finance & Business Management entry level Analyst - Bangaluru
advice:
JPMorgan is a great organisation that has learnt and improved its internal processes and employee friendliness through decades of trial and error, and I hope they do the same with some of the cons which although small, are important to fix. 

There are many places/cities in the country which also produces top talent in the fields of Finance, operations and IT (Chennai and Pune which are large hubs being prime examples), it will be great if JPMorgan expands their office footprint to such places in the country so as to mitigate their employee turnover and also giving their current employees the opportunity to work close to/in their home towns.
pros:
- Friendly and open work environment where there isn't a superior and subordinate relationship, and everyone at all levels are treated as equals.
- Colleagues go out of their way to comprehensively give training to understand the job and its processes end to end.
- the top management goes out of their way to create a great work environment where the collective team is encouraged to share automation ideas and best practices every week, this makes every team member feel important in the team.
- The entire organisation encourages its employees to completely switch off from work on the weekends and stresses the importance of work life balance.
- Internal mobility is highly encouraged after 1 to 2 years in the organisation, and you can openly talk to the management about your career plans and they'll go out of their way to help.
cons:
- The slow phase out of remote/hybrid model: Although it's required for some of the roles to be done in office, for many roles where it's not a primary requirement, a hybrid model should be maintained. The top management of the organisation needs to take its time and evaluate different roles and then implement a system where some roles require 5 day office days and some other roles can continue to be hybrid.
- High concentration in a few cities (India specific con): JPMorgan India as of this review, has offices only in Bangalore, Mumbai and Hyderabad. Concentration of large offices in only three cities with some of the highest population density in the country can lead to many disadvantages. I've seen many talented individuals that liked the organisation leave due to this location constraint. The company will also face many challenges and disadvantages due to their concentrated presense.

advice: Please be kind to people on parental leave!!
pros:
- Opportunities for professional development
- Competitive Salary
cons:
Working at JP Morgan has been a rollercoaster of highs and lows, with the lows overshadowing any semblance of professional fulfillment. Despite dedicating myself to quality work and commitment, my experience at JP Morgan during my maternity leave and beyond has been disheartening and demoralizing.

Firstly, the company's attitude towards employees during maternity leave is deplorable. Instead of acknowledging dedication and hard work, they choose to focus solely on in-office attendance and not the actual attendance, work that you put in even outside of working hours, disregarding the sacrifices and contributions of individuals. My rating during my parental leave period was unfairly low, despite consistently delivering quality results.

Moreover, the absence of flexibility within the company culture is glaring. The rigid policies and lack of understanding towards personal situations create an atmosphere of stress and apprehension. As a working parent, flexibility is not a luxury but a necessity, one that JP Morgan fails to recognize and accommodate.

Adding insult to injury, the workplace is fraught with office politics. Rather than fostering an environment of collaboration and support, it's plagued with favoritism and internal power struggles. Professional growth and recognition seem to be contingent upon one's ability to navigate these murky waters, rather than on merit and performance.

In conclusion, my time at JP Morgan has been marred by unfair treatment, inflexibility, and office politics. It's disheartening to witness the disregard for employees' well-being and the erosion of professional integrity within the organization. I would caution anyone considering employment at JP Morgan to thoroughly evaluate the work culture and weigh the potential repercussions before committing to this environment.

cons: Work-Life Balance: The main downside is the difficulty in maintaining a good work-life balance. The work can sometimes become overwhelming, leading to long hours and high stress. However, this seems to be a common theme in many big financial firms. Bureaucracy: Like many large corporations, JP Morgan suffers from its share of red tape. Decisions can take a long time due to various layers of management, which can be frustrating for those used to more agile environments. Technology Stack: While the company is making strides in modernizing its tech stack, there are still pockets where outdated technology is in use. This can occasionally make software development more challenging than necessary.

summary: The most toxic environment I have ever worked in...
advice: Please build a leadership culture where you have good "leaders" (and not executers lacking basic empathy), understand people who do the job on the ground are human beings (and not commodities), ensure you don't hire backups into redundant roles (and streamline your teams / efforts for redundancies), improve new-employee experience... (and so much more)
pros:
Reputed Brand
Decent Campus / Office Building
Good Benefits (though Low Pay)
cons:
In my ~18 year career, JPMC is possibly the worst environment I have worked in. Make no mistake this is not a Tech company in any sense.

From Bad leaders (workers vs knowing how to lead, saying really weird stuff, not managing toxicity well and having inability to apologize to mend things).

The company / firm & these leaders puts new employees through a terrible new-employee experience and simply does not care. The role is sold as a grand ownership responsibility, timezone expectations are not communicated (just to attract talent) & then de-scoped or changed within first 6-9 months and managers may ask you to work really early or late (on a regular basis) or give you hints to "start typing your resume".

Not knowing about parallel teams (especially in Core Tech & Platforms) working on same areas, makes a newly hired member already redundant and creates a huge amount of toxicity, with leaders saying really weird stuff and their managers not holding them accountable. 

Considering people hired in specialist streams (SMEs) as commodities that can be moved around anywhere, is unproductive waste of everyone's time & experience.

Then there is the case of constant org changes which is branded normal industry standard (having 3-4 managers in less than an year is not how re-orgs work per my experience at some big / great companies).

Also there is a lot of process churn, with everyone having their own ways and the company having so many processes, that you cannot get anything done, but have to cater to unrealistic KRs & Timelines (leaders should understand the system they operate in).

Please ensure, to vet your team for most of these things aka - a good leader with human empathy (vs thinking of experienced people as commodities), how would you be onboarded & made effective, which other teams are working on the same things, what is the state of Operating Rhythms & Processes, Timezone expectations etc.

Such a waste of everyone's time.

advice:
Listen to employees when they try to speak up for the product and technologies. When a deadline is unreasonable, listen to employees' reasoning and set reasonable goals and outcomes for the project(s).

Watch employees and understand them. When you are disassociated from what is going on, it's easy to think that the employee who talked the loudest contributed the most and is the most passionate about the project. Rather, it's the ones that are brave and speak up about issues that are honest and are looking out for the project and the firm the most.

Talk to employees and clearly articulate what the vision for project(s) are. Not clearly communicating leads to misunderstandings and can be manipulative. Oftentimes, it felt like information was held back to manipulate employees. Deadlines are arbitrary and often "not negotiable" to get employees to work hard. Promises that there is plenty of work and investment in the current project are lies to keep employees busy and from seeking employment elsewhere until the unavoidable lay-off, leading to resentment.
pros: JPMC is a large company and is very well-funded, meaning that mobilizing to another team is relatively since there are a lot of development teams and the company is more recession resistant compared to other companies. As an example of that, during COVID, despite massive lay-offs, JPMC still performed well and there were no massive lay-offs. Another plus is that you get the opportunity to meet a lot of people and network and socialize.
cons:
As a banking and financial firm-first, they are profit-driven and tend to promote narcissists because they are more interested in results and those who are able sell themselves the most. It doesn't matter how many years of experience you've had, whether you picked up a lot of leadership tasks, they would use your promotion as a way to squeeze out as much work out of you as possible.

A funny joke that employees also share amongst each other is that JPMC stands for "Just People Meeting Constantly" because people would rather appear busy and schedule meetings over results - they don't mind wasting developer time in meetings while expecting results happen overnight. 

Technology stack is often chosen without much thought into whether it makes the sense for the firm. There is also little trust in employees since they're known to track their employees with their webcams and badge-ins.

Management would rather cut costs than do what's right for their users. Although I'm just a disgruntled employee, they shuffled teams working on a particular project and laid off entire teams with short notice to outsource projects without much thought into how challenging it is to transfer knowledge of the project to off-shore teams in India.

They say they invest in people, but most would rather do what's most profitable for themselves. They claimed to help laid off employees find new work internally with a fancy redeployment program, but did absolutely nothing to refer developers internally. They would also ask laid off employees to take salary cuts than let them mobilize to another team. They would also appeal to your state's unemployment and protest against your claims for unemployment because they don't want to pay it.

advice: See my comments above regarding promotion opps and the ED/MD path. Having lots of friends go through the recent tech layoffs, big thumbs up to the HR teams for helping so many good people stay with the firm and find new roles including some help pay for relocation to another site! Lastly, the RTTO/WFH debate. We all know Jamie wants people back 5x/week but this shouldn’t apply to every role, especially tech. You can argue “culture/team” building all day, but the reality is over 50% of us still sit near people not on our team, all of our calls are on Zoom to people in other locations, and we do the opposite of the firm’s lofty Go Green initiative by burning unnecessary gas commuting along with lost hours every week. I get real estate costs are the key driver as are state tax breaks for occupancy, but true hybrid means letting leaders and teams decide how many days/week make sense for them so the open seats can be saved for teams that truly benefit from peer sharing and local meetings or people that like the social aspect of the office. With everyone on Zoom in an open floor plan talking way too loud, it’s very distracting for most.

advice: Take a look at the average age in your tech teams and you'll recognize there's a problem. Millennials and Gen Z aren't interested in working in tech at JPMC because you've fostered a culture where the bankers are the jocks and the techies are the losers. You also have a really weird reward system - bankers are rewarded for the bottom line but technology isn't, when in reality AI is cutting your headcount and contributing to your bottom line more significantly than anything else. The culture is toxic... its time to rethink who you're idolizing and who's getting rewarded.
pros: JPMC is an extremely diverse firm with people who are passionate about what they do. Every call I am in is evenly split across gender, ethnicity, and sexual orientation. Because of this, there is very little room for bias and people are more thoughtful about understanding their unconscious biases.
cons:
1) The company claims it wants to be the tech leader within the finance industry, but doesn't show the willingness to compete with tech firms. They hire within, transferring people with finance/operations expertise into product/ program/ project roles to keep salaries low. Not hiring outside industry experts reflects on the quality of its agile performance, and on product's relationship with engineering. Those with more expertise in tech tend to bear the responsibilities of those who are hired within, and are expected "wear many hats" without additional reward.

2) JPMC idols its bankers but doesn't appreciate tech's contributions to the bottom line (i.e. in one year I cut headcount by 10% but I don't see it reflected in a bonus, but bankers who land a couple of good deals that will take years to materialize are rewarded significantly in their bonuses). 

3) Finally, due to JPMC's transfer of employees from teams with vastly different cultures and due to its over-idolization of bankers, there is a ton of competition within the technology teams (and not in a good way). The company lacks a culture of respect, recognition, collaboration and teamwork. There is a lot of secretive work left off of roadmaps, and everyone is very calculated about who they share ideas with because they don't trust that their teammate won't stab them in the back and steal their work. It's counterproductive and a very toxic environment, and I after years of optimistic hope I unfortunately can't see it changing soon.

advice:
Create a separate position to handle all of the administrative responsibilities, so that this role can truly be a "trainer" position only.

If you do not create a separate role than update the title of the position to reflect the true responsibilities you require of this position, AND compensate your manager/trainer accordingly.

This position is two positions into one.  1.  Manager/HR/Admin and 2. Trainer

Don't think you can pay your new hire as a "trainer" ONLY to turn around and require them to do all the additional manager or HR type of responsibilities.  

A trainer needs to focus on preparing their training material and keep the classroom engaged to get the learner learning.

All the side coaching calls, payroll, name change, leave requests, and attendance coaching calls all take away from the trainers true responsibility, which is training.
pros:

Several recognition programs, which were good.

cons:
I worked many more hours than my direct line managers.

Trainer title is misleading because the pay reflected a "trainer" only position. This is NOT just a trainer position as you are led to believe in your interview. You WILL have many other responsibilities- managerial responsibilities and you WILL NOT be compensated as such. 

This position should be called a "training manager" position as you also were expected to fulfill the roles of a manager like payroll, leave requests, name changes, disciplinary coaching, documentation of all of this of course- almost become a bigger role than the actual 8 hour in class training.

You were not compensated for the additional responsibilities.

Management overlooks your feedback about, which trainees are not making the cut to go onto the call floor. The call floor then received many new employees that would reflect poorly on the brand since the customer would be able to detect that "they didn't know what they were doing". This leads to many errors, and loss to the company in reputation, and expensive mistakes all losses for the company.

Human resources was booked through an app, which made HR very hard to reach in a timely manner.

Many of the additional benefits like classes on mindfulness, mental health, etc. were offered during business hours, so good luck trying to get your boss to let you attend one of those.

This is difficult to answer, I worked in 1 LOB and there are 5.  Management are made up of individuals and we all can have certain flaws, I would like to think I had 3 good managers during my time.

I would like to suggest that everyone doesn't have the "people" aspect to be a manger.  It appeared that some individuals where promoted base on time in position.  Additionally the management structure can be improved.  The hierarchy is:
1. Managing Director (MD)
2. Executive Director (ED)
3. Vice President (VP)
4. Associate

I was a VP and reported to a VP, and there where some ED’s that didn’t have any reports.

One thing I would encourage managers are every level to do is encourage/instruct your direct reports to respond/assist/help others regardless of title.  There have been time when an Associate or VP couldn’t get a response because they weren’t seen as important, however, when it was escalated to an ED/MD they suddenly had time.

The Firm is a good place to work. You will have unlimited access to training sites; both external (Udemy, O'Reilly, Datacamp) to name a few and internal sources. Another things I was happy to see were the number of available Business Resource Groups (BRGs), that you can join to increase your employee network, and visibility.

Jamie Dimon, Lori Beer, and Jason Witty (formally) are intelligent and smart individuals, if the opportunity presents itself follow and listen to them.
cons:
One thing that concerned me are the unexpected and unannounced Reduction in Force (RIF), essentially a layoff. When I first started there was on that happened about 4 months after I started. I was told they happen every year (normally have in April and October). The RIF can happen to any Line of Business (LOB, think of departments within the Firm). You won't know about it unless you are affected or know someone who has been notified. Another issue regarding this practice is that after they layoff people new positions are opened for the same role.

One the bright side if there is one is the Firm will give you 45 days to find an opportunity within the organization and severance if you qualify based on role and time of service.

Note: Being RIF has a negative connotation and some hiring managers won’t hire you, even through there is a program in place to support those individuals.

Let’s talk about nepotism, I have seen so many people get special project, promotions, etc…. All based off of the level of brown nosery, or if they are family  and friends with management. This seems a little not fair seeing someone working accounts less than a year and failing metrics, get picked to work on a off the phone project when a tenured rep who has been meeting metrics, and knows the material is passed over.
pros: Awesome direct managers who communicate well and are generally understanding. Great company title to have on a resume as well. Skills learned are useful in more than one career in the Banking industry and are transferable elsewhere. They additionally offer training periodically for additional skills, such as credit card fraud, fraud recovery, card collections and merchant disputes - however no increase in pay with learning these additional skills to better service multiple client types. The center has low tolerance for client to agent abusive language or threats allowing reps to disconnect and report the caller. I’ve also witnessed the business has low tolerance for abusive, sexual, or outwardly racist remarks making it a comfortable and safe place to work. They have work from home opportunities that are pretty great, and a hybrid schedule (3 days in 2 days out during the work week.) they offer education tuition reimbursement, though this can be a double edge sword if you graduate and don’t find a promoted role within the organization as they expect you to stay with the company a year after graduation for every year you take tuition assistance. For example you take four years of tuition assistance, expect to stay at the company 8 years. (4 year you took the tuition assistance, and 4 years after you have graduated). The benefits are okay, with health, vision, dental and employee assistance programs (this helps with medical expenses occasionally such as counseling and therapy and only when the provider accepts EAP.) Additionally they provide a 401k that they match %100 of your contributions to, up to %5 of your total compensation. There had been pensions, though I don’t they they do this anymore as of 2019/2020. They have also given a bonus in December around the end of the year, a holiday gift, this is between $850-$1300, and is applied to your 401k.
cons: Pay is pretty okay, with 10+ years experience I would expect better pay. They hire new agents in at a comparable salary to tenured ones so that doesn’t feel great. Raises aren’t great usually between $0.10 - $0.25 annually with a pay cap. Call center environment that micromanages every aspect of your day. From the amount of time you spend on calls to the amount of time you have to spend working after calls down to the amount of time you take outside of your regular schedule including if you need to use the restroom and log off the phone. Additionally, they keep lowering the trackable metric for talk time but increasing the amount of work needed to service client accounts making it harder to achieve a passable rating. The call volume can feel daunting at times, with back to back calls from 6:00 am - 12:00 am leaving little to no breathing room to adjust yourself and prepare for the next account. Upper Management is terrible at communication or lacking when there are service issues, tool issues, or procedure updates. The center also tends to have teams working on federal holidays, even when the bank is closed (With holiday double time) and typically expect to work a weekend day Saturday or Sunday. Promotions and projects often are chosen off of nepotism instead of skill, merit, or tenure. This may not be a reflection of the company however with the line of work (Fraud and collections) customers tend to be upset or down right abusive. Though they are great about abusive clients and allow us to disconnect for bigotry or abusive language directed at the agent instead of having the agent stay on the phone and take the abuse.

advice: Chase needs to enter, stay a while, speak with ALL employees and fix the chaos. This is a high turnover facility for a number of reasons. Make it a safe place to work with policies that apply to all and offer guidance and resources to every employee with clarity that goes up the chain. This office runs on a buddy system for achievement rewards instead of merit for hard work and ability.
pros: Great team in the one department. Loved the managers and peers on specific teams. Other departments are NOT a place anyone seems to want to be. OT pay plus OT when working holidays. Extended unpaid lunches for appointments (although I was not aware this was an option until after working here for over a year). The position is fun and helping people with travel is a blast! In-bound calls, no selling, just helping people have amazing vacations by booking their travel,
cons:
Promised raises never received even as a stop performer with perfect scores, attendance and volunteering for OT when needed. 
Mandatory OT.
No set schedule. It changes every few months from day to night and weekends included.
High stress position with little rewards. Everything you do is micromanaged.
Employee retention horrible, Their doors are ALWAYS revolving with people quitting and new hires.
New hires received higher pay at entry level than tenured agents working there for years. No pay raises after requests made to receive not more, but EQUAL pay to brand new hires.
The call out system is 3rd party and often will log you as a No Call, No Show that takes months from management to correct and this directly effects your schedule.

HR is also a 3rd party from overseas that you can only contact via message center online and the responses are automated. 
Pay is constantly screwed up for numerous people every week from payroll center. If you are able to finally speak to someone, they don't know how to fix it and promise to get back to you... which often takes weeks and may not be resolved the first couple of times of reaching out.

There are blocked times on nights and weekends for the entire year you are not allowed to request off. Holidays are mandatory. Scheduling system is also created by the same party that marks you as a No Call No Show while you are at work or gives you points for being late when the system is down and often takes your PTO when you did not have time off, which is a nightmare to be fixed and takes management involvement and often 3rd party HR has to be contacted from the other 3rd party scheduling department to be corrected.. and many times does not happen correctly.

Scheduling department does not track PTO correctly based on PTO in your employee dashboard therefore causing requested PTO to be denied based on missing or wrong hours in their system.
Management, employees and corporate are almost never on the same page. 

Corporate will send out a newsletter about changes or perks that do not apply to your department (so we're told) after employees try to utilize them. Management has to approve and send off for perks, but they won't as they claim they don't apply to cxLoyalty employees, so you do not receive employee perks or rewards unless Chase is in the building and passing them out. Employees on each team are treated differently and receive different benefits/rewards.

You will hit a glass ceiling in the Travel Department with no where to move up and you are not considered for other positions within the company and no opportunity to train in other departments for a chance at a career. You do not receive promised raises for staying where you are as advertised in your orientation. New hires will make more than you even if you become a supervisor with a perfect record. 

There is always drama and fist fights that break out around your cubicles. The only way to be promoted or get the schedule you need based on school or a second job is to be well liked by management. 

The more you're liked by your manager, the better your chances of be treated fairly. I have watched threats and physical fights break out over rumors about new employees that had no clue who the people threatening them were. You must be tough to make it through your first few months here. There is also a major issue with theft inside the building. Your items will be stolen if ever left at your desk. This includes a sweater on a chair, jacket, lunches (out of the breakroom refrigerators), umbrellas or medicine. Pretty much anything that isn't constantly being locked away in a locker (that you must use as purses, phones and smart watches have to be locked away and are never allowed near your work area). If they run out of lockers, you must leave everything in your car and parking is hard to find and not close to the your office area in most cases.

This company was acquiesced by Chase, but never fully merged with Chase's policies and procedures. cxLoyalty considers themselves their own company and maintains their own policies and procedures inside their building regardless of Chase's merger. Each Team Lead tells their employees different information and no one seems to be on the same page resulting in many people feeling lost, confused or failing with reprimands and not knowing why as they followed the directions from leadership. There is no HR department in the building, but a liaison was placed in the building recently whom has explained she is not HR and has no HR training, but will forward information shared with her to an HR rep off-site. Any time someone asks to speak with HR about an issue, bereavement or pay they are asked to speak with their managers instead or directed to a 3rd party online message board which usually receive automated responses.

summary: Not for the faint of heart
advice: It’s an honor to be hired by a company like JPMorgan Chase. I felt very proud when I started, and I think the company does some good things, but onboarding process needs work. Training or some kind of structured shadowing and mentoring is desperately needed with realistic expectations for ramping up. Managers should be trained and accountable for how they communicate with and lead their employees. A lot of good people working hard for the firm but they can’t voice concerns with the current Employee Opinion Survey, the way it is worded. If you want honest feedback you need to redo the survey accordingly, especially as it relates to how they view their manager, training oppys, the current hybrid model, workload, etc.. Currently only one open question.  Employees need to truly feel it is anonymous. Small teams afraid to speak up because they worry they will be “found out”. Please rethink the rigid RTO, hybrid model, attendance dashboard and “big brother” mentality and policies. We’re not children. If you’re serious about embracing DEI, please reconsider how remote work could help people across the company. Also take a step back and look at your ADA accommodation process. It’s demeaning.
pros: Compensation and benefits are good.
cons: No training, expect you to figure it out on your own by navigating complex matrix org with no clear understanding of who does what, but have high expectations. Churn and burn culture. Some good leaders across the firm but direct manager is not one of them. Very poor communication and will talk down to you and use indignant tone if you have questions and can’t read their mind. Beware the company closely polices the hybrid work model with an attendance app, and I understand there is intense monitoring of everything we do throughout the day through WADU. If you fall below 60% in-office attendance, it is grounds for termination. Very difficult to get an ADA Accommodation to work remote, even if you furnish multiple letters from doctors. They will decide if you can work remote at their own discretion.

advice: If you are not comfortable with disabled people and their accommodations, be transparent about it.  Don't destroy their careers. Be open to feedback about what things they are facing as obstacles, which you may not realize from your point of view.  Also, pay attention to women who are doing more technical work than men in the same roles but getting paid less, regardless of their level (602 vs 603) and promote them when they deserve it.
pros: Lots of options for roles, mobility, and education/training benefits - as long as you are healthy and conform to being normal. Benefits seem great, but I also pay roughly $700/month for basic just me; still, the in house benefits are pretty great. Free employee assistance program with mental health, free education benefits annually that never run out ($7500 a year for advanced degrees and some partnerships with institutions like Purdue and LSU, etc). Excellent PTO - 4 weeks, plus sick time, some personal days, and even volunteer days. Anything in tech you want to do, you really can - and there is internal training to move over if you started elsewhere, too. All open to you only if you are not disabled, as I discovered first hand. If you have a great manager - and there are so many really great ones - you will have the world.
cons: If you are disabled, you will face significant challenges - doors will be closed to you. You can contribute to many extra curriculars and work well above and beyond, but be invisible as a woman and as a person who is disabled. You will be foremost in your field and top in education and experience, train the dudes on your team how to do the job, and still watch them earn $30k-$40k more than you annually, all while telling the world how advanced in DEI we are. Very little work life balance while you try to chase a promotion for years and years, which you will not get if you are not a conforming person in every day - I hate to say this, but it is absolutely the case. Managers who treat you poorly have no risk in doing so - the company still celebrates them, which can be really difficult to stomach when you've seen them treat people terribly. Pay is below market for the level you provide. I was involved in hiring for a few years and that was a very common complaint and reason we lost great talent. If you do not have a great manager - and there are many who are not - you will never get promoted, you won't ever get a raise, and you can even kill your chances for mobility. The worst thing at chase is the roll of the dice you take with managers. Good ones are incredible, bad ones kill your career.

summary: Highly recommend avoid working in J.P. Morgan Payments Merchant Services.
advice: In summary, while J.P. Morgan Payments Merchant Services offers notable employee benefits and internal opportunities, it is severely hampered by its management practices and workplace culture. The high turnover rate and lack of experienced leadership are major red flags that need to be addressed for the company to realize its full potential as a leading employer in the financial payment processing services sector.
pros:
Merchant Services presents a mix of both commendable and concerning aspects as an employer in the financial services industry. On the positive side, their commitment to employee benefits is noteworthy. The company offers comprehensive health benefits and education opportunities, reflecting its investment in the physical, mental, and professional development of its staff. Additionally, there are internal opportunities for career growth, which can be beneficial for those looking to expand their skill set within the company.

However, the organization faces significant challenges in its management structure and workplace culture.
cons:
Reports of poor management, from the top down, are a major concern. The feeling of being treated as a number rather than a valued team member can have detrimental effects on employee morale and job satisfaction. The lack of camaraderie and teamwork further exacerbates this issue, creating an environment that is not conducive to collaboration or shared success.

Moreover, the management's tendency to prioritize upward visibility over employee support is disheartening. The lack of support for growth and opportunities, combined with a tendency to pass blame rather than take responsibility, can create a toxic workplace atmosphere. These issues are further highlighted by the alarmingly high turnover rate, ranging from 45% to 60% annually, which raises serious questions about the sustainability of their workforce practices.

Another critical issue is the lack of experience and knowledge among managers, particularly in key areas like payment processing technology and onboarding. This gap in expertise can lead to inefficiencies and a lack of proper guidance for team members.

Lastly, compansation for Merchant Service employees are some of the lowest within the bank.

cons: The only issue I encountered, was once I graduated from college I wanted to move up in the company and begin working in my field of study. At the point of graduating I had been with Chase for a little over three years, and being that I had been with the company for that long, it was very difficult to get hired within for a different position out of the branch. I had spoken with several senior employees over the phone about my goals and aspirations and applied to several different positions, and after a year of doing all of that, I really got nowhere. I kept being told I need to have worked for Chase for 3-5 years, and I had been there for over three years. I just didn't expect it to be so difficult to already be a dedicated employee but to have such a hard time moving up.

summary: Ton to learn, because so much is outdated
advice: Fight for your devs. So many people within JPMC seem to function purely on fear. Fear of deadlines not getting met, fear of what will happen if a deadline is moved. Fear of what happens if something isn't delivered the way it was promised. The whole hierarchy of management continuously presses harder and harder as each person fears they might "look bad." No one wants to say "no" or tell someone their workload is too heavy under any circumstances. Ultimately the buck stops with the devs, because we can't pass it on to anyone else. So when someone does the work to prevent devs needing to deal with all the pushback, it is an immense weight off of our shoulders and a way for us to focus more energy into actually doing dev work.
pros: There is a ton of opportunity to build skills into your resume from working here. There is a company wide push towards AWS and React which I have had issues acquiring skills for in my spare time to appeal to other career opportunities. JPMC being as big as they are also supplies a wealth of knowledge that I have not found in other workplaces. Granted it is quite unorganized, so you have to really search for it sometimes. But any kind of language/framework/tooling you can imagine you're likely to find some space to facilitate learning or demonstrate its use.
cons: Work From Home (Hybrid, 3 days in office/week): Jamie Dimon absolutely HATES the idea of WFH and it trickles down to every level of management. My team is split between people in DE, OH, NJ, NY and even India but we all HAVE to be in office for those zoom calls Office: The firm seems to be really focused on getting everyone back into the office while holding onto cost savings from COVID restrictions. Everyone has to "hot-desk" so there's no assigned seating. Full blown open office spaces galore, I've worked in call centers that didn't feel so loud/cramped. But don't worry, the upper management still get their cozy little offices. Work Culture: JPMC is the first FinTech company I have worked for, but holy mother of Tech Debt. There is such a spiderweb of dependencies between teams and no safeguard against backwards-incompatible changes that the majority of the work ends up being migrations because "team ABC has decommissioned their API, now we have to use this." There is the typical corporate culture combining oversimplified requirements and then being inflexible with deadlines. That much I sort of accept at this point. However, what JPMC seems to be particularly good at is allowing projects to barely reach a functioning state and marking it as "done." The team gets moved onto another project with the same expected capacity getting done each week but pretends there isn't another 1-3 months of support needed for the app that was just finished. What's worse is that 1-3 months of support is really a pile of "requirements" that were never brought up to begin with.

summary: JPMorgan Chase does not stop the flow of illegal Chinese money
advice: Have compliance look at this issue and establish proper procedures to protect Chase from potential conflict with the Chinese Government.
pros: JPMorgan Chase is a good company to work for. Security and compliance with rules and procedures are important, and employees are well trained.
cons: Despite all the effort to comply with security procedures, and to comply with state and federal regulations, Chase looks the other way in regards to illegal Chines money flowing into its US accounts. China limits the amount of money each person can take out of the country. For a Chinese person to buy a home in the US, they need much more money than the country of China will allow them to remove. So these Chinese get all of their relatives to wire small amounts of money to the same account at Chase. Then they work it out on their end in China to pay everyone back. The Chinese government would not see the illegal activity, but it is obvious on the Chase side because of the way the money flows into one account. I have no empathy for the Chinese government, but I'm surprised that Chase allows this since Chase is an international banking company.

summary: DO NOT EVER JOIN THIS PLACE IF YOU CARE ABOUT YOUR MENTAL AND PHYSICAL HEALTH.
advice: Stop micro managing the company and the dirty politics.
pros: To be honest, none at all.
cons: I raised the concern to the Leaders about my mental health. I made them aware about the fact that I was not from a call center background and that it was very difficult for me to talk all day. More over I had never worked night shifts so my body was just not taking it well. I am a 34 years old woman who had put on about 25 kgs of weight, got PCOS and other hormonal imbalance due to this lifestyle. I was struggling so bad that either I was unwell physically or not in the right state of mind to work. I was not happy because I couldn't see my growth or where I was going in this organization. All I wanted was a little guidance as to how I could take an internal movement. And there were many like me but not all of us have the option to take a break, or leave our current jobs until we have got another job offer in hand. I had no intention of leaving either 😪 but I just couldn't take it anymore. Initially when I joined JPMC, I signed up for this thinking that with time I'll be able to grow internally and look for a profile that matches with my skills and work experience. I joined during Covid when there were barely any job openings in the market so I took the job I was offered, again with this in mind that I'll find opportunities to grow internally. There came a point when every single day for 2 weeks in a row, before my shift would start, I would sit with my manager and ask if he could help me get a back office profile or put me on a temporary project so that I could learn something new or help me move to a day shift department so my body gets the rest it needed and deserved. Or if nothing, at least get an approval to waive my notice period as an exception because I was not able to take calls. You cannot expect someone to talk to clients when they are not in the right state of mind. But our job was to take calls, so no matter how much the employee was struggling, we had no choice. The saddest part was I clearly communicated this to my managers, in the hope that they would understand 😔 but I was wrong. My last working day was August 2nd 2023 because on 3rd I sent an email to the leaders saying my goodbye to the firm. This was my experience with JPMC. The best decision I ever took for myself was to leave this toxic company because I chose my mental peace over money.

Yearly reviews are VERY IMPORTANT! They can make or break your reputation at The Firm and it only takes one subpar review to damage your career for quite sometime. pros: Here are just a few of my favorite things about working at J.P Morgan: - Great pay, benefits, and resources - Quick hiring process - Friendly co-workers and upper-level management - Beautiful office campuses - Some travel opportunities - Great lunch cafe and on-site events devoted to diversity and inclusion - Business Resource Groups (I recommend joining one or a few to build your network) During my time at this company, I was happy to be apart of such a large corporation and seeing how all the small entities of it worked to create the big picture that is J.P Morgan.
cons: Here are a few things that I did not like about working at J.P Morgan: - Your brand is dependent on you always being on camera and if you don't, it knocks your brand down - The working model is hybrid however, 3 days are mandatory on-site no matter the location and no matter what your manager says. They can track how many days you come in a month and there is an in office percentage you must meet every month; 60% (unless you have managerial approval) you also must log WFH days via outlook and time tracking system - Seating arrangements; there is no assigned seating and people will make you get out of a seat you've been sitting if they booked that seat no matter how late they arrive at the office; too many departments working on top of each other and no one has anywhere to sit - They are implementing a new productivity monitoring system that is slightly nerve racking especially when you're working from home that they say won't be used to judge employment (but it will for sure play a factor into your bonus, and annual salary increase) - Video conferencing using Zoom, they are transitioning out of using it and moving to Teams full-time but it won't be fully available for another year or so

In my humble opinion, the management could really benefit from greater employee loyalty if they aligned some major leave policies to peer group especially in India. Secondly, most major decisions and decision makers are based in the US. It would be encouraging to have a say and be included from a real time, operating role outside of the US rather than having token representations.
pros: - The firm is pro technology and recognizes the importance of embedding and adapting to advancements in the new technologies. All the processes are continuously upgraded on par with best in class product organizations. - The firm has solid roots in respective business lines owing to over a century worth of business experience and is capable of foreseeing plausible risks, changes and adapt it's strategies accordingly. - Growth is of paramount importance in revenue, profits, service quality. Therefore all businessesand support teams are aligned to cater to this vision with an emphasis on pushing the envelope to constantly innovate to benefit the whole.
cons: -The firm is extremely large and some of the processes can be quite beauracratic. - Leave policies, especially in India aren't aligned with peer group. For context, there are a total of 12 sick leaves, 20 days paid time off per year. You are allowed to only carry forward 5 days every year that is required to be exhausted by end of March the successive year else they lapse. - Though you can be smart and manage your work time best suited to you, the insistence of 60% attendance at any given point in time, deliberate tracking & monitoring, compulsion to be in office either on a Monday or a Friday has skewed work life balance. This is not aligned to peer group and is causing further unrest on the ground. - The firm strongly advocates importance of mental health but has no leave policy to cover this. - Some of the tools currently in use are cumbersome, lethargic and not optimized. The technology available to run backend processes are not aligned to the advancements and focus lavished on client facing tools.

cons: If you work at JPMorgan Chase & Co. or are thinking about working at JPMC, you need to know about their employee surveillance tool called WADU. WADU is an acronym for Workforce Activity Data Utility. Every employee at JPMC has a profile in the WADU database. I think everyone expects their employer to track them to some extent. It is pretty standard practice for employers to monitor and run analysis on things like building badge swipes and the amount of time spent connected when working from home. It has also become very common place for employers to record audio and video at the office. WADU is on a different level. It is an artificial intelligence & machine learning system for workforce human behavior. Starting at the moment you arrive to the building, WADU is tracking you using facial and speech recognition. Most JPMC offices and branches have been outfitted with some of the best HD AV security cameras. Whenever you are at your desk, know that there is a HD camera tracking you the entire time. WADU uses the array of HD cameras at the office to monitor all of your non-verbal body language all throughout the day. The collected information is then fed into the AI/ML system and it is used to update your WADU profile in real time. Every manager gets access to a dashboard that lists all the metrics about their subordinates. The productivity metrics about an employee start getting updated immediately after an employee logs into the system. If the employee is at the office, two bio-metrics are available, attention/focus and stress. The bio-metric feeds are updated from the facial and behavioral tracking. Having a bad day? Stressed about something? WADU has already noticed this and alerted your manager. Can’t focus? Not working at your usual pace? WADU has already noticed this and alerted your manager. Did something you normally don’t do? It’s possible WADU flagged it as suspicious and alerted your manager. WADU is also why they are pushing RTO or “return to office” so hard. Upper management does not care if some employees are more productive when they are working from home. They want everyone back in the office as much as possible so that their WADU profiles are being refined. Enhancing their insight into you is more important to them than better productivity from working from home. A lot of teams are now required to come in two to three days per week. Director level and higher are required to come in four to five days per week. Upper management wants to see everyone at all levels back in the office five days a week. They have invested millions into the WADU system, and they want to get a return on that investment. That only happens whenever people are in the office as much as possible. WADU is also watching and listening whenever you are working from home. If you installed Citrix Workplace on your own computer, and you permitted Citrix to access your web camera and microphone after login, you have connected those devices to WADU. If you are using an issued Chromebook, those permissions are already conveniently accepted for you. You’ll notice that your web camera will flash right after login. This is not an “initial connection” flash. Your web camera just took a burst shot of pictures and sent them to WADU. The pictures will be scanned for anything deemed unprofessional or unsafe. Recreational drug paraphernalia, TVs, game consoles, and several other things are all flagged if detected in the pictures. If you see your web camera flash randomly, that was your manager or someone in security requesting a burst shot of pictures from your web camera. You’ll also notice that your microphone will go hot shortly after login. Anything you say will be processed by WADU. All background noises will be processed by WADU. Say something bad about your boss or other superior? WADU flagged it. Say something bad about another co-worker? WADU flagged it. Have a moment of anger or frustration? WADU flagged it. These are just some examples, WADU is trained to detect a wide variety of keywords, phrases, and sound events. Your manager can also connect and listen to your audio feed live. WADU is also able to detect keyboard pokers/bumpers and mouse jigglers/movers. It doesn’t matter if it is a completely external solution, WADU will be able to detect it by analyzing the repetitive input pattern. Your manager will be notified that your under suspicion of faking productivity. They will then connect to your session and see what is happening live. Action will be taken if the suspicion is confirmed. WADU determines how productive you are by analyzing a variety of metrics about your session input. This includes words typed, mouse clicks, application activity, and many other things. The analysis also determines if someone is a unique contributor or if they are a regular worker. In overall rankings, unique contributors are always ranked higher than regular workers. The same analysis can also determine who is essentially dead weight. These people are ranked last. You may have noticed at some point that you started getting job postings sent to your personal email. If you click on any of the links in these job list emails, your manager will get a notification on your WADU profile that you are actively looking for a new job. Even if it was just browsing, it can negatively affect the employee who clicked the link. If you installed the JPMC workplace app on your phone, you have connected your phone to WADU. The workplace mobile app will collect a variety of information from your phone and use it to update and refine your WADU profile. Right now, the only way to reserve a desk at the office is to use the workplace app. The web version of the desk reservation system is still “coming soon” and you are pushed to install the app on your phone. It will probably still be “coming soon” in 2040. Upper management pushes a narrative that all this surveillance is required to safeguard the firm against insider threats. While that may be partially true, the main reason is to train and refine the AI/ML system. They want every employee profile to be as accurate and as detailed as possible. They say we are not supposed to use anything from an employee’s WADU profile to make employment decisions. It is kind of hard to ignore a ranked list of subordinates with productivity forecasting. Here is how you can minimize the privacy invasion while working at JPMC: Keep your web camera covered and microphone muted unless on a Zoom Most modern laptops have multiple web cameras and microphones, make sure you are aware of all potential recording devices on your computer Use your own desktop or laptop at home instead of an issued Chromebook Do not grant Citrix Workplace access to your web camera or microphone Use Zoom outside of Citrix when you are at home Consider getting a phone and number solely for work purposes Do not install the JPMC workplace app on your personal phone If you need the workplace app, factory reset an old phone and install it on that Know there are no blind spots, you are always on camera at the office Know there is no privacy, all conversations are recorded everywhere at the office Know all of your behavior at the office affects your WADU profile and ranking It would be a good idea for you to print a copy of all performance reviews at home

advice: Communicate clearly and frequently: Regular communication with employees is essential to build trust, address concerns, and keep everyone aligned with company goals. Ensure that employees understand the company's mission, vision, and values, and provide regular updates on business performance. Lead by example: Managers should model the behavior they want to see from their employees. This includes demonstrating ethical behavior, accountability, and a commitment to quality and excellence. Encourage feedback and collaboration: Encourage employees to share their ideas and feedback openly and honestly, and provide opportunities for collaboration and teamwork. This can help to foster a culture of innovation and creativity. Provide opportunities for professional development: Offer training and development programs to help employees develop their skills and advance their careers. This can also help to improve employee retention and engagement. Recognize and reward performance: Acknowledge and reward employees who perform well, and provide constructive feedback to those who may be struggling. This can help to motivate employees and improve overall performance
pros: Reputation and brand recognition: JPM is one of the largest and most well-respected financial institutions in the world. Working for such a prestigious company can be a source of pride and may open up future opportunities. Career development: JPM offers a wide range of career development opportunities, including training, mentorship, and promotion from within. Employees are encouraged to pursue their interests and to develop new skills to advance their careers. Compensation and benefits: JPM offers competitive salaries and benefits packages, including health insurance, retirement plans, and paid time off. The company also offers bonuses and incentives to reward employees for their hard work. Global presence: JPM operates in over 100 countries, giving employees the opportunity to work with colleagues and clients from diverse backgrounds and cultures. Social responsibility: JPM is committed to corporate social responsibility, and employees are encouraged to participate in volunteer and philanthropic activities through the company's various programs.
cons: Workload and stress: Working in finance can be stressful, and JPM is no exception. Employees may be expected to work long hours and manage heavy workloads, especially during peak times such as earnings season. Hierarchy and bureaucracy: JPM is a large organization with a complex hierarchy, which can make it difficult for employees to navigate and advance. Bureaucracy can also slow down decision-making and limit innovation. Lack of work-life balance: The demanding nature of the job can make it difficult for employees to maintain a healthy work-life balance, which can lead to burnout and reduced productivity. Intense competition: JPM is a highly competitive company, and employees may feel pressure to outperform their peers in order to advance their careers. Ethics and reputation: JPM has faced numerous legal and regulatory challenges over the years, which can raise ethical concerns for employees. Working for a company with a checkered past can be uncomfortable for some individuals.

I don't think there is anyway around horrible work life balance.

summary: It can be good, but it's not for everyone
advice: Simplify the processes. Invest in technology as everything at JPMC is a serious PITA. Allow some positions to be work from home only. There's no sense in having so many analysts in office. Zoom will do just fine. Invest more into training as it seems a lot of training is on the job resulting many errors and hours spent on figuring out what's missing. It's ok to slow down sometimes!
pros: JPMC has a lot of pros and they do know how to attract employees. Pay is decent for analysts as well as health benefits. Lots of choices for health insurance. But watch out - biometric screening is required in order to keep paying lower insurance premium. Generous PTO. Depending on your level, you can start with about 3 weeks of PTO. Lots of learning opportunities and very helpful and friendly coworkers. This being a global firm, there are international opportunities as well. Diversity and multiculturalism are great. If you're curious, willing to learn and show great attitude, you will do great.
cons:
This being a humongous firm, there are many positions that lack good work-life balance. Some days you just don't know when you will finish, if you'll finish your work that day at all. IT department is bad. In some positions, if certain processes fail, it may take about 24 hrs to restore everything, so work will be seriously delayed. Late nights can happen. There seems to be no improvement as problems show up almost on a daily basis. For reporting they use Tableau which errors out most of the time. It takes patience to run some reports. Again, little has been done to remedy the situation. Coworkers while tend to be great, they don't hesitate to gossip and strike up weird conversations. Listening to music helps to mitigate this nuisance. They love you when you're doing things right and the opposite when you screw up. You can even sense the tension on those calls. Some errors on your part may result in an avalance of fecal matter flying all over the place. Little to no privacy in office. They don't use cubicles, they use work stations. Everyone can see everyone. Zoom is used for meeting and the unspoken rule is everyone must turn on their cameras - you're probably on camerca at all times. They even have landline phones with cameras!

One addition needs to be made: Some teams are very fast paced and have lots of new staff. You may end up being trained by someone who's been on the job for way less than 1 year. I've never seen it before anywhere. Their training is subpar; however they expect great results with great accuracy a few months into job.

cons: Depending on the office you're in, there will always be an element of office politics, which regardless of performance will hinder you from growing, people in leadership roles especially in the lower end of retail banking always have favorites and as your individual performance is only a single contributor to the stats of your BM, who is only a single contributor to your overall DM, you really have to network in order to get anywhere, and really raise your hand so to say or else you'll be overlooked by those that you would expect to put you in position to grow, again performance alone won't enable you to grow as it will serve as double edged sword in the sense that you will be recognized for it but there will be an effort to retain you in that position which you will need to break through by networking, on a separate note don't let them fool you with the concept of potentially getting promoted or you'll spend the rest of your life in the role, NO ONE gets promoted, you literally apply for the position you'd like to move up to, go through the screening process, likely multiple interviews, then an offer is made, same process as an external candidate, when a colleague goes through that process management likes to spin this narrative that they've been promoted when the reality they interviewed for the position and got it

cons:

They lack accountability of Leadership roles being overstepped and allow Leadership to do many things that are not allowable of other Coworkers.
They allow Leadership to discuss Coworkers Metrics, Disciplinary actions, Medical Information, Personal life information and other information that is or should be confidential at Managers desks in a area that is or can be overheard by all other Coworkers.

The whole structure of how JPMC runs its trickle down management, pay structure, and how they went about return to office.

JPMC has two glaring red flags with management. 
First is that every development team is required to have a certain percent of contractors so if any budget needs to be cut the contractors are the fist to go. This allows JPMC to save face and say they are not firing anyone. 
Second red flag is how they do 'value adjustments'. Your manager can tell you to your face that you should be earning a salary 10k more than what you make, and JPMC will give you a bonus if you stick around until next February to 'compensate' for that lack of salary. They won't raise your salary to meet that level, just write a check and hope you don't notice how expositive this practice is. 

As for the return to office (RTO) - at first they gave us a 2 week notice to return to office in the middle of the 2020-2021 school year. Then, because management did not have a practical plan to keep social distancing and not everyone could be vaccinated at the time (NOT because it was a 2020-2021 school year where most parents needed to work from home because their kids were learning from home) they back pedaled and kept changing the return to office date and means. It was over two months of consistent changing of the RTO plan(s).

advice: Really need to promote recognition for employees on your own teams and provide opportunities for growth to retain talent. Some people get frustrated and leave the team and stay within Chase which is good, but others get SO frustrated that they leave the firm.

Medical benefits recently were made better for us as part of a health industry initiative Chase is part of. Work-life balance is decent and getting better. Some positions allow for Work From Home flexibility.
cons:
Once reaching the Associate level, it can be hard to be promoted within your own team as many managers seem to prefer to hire VP-level folks from outside of their own team instead of promote from within and back-fill. In production environments, that's not necessarily the same, but in the project management/tech jobs, that's what it seems like.
