summary: If you like growing as a developer, don't work here
pros:
- relatively good benefits (health, 401k and matching, pension)
- relatively stable workplace (don't feel like I could ever get fired lol)
- this isn't true for all teams, but my team has been very flexible in allowing me to work remotely full-time which has been great for me
- if you like finance, working for a bank, specifically as an eng in the IB, gets you as close to traders as you could get which can be interesting if you like that stuff
cons:
Working for a bank obviously has its cons but the biggest things that stand out to me:
- we don't retain good engineers (everyone leaves) and we also don't listen to the concerns of our engineers
- we don't have competitive pay compared to other tech companies
- lack of diversity in engineering (specifically among females and BIPOC)
- very hard to make it above VP level and we really don't promote women or BIPOC into leadership (levels are analyst, associate, VP, ED, MD, e-board)
- we don't adopt new technologies frequently so engineers skills remain stagnant
- tech stack is very internal (a lot of stuff was built in house so skills are not very transferable)
- teams are overstretched to the point where everyone experiences burnout (we don't backfill positions when people leave so team is still operating at previous level with less people)
- team has on-call rotation which progressively gets worse as people leave/we onboard newly built technology and our production support team effectively does nothing to help (so half of your job is site reliability which isn't for everyone)
- overall, seems like everyone hates their job which isn't the best work environment

summary: JPMorganChase - know what you're getting into
advice: Practice what you preach on work life balance, flex work options, and being a "best company" for working mothers.  These are all areas, in my 10 years there in several different groups, that are only given lip service.  It is hilarious to me when JPMC ends up on the Fortune list of best companies for working mothers, etc.  Must improve the HR function.  It is extremely weak.  Results in lost opportunities for employees career progression/development and lost opportunities for the firm for maximizing the talent pool across all lines of business.  Further, administratively it doesn't work very well for employees.
pros: A challenging and dynamic work environment.  Good experience and a good name to have on your resume.  Good benefits.  Opportunities for growth and exposure to many areas of banking (though networking is key to opening doors).
cons:
The pace of change is extremely fast.  One has to be able to handle this and thrive in this environment.  There is very little time, even for new employees, to get up to speed on their job.  

The size of the organization can make it somewhat impersonal, esp. if you are dealing with unique personal circumstances (they will just pull out the HR playbook, not tailor solutions creatively to your needs).  

Your work experience will be 99% dependent on the demeanor of your direct manager.  The company doesn't promote one management style or philosophy so it is rather hit or miss as to what type of group you end up in.

It's still a bit of an "old boys club."

summary: Great start, destroyed by constant re-organizing
advice: Stop re-organizing so much, figure out what's the problem, and measure for it in every action you take. Focus.
pros:
- Very skilled and competent managers that are actually well trained at management. (not all, but the ones I had where good and it seemed to be common). HR does a lot of work to train their managers in leadership, coaching, and managing. 
- Great list of products: among the best in the Credit Card industry. I worked in the card division.
- Great project managers--among the best I've worked with. So, projects will run better and creative/strategic work is easier to accomplish because great PM's handle tracking deadlines and deliverables for you. 
- Good team environment with how projects are executed. 
- Good health benefits back when I was there, decent pay, and small cost-of-living adjustments were pretty regular. Small bonuses were also a regular thing.
cons:
- constant re-organizing. Teams get shifted around and you end up working for multiple different managers (all within the span of one year). I've heard from folks who are still there, and they tell me the reorganizing continues. Re-orgs seem to happen with no metric for success, so before the previous re-org has settled, leaders are initiating another one. 
- constant budget squeezing while executives continue to get lucrative bonuses. 
- Increased scrutiny from government/regulatory agencies is making the marketing work harder and harder, and the company pushes some of that work on marketing folks.
- Hard to get raises. Competitive review process ensures that only 10% of the top performers get decent raises or bonuses, and it's not so much based on performance, but rather on whether you did one or two stellar things/achievements.

summary: JPMorgan Chase: pays well if you have a strong stomach
advice: Don't believe anything your direct reports or their direct reports tell you. Come all the way down to the trenches if you would like to learn truthful information.
pros: JPMorgan Chase is a "target-rich" environment for technologists -- there's always something to fix, or something to break and then fix again. The benefits are good, the pay is very good, the Columbus facilities are nice, and they have a lot of money to throw at shiny new toys. Some programmers and engineers have more stressful lives than others, but there is nothing like the horror stories one hears from game development shops. You can come across the occasional diamond in the rough or guru while working there, and it is a good place to network for future job prospects.
cons:
JPMorgan Chase is not a technology company. There is little respect for technical analysis or input. Management often overrules or ignores the actions of the technical staff, and there is almost never any effective recourse.

There is little room for advancement for someone not interested in management or finance. As a multinational bank, JPMorgan Chase must be one of the largest users of technology in the world -- yet as a rule, they give their janitors and their engineers roughly equal influence over the direction of IT.

Design by bullet point is a pervasive practice at JPMorgan Chase, since half of the people there are apparently functional illiterates. Death march projects are common. Often projects exist or proceed the way that they do solely to perpetuate various middle management fiefdoms.

advice:
The highest level management seem to be driving the company quite well, as reflected by profits and dividends.  However, they clearly are unaware of how the mid-level management functions, or how many levels of managers there really are.

Recognize and appropriately reward your employees.  Getting a bonus of $4000 at the end of the year is nice, but if you break that down into how many evening and weekend hours actually worked, it winds up being just a few dollars an hour.

Employee Satisfaction Surveys are completely invalid, as the user must enter their SID, and the reports go back to managers who only have 10 or fewer direct reports.  It's very easy to figure out who said what and the takers of the survey know that, so they lie.  Use an external company and don't require an SID.  That will give you a report of actual feedback.

Be aware that the "good ole boy network" is alive and well at JPMC.  There are people who only have the job they have because of it.  It's costing you money.

Any manager should have manager training and learn how to encourage their staff.  Managers should be rewarded based on the team output, and the team satisfaction.

pros: For someone like myself that doesn't know exactly which line of business or role will be the best fit for themselves, JPMC is an ideal company to work for. They offer opportunities, and often encourage branching out to other LOB's after you've satisfied your one year commitment in your current role (and sometimes sooner depending on demand and workload).
cons: If you are hired mid-year, and are looking for a fast track for promotion, it is difficult to achieve this after your first year. Your EOY performance reviews play a key role in determining your eligibility for a promotion, but if you're hired mid-year, you will not have been working for the company long enough by the end of the year (because you've only logged six months worth of time invested in your role). So you'd be looking at a realistic opportunity for advancement at the end of your first full year working there. Additionally, promotions are based on availability and need for each of the positions, so even though you may have superior marks and reviews, if the need for the next role above you is limited, you may have to wait another year before being promoted, as the company only promotes once a year.

advice:
* Stop Managing in the Moment *
-- Short term cuts to the bottom line in order to gain easy performance appraisal bullets invariably reveal inherently short-sighted, "path of least resistance" thinking after you have moved on.

* Do your ROI homework *
-- Make the case for investing in technologies that have an upfront cost (yes, there's a bill - deal with it) but end up paying for themselves many times over in the form of vastly increased productivity and streamlined processes.
-- Learn how to quantify lost hours spent compensating for a second-rate solution and *sell* the *right* solution to senior management.  This is a high risk move, but will pay out huge dividends when it succeeds.
-- Listen to your staff for clues on where to look for long-term investments - after all, these are the folks that will be supporting it on a daily basis, and can highlight current process strengths and deficiencies you may not be aware of.

* Lose the ranking system *
-- You don't need the current ranking system to reward exceptional performance, and you know it.

summary: Glad to have been there, but glad I'm gone
advice: Reward "outside the box" thinking and encourage a bias for action. Streamline decision making and remove bureaucratic obstacles. There are many good people in the middle and lower levels who are utterly frustrated and stymied by managers and organization structures that prevent them from doing their jobs in an effective manner. Jamie Dimon talks a good line about cutting out the bureaucracy, and I believe he truly means what he says, but it is absolutely NOT being carried out in the lower echelons.
pros: Exceptionally good benefits programs and liberal vacation allowance. Compensation is on a par with, or perhaps slightly better, than peer companies. Opportunities for career and personal development are widely available, but need to be aggressively sought out -- management is lax about providing these opportunities to staff.
cons: Very high stress levels, minimal acknowledgment for a job well done. Recognition is highly inconsistent across departments. Some departments praise and reward staff for minimally doing a competent job; in other departments, staff can consistently produce exceptional results and barely receive an acknowledgment that they contributed anything at all. Training budgets are miserly. Reorganizations occur with dismaying frequency; any given structure is hardly in place and starting to function before the apple cart is upturned. There is an appalling lack of personal accountability for quality across many areas, especially in technical and infrastructure support areas. Staffing in technical support areas is barely adequate in many cases, leading to excessive work hours and high stress levels.

Engineers and project managers are overworked and treated like red-headed stepchildren. However, a number of times I was asked to work on a Saturday that I had scheduled off with just a few days notice (sometimes working 4 Saturdays in a row in a branch with 6 bankers).I was also asked to come in for 2 hours to cover an employee's lunch on one of my "off" days during the week. The HR policy clearly states that you have to have employees scheduled for at least 4 hour time periods, but when I called HR about this issue, I got no help. 
Also, if I called in sick, the manager would beg me over the phone to come in even though I was sick! Overall, I would not recommend this company if you are considering branch banking. Do your research on the current manager before you accept your offer!

advice: The majority of your clients did not start out being trust fund kids. They started out small and increased their wealth over time. Your policy of no compensation for trades under $50K is not well thought out.
pros: Company has Great benefits. Bankers get compensated to set appointments for you. You control your schedule.
cons:
In 2015, the pay structure for Financial Advisors changed dramatically. FA's don't get paid on trades that are less than $50K. That is no problem if your bank is in a wealthy part of town. Many banks are located in areas that have customers that are well educated and have great FUTURE income  potential, they are just not there yet. Their trades are often less than $50K. I have built my business on helping them with the small trades, knowing that as their income increases, so will the trades that I do for them in the future. So, the concept of "Location, Location, Location", is important to succeed with JPMorgan Chase. IF, you have a good location, (Bank location that is..), there is a better chance you will succeed. 
The company's comp policy says, "We don't want to mess with the small fish, we only want the whales". A bad business policy for the clients, financial advisors and banks that use to provide  a great service to their client. While the comp policy is expected to change a little every year,
this change is one that is great for the company and bad for everyone else.

I work in compliance, specifically AML, and I have to say that joining this firm was the biggest mistake I have made to date. The attrition rate here is so high that I've had 4 managers in as many months. Because the firm rarely hires and promotes from within, most of the new managers need to be trained by their subordinates. This is unacceptable, illogical, etc. 

Compensation is another issue altogether. You will be paid under market - way under market in fact. My bonus this year was less than a month's paycheck (and I fared well considering many folks got nothing). To add insult to injury, salary increases did not exceed 2.0% for most of my colleagues, and the majority reported 1.5% increases. This is municipal government quality compensation - not compensation for people in financial services. Most of us can literally no longer afford to work here and live in New York.

summary: The company makes promises to employees but will never let you progress
advice:
Stop taking a blind eye to what's going on in your company.  The Management team is lying about the numbers to make everything appear to be ok, thus playing a mathematical game with the statistics.  They will never let an employee progress unless its an employee they can forever keep in their pocket.  If you really check most managers working for you do not possess the educational background required for the position and most have been recruited from other companies where they were terminated from.  

Do an overall assessment (third party), and try to benchmark your operations from some of the leaders in the industry (BOA).  Clean up house and start from the top!
pros: JP Morgan Chase is an old reputable company and its better to have a job than not have one!
cons: The company has the lowest payscale of any other bank.  The company will not support tuition reinbursement even though they offer it.  They eventually ask you to multi-task and perform management related duties but never increase your salary.  The management team is so detached from their employees.  The management often sladers the lowel level employee and the supervisors have now clue and depend on their staff to save the day.  Overall its a hightly stressfull, understaffed, unprofessional, and depressing place to work.  As soon as I found a better job, I resigned with a two week notice immediately!

summary: Great Place, but treatment depends on location branch
advice:
Listen to your employees and work with them. They will be there for you, if they think you will be there for them.  Don't downsize your employees if there not in a high-profit branch, everyone should be just as important. Especially if you're going through an employment shortage and transfer people from one branch to another. 
Also update your dress code, or at least go to more sustainable clothing with natural fibers that decompose such as cotton and linen.
pros: Very well structured training and helpful coworkers and managers.
cons:
I originally liked it, but after I was trained in one location and moved to my full-time working location, the quality of the workplace went way down. And with that also the treatment of the employees and respectful customers.

There are uniforms ordered through Lands End with the Chase logo and colors in white, gray, and navy. And they for one are mainly polyester and ill-fitting. It reminds me of working in a retail shop, rather than a respectful banking environment. You would be better off having the employees dress in business casual within Chase's selected colors. Even customers thought it was too casual to have employees wear denim, yet your company thinks khaki is too casual?

advice: care about who cares about their job . care about who can do more or who can do more in other fields. care about each individual talents and skills rather than standard frameworks and who they know to use their talents. please cut the who knows who specially in higher ranking and management positions. If they know some body that does not mean they can do the job. The loss of the company starts from the horrible high managemnets that you have coming down and the profit starts from the tellers and bankers who is geniounly working with the lowest pay checks. Value the low level and get rid of all those high paycheck no knowledge and skills high managers
pros: good and stable company to work for. if you try your best , you can get to some steps of success . Insurance and benefits are good.
cons: just like every other company , it depends who you know a loooooooot. education and degrees not really matter unless some body makes it big and matter. very long hours of work and low pay check. strict policy for second job even though they make it impossible with working hours. lowest pay bank. the higher the management , the lower their education.

advice: Be more upfront and honest with employees about the direction of the company. Employees shouldn't have to read the letters to shareholders to learn about the reduction of expenses. Restructure the PL to bonus branches based on YoY growth on not based on peers. Simplify incentive programs for bankers and follow through on payout. Provide more career management resources.
pros: Benefits, holidays, vacation and sick leave. Match 401k 5% with a pension of 3%. Decent incentive opportunities. High focus on doing what's right and providing exceptional customer service. Great CEO.
cons: Middle management could be more effective. Communication from upper to lower management could improve as well. Compensation plans change every year with a steady decline in payout, though last year remained relatively stable. Politics like most organizations. Growth opportunities can be minimal as they have recently contracted. A few items in the incentive plans don't make sense and they look for ways to not payout through small intricacies. The PL structure just changed for the better but it is designed where only the top performing branches in their peer group will get bonus even if a branch's YoY results are superb. Superb results for a branch in rural america compared to a branch in Chicago or Miami is not just.

summary: Best Company I've Worked for Yet
advice: Keep doing what you're doing but with employees interests in mind.
pros:
-Great benefits (20 days PTO at the VP level starting, 3 personal days, 9 paid holidays, 401k match at 5%, pension at 3% of your salary, medical/dental options, work from home opportunities, 16 weeks parental leave paid at 100%, medical covers IVF)
-Best work/life balance
-Flexible
-Intelligent and transparent management
-Ethical company
-All bank holidays off
-Great CEO and face of the company
-Stock price is always going up, so it's worth investing in ESPP and/or investing in JPMC stock in your 401k plan
-Roth 401k is offered in addition to the tax deferred version
cons:
-The Employee Stock Purchase Plan is only discounted at 5% and is paid quarterly
-From my observation, once you get into senior management, it seems like you go from awesome work/life to none. I think you get paid the big bucks but you will be working 12+ hours a day
-Unless you're in a hub location (Columbus, Phoenix, Dallas, New York, San Francisco), management opportunities are far and few between
-If you're not in a hub location, the offices are something out of an 80's movie with hardly any amenities

summary: Good for early career, but don't spend too long here
advice: Pay your top performers.  If teams are already distributed, let them work remotely.  Get a better method to get feedback on managers.
pros:
Early on, JPMorgan taught me a lot and gave me a lot of opportunities to grow. My role was expanded multiple times and I was given a decent sized team to manage for my age. 

I had some great managers who have taught me a lot and been great mentors.
cons:
My compensation never kept up with my expanded responsibilities. I found out that external hires in similar (or less senior) roles were often being paid 50%+ more than me. Despite being a top performer (based on my performance reviews), I never was paid market rates.

I've had some pretty crappy managers, and have had no avenue to talk about them with anybody.

The recent focus on D&I is great. However, JPMorgan is using a system where senior managers get "points" for their diverse hires- which limits the mobility of anybody who doesn't fit into one of those categories.

Too many people think that they are very important, and come with demands with very short turnarounds. This makes for a very stressful environment and ruins the work/life balance

summary: Good work life balance, benefits, job security. Needs better comp
advice: Management is generally good but the way the structure and rules are set up, it is hard to work your way up the ladder as previously noted. Would be nice to have a better sense of upward mobility where I can work harder and get a promotion based off what I have learned and proven, not just by only doing required work over longer period of time.
pros:
Based on my experience, things change between teams but from the 2 teams I worked on, these are my notes
- Work life balance, only expect 40 hours per week of employees
- Job security, only 1 person I worked with was ever let go during my 3 years here
- Internal mobility, many open jobs internally for changing teams
- Good benefits
cons:
- Climbing the corporate ladder can be difficult here, generally takes time but working harder or more won't necessarily get you noticed
- Compensation could be better, I ended up leaving for a 50% salary increase at a different company. They will only really raise your salary significantly if you make it known you are looking to leave by having other job offers
- They will also hire new employees with less experience at a higher salary than you

pros: I do not recall any pros of working here. It was all bad.
cons: There are too many to name

summary: Lots of data, but a diffiuclt environment for developing innovative analytic solutions
advice: Encourage technologists to be involved with open source projects and learn and develop skills outside of work or on their own self-driven work-related side projects. Also for technologists, there needs to be a compensation adjustment to make the salary comparable to tech firms.
pros: Very interesting, rich, and valuable data. Lots of "extra curricular" activities and opportunities to network and figure out what's going on. Many opportunities to learn about other roles and lots of internal mobility.
cons: If you're excited about making innovative technology products and using open source tools, this environment, like many other large companies, that will prove difficult.  I was sold on the fact that there was so much data to use and could do so many innovative things with it, but it proved very difficult to move beyond ideation stages with many projects because of management changes in priority and legal/compliance conservatism. It is a difficult environment for an ambitious technologist who's not willing to put in the time and effort to win political victories to push her or his work forward- overhead that you would not have a tech company - but also not a learning opportunity you would have in a tech company either.

advice: Your website talks about a great culture that you have. However its a lot different when you get hired. You don't need to be roude to people and treat them like your children. There are plenty of other companies that pay better and treat their employees better.
pros: Benefits are great. I met some nice people there. They want to be a company that gives equal treatment to everyone but they fall short...If you are a woman looking for management opportunities, you will fit right in (most man are not welcomed)
cons: Be ready to accept a position for a lower pay then you expected. You will not be promoted in a year. Getting promoted is very difficult at JP Morgan. You have to know some one or if your parent is an executive director that helps too.  Most of the managers are roude. You will be embarrassed in front of your colleagues at least once by a manger and yelled at. Bonuses for managers are very important. A lot more important then you. Remember its what best for the FIRM not your family. If you want to get promoted or keep your job make sure you work at least 50 hours per week.

advice: Please provide better training to managers especially in terms of sensitivity training.
pros: Opportunity to work for a large firm, if you play your cards right you can network with coworkers located in London, Mumbai, Singapore to name a few. This can also open the door for working abroad to one of these countries if this is something that you desire to do. Like any company, if you play your cards right you have a wide array of different career paths that you can take internally.
cons: Corporate Culture - It is rather common to hear about nightmare manager stories from other employees if this nightmare scenario is not happening to you. These scenarios can range from, micromanaging, public embarrassment, and poor work/life balance to name a few. As I said in the pros section, your career at JPMorgan is really based upon the hand that your dealt upon starting at the company. This means that if you start off with a manager that is in a poor standing with their superiors they can and will destroy your career to save theirs. Make sure you document everything so that when the time comes to throw someone under the bus to save yourself, you have the documentation to back you up.

advice: This isn't a company where you can feel like you contribute or build a career. It's an assignment and sometimes what you do might matter, but mostly it won't. There is plenty of training listed as available, but it has no value. This is a global company, so you are 1 of 100,000+ people with no culture or identity. Find exactly what you want or leave.
pros: Some technology. Decent benefits. If you know how to play the game and move until you find the right situation, you can advance. There are decent groups where work can be rewarding.
cons: Much of the IT is hurry up and waste your time with little chance to advance. In these poor areas, work/life balance is preached but not practiced. In the same poor departments, you only have about a 2% chance of ever being promoted - ever! Took a very large leap just by doing the same high level of performance under a different manger. Top performers get varying bonuses but rarely advance. All culture has been eliminated. Tools are watered down to the cheapest available or to the lowest denominator. Socializing is reduced to the Starbucks break or corporate sanctioned community service.

jobTitle: Business Analyst - Corporate Investment Bank, NY
summary: Full Time Permanent Business Analyst for Corporate Investment Banking. Been with the company for 3 years.
advice:
- Show you care about your employees
- Help employees achieve a work life balance
- Preach what you practice. If you are dishonest then own it and stop shoving mandatory compliance courses down good employees throats
- Get rid of super aggressive middle managers and leaders you have in your organization
pros: Compared to other comparable companies, people are open and collaborative in sharing information and supporting your work. Very talented pool of coworkers and leaders but extremely aggressive in keeping in mind to get ahead careerwise and pushing their own agenda to the point they might seem very cut throat. Definitely a very process oriented place, where hard work and talent is valued and rewarded at the year end review.
cons:
No chance to move to other projects across Lines of Business except if you know the hiring manager etc.
Very long hours with no concern for work life balance for folks with families and kids. Managers do not care about employees at all except to get their job done faster and quicker. Management is somewhat cutthroat. 2014 bonus was very bad during to Q4 2014 company's bad performance.

advice: do better.
pros: money, learned a lot about portfolio management and banking.
cons: no work life balance, poor DEI

advice: Find ways to identify true competence and dedication in your employees and remain true to the system you have in place for scoring branches & departments which are under performing.  Get rid of those who have done poorly over the long run.
pros: This company is a marketing machine.  They offer a great brand name and their system of collaboration is nothing short of outstanding.  The benefits are great.  If one is fortunate enough to be placed in the right situation, career success is virtually assured.
cons: If one is placed in an unfavorable situation, there is very little that even the brightest & most ambitious person can do to overcome and succeed.  Disrespect from management to their direct reports seemed to be a corporate cultural problem.  Politics is also a big problem here.  Shocking how common it was to see managers undermine their own long-term success in favor of short-term pettiness and desire to get full credit for the job being done.  There seemed to be virtually no understanding of the cause-effect relationship with departments/people which were doing well and those which were not.

advice: Don't forget from where you came!  There are things more important than your sick & demented need to always make money no matter whether it is harmful to the employee!  Think first of your employees.  If you treat them right then they will do more for you & will look forward to coming to work every day instead of going to just a job.
pros: Stock options.  Nothing else that I can think of.
cons: Very oppressive & severe working conditions!   Cares only about making money at the expense of the employee! Management closed down the building I was working in at Hicksville, NY as he decided to outsource our jobs to India.  Some 1500 employees were laid off.  Most of these families had families. If the employee decided to remain with the bank then he/she had to transfer to either Tampa (which the bank later closed after a lot of employees had moved to), San Antonio, Tempe &/or Garden City where they still had to endure the same harsh conditions.  While the bank was willing to pay the move of the employee & his/her family together with giving them $5000 cash to restart life, they stated that if the employee were either fired or quit in their first year the employee was required to reimburse the bank all the moving expenses & the $5000!

summary: Worst Company I've Ever Worked For
advice: Communicate with your team. Be sure to let them know of new regulations are changes within the company. Show up to work, if you expect your team to respect you, and stay with the company.
pros: This company pays good for the area that I live in, especially for not requiring a degree. The benefits are outstanding and they offer three weeks paid vacation a year plus 5 sick days.
cons: I did not have a single check in 2013 that was accurate. I had to open a case every pay period for HR to research my pay. This took typically two weeks to resolve, so I was always behind on paychecks. You have to put in your vacation requests a year in advance and changing schedules is nearly impossible. Management is usually good, but they never stick around. I was there for almost four years and had 12 managers. Changing departments or moving up is very difficult with the company, as they only like to hire from outside. Calls are completely scripted and it is extremely easy to get a bad audit due to saying one word incorrectly - which leads to a write up. Policies are always changing, which also makes it easy to get a write up. The company is money hungry and does not care if cuts or changes will affect their clients negatively.

pros: NA bad experience overall it is
cons: Lot of things bad management

pros: Good bonus and good salary
cons: worst work, worst team leader and management, only hindi people can survive

summary: They try to cover up company issues by offering a higher salary
advice:
- Value your employees more and show that (having to buy a keyboard just to be able to do the work is honestly outrageous for such a successful firm)
- When you do 'recognize' company achievement, don't just recognize those making under a (very low) threshold 
- Retrain your HR employees to actually tell the truth during negotiations (I was promised bonuses, benefits and a lot more than I have since found out is not applicable)
pros:
- Company name recognition
- Looks good on a resume
- Salary is the highest in the area
cons:
- No trust from higher ups
- Lack of company structure (many reorgs, title means nothing, unclear goals for reporting structure)
- They nickel and dime everything (you have to buy your own supplies, your area gets charged for calling support, the conference rooms are terribly dirty and unkempt because they won't pay for cleaning crew)
- The entire leadership structure is filled with self promoters and they will throw anyone under the bus to move up
- Benefits are terrible (expensive health benefits, and almost nothing beneficial starts until you have been here for more than a year)
- No work/life balance (I work 50-60 hours a week at least)
- It's impossible to get 'sponsored' for leadership. You can only move up if you leave and then get hired into another role.

pros: Good benefits, networking opportunities, generally people are very smart and willing to help, good name to have on resume
cons: In a company that is so large, you are just another pawn in the system. They expect loyalty, but if it benefits them - they will get rid of you in a heartbeat. Many promotions/opportunities are based on who you know and not your skill or performance. IF you are promoted, pay increase is abysmal, which is why so many people leave and come back later. Have a hard time keeping diverse candidates because they are often overlooked or misunderstood. People are very quick to throw each other under the bus. Bureaucracy is a major problem - projects take so long because there are so many levels of approvals, leaving a lot of wasted downtime filled with unnecessary busywork. It is very hard to change lines of business, as every line of business has its own analyst program. For example, the Investment Banking programs only recruit from top level schools, operations programs recruit from state schools. Extremely hard to make the switch into the revenue generating side unless you know someone. Managers can make or break your experience.

summary: Work 18 hours a day and belittle your co-workers
advice: Get out of your office and get a life!
pros: If you enjoy working all hours of the day/night and having your boss checking on you constantly to be sure you are logged in and available, this is the company for you! If you enjoy hearing a department "leader" (Managing Director) tell your India counterparts that their English is bad, this is the place for you! If you want to hear from your immediate boss that she inherited you in a role that is not her specialty (and she is not happy about it), this is the place for you! If you want to work for a company where you feel unwelcome, this is the place for you!
cons: My experience was so bad, I refinanced my home so my mortgage is with another lender. I would not give JPMC another dime of my money. I will never bank with them. Very unorganized company. Internal technology needs to catch up to the times. People work non-stop because processes are so manual. The long-tenured associates like to do things "the way they've always done them" even if it means it's more time-consuming and they dedicate all their time to this institution. If you work here, you will not have a life outside work. They also like you to log your whereabouts when you are on vacation. It's an invasion of privacy.

advice: lol
pros: Great benefits, okay salary, good overtime pay and yearly raises. They have written rules and regulations that can be found by any employee. It's an alright job if you do exactly as you're told, arrive early daily and enjoy long hours.
cons: Overworked. No say in anything, they try to make you feel heard but it's just for show. You are micromanaged down to the millisecond; prepare to get to work at least 10 minutes early every day to make sure your ancient computer boots up fast enough for you to clock in on time. If you log in even a minute or two late more than a few times, prepare for a very uncomfortable conversation with your boss. They love to call everyone "family" which is manipulative. If you deny overtime, again, prepare for another uncomfortable conversation with your boss. Work, work, work, work, that's all this company knows. They are big enough that if you quit, retire or even die, they can fill your spot in a second. They do not care about you. Also, they do not care if you are being harassed or bullied by your coworkers, unless someone straight up hits you or inflicts some sort of physical pain unto you, HR doesn't care.

summary: Overload of work with limited opportunities for growth
advice: Hire employees who already work in the department who understand the SOP’s than hire someone else from a different department who do not understand how the department works due to not having experience working in it. It will help with more growth opportunities with employees within the department. If the wait times to speak to a representative are long, instead of pushing the employees to speed up the calls. Jump in on the calls and help! that’s why your in the position of management. Do not belittle your employees, show more appreciation for the hard work they do.
pros: Positive aspect about the job were my co workers and our team potlucks.
cons: Company did not pay nearly as much as they should offer from the work load that you will have to do. You have sets of eyes staring over the back of your head if your call time is over 7 minutes. You can not put yourself on hold after you finish a call if you need to finish up putting notes in an account. The leaders would be upset if you do and will constantly ask what is taking so long. You are undervalued for the hard work that you put into.

summary: Great place to work if you are in the right department
advice: Increase pay and rely less on contractors.
pros:
Its a very relaxed atmosphere, I was lucky to have a hands off manager who left me alone. 
To get ahead you need to know the right people and then prove you can handle the projects assigned. Once you do that and the upper management knows you are set and you will get all the good projects. 

Being a huge company there are lots of opportunities to join extra curricular activities such as volunteering, mentoring, recruiting, and etc. 

I met a lot of great people here, sure there are cliques but generally people are friendly and open.

The work life balance is generally good from my experience. You are allowed to work from home whenever you need to.

Good PTO.
cons:
Pay is somewhat low. I did the same amount of work as people getting paid almost twice as much as me, but because they worked here longer they got a lot higher paycheck.

Lots of red tape if you are a developer, the computers are bogged down by slow software. Its affects productivity a lot. If only they spent more on technology such as projectors/wifi in conference room, employees can be more productive.

advice: Consider hiring managers who aren't your close friends.  There's a long list of qualified candidates out in the world who would perform much better than about 75% of the management you currently have in place.  Example - in one dept, the AVP only had collections experience, yet was overseeing a mortgage lending dept chock full of experienced knowledgeable mortgage professionals, yet when suggestions or ideas were offered, they were repeatedly rejected, only because it "threatened" the image of the AVP.  This example is typical across the board at Chase.  Its who you know, now what you know - the old saw.  Unfortunately shareholders could care less, and the board of directors could care less - just keep churning out the profits and screw the talented people.
pros: I worked at Chase for several years in the Loss Mitigation dept.  The people I worked with were all very professional, smart and easy to work with.  Nice facility.  Plenty of parking.
cons: Middle to upper management seem to operate in a different world than the rest of staff.  Just about every decision that came down, made little sense in the real, on the floor day to day operations.  The people in the middle to upper management positions were for the most part inexperienced, had little to no actual management experience which showed in their poor people skills and inability to effectively lead others.

summary: A great place to work for right out of college. CDP Program
advice:
Provide more career advancement/promotion oppurtunities.
Consider balance workload on team over specific individuals.
pros:
Training is available depending what set of skill is available but learning really occurs from your coworkers or outside your team. The CDP program has dedicated 4 week training to provide guidance for those that may need step in to the work force.
Company recognition/visibility for hard/smart workers thinking outside the box, owning hot items(I.e. running to the fire), leadership opportunity, and process improvements. Depending on manager
The time off policy vacation/sick/personal/compensation great compared to other companies.
Getting an exceeds rating in the company allows employees to get school compensation opportunities belive its around 80% for selected schools.
401k Rate match to a specific percentage point, company stock option, health plan, life, legal insurance available.
cons:
Work life balance especially in the IT support area.
Advancement/Promotion oppurtunities have to work beyond the next pay grade available to get promoted. Think of working 2 pay grades above to get promoted 1 level.
Workload ownership.
Dont be surprised of pay gap differences when doing same/above job roles and responsibilities.
Bell Curve rating system.
Management styles varies so expectation in certain area may weigh in to your rating which could be in your favor or not.

summary: Great company, management personnel could use some tuning though.
advice: This advice is for upper management. Train your people correctly. Let them do their jobs and stop pressuring for more to be done when it is nearly impossible. Don't lay off veterans that you say you support, just because your refinance loan rates go up. This doesn't coincide with the "hire 100,000 veterans initiative". Its a load of crap. This will fall on deaf ears but I suggest the company stop trying to make as much money as possible and concentrate more on its people and the communities. Making too much money is whats wrong withe the world. You can't take it with you when you die, so whats the real point? All we're doing is earning the board and its chairman more money.
pros: The pay is great and the colleagues are wonderful. Everyone is very helpful with each other and its a great work environment. The moral is great until upper management steps in and spoils all the fun.
cons: Management. The management has such pressure to meet goals that they sometimes overload the employees. Its not always their fault as their job is on the line too. Working for a bank is strenuous and mundane. All they care about is money. It'd be nice if they cared more for the employees.

pros: Nothing was good about it
cons: everything was terrible about it

advice: There needs to be more emphasis and accountability on managers to develop their staff, provide regular performance feedback, and be up-front and candid on promotion opportunities (or lack of). There should be more transparency into the promotion discussion process. Remember – Great people management is critical to be a great place to work.
pros:
1) As a large company, J.P. Morgan Chase can offer opportunities to do many different things and the bank has gotten better at supporting internal mobility. 

2) The bank has resource groups to support different groups and interests - women, young professionals, etc. The BRGs provide opportunities to get involved and network.

3) J.P. Morgan Chase also has a very strong brand recognized around the world.
cons:
1) As a very large company, the environment can be very different across the firm depending on your line of business, management, and location. Compensation and promotion rewarded for doing a great job and working hard seem very inconsistent.

2) For advancement opportunities, it’s critical that you align yourself with a supported line of business and supportive management in your location. You need to be savvy to recognize your environment and work to change teams/roles if needed.

3) In early 2015, the bank got strict with the work from home policy.

advice: Work on developing your people.  When someone gives you feedback, really listen to it instead of taking a defensive pose.  As employees we're expected to take feedback and work on ourselves and be better, so as managers when we offer feedback it should be the same way.
pros: Chase is a great company to work for.  Work hard & have a great work ethic would be my advice to anyone at any job, but it's doubly true at Chase, or you won't get anywhere, period.  It's very competitive and fast paced, & there are a lot of opportunities for advancement BUT you must be willing to go the distance.  Chase has great programs for wellness, wonderful benefits, and competitive pay for the area.
cons: It's incredibly stressful.  You're not always going to get a manager that knows what they're doing, either because they don't screen their managers well enough in my opinion.  Things constantly change, and that causes a lot of stress with trying to keep up without constantly feeling like you're doing something wrong because you can't keep up with the changes.  It's way difficult to advance because it's so competitive that there's literally 20 people who are just as good as you applying for 1 position.

summary: If you want work/life balance work here. If you want to work on latest Technology look somewhere else.
pros:
- Great benefits and good pay 
- Amazing work/life balance (mostly will depend on your manager)
- Helpful people, although there will be exceptions just like any other place
- Internal mobility is good, although it never worked out for me because all the interesting things I wanted to work on (Tech wise) was either in New York or Texas.
cons:
- Promotions take a long time depending on what level you join. So make sure when you join the firm, you come in at a position you want to be at. Because you'll be there for a long time. I've seen people quit and come back after a few years just to get a higher position.

- If you're working for any of their Technology departments, you will not be working on the latest technologies. JPMC being such a large organization, implementing any technology takes FOREVER.  For example: It's 2019 and my team still supports 2008 servers for some projects. Even Microsoft doesn't support it anymore.

- There is a lot of bureaucracy and unnecessary paperwork that will get in your way. This will get really frustrating, really fast.

summary: OK, but needs to have more hands on training
advice: More experience actually talking to people on the phones before kicking them to the floor.  There is SO much to learn, and you can't remember everything in training and it's hard to look up in Chase Answers unless you know specifically where to find the answers, and the team leaders do not always know the answers, and that makes it hard . I've seen very good people leave or get fired over knit picking things.
pros: They are always having games, fun, etc. Free coffee, on site cafe, 3 weeks paid vaca first year, 3 sick days a year, 3 personal days, paid holidays.
cons: They give you 10 weeks training, but when you hit the floor, you BETTER not mess up. Depending on who your manager is, they will "coach" you, or write you up for every little thing, even if you can't find the answer on their site.  Even if your boss tells you what to do, and it turns out wrong, you're written up. Some people are there just to talk the whole time and it's hard to get your work done with people laughing in the back ground or being loud.

advice: Beaurocratic mgmt
pros: Database platform mgmt, gti planning
cons: No career growth , time pass mgmt, try to adopt west coast technology

pros: good work environment, decent benefits (401k, ok medical and vacation), decent incentive compared with the other banks. Pretty good technology compared to other banking jobs I had.
cons:
Sick time is only one week, if you get Covid be prepared to use your vacation time. Company keeps changing incentive plans and cuts incentive each time the plan is revised, the bankers who bring the business get paid last after everyone in line gets the cut. Bankers always have to stay on top of their incentive tracking to ensure they get paid. The automated system that tracks referrals needs to be more streamline, otherwise there is a perception that it rearranges incentive on purpose to get bankers less in bonuses. 
No pay raises whatsoever. Never worked for a company that does not give pay raise every year. (complete disregard for inflation) It also was not communicated to me when I was hired.
You have to be a notary, and notarize external documents which does not give you any more money, puts you at risk of being sued and takes away your time from work. 
Investment bonuses cap for bankers don't make sense for business. Incentive is highly dependent on location

summary: Stay away from this company, it's trouble.
advice: Be glad to got ride of your subprime mortgage division, they were a lawsuit waiting to happen.  And for advice, take a good hard look at your management structure and then replace them all.
pros: This is a huge company with lots of possible positions to apply to change to if you are interested.  Also this company had great benefits and decent pay scales so you are in a fairly good situation both financially and beneficially.
cons: This company if filled with people who have been inappropriately promoted based more on politics then on ability.  In my time at this employer I worked in an entirely female managed group and I heard on multiple occasions statements made to say that they planned on keeping it that way.  Being a male employee I was treated very poorly, and I ended up being unfairly fired.  There was NO recognition for good work done and you were hammered when you didn't do a good job.  I personally got TONS of praise from my outside contacts but my internal management gave me no credit.  I was punished for doing TOO good of a job at my duties and I was unfairly treated.  When a manager got concerned that I would replace her she had me fired for a completely false accusation, and I wasn't given an opportunity to defend myself.  STAY FAR FAR FAR away from this company.

summary: A bureaucratic nightmare of poor documentation and poor programming practices while being surrounded with great people.
advice:
Focus on quality over deadlines. It appears counterproductive to push code design and creation as fast as possible before requirements are complete or the necessary tools are requisitioned. To me, it seems like it produces much more work for testing cycles and operate support, when if the code was done properly these teams should ideally have little to do.
An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
pros:
The people are the main reason to work here, they are professionals and have a nice inclusive culture. Also, there is high mobility to move throughout the company, so potential to work anywhere in the world.
However, since it is such a large company, it is possible your mileage may vary depending on which group you are in.
cons:
The heavy red tape that is involved with getting anything done is the largest challenge. Something that should take 10 minutes for a knowledgeable individual can take up to 3 weeks due to permission requests.
Also, the culture is borderline workaholic, with cars arriving at 8 AM, not leaving until 6 PM, and many people taking desk lunches.
As with the Pros, these might vary between departments. I have heard from others who barely work at all.

advice:
The daycare is amazing, but because our facility is quite large, it fills up quickly. It would be great to expand it. 

Create a better process to report issues, and a more robust approach to ensuring people have access to all the information they need around their rights.
pros:
Recently had my first child and they provided 16 weeks paid maternity leave, in addition, my manager and senior leaders for my group have been flexible and sensitive with my transition back to work. I've been allowed to work from home, start work early and leave early to accommodate for my child care. They offer 8-week transition daycare and emergency day care on site.  

Other then my experience around maternity and flexibility, my experience has been positive. My manager is forthcoming with feedback and honestly wants to help me succeed.
cons: Only issue is that culture and mobility is very dependent on your manager. Prior to my current role, I worked in the same area under another someone else. That individual created a very hostile environment that resulted in me becoming sick both physically and emotionally. Because I am in HR, the team was not set up to allow for easy reporting as my manager knew all the HRBPs and those in ER.

summary: Chase has a big head but no eyes or ears.
advice: Treat your employees like autonomous human beings and not robots.  We aren't all the same.
pros: The company provides a okay but not great wage, benefits are acceptable, they work with your schedule pretty well.
cons: When Chase as a corporation decides it's going to do something, it does it regardless of how it's actually working in the field. For instance, the branches are now forcing employees to stand in the lobbies with tablets, resulting in longer wait times for customers, more annoyed customers who are not interested in the performance and just want to do simple transactions, and less productivity due to slower devices that cannot multitask as well nor perform as many functions as the vastly superior computers we've all been using forever. They have also recently decided to give all responsibilities and liabilities, from the top down, to the bottom of the totem pole; "associate bankers" are now required to perform all the same functions as the real bankers and a great deal more, for a considerably lower pay rates. In one short year this company has transformed from one I begged people to apply for to one I insist they stay away from. I used to be so proud of my job, now I dread every day.

advice: Give the new kids a chance
pros:
Its the last bank standing - whats not to love. There is tons of opportunity in the various depts. 
for the most part you will be challenged and your peers will actually challenge you harder, which at times can be scary. Overall the training and knowledge that you learn here you can take any where. My advice would be to stick it out in your respective dept as long as you can and then see if there are opportunities overseas which most departments will look into for you. however given the recent state of the world financial industry that practice maybe null and void.
cons: the stereotypical male, white, and over 60 are all still here which is very upsetting it ;leaves no room for growth and many of these individuals have made enough money to compensate an entire team. Bottomline, dont come here if you think that the bonus will be at least 6000k (after tax) because that hasnt been the case in a very long time. In addition, there is no point going to HR because there is over 1000 HR representatives who are soo specialized that any assistance you need will not take place. Again, join JP for the resume booster and take your knowledge elsewhere.

summary: I would describe my experience at J.P. Morgan to be different.
advice: I beseech you to please seriouly consider employee feedback and suggestions.  Also, there is a great need for management to treat all employees with respect.  It kills employee morale when threatening to take employee jobs just to produce greater results.  Motivating employees and ensuring that all employees are happy is a much better way to inspire employees to produce greater results.
pros:
There are a myriad of opportunities globally within the firm.  It appears to be common to take advantage of opportunities across line of businesses.  Also, it is very common to communicate with colleagues across the globe (i.e.: London, Bangalore, Manila).  

People at J.P. Morgan also have a very deep knowledge regarding their respective industries.  The firm provides the resources needed to acquire industry knowledge (including competitor intellegence).
cons:
Improvement is needed in regards to process efficiencies.  Also, I believe that the firm should consider making a greater investment in the new hire on-boarding orientation & certain job-specific training (i.e.: organized job-specific training to ensure that new hires obtain the essential knowledge regarding the firm's systems, groups and processes).

Lastly, management should seriously consider treating employees with better respect and have an ear to hear employee feedback and consider them.

summary: Learned a lot of skills with the company and met a lot of great people.
advice: Share the wealth! Every time numbers outperformed the prior year the incentives were pushed higher and were made harder to hit. I understand that's how numbers keep growing but it just puts stress on one of the most important ingredients to a business being successful, it's employees. Give them raises every year and share the wealth.
pros:
I think the management and co workers you work with definitely make the work experience good or bad. Fortunate enough to work under a caring manager and great co workers which helped me succeed and pushed me to grow as a person.
Great systems and updated technology gives you the tools to be successful.
cons:
Big company that at times felt like they only cared about profit and their clients more than their employees. Every time numbers outperformed the prior year the incentives were pushed higher and were made harder to hit.
Depending on the managers, co workers and clients, people could definitely be a pain to work with and give you a negative experience.

summary: If I could do it again, I wouldn't.
advice:
Be honest with your employees.  If you hire and tell people they will be moved to a similar job at the end of the project, stay committed to that.  You're dealing with people's lives here.
Bring people in that actually understand how to manage a project.  I understand that there are certain things that are out of the company's hands, but you can control how everything is run.  This is the first place that I have worked that wasted months of time because of poor leadership.
pros:
Excellent vacation policy. benefits, and pay.
Great name recognition on a resume.
Comfortable chairs and spacious desks.
cons:
High turnover rate for managers - it seemed like every few months, I had a new one.
Dishonest leadership - a whole building essentially became temporary staff after being told we were permanent at the time of hire.
Inconsistent performance management standards - you might be rated high at mid-year, and then have the exact same review for year end, and end up lower, with no explanation why.
Analyst-level staff are treated poorly, which was dictated by leadership.
Project ended, everyone was laid off.  Talent reassignment has been a joke.  Three months - no interviews.  The company doesn't seem truly committed to retaining employees.

pros: Great benefits for part time. 3 weeks vacation and 12 paid holidays. Pay is decent. Company gives allowance to purchase company clothing.
cons: Onboarding training is unorganized due to no clear direction of where to get started in training modules. Training is held at a center branch within a general area of where you will be working. Training consist of virtual training: watching videos and having conference calls with training facilitators. No true hands on training is had during 3 weeks of training which leaves you unprepared to properly be efficient in your job once you go live at your branch. No HR representative goes over how to enroll in health benefits or order company clothing which is part of the dress code.  Full time for teller/associate banker is 30/hrs unless branch does not have the staff to cover branch needs then more hours can be worked. Company is undergoing a change on the branch level by introducing the Associate banker which is a fairly new role. This role will most likely do away with the teller and banker position.

summary: Work life balance? What is that?
pros: Great technology, prestigious company name to have on resume that will help you get another job, nice building, professional looking staff, team environment, organized, made good friends and connections. Perfect environment for a hungry, aggressive, just out of school Ivy Leaguer.
cons: Overworked, miserable, underpaid employees. Fake, pretentious upper management that can care less about their employees on a personal level. Managers take credit for work done by their team, no "job well done!". bureaucracy, backstabbing and b*tt kissing is essential at getting ahead, not fair evaluation and raises are minimal with upper managers taking in good chunk of dept bonuses, no clarity or explanation - 'projects' just get thrown at you. people working in technology or branches are treated like 2nd class citizens compared to other areas of the bank. Having any kind of personal life outside of work is unheard of. No one cares if you have a sick kid or had trouble getting to work due public transit, its going to make you look bad and you will pay for it at compensation time.

advice: Overall,  what a stressful and unsatisfying experience. Having to play the game of politics and all the bureaucracy that comes with it is not fun. It was an unhealthy environment for many. We faced discrimination on a daily basis, (race,  gender,  lead source,  etc)  as there was definitely not a fair playing field in Consumer Direct. I have given so much over my ten years with this dept, I feel like the life was sucked right out of me.
pros: Worked with some great people. I wish I had more positive things to say. Unfortunately,  the benefits,  pay, overall work balance was great when I started in 2002. Everything went downhill,  hence,  why I left.
cons: I worked in a call center taking inbound calls as a Mortgage Banker. The leads were not distributed on a fair basis. They had a way of keeping the top dogs on top and bottom dwellers at the bottom. Hence,  why there was a huge settlement after the dept was sued for discrimination.

summary: Mortgage business in the penalty box and it may never be released by executive management at the bank.
advice:
Spend money on technology but let the business decide what it needs and not let the IT folks run the company.  
Worry less about where managers are located and focus on retaining good leaders because of what they bring to the table. This is 2015 and location should be more irrelevant.
pros: Good benefits, good people wanting to do the right thing for the right reasons.
cons: Too many chiefs, salary and promotion strategy archaic, company does not engage or embrace technology to help it in important areas. Legal is too conservative in its approach and its influence has far reaching effects on processes and procedures that often conflict with business models from both a customer service and expense mode. I feel the company lets it's legal and IT people have way more influence than its business leaders which creates an environment of frustration for managers and employees. These two groups should work with the business to support them rather than just saying no to everything.

summary: This company has diversity issues at all level
pros: Nothing for non-white people full of bureaucracy. The CEO knows it’s and he say he wants to fix it but it’s hard as I mentioned my review
cons:
, it’s primary run my only white people at the leadership level they pretend to run the diversity program but it’s a sham ) 
obureaucracy and underline racism And bullies , due to this kind of leadership which is been a primary white people company there is so much bureaucracy and Red tapism that other race people can’t get anything done they have white folks in London and UK along with white people in  America controlling the IT teams and business teams , I was an executive director there for 11 months and I am from India and I experienced it first hand being in the leadership role , they didn’t let me do anything and ultimately I resigned !  I liked Jamie Dimon that’s why I joined but it was a stressful experience dealing with the bureaucracy!!
