advice: Middle management is not good, rather than having a meeting with 100 folks, spend time on having one on one conversation. Every time something happens, you create a survey. Your day/week is full of surveys. There aren't many black people in the middle/lower management, may be two in every 100. Minorities, people of color are under represented. People of color are in top management often get highlighted and the company assumes we have good balance.
pros: 1. The CEO is doing very commendable job , he has steered the ship very well through various crisis
cons:
1. Wells Fargo is poaching a lot of people similar to how JPM has poached people from AMEX  
2. Does not pay well
3. Middle management is very bad, it is leading to a lot of good people leaving the organization. There are no growth opportunities.
4. The company has created a lot of processes and amidst of all this they forgot employees are their best asset. The middle management does not have time to nurture people.  Employees are there  just to produce output and reports.

summary: Banking Company that is moving with the times - less robotic and more engagement for the customer
advice: Just a reminder to be consistent and to recognize that employees should never be pigeon holed.  Call center people can be bankers in the retail world and vice versa.  Investment people can grow out of other areas of the bank.  A college degree is a measure of commitment not knowledge necessarily.  Once you manage people the job tasks are learned behavior.  Managing people is all very similar no matter the environment.
pros: For a bank this company understands it has to do what is right for the customer.  It also understands it has to develop the right people to lead the teams to encourage the right behaviors within it's employees to engage their customers.
cons: Because it is a bank...regulatory agencies and laws can sometimes create required scripting that is not so customer friendly.  Because of this sometimes the changes take a long time to get through all the red tape to allow the employees to become more customer focused.

advice: Train the management team on leadership development, basic  management skills and choose them wisely. Employs are looking for competent mangers not someone who you have to daily consider what mood are the in; or how he is going to chastise u for asking a business related question. Also those daily huddles need to go such a waste of time on so many levels, what is the purpose of them beside belittling employees and telling them how they suck. Also how  are employees suppose to get a meet or exceed expectations when they done know what they are measured on. you only come to find out how you were evaluated on the day of the evaluation and even then its not clear how your manger evaluated ur performance.
pros: As an organization they are great. I would go back and work for them; however, i would never go back to any of their small offices. Great benefits insurance is so so but everything else is great.
cons:
lack of upward mobility
Unskilled management on many levels
unrealistic work expectations 
no life and work balance 
Favoritism

summary: Poorly made decisions by people unqualified to be in management
advice: Stop giving authority to those who cannot handle it.  A true management training program would be beneficial, so that those who are looking to move ahead have the skills and opportunities to do so.  Too often people are promoted to management positions with no experience due to the business needing to fill a position.
pros: The pay is good.  A common joke around the office is that we are in prison and that bail is too expensive to get out.  People stay with Chase not because they can't find better jobs, but they can't find the same pay.
cons: Management is very poor.  It is like watching little kids dressing up in their mommy and daddy's clothing.  People are promoted based on who they drink with, not based on performance and merit.  The arrogance of management is astounding as well, as certain managers are 100% convinced that their decisions are always correct, and though they "encourage" feedback and discussion, really only want people to agree with them.  Anyone who objects ends up being labeled as "difficult" and is blackballed.

summary: Great name - too much politics, too much resistance to change
advice: - Aggressive for the sake of being aggressive isnt good enough. Share your strategy with the rest of the team - they will step up to help. Just pushing people will push them out the door.
pros:
- Good name on your resume
- Good Bonus structure
- decent salaries
cons:
- Too many people who have been at Chase for MANY years - they are reluctant to change, and can be hostile when change is introduced.
- Company wants to be more nimble - but in an oxymoron fashion, creates committees to figure out how to be more nimble. These committees then have to go to other committees to get approvals, and those committees have people who are too comfortable in their jobs.
- Some groups are hiring extremely talented people at high pays to bring this change - MOST of those people realize they can't fight the currents, and leave. Those who are left behind either convert, or shut up. 

DISCLAIMER: JPMorgan Chase is a VERY large company, so it is hard to generalize a review. This is specific to the retail side of the house.

summary: I had great growth opportunities and worked with great people all over the world.
advice: Get resources with more technical minds in management and the business side to provide balance to the pure management types.  Stop reworking budgets as often and follow through on the plan.  Get ahead of events by spending on fundamental components rather than always reacting.  Be more flexible in working locations you can retain talent that otherwise will be lost.  Service Oriented Architecture only works if everyone is willing to cooperate.
pros: Lots of very talented people working hard in a client focused culture.  Good benefits by today's standards.  Rewarding experience bringing products to market that serve the clients well.  I would still be there if job locations did not change but I did not want to move.
cons: Overly political much of the time.  The MBA's are a thick middle management layer that could use some thinning with some technical people.  Not enough hands on resources.  Budgets are constantly in flux as management reacts to events rather than be ahead of events.  This can make bringing a program to fruition very challenging.

summary: No upward mobility or consideration for the disabled
advice: Treat your employees with respect, value all of them, not just the ones who are top performers or brown nosers. Work with the employees who aren't perfect, have a heart. Not just for your customers but your employees too. Without your employees, you have no business.
pros: Good place to get your feet wet in the call center environment. When I started working for the company it was converting from Bank One to Chase. The culture was very laid back, and management listened to their employees. The benefits package is great.
cons: Was told in training that you should leave your heart at home, because there's no room for it at Chase. No upward mobility, rarely promoting from within. They prefer to hire from outside sources for management rather than promoting. Quite a bit of favoritism for the yes man. If you're an honest, hardworking employee, they don't care. Don't bother applying if you have a chronic illness or disability. They will find any reason they can to target you and make your life miserable if you're sick. There is no accommodation for people suffering from anything other than cancer.

summary: Factoring in Cost of Living and Hours Worked Not Worth the Hassle
advice: The tech firms are stealing your talent due to equivalent pay, half the hours worked, and higher quality of life. The investment bank "up or out" employment model only works if you aren't being disrupted. Less rent-seeking bonus-based compensation, more long-term stock-based compensation thinking please.
pros: Interaction with CEOs and management teams of Fortune 500 companies. The long hours translate to a lot of experience crammed into a short time. The number of resources available to enhance your work is staggering.
cons: Company pays lip-service to employee value. For example we have free annual health care checkup and flu shots, but no gym (and no time to go to one). The kitchens are stocked with cheap low-quality coffee, which I can only presume is there to try to limit our time away from desk. In some ways the work can be degrading (printing out copies for your boss, acting as a low-level buffer, doing the work nobody else wants to do). The technology we use is horrifically outdated, resulting in a lot of time spent doing menial work that adds no real value.

advice: fewer meetings, more cross team accountability.   Oh ans schedules aren't king, productivity is.
pros: JP Morgan is big big.  the benefits are great, the pay if great and the services are great.......  but read the CONS....
cons: Again JP Morgan is big big.  To many people running around trying to do too much.    It is hard to get things done.  Hard to get started and hard to communicate with fellow team members and internal groups.    There is little cross team accountability.   What JP Morgan loves is meetings, meetings and more meetings.  Let's have meetings to discuss the status on the last meeting, and let's have a meeting to schedule the next.  And let's include everyone in every email, so you'll have to read through 50-150 every day, least you miss something critical. Don't forget the stand-up meetings.   Overall I was dissatisfied, when I raised concerns, regarding requirements and others not fulfilling their deliverables,  we schedule a meeting not address the issues.  Easier to push things out.... but let's not change the deadline.....

advice: Your talent is frustrated.  Listen to them and give them opportunities to improve the organizational culture.  IT work is knowledge work and people are not interchangeable parts (fungibility)
pros:
Large company with unlimited options across the global banking industry (consumer, mortgage, investment banking, etc) and technology domain (infrastructure, middleware, mobile, etc) if you're willing to go through a few relocations.

Easy access to very intelligent and highly motivated people; healthy options for those with talent and motivation.

You will learn to operate systems at scale that are unrivaled many other places.
cons:
Being a large bank in today's world technology moves slowly unless you happen to be in an "innovation center" and usually trails the leading IT trends and services by 3-5 years.  

Lots of bureaucracy and red tape.  Way to much paperwork in most cases.

Lots of reorganization and a major site strategy underway, make sure you find yourself in a strategic location.  If you're good at our job there are enough mobility options inside of the "hubs"

The old adage "a penny-wise but pound foolish" occurs far too often in decision making from upper management.

jobTitle: Assistant Vice President - Technology Project Manager
advice: Treat others as you would like to be treated.
pros: Great benefits, though the stock purchase plan and 401K contribution were not as generous as other companies.
cons: I can speak only from the technology realm.  The company downsizes on an annual bases in the double digits to make their numbers. Replaces US employees with offshore employees or with H1B visa consultants. There is no such thing as work/life balance and there is no such thing as comp time. I did get comp time once after I had spent a summer working 14-hour days during the week and working several weekends, my manager smiled and gave me a day off. Management is rude and demeaning to their employees. In my area, there were several people who applied for jobs elsewhere in the bank but were blackballed by their managers. The only people who got out were the folks who knew the hiring manager first. It is a finger-pointing organization and highly micromanaged from the top levels. You constantly have to CYA. Also, in the 6 years I was there, I only received 2 raises. After 2008, no one in my department saw a raise except for a couple of people, and they weren't happy with the raises they got. If you're in technology, stay away!

summary: Solid company, good comp and benefits, but still very traditional
advice:
Apply 360 leadership "talk to walk" -- require specific feedback of managers rather than "write in boxes," which encourages a lack of response. 
Better staff HR in Markets; there is 1 HR person for every 250 markets people, and it's clear they work for management, not in favor of the little guy.
pros:
Average compensation, average benefits for industry 
Great analyst and intern training programs
Strong brand recognition / strong reputation in finance 
Clear path to promotion from Analyst to Associate, from Associate to VP
Internal mobility - decent movement between functions, geographies
Jamie Dimon's commitment to recruiting minority groups and providing spot bonuses to lower pay employees
cons:
Management in CIB still very traditional in thinking about role definition
Lack of "safe space" to provide critical feedback to direct management
Lack of clarity around ED and MD promotion criteria (many stagnant VPs) 
Insufficient commitment to environmental sustainability  (doing well on community support though)
HR works for management, not the little guy (everyone more junior than an MD)
Lack of female professionals at the ED+ levels

summary: A bank, not a tech firm. Pay is good, but the environment is alright
advice:
• Everyone on a team should be guaranteed a seat. No one should be left behind just because they want to squeeze in as many people as possible due to absences. Having "80% coverage" in seating is not ideal for teams and people who just want to work.
• Managers should be more technically knowledgeable of what we're doing. Otherwise, we're at the mercy of unreliable metric review and people showcasing what we've done to really know anything. This does not play well with the political landscape.
pros:
• Good pay. As a software developer that did not finish college, I started with a very good starting salary.
• Mentorship opportunities to learn
• The application functions are simple. As long as the codebase is somewhat clean (very important), the work is not too complicated for strong developers. However, this point is based off of my limited experience.
cons:
• The overall software in J.P. Morgan isn't very "current"
• There's quite a bit of politics that goes around
• Management isn't very technically knowledgeable
• The more legacy application deployment process is very inefficient
• Open office seating system

pros: The job will help you work on a lot of core skills including, writing, critical thinking, public speaking, financial modelling and analysis, and relative valuation/idea generation. You also benefit from access to a broad array of resources working on the sell-side that may or may not be there on the buy-side. Overall, a great way to "cut your teeth" and learn many skills that you can take with you wherever you go.
cons: As a junior analyst you will most often need to look outwards (either for another role within J.P. Morgan or at a different company) for upward mobility given that the next rung on the "corporate ladder" in the group is to be senior analyst and those opportunities will depend on luck and timing (relocation can also be a way to make senior analyst. Not exactly a "con" but the other consideration you should think about is that you work in a small team so communication and developing rapport with the senior analyst you support is a MUST.

summary: Pay is not competitive at entry-level
advice: Managers should foster growth and not complacency in employees. It should be commonplace to be moved to different workgroups or projects  frequently, people get too used to doing the same thing and focus on just meeting numbers instead of having a big picture understanding of their job.
pros: Benefits like vacation time, sick time, healthcare, facilities, etc... are above what I expected.
cons: In my experience the pay is not competitive compared to several other financial businesses in the area, however, the benefits may outweigh the difference especially if you have children. Some people may complain about career mobility options but that largely depends on your education (degree vs. no degree), experience (time in your position with the company or in a similar role outside), and your personal drive (you need to exceed expectations and clearly communicate with your manager so they know how to help with your goals). If you're aimless, no one will guide or push you unless you have a true gem of a manager.

summary: During my time there felt like the most dysfunctional family or being in high school.
advice: Having employees take 2 to 5 hours a week out of their actual work to answer to the status of the loans in pipeline with three different members of management is unproductive. New employees should not be penalized for the loan files that are anywhere from 60 to 90 days old when transferred to the new processor. Demeaning and bullying employees is counterproductive and highly unprofessional. If your intent is to hire only to harass our employees than your business model is sorely lacking. Working with management that are either still drunk or hung over from the prior evening makes for a hostile and frightening work environment. Yet these are the types of people who are promoted through favoritism.
pros: Pay and benefits (specifically medical)
cons: Too much micro-managing, not enough working, sarcastic management and team leads, unprofessional managers and team leads. Coworkers were often in tears or swearing loudly (management did nothing to stop these outbursts). In fact one of the team leads spent 7 hours out of 8 swearing. The manner of answering the questions of a person in training  or  existing employees was always rude and unprofessional.

jobTitle: Licensed Relationship Banker Small Business Specialist
summary: Becoming too corporate, less focus on customer service and employee satisfaction, More focus on being a car salesman.
advice: Management takes strong leadership, take responsibility and own your branches. Use common sense. There is a growing amount of spineless women being hired as managers because they are easily influenced and controlled. When i first started in 2010, I only had women management and they were great, all formerly managers from Washington mutual. Chase has stripped all independence from their managers and you are now robots working for the man, instead of regular people helping customers. You are now just a Big business that hooked a great population of consumers on an idea of a big bank with a small bank feel, but now that you have all the customers, you car just going back to a corporate big bank that only cares about the big fish.
pros: commission, some coworkers are enjoyable, get you licensed
cons: poor management, clear trickle down effect. Very few managers are individuals, they are simply robots transferring information from higher ups.

summary: What goes up must come down
advice: I understand one of the easiest ways to increase revenue and profits is to cut compensation. However, do not forget that the talent pool being taken advantage of are the ones driving the sales. What is easiest is usually not the best way to do things.
pros: Good overall company with lot's of opportunity for those willing to go the extra mile. Strong focus on building client relationships and retention of assets. Great place to learn the business as a starting point in your career.
cons: Every year it seems like they find ways to pay us less in our compensation plan. The latest cut back ties our yearly bonus into our monthly paycheck, so if we are not on pace to meet their goals we are penalized what comes out to thousands of dollars of years. This is especially true if you have been with the company more than three years. Not competitive against other financial firms since most firms pay 40% commission on financial solutions you provide.

summary: Can't get any better exposure to business than this.
advice: Maintain more transparency across all levels. Encourage and invest in development of your existing  employees. Retain the top notch candidates you have and incentive for their efforts than throw away money on new recruits from competitors who know little about technology or the business when compared to existing employees
pros: You would get to work with great people who are in the business for good 15+ years. Great deal of experience gained while working with them and the problems you would try to solve are at the grand scale and helps make money for the company in big way. Great vacation package
cons: Not everyone is collaborative, typical big corporate politics and finger pointing when things go wrong. If you are technology geek and want to be part of disruptive industry then you got to look elsewhere as people weigh more on your financial domain experience more than anything else. No bump in salary for 3 years which is ridiculous

advice:
Be open to listening to suggestions and consider all options for a successful work environment.
Make sure that employees have, or can receive, appropriate training for the tasks they are to perform. Upward mobility is excellent if given the right tools; disastrous if not.
pros:
I worked first in the Kansas City, MO office as a designer and that was an excellent environment. I had an excellent manager who recognized everyone's skills and talents and was very open to suggestions. 
In general, the environment, management, compensation, benefits, etc. were excellent and I would welcome the opportunity to work with Chase again.
cons:
When I moved to Pennsylvania, the situation was quite different. It was an office that was comprised of people that had "fallen" into their jobs through a series of mergers. Many people were in positions for which they did not have appropriate training. 
Found that the mentality of "we've not done that before so it won't be successful" applied to many.

summary: Good place to start - Learn and leave
advice: Increase head count - Managers should be retasked to prioritize pursuing and implementing efficiencies to existing processes. They spend too much time on calls updating stakeholders on problems instead of seeing the fixes through.  More people are needed to free them up to do this. Current model is heavily dependent on line analysts to execute change. It's not realistic. The people flying the plane are too busy to rebuild it at the same time and its magical thinking to expect that.
pros:
Lots of independence to own processes
Lots of opportunities for growth
Lots of internal mobility opportunities
cons:
Stifling bureaucracy - implementing changes and improvements to processes happens over months due to poor internal coordination and opaque team dependencies. Its hard to get anything changed for the better. Tactical ad-hoc workarounds devolve into BAU SOP quickly here.
Severe workloads - head count is not where it should be. You can work 60+ hours a week and still feel like you are falling behind

summary: A great place on paper & very challenging, but not geared towards developing young talent!
advice: I think young people want to learn the best industry practices and specialized knowledge of particular fields. If the management can encourage more senior workers to help mentor younger workers and additionally provide improved training systems which can be accessed at no cost.
pros: Having JP Morgan Chase on my resume has drawn a lot of positive attention from other employers which makes it a great marketing tool in the job market. JP Morgan also have very disciplined banking practices and will teach you exceptional methods of multi-tasking & time management.
cons: My line manager at the office was an exceptional mentor and taught me invaluable skills, however the company as a whole did support his ideas and often at times he would take time out of his personal life in order to teach me things rather than be supported by upper management in helping younger employees to learn. Additionally, the training systems are very old and out-dated.

advice: Please only advance people to management who are emotionally mature and fit to be managers.  My manager would whine all day that she didn't want to be a manager.  Then don't accept a position you are not suited for!
pros: Good company to put on your resume since the name is well known.  Nothing other than that.
cons: Oh boy!  How much time do we have?  The place is a sweatshop.  They expect you to work 70-80+ hours and then some.  You are given a lot of vacation time but they expect you to work on vacation too.  I can't tell you how many times my manager called/texted on my days off.  My manager used to pound her fists into the desk, throw papers all over and stomp her foot like a baby that needs a bottle!  Unbelievable.  The environment is downright abusive and intolerable.  Technology is antiquated at best.  If you are a current employee who is suffering, I feel your pain.  Find another job and know that life will get better.  It is so not worth your health and well being.

advice: Consider us for sales positions even if we don't have the minimum "retail banking experience". We are working for the firm after all, we're familiar with the product and we love the Chase way; those of us who are interested in moving lines of business should at least be given the opportunity to interview. Also, the "shift-bid" needs to go, the number one reason you lose good people.
pros: Pay is comparable to other call center jobs, my personal dept only speaks to Retail Bankers, so we don't have to bid on Holidays off, never work Sunday's and we open late/close early. Great benefits, and people are friendly. The company does a lot of employee appreciation events (provide free lunch, games, snacks and chances to win prizes), Chase definitely knows how to treat their employees to a good time.
cons: Career mobility (moving LOB) is extremely difficult, we're FORCED to bid on new schedules once a year, so if you're receiving a shift differential it's very possible you will lose it. Growth within the company is nearly non-existent (in this particular LOB) and frequently take advantage of talented specialists, moving them into temporary management roles and then removing them. Constant revolving door.

advice: Continue to strive for excellence within your teams, ask for more input from your teams on day to day processes. Work on being more timely with monthly score cards.
pros: Not your traditional call center job, jobs is rather easy once you get all processes down pat, leadership is always available and willing to answer any questions and listen to concerns. My particular manager has done an excellent job at boosting my chances at being promoted by recommending me for different projects, and supporting my ideas to better the department. Requesting vacation time has not been an issue, overall a great job/ department to be a part of! 10/10 would recommend for driven individuals!
cons: Growth potential within this department seems to be rather stagnant, a lot of people transfer to this job internally which makes it more difficult to be promoted due to lack of availability. Hours are not always optimal, and pay could be higher especially for those individuals who has considerable saves for the customers and the bank as a whole. Switching schedules to achieve a better work life balance has proven difficult but I understand that has to do with the needs of the business and space available.

advice: Duh , Career advancement , I hear a Man was getting 23 an hour to do my old job yet I was getting 11.50 with more years of Experience , Go figure.  My MBA seems like a nice napkin at Chase , because it's not from Harvard or Yale like the CEO's.
pros:
Stable good benefits just So-SO on pay. , I wanna Leave this job for better but 
the chase You halve to talk to HR ( and DIE waiting on the Phone) as managers can not discuss employees to potential hiring firms , thus keeping me shackled to this lackluster Entry level job. 
I was a Lone officer it was more interesting .... 

Job of depositing ATM checks is so easy a monkey could do it in their sleep.
cons:
Pay to Women is a Joke for An MBA ,even without an MBA Joke. 
And if I were to get my CPA I could make far more Money outside of Chase. 

 few opportunities  for Advancement into management or newer positions often managers with half my education often stonewall advancement, 

recognition as a Senior Employee begins with Senior citizenship most firms after 5 years.

summary: Progressive, Innovative in the Financial Services Space
advice:
Be visible and evangelize your commitment to the culture, space and technology  to enrich collaboration, innovation and the employee experience.

Institute a TRUE 360 feedback program (similar to Glass Door and/or Yelp) where employees can offer regular, and pulse feedback regarding the people leaders in their chain of command. It would allow people leaders a real time means to implement course corrections, and a method to weed out toxic people leaders.

Truly support work autonomy, skill-set mastery and instilling unity of purpose to elicit higher levels of employee engagement. Oh, and make work and the workplace FUN!
pros: JPMorgan has put significant effort and resources to evolve as a progressive market leader steeped on a trusted reputation who's leading the industry cognizant of culture, space and technology changes required to enrich collaboration, innovation and the employee experience.
cons:
Pockets of reluctant adopters of change (Lines of Business), especially changes that enrich collaboration, innovation and the employee experience.

Sometimes slow to remove toxic people leaders.

Primitive (time consuming) on-boarding processes and technology...from candidate interest to candidate vetting to making an offer to a potential candidate takes to long, and in the process lose candidates to other offers.

summary: Good company brand, certain roles are better than others
advice: Invest more in retaining employees and developing lower level management. Support the little people. Reward high performers or they will continue to leave.
pros: There are many opportunities, and if you managers like you, they will make opportunities for you. Good perks, company sponsored networking events, and solid job security. Some very intelligent colleagues. Most people are collaborative, and take accountability. Good technology, good vacation policy. Opportunities for internal mobility. For a large company, it functions very well.
cons: Senior management boasts work-life balance, but it's not realistic. Long hours, weekend, & holidays required as work days. Salary is too low for the amount of work, the responsibilities, and the yearly increase aren't enough to cover inflation. Internal mobility traps you in the same salary. High turnover rate causes talent to leave the company, but it's the only option if you want to advance in your career. I saw almost 95% of my division, including managers, leave in a short period of time. Some colleagues make huge errors, are not team players, and have a "that's not my job" attitude. Bad maternity and paternity leave. The new healthcare coverage isn't as good as the previous plans.

summary: Good firm, pay's not great, and it is a bit too big these days to adapt to change
advice: Be careful on the amount of cut-backs.  The firm has become way too top heavy and cutting resources from operations groups are causing a real strain on morale.  Cutting one low level operations person making entry level wages should not be considered the same as cutting a senior manager.
pros: Truly believes in career mobility and senior management genuinely understand that talent is their most important asset.  Good CEO and senior management team.  Relatively good job security given current market conditions.
cons: Low pay in comparison to the industry.  Do not appropriately reward high rated employees that are loyal to the organization.  The best option to earn a market competitive salary is to leave the firm to work for another.  Lastly, every firm is having to cope with a sizeable amount of regulatory change, but getting swift and decisive action is difficult in a firm this size.  They tend to project manage everything to death and expect way too much given allocated resources.

summary: Review of a former IB Associate
advice: Find a way to retain talent.
pros: J.P. Morgan was the ideal place to begin a career.  The company boasts a world-class training, analyst and associate program, and exposes you to some of the smartest and most driven financial experts on Wall Street.  Additionally, the breadth of J.P. Morgan's reach allows you to touch a number of different industries and products, allowing you to develop a wide scope of understanding and context in the financial markets.
cons: Although this is more a function of industry dynamics, the increased regulation over the past few years as well as what it looks like going forward has an impact on your ceiling.  Working at a major investment bank such as J.P. Morgan can provide dividends in terms of its reach, your opportunity to work with a considerably large population of very smart and driven people, but it will ultimately limit your salary and career growth compared to other less regulated companies and industries. Like any major company, there is also a lot of internal red tape and politics that you'll need to learn to navigate (along with a little bit of luck) to succeed on a long-term basis.

summary: GREAT PLACE TO WORK IF YOU ARE THE COMPLACENT TYPE WHO DOESNT ROCK THE  BOAT, BAD PLACE FOR CREATIVE THINKING INNOVATORS
advice: Management is just idle and in most cases, they wont improve a function or process unless it is severely impaired. Management doesn't address employee dissatisfaction about career growth opportunities and do not provide a career path to driven, talented employees. Make the workplace more attractive to retain talent. Provide a clear career path, and recognize those who exceed expectations and reward them.
pros:
-Brand recognition
-Competitive starting salary and great benefits
-Diverse corporate culture 
-Great networking events/groups to join within the company
cons:
-Internal transfers are cumbersome, and you will have to wait till following February for salary adjustment - and even after the salary adjustment (in the event of promotion) you will be making far less than someone who was hired externally for that role. THIS STATEMENT HOLDS TRUE THROUGHOUT JP MORGAN CHASE.. regardless of your division 
- Red tape/bureaucracy, 
-Old fashioned, antiquated database systems in some divisions, limited technical support, lack of innovative thinking 
-Management doesn't like creative thinkers, old fashioned institutional setting, "if it isn't broke, don't fix it" mentality. 
-Limited funding for creative projects

advice: Fire the bad incompetent managers and keep the good hardworking ones
pros: None that I can think of
cons: There is high turnover since management is incompetent, childish & useless.  Lots of incompetent stupid managers with lots of insecurities and drama. In my dept the good managers got fired and the lazy, stupid incompetent managers who flagrantly disregard the rules but are kiss ups to senior managers remained. Management doesn't want to fire you since the company doesn't want to pay unemployment so they make your life miserable in the hopes you'll quit so make sure you keep a copy of your conract and detail notes of any meetings with management and any incidents. Because management lies. Also they are a greedy transactional company, they don't care about their customers or their employees so if you care about your customers or co workers you'll not last long at this company. Very low employee morale in every dept, everyone hates their job and the company, just read a site ( google it) to see how much the company screws its employees. Be very careful and read your contract very carefully the job is not what they say it is. Management is deceitful and incompetent. Technology is outdated and crashes all the time. Lots of incidents of racial discrimation & sexual harassment that management cover up and HR ignores. Keep detailed records of all incidents.

advice: Salary/promotion is based on investment bankers who leave all the time for other firms. If you want to retain staff, you need to pay adequate raises, especially on promotions. Hiring replacements costs 150% of salary. Paying 3% to the employee would save you alot of money.
pros: Room to use your vision to make an impact - project managers who do more than just process will be very successful. Diversity is valued.  The company is trying to become more innovative and creative, and to encourage employees to offer suggestions. Excellent company for veterans, with a strong focus on hiring them.
cons: very direct culture, often "New York" rude by midwest standards. Complex bureaucracy with lots of controls and policies requires you to learn the systems to get thing done. Expect to work more than 40 hours per week. 50 hours is common. Raises are below cost of living. You cannot afford to work for Chase for more than 5 years or you will be underpaid for your skills. Major re-orgs in top level technology leadership happening. Everything could change over the next few months, depending on how the re-orgs shake out.

pros:
Employees are our greatest asset, and we strive to attract talent from the broadest pool to foster innovation, creativity and productivity. There is tremendous power that results from this kind of diversity. In fact, creating a diverse and inclusive environment is critical to our success, and we are deeply committed to hiring and retaining employees from different backgrounds, experiences and locations.

cons: The Chase Bank fee structure is one of the bank’s biggest downsides. Unless you have direct deposits, are eligible for a student account, or keep a substantial amount of money in your account, you can expect to pay a monthly fee between $12 and $25.

summary: A nice job. But after a month there I want out...
advice: We need more tellers!
pros: The hours are pretty good except there are some long days at times (8:15-6:45pm). Having a nice team behind you makes it worthwhile. Not too many other pros to be honest....
cons: It's a quite challenging job dealing with people's money and as we all know that can cause a mess. I feel like I'm on pens and needles each day since I am very new to banking (my background is retail). There is not much room for mistakes. My location does not enjoy working around school schedules so students beware. Also, because we are understaffed, I was thrown into a register and pretty much had to make mistakes to get better. It's hard to constantly ask for help while other tellers are busy with other customers and you have to continue to interrupt them. When it gets busy and there are 6 cars in the drive thru you just want to give up. If your location is completely staffed there will be someone helping you every step of the way until you get it right. At this point, I stress going to work everyday.

summary: Where Technical Talent Goes To Die
advice: Trade your CTO and other technical leadership for someone who knows how to run a software company. The engineers you have are really good ones, they just lack a solid leader in the technical domain.
pros:
Amenities are great at Plano, TX location.
JPMorgan Chase really showed their true colors during the Covid-19 pandemic, Covid days, extending vacation usage periods, remote work without the hassle.
Medical Insurance is amazing.
Prescription Plans, you hardly pay anything for most drugs, most of the time they are actually free.
From a company perspective, as far as treating employees, it is a great place to work.
cons:
From a technology perspective, this place is a complete trainwreck!
This organization literally has redundancy baked right in. There are dozens of teams all working on the same type of software products, dashboards for measures all kinds of metrics. Some written in React, Angular, probably even Cobol somewhere.
Technical leadership lacks vision and direction.
This place is basically your camp if you want an easy job, low responsibility, and you desire next to no career growth, in software development that is. I cannot speak to the other domains.

summary: JPMorgan is top notch at balancing the employee and business need to create a secure positive work environment.
advice:
Promote those who will be best at the job they are being promoted to, not the job they're currently in. Some employees may be highest performers, but cannot thrive when managing people and there for we suffer by taking those talents off of the floor and into an office. 

Always remember that training and stretch opportunities are imperative to an employee's success and we need to make time in our work day to continuously grow employees, not just master the current role.

Take time to talk to your team one on one.  Every employee has something to say and every employee opinion matters.
pros: Benefits / competitive salary / highly skilled employees create challenging work / top financial industry world wide / opportunity for growth / desire to encourage internal mobility
cons: In my experience, in a large corporation of this size, everyone is replaceable and therefore employees are more concerned with protecting their own jobs;  verses working at a team to create a universally better process and product for clients. Lacks a company culture that encourages creative and unified thought.

pros: The best in the industry. That is a level of stature that comes with working at a place like this. Can have access to great contacts, smart people, the sky is the limit if you want to put in the time, effort, and make your job your life. Management at the top of the house is top notch.
cons: It comes with a price. you work hard and long hours, even in a support function. If something comes up you are expected to drop everything. And you are not making the salaries that the executives who are asking you to bend over backwards are making. In general, they don't value loyalty and longevity at the company. I've been a strong performer and always had solid reviews but am undervalued and repeatedly looked over for promotions and bigger jobs. And when they bring in people from the outside with inflated salaries, they just usually don't work out and I am left picking up the pieces.  I wish management would not have such short term memories and remember the loyal contributors who have stuck by then through thick and thin...

summary: A good job that could have been GREAT.
advice:
-Focus on elevating charismatic and EFFECTIVE leaders, not just anyone who fits the qualifications on paper

-Leverage the INSURMOUNTABLE amount of funds and influence you have to fix the gaping holes in your system. Become the trailblazer for the rest of the world, don't wait for a scandal to do better.

-Take care of the level 1 workers. Do better by them, if you have the heart to give a little, give some more and see the difference.
pros:
-Base pay = $16.75/hr (much higher than most entry-level retail jobs)

-High-pressure, fast-pace, no slackers, lots of responsibility (this job is not for clowns)

-Full healthcare, dental, vision benefits for part-time employees (20-30 hrs/wk, great for HS grads just getting started)

-Moving up is easy or difficult depending on how bad you want it. You ultimately decide whether you move up with this company.
cons:
-Incompetent and lackluster managers, close-quarters workplace, corporate brown-nosing, volatile clients

-ANCIENT computer hardware and software, difficult to manage at times.

-They will laugh at you if you ask for more than 20 hrs/wk. Expect short and brutal shifts, random and revolving days off during the week, Saturdays are mandatory. All of this will somehow end up as 20 hrs/wk

summary: Be ready to deal with the red tape
advice: I would really encourage you to work on providing more resources for development and applying your resources well across all markets you have a presence in. Truly today the experience you get in California or another large market for the company is vastly different then you get in the Midwest or South which is disappointing for several who travel through or extend their stay in these places.
pros: Working here certainly has its perks. You know you will never have to come to work only to find out your company has gone under or is in deep financial crisis. They have a great vacation package and are working to make it easier to move around the company based on your goals and career choices.
cons: This company is huge and that means you are a number with no name and your opinion, unless accompanied by 10's of thousands of others, means very little in the grand scheme of things. Also, expect to hear the same corporate lingo and "attaboy" talk while the work on the real deal and business plan behind you. Often you will find yourself working very hard with little reward.

summary: Last place on earth I'd ever work at.
pros: It was a pay check only
cons: Incompetent workers, managers and Sr. Management

advice: Nothing will change under the Dimon Administration.  Probably - and unfortunately - have to wait until legal and regulatory action break the Firm up.
pros: It's the right place to be if you're looking to pad your resume and gain experience for just a few years. Or if you totally run on adrenalin and enjoy stress and being second guessed.  Or if you have a rabbi on high to protect you. If you want to work hard, develop a career and have your contributions appropriately acknowledged, look elsewhere.
cons: The Firm is way too big and the left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing. Overly obsessed with operational and risk-based controls (sort of like locking the barn door after billions of farm animals escaped), even when the risk is marginal. A lot of bureaucratic and administrative obstacles. Little to no salary increases and dismal bonuses (each December you hear how badly the Firm is doing - EVERY year).  Adversely affects those who have been employed for a long tenure with predecessor entities, who now make better money; easier to downsize those close to lifelong careers and hire a younger workforce for cheaper salaries. Bank One's 2005 acquisition ruined a really great place to work. Colleagues used to be like family, too. Not anymore, when everyone had to look out for their own backsides.

advice: Take a look at whats going on in your Technology department (particularly workforce technology headed up by SW)  Note the nepotism going on there particularly around how friends and family of the crew in Ohio are empire building moving jobs out of places like delaware, nyc etc.  Look at how much money this part of your organization has thrown away on projects that failed because people were put on them who were friends and family rather than qualified people already in the org.
pros: Pension and good 401K Match
cons: Management doesn't care about employees or want input, at least in the technology org.  People are treated as expendable and replaceable.  Decisions are made about technology by people who aren't end users and those responsible for doing configuration and supporting applications are mere order takers.  Performance review process at this company is archaic and a total waste of time.   Decisions are made regarding who will get bonuses and how much even before the reviews are completed.  Its very political.  When employees leave the company, management doesn't even conduct exit reviews because they could care less what the employee has to say.  That says alot about a company.  I guess they figure that because they give out decent benefits the employees should should shut up and be grateful.

advice: Adjust the personal bankers incentives to reflect branch traffic! Everyone should not be held to the same standard. A banker little Alexandria, Louisiana should not be put up next to a banker in Manhattan and expected to be putting up the same numbers.
pros: The management I've had so far has been very helpful. I have not had much interaction with upper management, but on the branch and district level, they have been nice. They train you very well and try to prepare you as much as they can for what you will be dealing with. The hours are great, you have a 98% chance of getting off everyday before or at 6:30pm.
cons: The incentive pay should be calculated by branch traffic. You have to earn a certain number of points and if your branch is not busy or has very little walk in traffic, your points WILL reflect it and not in a good way. No real perks! It's a pretty big company so I think we should get a little extra something...at least a company picnic here and there!

summary: I wish upper management cared about the teller side as much as they cared about the banking side.
advice: Let the bankers do what they are paid to do and let that be the case with tellers. Also, if a branch needs help provide it to them. There is no business that is too strong to crumble.
pros: The pay is pretty good considering every other part time job is paying somewhere in the single digits. it preps you really well in knowing how to work quickly. The customers made me love what i do. As with any job if you have the right set of people you can work wonders.
cons: The inability to work with your personal life is something I disdained. Due to recent changes in my district they are no longer hiring tellers within our region. This leaves many of the branches understaffed. Upper managements response is to let bankers jump on the teller windows and assist if need be. This creates an atmosphere of chaos leaving customers irritated. There have been many instances where customers would ask us "where's the staff".

advice: Please fix your training process and set realistic goals for personnel.  Also, numerous employees use their work from home overtime to obtain their daily goals and sit around during the day on their devices but no one seems to care because goals are met.  Unfortunately you are paying time a premium because of people doing this.
pros: Salary was OK and you can leave your work at work if you choose to do so.
cons: So much emphasis on production that quality suffers.  An employee can surpass their goals  on one day and have to send their manager an email the next if goals are not achieved.  Unfortunately not all work is equal but the daily goal is always the same.  Training is all over the place and procedures change too frequently.  OVERTIME IS EXPECTED and this is OK if you want it.  I was told that if I wanted to increase my rating that I needed to work overtime.

advice: they need to treat every employee like they matter,  to be with them and encourage them along the way.  This  has been the case in most every instance.   need to have open door policy and make themselves available on the floor
pros: This is a company I have worked for 24 years , this was due to the management staff, they were great in showing a great example on how to be.  The training was tremendous and I was able to pass this down to my advisors that reported to me.  This company has grown a  lot in the over 100 years they have been in business.  I have been compensated very well every year,  Based on my performance,  this was very encouraging to jump into the next year with a good sense of pride.
cons: as in anywhere you work you are going to have people who did not get along,  I felt our HR department was no quick to get in the issue and help resolve

summary:
Document Review Senior Specialist II
Customer Service Specialist
National Subpoena Processing
advice:
If you truly want your employees to be “customer obsessed”, don’t put time constraints on them.  Each customers situation is different and some take longer to resolve than others.  Don’t make your employees RUSH through a call trying to meet a certain quota or number that you think it should be done in. That’s no way to be customer obsessed. 

Also, don’t treat your employees like they’re just a Standard ID. Recognize those who are truly committed.
pros: Good healthcare coverage.  Three weeks vacation your first year, plus sick time, personal days, and paid holidays. Most of the mid-line managers do really care about their staff.
cons: They want you to be “customer obsesses”, but expect you to do it in a minimal amount of time. This doesn’t make the customer feel like you really care about their circumstance. Weed out the managers who only care about meeting a number and advancing their own career, but pretend to care about their staff.

summary: Perfect fit: driven by money, need your ego pet, enjoy constant banter with people
pros: People. Salary. If you're passionate about finance, endless opportunities for networking and growth.
cons: Morning meetings were painful. Attendance was at an all-time low when I quit. The job itself was very operational and mind-numbing. 75% of daily duties require virtually no thought. As an analyst, you're expected to 'show face' and work evenings. While there were some nights my workload demanded the longer hours, there were more times I was there to kill time, which I found infuriating. If you're extremely productive, he/she is condemned for not having enough on their plate. If you're not, he/she is praised for working hard into the night. Flawed system. Lose-lose from my perspective. After 6 months,  most analysts were generally annoyed and unless absolutely necessary, nobody really had each other's back in balancing workload during busy seasons. I can't blame them. Large egos in VP+ roles. Hard to take myself seriously in PB.

cons: The team leaders and other management does not know how how to manage their employees in the call center.  Higher management needs to train their team leaders and floor management on how to treat the emplyees with fairness.
