pros: The people are amazing and it was an enjoyable and interesting place to work. Lots of opportunity for movement across departments and functions. My direct leaders were focused on helping develop my skills and assigning me projects that kept me challenged and engaged.
cons: If you start in an entry to mid level role and move up you are not compensated very well. You will receive your annual performance increases of roughly 1-2% but rarely will you get a "promotional" raise. I had 5 promotions in 4 years and made significantly less than my peers.

summary: Great place to work -  for the next 60 days
advice: Take some time to figure out what you've purchased before dismantling acquired companies and pooping thousands into the unemployment line...three or four thousand jobs will disappear in Seattle almost overnight.  WaMu was a company with a lot of really talented people but some really bad leadership.  You're missing an opportunity here.
pros: Hmmm....not sure what the best reasons to work for JPMC are - as they recently gobbled up my bank, Washington Mutual, and then laid me off (with several thousand of my close friends).  I would however, give a gold star to their process for laying people off....they're very professional, reasonably generous, and very efficient.  They've obviously done this many times before and perfected the process of takeovers....and I'm not being a smart-ass when I say this.  A lot of companies are pretty ugly in this department.
cons: I can't really say anything bad, other than the fact I'm soon to be unemployed.

summary: High stress call center, but rewarding
advice: Reconsider deskilling your workforce. Having specialists in each of the areas of annuities, securities, mutual funds, retirement plans, tax information is better than a department full of average-knowledge associates.
pros: I was pleased with the amount of training that went into each associate's time in the inbound call center. Weekly training sessions to maintain knowledge base were crucial. Peer training kept us on our toes with the ever changing regulatory environment. Fast paced and high stress, the top performers were well-rewarded.
cons: Rigid time schedules in the call center meant it was difficult to get time off for personal needs. Tax season stretched from mid-November through mid-May and it was nearly impossible to get time off as a result. As departments decreased in size, associates picked up more knowledge and responsibility, which resulted in a general de-specialization/deskilling that I personally felt hurt promotion opportunities. Incentive programs were mismatched. The entire department could meet or exceed their expectations, but only the top 25% would receive bonuses.

advice: The culture of an organization goes a long way with employees. If employees know that management does not care about employees and is centrally profit driven, the relationship doesn't work.
pros: Great company name to have on your resume. Co-workers are pretty good, you just have to really be outgoing and speak to people, as many employees keep a very low and quiet profile as to not bring attention to themselves. Good stock purchasing program!
cons: If you accept a position at Chase, the most important thing to remember is to NEVER take any type of FMLA. Those who use this benefit WILL LOSE THEIR JOB!! The downtown mortgage center in Cleveland, OH is notorious for taking this action. This means that if you are pregnant and are taking leave, your should look for another job while you are on leave. If you have a health problem that takes you out of work for more than one week...find another job while you are out. If you return to work, you will undergo a systematic process to phase you out of the organization. Please do not be fooled by what management tells you, your job is being eliminated!

advice: Empower junior employees more - all of the company's assets are the employees, need to encourage and value the employees. Also, J.P. Morgan is notorious for being the last company on the street to "match" other bank offers - they were the last to raise salaries, bonus ranges, and other perks (dinner, travel, etc.) and only did so because they were forced to. It is pretty obvious that JP didn't want to make our lives better.
pros:
Great opportunities present themselves after completing the Associate or the Analyst program.
Free dinner on weekdays and weekends plus travel.
cons: Investment banking is a glorified broker role. Very little actual value added analysis is conducted or unique thoughts generated. People just care about getting deals completed. Junior people's thoughts and recommendations are not valued at all - want you to just get the work assigned to you completed quickly. The pay for actual hours worked is very little, probably get more money per hour working at a restaurant or bar.

summary: A solid and valuable company to work for.
advice: Just because you're in banking doesn't mean your offices need to be so darn boring looking! I would have loved to have seen a more modern, innovative, social, and open work set up in the offices as opposed to the outdated land of gray cubicles and 80's era artwork.
pros:
-Training was very organized and thorough
-Had great extracurricular programs for networking and community involvement
-Competitive pay and benefits
-Lots of room for lateral movement into other areas of the company
-Overall a great company to have had on my resume to get to that next step in my career.
cons:
-Because company is so big, getting a good manager is hit or miss, much like going to a large university, some will be awesome, some not so much.
-Office environment is very corporate and traditional, bordering on impersonal and lacking human element, though if you're in banking one should expect this anyway.
-New and innovative ideas will likely go unnoticed as the company is pretty set in its ways.

summary: The ups and downs of being a Wamulian
advice: Respect your employees enough to tell them the truth and take responsibility for you actions.
pros: Benefits are very competitive and affordable.  The employee portion is based on your salary so the higher your salary the more you contribute to the benefit package.  This is very helpful for lower level employees who are not paid as much.  The atmosphere at Wamu was very pleasant and it was an enjoyable place to work, but as pressure increased to push through loans the feeling became more of a sweatshop than a bank.
cons: There is a lack of communication.  Even during the time when we knew the company was going under, the official communications we recieved still stated we were in a strong  position and to provide that information to customers as well. To continue to encourage employee participation in stock plans that were doomed to failure is gross negligence on the part of the company's leadership

summary: Good pay and benefits, not so good work-life balance.
advice: -- Tone down the IT Risk Management stuff.  It's nearly impossible to get things done sometimes when you don't have the tools or access you need to do what needs done.
pros:
-- Good pay and starting vacation time.  The benefits as a whole are good.
-- They allow and encourage internal mobility as well.
cons:
-- Way too much beuracracy in the IT space.  Most projects that impact several groups will end up getting delayed because one or more teams end up stumbling over some red tape.
-- Work-life balance is not so good.  If it comes to it, you really have to just put your foot down and let them know you're unwilling to put in the hours demanded, or else your personal life can suffer.
-- In some departments, the offshore development model is very effective.  Keep in mind that if this is in place, you will be doing almost 0% coding and will lose some real job marketability.

advice: Upper management is almost certainly not reading Glassdoor, waste of time.
pros:
A multinational behemoth with a diverse range of opportunities and challenges to tackle, JPMorgan touches almost all financial services domains, so there ought to be someone doing something you are interested in, from technology to strategy to product development to operations to compliance. 

Most managing directors are well-rounded and interested in identifying and developing talent for their organizations. 

Once on board, it's imperative to actively grow your network because paths will cross unexpectedly.
cons:
JPMorgan is similar to what Winston Churchill said about the US during WWII, in that they "will do the right thing in the end, but only after they have exhausted all other options." 

From a cultural standpoint, the bank is conservative, so radical changes will take time to implement and low ranking staff will see the need long before steps are taken by senior management to implement the strategy, usually after the competition has tried and failed.

summary: Very relaxed atmosphere to work in.
advice: I was say, at least from my perspective, please keep up the great work when communicating with your employees and giving feedback.  This is one of the things that made me absolutely love working for JP Morgan.
pros: Very relaxed atmosphere to work in.  The management is focused on helping you improve your career and build experiences that will take you to your next level.  All three managers I had the privilege to work with had been extremely helpful in communicating what they needed from me and helped me along during my stay there.  The work can be slow sometimes but you can almost expect to work 40 hours a week and go back to your family on a regularly basis.
cons: As mentioned above, the work can be slow at times and you find yourself looking for things to do.  This can be a beneficial thing when trying to balance work and personal life.

summary: Big company with a lot going on, can move internally.  Very very bureaucract to the point of not being able to move.
advice: Trust your IT employees and let them work!  I understand regulations and government intervention and I don't believe it has to be this way.
pros: Salary and Benefits very good.  The company seems to be supportive of internal transfers.  The federal government has declared them too big to let fail.
cons: This only applies to IT because I believe it's very different from the rest of the company.  They are at least 10 years behind in technology.  If you like staying up with technology then stay away.  The bureaucracy is absolutely incredible.  IT workers don't have access to the tools they need to do their job and can't access systems to do their jobs.  10 years ago I estimated that Chase required 10 IT workers to do the work of 1.  Today I would estimate it to be around 20 to 1.  IT workers are not trusted to do anything.  IT employees act out in passive aggressive ways to get out their frustrations.  Technical people do not stay.

summary: Great People working for not so great management.
advice: Please pay people the respect they deserve. Do no treat them like "Object" and start treating them like "People".
pros:
I have worked at JPMorgan for over 10 years and in different LOB's and a few things are consistent across the board. 

- Lot of benefits right off the bat.
- Lot of room for growth & mobility options. 
- Great colleagues, hard working and exceptional bunch of resources .. it was fun to work on every single team.
cons:
- Leadership do not care about talent and skill retention. 
- work life balance is non-existent as they heavily rely on you if you are SME. Leadership do not give you resource to train or help out. 
- The pay could be better. past 5 years the pay increase did not even meet the rise in living standards which I think is ridiculous for the top ranking bank making billions in profit.

advice: Expand the training for online services.
pros: The benefits, paid time off, and resources to perform the job were good things about this company. Day consisted of taking inbound calls to assist customers with questions on their checking/savings accounts. Things such as: balances, fees, times & dates for when a transaction occurred. Any disputes would be transferred over to anothe department. Lunches were an hour long and there was a cafeteria that served food. There's a track that surrounds the call center floor to promote health and exercise. Also a daycare, quiet room and nurse's office are in the building as well. 10% shift differential for working anytime your shift started at 10am or later.
cons: High call volume and having to deal with a lot of angry customers. Working weekends (typically 1 weekend day) and working as late as 11pm. Training for the online portion of the job could have been a lot better by being hands on & longer than a week.

advice: Great job! Keep up the good work.
pros: I was at JPM for over 10 years and then they decided to close down our EFS group and get out of the EBT business. They notified us of this decision well over a year before the layoffs started in our department, which was very much appreciated. This was a great company to work for and the people in my department were hard working and professional. JPM always expected a lot out of you but they paid well, had good insurance, gave raises and bonuses.
cons: Long hours and working while on vacation. Management never "made" me do this it was part of the job. My entire team always worked non-stop to meet deadlines on our numerous projects. Not complaining, it is just the way it is at JPM. They do let you manage your own time and treat you like the working professional that they hired.

advice: Sometimes just  being the best isn't good enough.  You actually have to care!!!
pros: #1 bank in the country,  smart and professional co-workers.
cons: Just a number, won't consider tenure, heavily bureaucratic, completely hypocritical when it comes to the firms own business practices and the reflection of that on company culture.  To clarify,  if the firm does something wrong as far as compliance or conducts unfair trade practices or conducts illegal business activities outside regulatory framework, they are simply reprimanded and fined heavily( which they can afford) or they lawyer their way out.  Proof of this is  the roughly 18B spent in legal fees since 2008 and roughly 10B in regulatory fines they have doled out.  Unfortunately, they do not extend those same curtsies to their employees and most employees if they disagree, with a internal decision or forced resignation or otherwise, they general don't have the means to fight back at them in court.

advice: More solid pay for employees to reduce turnover and increase customer satisfaction.
pros: Company really cares about its employees at the corporate level.  Sometimes this gets lost at the middle management level.  Stellar  benefits, great training, innovative and top notch tech. great communication.  JPM knows how to do everything correctly (rules & regs) and the company is very ethical.  Most managers are incredibly respectful of their employees.  I had some of the best managers in my career at Chase.
cons: Very high turnover across all lines of business.  From tellers to bankers, advisors, mlo, managers, there is constant employee turnover and the clients become quite displeased, making it difficult to earn their trust and share of wallet.  Customers consistently complain about the turnover.  Benefits are great, but pay is one of the lowest in the industry.

advice: Management can't be helped.
pros:
Love the work and using tools.
A hands on type of job.
Cool knowledge of building and use of tools.
Loved reading and building these trucks
cons: 2022 the management and select few supervisors all work together against employees, like it's a game. Employees 3+years original pay were just over .50 then the new hires. Sexual harassment cases. Allowing fraudulent documents from employees. Employee favoritism. Shortages on parts to make a body or tools. Carelessness of employees knowledge when hired in. Overworked knowledgeable workers. Negative feedback constantly from Management. Blame the employees for overtime. This plant is run by a narcissistic management. Supervisors are liers, careless, and lazy. Numbers are more important than quality. We appreciate the work this company wants and the dream of building but this plant is crooked with poor management. Communication or a big cleanup between supervisors and management needs to happen. Improper business. We can't address an issue if management is friends with HR. What happened to pride in the work? Success is lead by leaders, not tyrants. We are not slaves.

advice: There's just so far you can take the practice of making employees work like machines and trying to see how much mileage you can get from them.  Eventually, financial firms need both a brain and a heart to be able to achieve customer loyalty,  and of course employee loyalty.  At present all JPMC employees are perfect mercenaries and everyone in the firm knows it.
pros: Large company has large amount of resources to allocate; can distribute risk internationally; company is genuinely interested in audit compliance and following the rules
cons: Corporate culture is cold and prickly.  Those who succeed without ruffling the feathers of others are exhaulted publically.  All the others are treated as non-entities.  This firm systematically identifies what it feels are it's "bottom 20%" performing employees and finds ways to cut them.  The "bottom 20%" are in fact just the ones that management simply does not like for one reason or another.  Thus, this practice (supposedly recommended directly by way of consultation by Jack Welch) is just a way to justify their subjective prejudices.

summary: Mostly great people at lower levels, but as you move up the organization, politics and self-importance start to dominate
advice: Think about this, you continue to wring salary, benefits, work-life balance, education from employees. Then you move jobs off-shore. What is the logical outcome of this path? Using Chinese prisoners to do your work? Then how do you get a cost savings after that?
pros:
The people in our dept had all worked together for years and mostly we considered each other friends. 

The pay was good and the vacation (4 weeks + sick time!) was excellent (not sure if this is true any more).

Some opportunity to learn new technology.

Decent internal communication about industry events, internal policy, but not really supported by *my* line management.
cons:
Continuing pressure to do more with less at some point leads to completely unrealistic situations. 

World-wide organization with 100,000+ employees just too big.

Death-march projects. Everyone I knew (near the end, before our dept was moved to another state), had the *opportunity* to work 80 hr weeks for months on end, including a few 24 hr days on the weekends. Is that management?

summary: If you are considering this job, please read this before you apply
advice: Don't let the position get to your head, Don't be cynical, and actually listen to what your reps are saying, and considering the fact you all are salaried, give the reps paid time to get off early on Christmas and New Years. they are who bring the company clients and money.
pros: Good Work Environment, reps are friendly, that's about it
cons: 1) Quickly becoming customer service based, yet the position is for POTENTIAL customers. 2) Mass Politics, if you like to suck up to management, then this is for you. 3) Lack of direction, yet you are under the leadership of directors who just listen to corporate. 4) Vacations and Holidays seem nice, and while you get off on eve's (Christmas and New Years), they expect you to use your own time and/or go unpaid. 5) Call Volume vs. off the phone activity,  the volume is increasing exponentially, and management considers seasonal holiday decorations more important. 6) Shift changes. don't expect get your shift changed unless you have an extenuating circumstance or you can revisit #2.

advice: You pay more to hire external people instead of rewarding those who have remained loyal to the firm and who have longevity.
pros: Brilliant people are working there
cons: The annual salary increases/bonuses are a joke. Even when it’s an “up” year for the firm, employees got the same story that the bonus pools were smaller and it was a tough year - never expect a major bump in salary or bonus - even on promotion years.

summary: It was the best job….until it wasnt
advice:
Where their is smoke their is fire. If you have multiple employees reporting an employee the odds are good that employee is doing what he is not supposed to.
Overall Chase was awesome. It was only in the last 12 months of my employment with everything we were asked to do along with the Covid lending guidelines, reduction in people working it just became impossible. To do what was necessary to maintain much less increase my production and manage the additional work life balance of kids, online school and  everything else Covid was dealing out had to make changes.
pros:
Unlimited leads
Great co-workers
Great Benefits
They take care of their employees
cons:
Constant push to cross sell investment and banking products yet received very little or no compensation.
Continually adjusted down bps on loans
CSAT bonus is based off overall results so even if customer gives you a 10 but overall an 8 it’s a fail. 
System updates are always done the last week of the month and if the system issues keep a loan from closing and in turn effects your tier…to bad for you.

summary: Little boys club of low moral, zero family value employees
advice:
Perhaps I would have a different view of JPM if I hadn't joined the Global Risk Middle Office.

JPM= Just People Meeting....all VPs do all day is sit behind closed doors talking about nothing...they view the departments as their fiefdoms and act like they are Managing Directors.

I never felt that my life outside of work was of any value...god forbid you are a married male and only working 50 hours per week (and throw in a 3 hour total daily commute).
pros:
- Name recognition of working in the IB of JP Morgan
- Lots of training available 
- Employee discounts
cons:
- JP Morgan comes first before anything in your life!
- Employees who work 9-6:30 or 10-7 are viewed as 'harder working' and 'more valuable' than someone who works 8-6.
- Forced rankings: doesn't matter if your team has two people or 25...of course this is a popularity and pissing contest
- Extremely expensive health benefits (good coverage, but $$$$$$)
- Lack of admins and supplies: you never knew who to call if there was a problem or need for the department

advice: Hire a legitimate consulting group to come in and determine re-organization needs.  Have the consulting groups reduce redundancies - there are numerous redundancies and lots of waste (labor-cost wise).  Have management re-apply for their jobs.  Move out of the DE locations -  you get what you pay for remaining in a weak talent pool.
pros: Reputable name and people outside of banking seem to hold it to high esteem because it's the biggest bank.
cons: Disorganization - Everything changes every week and managers lack serious competency; you cannot seek their expertise (b/c they lack any).  Loyalty/Compensation- Management will try to low-ball individuals over their salary and have employees perform management functions without any extra pay.  Additionally, the pay is below the industry average.  Location- Newark and Wilmington, DE are less than desirable and living in a major metropolitan city (i.e., Philadelphia) is unrealistic now that the 495 is shut down.  Talent pool- very weak in the DE market and new employees are getting paid higher wages b/c of this, causing discontent among the workers who have been their longer and possess a higher skill-set.  Worker morale- Management presses for unrealistic numbers and there are rumors of/actual layoffs every month or two.

summary: They treat their employees with respect and they try to always keep you employed if a sitution happens
advice:
I miss working for Chase and I would love to come back. Customer Focus is what it is all about and what is most important and without the borrowers no one would be there... I think Chase has a great training class and train well. Many opportunities to grow. I made it through many layoffs but this last one I didn't make it and I feel it was because I was sick however I am better and miss what I don't have. 
Thank you Chase for giving me a wonderful opportunity to grow and learn more about mortgages. I was able to take care of my family and you pay your employees well.   

Thank you Donna Harvey
pros: I love that Chase takes care of their employees, Don't discriminate
cons: I had a manager who didn't respect your privacy when you call out for a personal reason. Everyone knew but the reason she told was not even why I was out but tried to embarrase me.

advice: Look at the culture in technology. It is in decline. People who treat analytics like an IT project don't know how to do analytics. Consider allowing remote work and other soft benefits. You are not competitive in recruiting technology talent because you don't invest in people.
pros:
1. Company is doing well
2. Health Insurance and MRA funds good plan especially for lower employee grades
3. Having JPMorgan on your resume opens doors
4. I had good equipment and technology.
cons:
1. Politically correct culture 
2. Too many middle managers (VP, ED, MD) are not good at their jobs especially in technology, HR, and other backoffice areas. There are exceptions of course!
3. Data security and access protocol is done in a way that it restricts work but does not necessarily make the firm safer. Just more hoops to jump through.
4. Hierarchical power structure. Being in New York City is an advantage to an employee even though most are located elsewhere.
5. Chase's actions suggest they don't really care about their exempt employees especially at the 601/602 grade (entry manager and just below).

summary: Job Satisfaction Depends Primarily on Managemet
advice: The vision at the top becomes warped at the middle-management level. The big picture doesn't translate well because the accountability measures are designed to quantify short-term customer acquisitions rather than long-term relationship growth.
pros: When working under a supportive manager who backed me, gave me some autonomy, listened to my concerns, and found opportunities to sing my praises, this company was awesome. I found myself promoting from a banker to an SBS in a few months, from an SBS to a new-build in a year, and into the BMT program a year after that. Each of those advancement opportunities had been catalyzed my respective manager.
cons: When working under an unsupportive manager, this company was unbearable. I had to relocate and fell under a new manager's umbrella. The company is so big that, without a manager who is interested in proactively marketing you for advancement opportunities, you can easily be passed up for positions that you're qualified for.

summary: Great company for a long term career
pros: J.P. Morgan is a awesome company to work for.  The benefits are great and there is strong push towards diversity and culture making a good atmosphere for employees.  There are thorough training programs put into place so regardless which role you take you will feel ready and capable to perform your duties.  There are a lot of opportunities within the company and the company is always hiring; you will never feel "stuck" in any position.  This company is also very stable and growing; lay-offs or job cuts are quite rare.
cons: Although the benefits are great, compensation is low compared to competitors.  Raises are minimal and bonuses are non-existent in some departments.  It also appears that the company prefers to hire externally rather than promote internal employees so moving around can sometimes be challenging.

summary: Solid place to work with great internal mobility
advice: Systems/training, a company our size should have better training simulators on the systems we actually utilize.  Training has been a series of lesson followed by very little drop in the deep end and swim (taking live calls) and saying you are good to go.  Proper training simulators (off line programs with full mock databases) would increase new hire confidence and reduce procedural and regulatory mistakes early on
pros:
-There is a lot of opportunity to move within the organization as long as you are willing to put in the work and look for it
-Very inclusive work environment
-Knowing I work for a company with a lot of great values
-Benefits with multiple health plans, psychiatry, paternal leave, legal help etc
cons:
-They pay less than many of their competitors
-As with most careers, your enjoyment will hinge on the people you work with (especially boss)
-Bonuses are small, but made directly to 401k (so good for tax purposes)

summary: Hard work to build a good foundation.
advice: More perks!
pros: Its a great company to work for.  They really give you great opportunities to move up and grow.  The training is thorough, and prepares you not only for the job, but for jobs down the road.  The reputation of the firm is well respected.  The positions are competitive.  People are smart and respectful.  Everyone works with a team approach.  There is no overbearing hierarchy with management.  Open discussion of issues are encouraged.  Everyone is very approachable and friendly.  The management works hard so you are naturally motivated to work hard as well.  Generally, I am very happy here at JP Morgan.
cons: Long hours.  Long hours. Long hours.  No vacation time. No vacation time. No vacation time.  The work could be grueling and mind numbing.  You sit and stare at a computer screen for 12-14 hours a day.

summary: Chase, a great stable company to work for.
advice: Run it like you own it.  Thats about it.  It has so much potential that it's silly.  I can't stand for management upheaveal, but this company needs it.
pros: Their benefits are world class.  I love the bank.  I wouldn't trade my experience for the world.  The culture is world class.  I couldnt say more about how it's managed etc.  Lots of great friendships were had here.  And for that I wouldn't trade my experience for anything in the world.
cons: I hate them.  They laid me off when I was having some solid months.  It seems that they are more interested in the outside world.  I loved the welcome calls and the information provided on them.  It was a unique enviornment.  I must say that it was fun as I loved the comraderie accoatied with the organization.  It was unique.

summary: So much red tape, it's amazing anything gets done.
advice: Stick with guidelines once socialized.  Stop relying so much on consultants.
pros: You can say you work at JPM Chase.  Benefits are good.  People are generally good, but sometimes not motivated.
cons: Red tape, beauracracy, change is slow, slow, slow.  Massive paperwork required and 10-15 signatures required to get a simple change put in production.  Extremely stifling for someone who is results-driven, especially having come from a high-caliber shop.  Working off a lap top as opposed to a workstation is another horrible experience.  Frequent re- orgs.  Management outlines one policy, and several months later said manager is no longer at jpm.  Typical response to an outage is: 1) freeze on changes for an arbitrary period of time.  2) have endless meetings (on a call, almost never in person) 3) reveal post-mortem for which the action item is to add another signature to any change.

summary: Where's the Forrest?  All these trees are in the way!
advice:
Fear stifles good ideas from being shared.
A genius working for JPMC would retire an associate.
Don't hire the disabled to do jobs their disabilities prevent them from succeeding at.
Fear has turned the organization into a bunch of "yes men".
Have an open door for things other than compliance issues.
Your people really only cares about their bonuses.
Being a senior manager doesn't mean your ideas are good by definition.
pros:
Great benefits.
To big to fail. 
Vision for change. 
Many good rank and file people. 
Numerous Opportunities. 
Every corporate culture is in there somewhere.
Once your established your financially set.
cons:
Inconsistent team management.
Profits transcend everything.
Pay and responsibilities don't align.
Death marches are a way of life.
Actual change is compliance driven.
Daily experience totally depends on who you work for.
Senior management clueless on how things actually work.
Priority is driven by what senior management is scrutinizing.
Ethics are preached but only really count if there is financial risk.
ADA is preached not practiced.

summary: Very smart people don't always make very smart leaders....
advice:
- A large part of incentive compensation for MD's should be based on the employee satisfaction rating for his/her group.
- You have the vision to fund strategic projects; have the business sense to staff them with qualified resources, not co-opted subject matter experts.
pros: The firm has demonstrated thought leadership across all facets of  the financial services sector - ranging from the calm reasoning of Jamie Dimon during the financial crisis, to the VP's and ED's providing daily leadership in industry organizations, committees and discussion panels.
cons:
- Despite the mantra from the CEO that the employees are the most important asset of the bank, that is not the reality in the bank.  There is a pervasive culture of fear.  
- Strategic programs / tactical resourcing.
- Incredible amount of time and effort expended by MD's managing up the chain.
- Failure to deliver at the MD level is often rewarded with promotion.

summary: great benefits but no work/life balance
advice: branch manager refuses to work weekends however, rest of staff is required to. if you work part time, be prepared to not have 2 days off in a row and/or to work 6 days a week for a few hours each day.  branch manager will promise you anything to get you to take a job.  pay is not great and you can make more money waitressing and still get full benefits.
pros: The health benefits, retirement, and time off are amazing.
cons: Constantly short staffed. Schedule changes weekly with very little consistency. no work/life balance. Customers are exceptionally grumpy because of long wait times to work with bankers in the branch. Bankers are coached to "change their mindset" when customers are yelling at them and to be sympathetic and understanding. Zero support is given by managers as they will not support staff when a customer is unhappy. Customer satisfaction surveys are given way too much importance.

advice: Leadership has no idea what they’re doing, and you will continue to be short-staffed while losing talented people who are becoming aware of their worth.
pros:
Benefits
PTO received as soon as you start. No accrual.
cons:
* Micromanagement - You have to clock in on at least 2 different systems that track your every move. Need to go to the restroom? You better hope it doesn’t take too long cuz it’ll be reflected on you not getting a perfect conformance score. 
* Incompetence - Leadership has no idea what’s going on, and their ineptitude leads to departmental failures which leads to the figureheads demanding mandatory overtime from workers who steadily produce and maintain quality work. 
Training is either non-existent or inadequate, yet you’re expected to be at 100% with zero errors at all time even though there s either no guidelines for your function, or your superior has no idea how your function works.
* No sense of Proactive-ness - you can bring up potential problems again and again. Doesn’t matter. It won’t be heard until things completely fall apart, and you’re told you have to give up your work-life balance to.

summary: Not impressed with how Home Lending business is being ran.
advice: Listen to employees more.  It seems since the Wamu merger, many top executives of JPMC were replaced by Wamu execs..doesn't make much sense to me.
pros: Decent benefits, good vacation time 20+ days, very flexible work schedule.  Generally work place is very casual.  There are opprotunities to move jobs however, pay increase is not an option.  So ask for alot when you come in otherwise you are stuck.  Once your in, your have to do alot to get let go.
cons: No Pay increase when moving within company.  Many groups doing the same job, even though this is pointed out..no one cares.  I would say there is a lot of waste that could be eliminated though, most of the time, people doing mundane tasks are hidden in the hierarchy.  Management doesn't listen to lower level employees.

summary: we work hard for our money, but there are good benefits.
advice: Have float relief people for retail. Especially in small branches, if one person is sick or on vacation it is too hard on everyone else. It's not okay to not allow someone sick time or make them feel bad about taking it because there is NO ONE else.
pros: Chase has good medical and retirement plans even for part-time employees. Plus they have backup childcare for employees which you pay based of your earnings.
cons: There is always turn around because they aren't allowed to staff enough for the hours and clients to be serviced. It burns people out. Average time employees stay is probably 9months to 5 years. I know very few who have stayed consecutively longer than that. It is also hard to change sectors in the company. if you start in retail you will most likely stay there forever.

summary: Call center is the fast food of mortgage lending.
advice: Strive to keep your talented people in positions that can better train the waves of new hires that surge into the company.
pros: The company has great name recognition with new customers and has a ton of current clients to market.  Their marketing efforts always had the phone ringing with someone on the other end of the line.  The income potential was six figures as long as you were quick and a talented sales person.
cons: The support teams of processing and underwriting were terribly slow at getting loans cleared to close.  Very frustrating to have you client waiting for months in order to close their loan, while the local broker in town was closing loans in 30 days or less.  The rates and fees are not negotiable and sometimes difficult to pitch to a non-Chase customer.

advice: Do what you say you will do  and try to be more consistent. During a job offer, if you claim a rep will get study time on the clock, you should do that. Also it is unfair that some people have 30 days to study for the 7 and some have 6 months. Also, 30 minute lunches just dont do it for most A few of the team leads and managers are extremely condescending in your Chicago location.
pros: opportunity to earn a series 7 and series 63.
cons: Constant high call volume, was a 45 minute lunch but reduced to 30. Was told would have time to study on the job for series 7, but once hired they did not allow for it. You work with about 13 different programs while on the phone with a client with very little training and very few people to reach out to. Sometimes a client will hold up to 20 minutes while waiting for help, but the time that a customer is on the phone is measured. This is a modern day sweat shop with very little recognition, mediocre pay, and sub standard training.

summary: Industry's gold-standard of service and sophisticated advice, tarnished by conflict of interest & employee intimidation.
advice: Take the high road and resolve the conflicts.  Be a leader once again and this time, save the financial system from this fatal flaw.  Jamie, you're the only one capable of pulling it off.
pros: Culture of excellence and expertise second to none.  Brilliant CEO whose work ethic, style, and confidence shines through to the front office, providing the ultimate model for those managers willing and capable of passing it on.
cons: Massive corporate arrogance.  Management by deception, vagueness, and manipulation by many front-line managers and practice leaders (many are wonderful too).  Rampant conflicts of interest.  Private clients and client advisors are used by senior mgmt as tools and liquidity sources for I.B./CorpBank/CommBank deals.  Lots of rhetoric with weak investment results.  Independent thinking is squashed and independent thinkers are defamed.

summary: Got a long way to go
advice: Reduce beaurecracy, promote from within, offer better pay, help people advance in their career
pros: Benefits are fairly good. Time off is good. Work life balance is good. People are nice. Brand name is good. We are among the last ones remaining which means the company is being managed well from a risk management and financial perspective. Some training opportunities (e.g. preparing for CFA) are funded. Generous number of days off - 22, sick days - 6.
cons: Culture does not promote from within, beaurecracy, pay is low compared with other similar types of firms, opportunities for career advancement are limited. Any move within the company is at the same level and same salary thereby decreasing the motivation. Career advancement is pretty limited unless you have the right contacts. People are not empowered enough to take decisions. There are several old school managers who have their own way of doing things with no inputs from other people even if others have better ideas. Promotions and bonuses are subjective. No clear career planning is available. Titles and experience for people do not match.

summary: It doesn't pay to be a high performer
advice: Reward your high performers for being high performers.  If you don't do this then they will leave and you have to hire new people that require training.  It blows my mind that the company and it's managers would rather spend money to train people instead of just taking that same money and paying their existing employees more.  People that feel taken care of will work harder than those that don't.
pros: Excellent work life balance in IT.
cons: Poor compensation increases.  Only way to get paid is to BEG or leave and come back a year later.  They pay people coming in off the street more than those who establish a career there.  Strange if you ask me.

advice: This is to corporate (regional directors and higher) Look at the eye opening success of the television show 'Undercover boss '- hide your identity and work a week (or longer) in the sales force at the branch level.
pros: Education is continual, cutting edge compliance with BSA and AML is second to none, upward growth potential is present yet limited by available slots, benefits package, sales training is excellent
cons: Low base salary, low incentive caps, low annual bonus, disconnect between policy makers and boots on the ground workforce, customer satisfaction is failing because of short staffed branches -- hidden by attempt to get 'old dogs'(customers) to learn new tricks in 'self service adoption' by promoting a new 'advice center' model. Customers want someone to talk with - not a computer to punch.

advice: The technology is state of the art but the bureaucratics are horrible.  There is so much turnover that the mortgage department feels like a training center. The department needs to learn how to treat their employees better which will help with turnover  and retaining good talent. The company should also review the pay of employees as there are big variances between employees and how Chase pays compared to competition. There is a reason why the top talent does not work at this location.
pros: Good benefits, good technology.  Well known company with the corporate environment. The co-workers made for a fun environment. Good work life balance and relatively flexible with vacations.  Great training program. A good place to learn.
cons: Very bureaucratic. Top performers are not recognized and the pay is well below average. They find ways to take away potential bonus if you make an error. Expected output with no errors are not very reasonable. There is a good amount of turnover.   The company has trouble recruiting and holding on to top talent in the mortgage department.

summary: Ok pay, good benefits and good opportunities for growth in the company if willing to jump around
advice:
Don't pass rules across the company that will affect the bottom line of individual departments.  Allow for advice from departmental management to be taken into consideration to take each department as a case by case basis for how they should operate.
More competitive pay will lower turnover rate.
pros:
Pension Plan
5% 401k Matching
Great Vacation benefits
Decent pay
Reputable company
Friendly professional culture.
cons:
Don't compete for pay as much with other Banks and the Tech industry because they're the leading bank in the world.
Enforced blanket rules across the company when each department is like a different company in and of itself.  Causes a lot of red tape and problems with efficiency and waste in funding.
Medium-high employment turnover rate.  Not many young workers willing to stay around when other companies are offering much more for their employment.

advice:
- Better training programs and networking events as "advertised" - don't make operations employees feel as obviously second class
- Transparency and hands-on program leaders 
- More competitive salary
pros:
- Working with people your own age and experience level (right our of school)
- Theoretical ability to see a host of operations opportunities within a large bank
cons:
- Salary is not very competitive and is based upon location in an illogical way (for example, NY offices make nearly $15k more because of cost of living, while Boston and Columbus, Ohio are considered to be on the same level)
- Lack of transparency into the rotational program
- Lack of interaction with others in the program
- Training at the beginning is a "one step forward, two steps back" mismanagement of time and resources

If you're a college senior deciding whether or not to take this job, please reach out to someone in the program at the office you would be working at to get their honest opinion. While there are opportunities at the end of the 2 year program, it will be a very long two years to cement your spot in the back office

advice: Focus on analyst retention
pros: Strong brand name on your resume. Phenomenal company resources for personal development (every morning starts with a 30 minute meeting on relevant topics relating to global markets/politics/macroeconomics).  Overall great place to start your career.
cons: Private Banking in general is a difficult industry to advance in as a young professional due to the high profile nature of clients.  Most successful MDs started their careers in other fields of finance and grew their network before becoming Private Bankers.  However, it is a great place to start your career if you are still unsure about the long term.  You will build soft skills that are pertinent to just about any finance job unless it involves financial modeling....technical skills lack in this role.  Additionally, another non-JPM specific con is that your experience is based entirely on your manager....

advice: Stop treating employees like children. Give us more flexibility and trust. Less micromanagement. Better technology to compete with the fin-tech companies like Sofi and Ally.
pros:
-PTO
-Food days if you like food
-Snack cart
-Good benefits
cons: The flexibility is awful. You are given a lot of vacation time. However it can be hard to get the days you want, because they limit the vacancy to 20% which makes it very difficult around holidays to take time off. They tell you to enjoy time off with your family around the holidays though they don't really give you the flexibility to do so. You will probably work Black Friday and Christmas Eve every year unless you have seniority. There is no flexibility to work from home either. I always thought they'd come around with that since so many other banks already have but they haven't. Hours are strict, you will not able to make your own and will most likely get crappy hours if you're just starting. There is also no career mobility in Milwaukee as it only houses home equity unless you want to work in a branch or move out of state.

advice: Listen to your staff.  Offer assistance to the staff to allow them to grow and move up with company.  Respect your staff and what they have done for the company.
pros: Excellent paid time off and benefits.  Opportunities to work within the community helping others.
cons: Not a lot of promotional opportunities unless you are in tight with management.   Management was clueless on what teams were completing, often times being pulled in different directions by their superiors.  There was a lot of secretive discussions not shared with the teams pertaining to their job stability.  Minimal assistance provided to grow with the company, often times leaving you stagnant in a position or shuffling from lateral position to another - regardless of your past experience and what you have brought to the company.  Low salary for for positions that demand higher pay in the competitive market.

advice: Put your employees first, always. There would literally be no Chase without the help of your employees.
pros: The pay was good and beyond exceptional benefits.
cons: Busy. There were days that I did not get a break. Always lines in the drive thru and lines out the door in the lobby. I was pregnant and didn't get a chance to eat sometimes and if I went to the bathroom it meant that people in the drive thru were going to be made when I got back. There was no way to keep customers happy with lines this long. When we were short staffed they would not shut down the drive thru or the inside, which didn't make sense to me because the customers were mad either way due to the lack of staffing, so why not shut the drive thru down to help your employees out. They were more concerned about their customers ratings than their employees. After maternity leave I decided not to go back to this place. It gives me anxiety to even think about it. Large turnover rate in my branch.

pros: It is easy to make an apointment because they are not busy.
cons: This bank that I worked for for over 20 years has lost its connection with the customer base. Chase is now about the bottom line and charges unreasonable fees to the everyday customer. Their focus has changed to the “elite” customers and Chase has lost touch with the everyday customer that represented 75% of the customer base at the branch In Brunswick,Ohio. I witnessed a loan officer refinance a mortgage with a family for a lower interest rate but the majority of the mortgage payment went to the interest., not the principal. This family made 15 years of payments and their mortgage balance was only reduced $10,000 in that 15 years of payments. Our recent changes in bank personnel are uncaring, impatient and rude and I have since left the company after 20 years of employment.

summary: Very disappointing, not what I expected from such a large organization.
advice: Management plays favorites and too worried about their own jobs to listen to their employees in the trenches. Too many chiefs, not enough indians. Stop being so bureacratic and do what is right for your employees and your department.
pros: Decent benefits, if you get a good manager you will enjoy your job. The facility is decent with a cafeteria but overpriced. Good retirement benefits.
cons: Management is very clickish and bureacratic. If you do not kiss the butt of the right person you will get no where in the company. Often times job postings are posted at one grade level, but once you apply they downgrade the job level, therefore there is no upward mobility, at least in pay; always a lateral move. Micro management runs rapint, employees are not respected enough to take ownership of their work. Recognition is cheap an unmeaningful, no real rewards or acknowledgement are given when it comes time for reveiws no matter how many kudos you rack up. I would strongly recommend not to work for this company, you are treated as just another number.

jobTitle: Personal Banker - Small Business Specialist - Manager On Duty
advice: Wake up.
pros: Very few. The people in my branch were fun, and it looks good on a resume. Otherwise, the grass really is greener on the other side.
cons:
Bankers are told by upper management (with 6 to 7 figure base salaries) that they don't understand why bankers are upset that their base salaries were frozen three years in a row.  Specifically, we were told that "I haven't gotten a base salary increase in years." 

Perhaps that would be comforting, if we got the perks and bonus package that she received.  The commission structure is constantly changing, and leaves bankers in smaller, slower branches facing decreases in pay. 

Moreover, Personal Bankers were told to direct all new accounts to Relationship Bankers, further hindering their opportunity to "decide their own raise" (how upper management justified not giving salary increases).  These bankers are also commonly scheduled as tellers, because the company continues to downsize branch staffs.

Middle management is constantly changing and downsizing, so the people responsible for promoting and hiring have no clue who even works for them. I was a Personal Banker and a Manager On Duty, helping run two branches, sometimes even helping at a third and a fourth, but got 0 support when I wanted to be promoted and compensated for the job I was already doing.

advice: Train everyone equally and that way, we will definitely sound and act like “one chase”. Every employee should be given an equal opportunity to grow latterly. That opportunity should not be based solely on one’s opinion.
pros:
Benefits 
Job security 
Environment aims to encourage Growth
Option to go to school
cons:
High turnover with management (employed since 2018) I’ve had 6 different managers. After a while, it begins to feel like employees are just numbers.

In the Fraud/ claims department, employees are not all trained the same. For example, when my group came for training, we were told that we would eventually be trained in compliance or maybe other up skills, (emm/ reso/ compliance/ aht and so on) however, that was not the case. 

We literally have tenured employees less trained than the newer. That’s not very organized in my opinion. Everyone should be trained and introduced to new things. Why bring in new employees and let other employees remain stagnant doing one skill? 

It comes down to the fact that it’s up to your managers discretion if you’re cross trained/ up skilled. 

Tricky when you’ve had 6 different managers, right?

summary: Not Mom and Dad’s House of Morgan
advice: Stop cutting incentive plans and putting more responsibilities on branch employees. Make it easier and transparent for good bankers to move up and if there is no opportunity to move up, pay them more to stay. You are sending people to school to then work for the competition because there is no where to grow in the branch level.
pros: You learn a lot about all areas of lending, business banking and investments if you apply yourself. Benefits are competitive. It’s a good place to start as a licensed securities professional. They are paying for schooling. Bank holidays are nice.
cons: No career growth once you reach private client banker unless you want to be a branch manager. Partner roles are near impossible to attain in Nashville market. Branches are understaffed, customers are relentless and unappreciative. Training is just power point slides, most of your coworkers cannot do the most basic duties of their job because they are thrown on the floor unprepared and untrained. Incentive plan has been cut every 6 months since I started with the firm before the pandemic.

advice: be more responsive to what your employees are telling you, we don't all drink the kool-aid, your teams are being stressed out because there is no staffing. Put more staff into the branches and get them more help!
pros: It's a large company so it has a lot of perks, full health, dental, vision, HSA, 401k both roth and traditional, employee stock purchase etc. Paid sick time, vacation time, and personal days. Reasonable hours since it's a bank and we get a lot of holidays off as well.
cons: Staffing model has changed a lot and the teams are getting smaller at the branch level which in turn is spreading the teams thinner and thinner. Which puts added stress on the teams especially if someone calls in. There is a lot more pressure now on the branch manager than before you are now the operation manager and the sales manager and  you do it all.

advice: Have a clear definition of what skillset and experience is needed to be promoted to the next level in positions (Associate to VP, etc). Reconsider work from home, as you lost a lot of experience and talent by changing that policy. Also, consider a few days work from home (3 days in office, 2 days wfh) for positions that able to as this is seen as a great benefit to employees this day in age.
pros: Maternity benefits were good. Health benefits are ok. Gained good experience working for them.
cons: Moved managers at least 6 times in two years and each manager had a different view of what is needed to be promoted to the next level. This meant everything you did to get to that next level was worthless when you were moved to the next manager. They changed their work from home policy and made it more difficult and more strict. Annual raise was minimal.

advice: Focus on People and do not treat them as commodities. Control the power grabs look into the ethical  violations and moral corruption among you senior leaders.
pros:
Company is huge so there are a lot of internal oppurtunities  to expand your career. Company also uses almost any kind of IT technology out there so if you are  a technologist there is ample oppurtunities. Corporate culture varies based on which LOB you are in,  drastic differences from fast paced to very relaxed environments based on which LOB / business unit you belong.
Company CEO is very dynamic and straight forward and projects a leadership role.
cons:
As with most companies this size there is a lot of nepotism  and old boys clubs.
Power plays constantly happening from NY, constant strategy changes of centralization of IT and then decentralization. Lots of bureaucracy and due to that bureacracy lots of middlemen paper pushers with power.

pros: Good benefits. The staff is fun to work with.
cons: Front line employees have not received a raise in four years. Keep on changing business model--one year have you constantly probe customers on very personal financial questions, ever if they sat with a banker a month earlier. After customers started to complain, this process discontinued. They next year they had bankers do everything for the customer. Then in my final year they decided to make the customer wait to see a banker, so the banker could keep up with the heavy load they placed on them. Chase has a more of a " chew you up and then spit you out attitude." They demand a lot out of their employees.  Each year they make it more difficult to reach you goal by having you reach more and paying you less in incentives. They micro-manage you to the extremes.

summary: JPM is a Great Place to Work
advice: Value employees more holistically.
pros:
They work very hard to maintain diversity and do things right by their employees. Effort is valued and a lot of work goes into evaluations in an effort to make things fair, yet reward achievement and excellence. If you are considered a top performer, you will be recognized. Manager are mandated to maintain a meritocracy. If you do what you are told to do quickly, things should be fine for you. 

Great leadership from top to bottom overall.
cons: Some managers aren’t great in administering the mandate that JPM has given. There is also a very strict definition of what success is based on the JPM culture. If you fall outside that definition in any way, you will be held back. So while it is a meritocracy, there are plenty of times where certain merits are ignored and not valued.

summary: big, bureaucratic, rampant cronyism, not a place for young, energetic, and ambitious
pros: Good benefits, salary, place to be if you are day-in day-out
cons: I observed rampant cronyism to the point when a people with only a high school diploma and no technology background were accepted into IT Executive Director positions, just because of "networking". The JPMC also goes out of its way to discriminate against straight white males, by using race, gender, sex orientation as criteria for promotion. The IT in particular is overrun by immigrants from India because Chase signed exclusive agreements with TCS and Cognizant (Indian IT companies) to provide all consultants, who are then converted into FTEs. As a result, it is common to see 80%  of the people on the floor are from India. Needless to say, it is just another form of discrimination.

summary: Great company especially when you put the work in!
advice: Don't be so hesitant and rigid when it comes to promotions, when someone deserves a promotion make it happen for the employee, don't weigh up time in role at a certain level, base promotions purely on promotion and effort put in - retention is key! People leave the company and then come back into the company to receive VP/ED level faster, I don't think this should be a thing, retain your employees and promote your employees when they should be!
pros: Great Benefits, great networking opportunities, diversity is rife
cons: Its very easy to get comfortable when benefits are good and salary is good but there are so many amazing opportunities so you have to learnt o balance your work life an attending events to ensure you are actively seeking new opportunities even when you love your job!

advice: Have your employees backs whenever they need it most. Covid has presented major challenges and talent will be lost to other firms that value what they bring to the table.
pros: Huge amount of money to be made, professional attire, good clientele, structured program, lots of resources.
cons:
Does not practice what they preach as a firm at the branch level. All about numbers, not about your value as an individual and what you bring to the table. Employees are naturally motivated to attract, and be attracted to large deposits, it’s how they make their money. “Little guys” often left behind because of this. 
Not able to own my clients issues, and instead spend a lot of time on the phone with the back office. Manager is Micromanaged which in turn requires me to be. Takes longer than it should to have a process/issue completed. 
Technology on the employees side is way behind the rest of the industry.

advice: Literally what management? Managers are treated just as poorly as the rest until they reach a senior leadership level. Senior leadership is paid far better but aside from that, their hands are tied by corporate decision makers so far removed from reality it seems like a joke.  The whole company is run by one person. It’s his way or no way.
pros: Benefits are good; vacation time is competitive; a lot of great people working there
cons: The pay is below poverty level for most adults with at least one child, productivity metrics are designed to be impossible to meet let alone exceed; new hires with no experience are paid $2-$3 more per hour than the current employees being tasked with training them. Rewards and promotions are based on who you are friends with and not on your work performance. The harder you work, the more work you are given to do without adequate compensation increases.

advice: Think about making the associate program length more flexible. Some internal transfers to new cities might be very successful and have a high ceiling but need an extra year or two to develop a network without worrying about getting cut loose. Set proper compensation expectations with people at the banker level and above.
pros: Best spot for a private banking analyst to learn from the best and be in a very structured program. If you are willing to go above and buying people are willing to really help you out and teach you the tricks of the trade. Being a holistic bank allows you the chance to learn not only about investments but credit and lending, trust and estate planning and wealth advisory.
cons: Given analyst and associate programs are a three year hard stop if you are good enough to stay all the way through to banker you now have age against you.

summary: Learning is good they have all kind of technology, financial growth is bad and there is not recognition.
advice: Give raises to your exceeds people and low pays to the new guys, they do the oposite and they always lose their Sr. Staff because of this.
pros: Always on top of technology day to day learning is awesome, for engineers is the place to be for 2 years and leave, chase will make you an expert on any field because they have all kind of problems.
cons: Management is weak, they dont fight for their people, they do the force ranking review that even if you are great you never get an exceeds because they have a budget (industry standard but is unfair) no raises, so be sure you cut the best deal before you get in, the new healthcare is realy bad you pay 3000 in deductible and 2500 coinsurance and month to month is expensive, very near to a private insurance.

advice: Greater attention needs to be paid to developing and promoting internal talent.  Processes need to be streamlined.  Do not require meetings on global corporate topics that have no impact on individual contributors
pros: The job was stable, you knew what was expected of you from day to day.  The work load was reasonable, and could usually be completed in a 40 hour week.   Once assigned a project, you were generally left to manage it on your own
cons: Worked on older technology, generally 2-3 generations behind.  Constantly bombarded by email about people and departments that you never interacted with.  Constant meetings that served little value.  Strict and often conflicting standards and policies imposed by various departments.  Very little chance for advancement as an individual contributor.  Training was not generally provided, and would sometimes need to research new technologies on own time

advice: Please pay attention more tellers and bankers. They are putting up with a lot from customers with little pay. I worked in a lot of different branches, and it is the same everywhere. Or at least change the policies regarding customer behavior.
pros: Loved my coworkers, even my manager and assistant manager. They were like my second family, and they still are. Health Insurance, 401k, even when I worked as part-time
cons: I felt that chase didn't care enough about employees, and prefered to baby clients. I had to put up with abuse from customers..and I am not talking about rude people, this went beyond that. People who were not happy with life were venting on the tellers and bankers, b/c they know they could. Especially if you worked at a busy branch, you had to put up with a lot. The only reason I stayed as long as I did was b/c of my coworkers.

advice: Involve the teams in most if not all of decision making process so they feel engaged. Need more team building activities to have cross-team knowledge share (sometimes people work in silos just because they don't know where or who go to).
pros:
They give you a ton of opportunities to learn, challenge and grow especially with extremely smart people working around you. Internal mobility is well received and expected in junior to mid level roles after you spend about 2-3 years in a given position. Work life is not bad (work from home etc. is accepted) but at the same time they want you to work HARD!

You may hear "too many meetings" but that also means a very consensus driven environment!
cons:
No matter how well you do, at the end, you are still that small fish in the BIG pond.
Extremely competitive (not necessarily a con), hours can get long if you are more in line work.

Benefits are okay.

advice: There's a reason why this department has a very high turnover rate. You know the reason why, but you won't do a single thing about it, so my advice is pointless.
pros:
Great for resume building
Great benefits and unbelievable vacation/sick/personal days
Atmosphere is very laid back most of the time, with the exception of meeting deadlines.
Many networking events available and mini events (non-JPMC sponsored events)
Paid on a salary basis with OT opportunity
cons:
Management is awful. analyst always loses.
Work is measured by work performance which is by the amount of work you complete ONLY!
Tedious work. You're essentially doing the same work everyday. Your typical 9-5 job you will dread.
Training is dry and most of the time pointless and a waste of time.
Consultants are treated like peasants/untouchables
Essentially zero promotion opportunity. Only way up is to move into another department such as asset management or consumer investment banking or find another company to work for.
Salary is below the mean for Compliance Analyst.

summary: Specialist II position for Sapphire Travel Cards- Ok but has flaws.
advice: Bring back incentive to be the best, to do well. People dont get fired for blatant call-avoidance, and even still receive a raise with people who DO their job, and do it well. I had no fear for loss of my job, but also no hope or motivation to go above and beyond when "not being god awful" is acceptable
pros:
-medical benefits are nice
-pay is decent
-hours are consistent
-co workers and supervisors are generally easy to get along with
cons:
-they recently removed a lot of growth programs, and you cannot grow or move within the company until after a year
-Internal physical changes are happening soon. While working, everyone had their own cubical and drawers for personal belongings. They will be moving everyone into non private, closely placed seating with no area for belongings. And customers had already complained about being able to hear other specialists with the better-spaced layout.

summary: If money didn't control the government, I would never work another day at a bank.
advice: Like the rest of Corporate America, you need to take a step back and realize that your success is only due to the sacrifices of us "little people." There is no justification for someone pulling a multi-million dollar salary while the rest of us work 65+ hours a week for less than $60K and are lucky to see a 3% raise.
pros: As long as people use money, there will always be banks, so it's definitely one of the more stable fields to work in, despite the recent economic woes.
cons: I work in the Technology sector of JPMC and, for as much as Jamie touts how critical technology is to success, the rewards are only reaped by a small handful of people at the top. For the rest of us, compensation and recognition are well below the industry average.

summary: A great place to gain experience and have a long and varied career
advice: Continue to treat your employees as valuable team members and realize that everyone can contribute, regardless of rank or length of service.  Recognize that the work environment is changing and allow for flexible options, locations, and activities to get the most from your employees.  Continue to treat everyone with respect and you will be more rewarded by your employees.
pros: Company provides a wide range of experiences in the financial industry, from personal banking to investment management, tax, asset allocations, etc.  The people are supportive and do not treat non-management like peons.  Company communicates well and discloses corporate information appropriately.
cons: Banking can have long hours, lots of travel which is great if you want it but can be difficult if family is of strong concern, financial industry has lots of ups and downs so be prepared to weather the storms

summary: Big exposure, but completely resistant to any innovation/progress
advice: Actually learn how to reward and retain people, your attempts are just following Goldman's lead at each turn. Try to figure out how to remove the self-made inefficiencies in our entire workflow that keeps us here through the night and on weekends, fix the expectation that clients have of using our resources for free at the snap of their fingers, analysts and associates are the only people that suffer from this, you don't...
pros: Huge exposure to large deals with substantive impacts to the world and the markets, Money is more than you'd be making in your first year out of college in most other jobs, huge upward salary trajectory
cons: No work life balance, money doesn't compensate you for the pain you go through and bonuses are very politically distributed to people (i.e. producing the best work at a junior level doesn't mean you'll get the best rank)

summary: Really good...right up until the end.
pros: It's a BIG company with great global brand recognition and marketplace leverage. Well known and admired upper management. Pretty decent pay and there are a lot of opportunities & benefits for their employees. Great little consumer perks and discounts from being an employee as well.
cons: Because of the size of the company it can be a little impersonal. Plus with its numerous global locations there is always the risk that your department could be relocated out of state or out of country. When it happens it's tough to deal with. However you have to always remember that it's not personal. A company such as this is in the business of making money for its shareholders as much as it is satisfying their customers needs. Unfortunately employee salaries are just another line on the ledgers to cut down in order to increase profit margins.

advice:
Deliver what you promise by promptly training and getting the new hires ready.
Getting rid of back office coordinators that used to help the new hires was a bad idea.
upkeep with tech trends
pros: Could be a great place to work for if it wasn't for all the cons.
cons:
All the way around inexperienced management and team of rookies.
Banker support phone line assistants cannot help the new bankers and are getting calls from other countries and hard to understand and do not understand what you ask them.
Promised training and advancement never delivered due to short staffing of under paid employees who are happy where they are.
Pressure to greet and help customers but short staffing result in bad "customer experience evaluation.
Technology needs to be better updated with the current trend; light years behind with constant system glitch and bad banker support staff.
New hires have no chance to advancement which makes them feel stuck

advice: Make it easy for employees to help the customers by providing more support (someone to call when an issue arises, instead of emailing a department).
pros: They care about the employees. Culture is a big emphasis. Great products and services and market reputation. Quarterly bonuses for branch employees based on client experience scores.
cons:
Bonuses are annual, so you can be doing great most of the year, but if your performance level drops in 4th quarter, then your bonus will be reduced.
You don't get much discretion on making local decisions, as it is a large company. Sometimes that's a plus, as you just need to follow policies & procedures. Hard to work with the call centers for employee support especially in the time of COVID. Sometimes there is too much "culture" activities encouraged (read "required"). Sometimes I just want to do my job. I don't need to share everything with people I work with.

advice:
- Shift to a compensation model that rewards high performers in tech; Use record profits to grow salaries and bonuses for technologists, not just for bankers.
- Embrace the Work From Anywhere (WFA) model for tech, it's a proven model that works. In-office mandates are archaic.
- Prioritize removing barriers/silos between tech groups (product/security/ops).
- Improve the digital product development lifecycle internally to ensure end-users are more plugged in with product teams and the changes they roll out.
- Build a culture that puts a larger emphasis on change/transformation from the top-down, and cultivates stronger partnership between business and technology.
pros:
- Job security and benefits
- Smart, high-performing, and diverse teams
- Reputation and integrity
- Market leader; Technologically advanced relative to other big banks
- Opportunities for networking, professional development, and continuous learning
cons:
- Bureaucracy and red tape
- Tech group silos (product, security, ops)
- Lacks work flexibility and compensation for technologists
- Resistance to change/transformation

summary: Chase is a good place to work
advice: Prioritize the most important issues and accept the fact that experiences and processes need to eveolve over time, rather than try to launch new initiatives perfectly.
pros: Chase hires very talented and dedicated people. There is a high level strategic and innovative thinking. This is balanced by operational teams focused on executing projects. The managers care about their direct reports and it is relatively easy to develop friendships with other employees. Most senior managers a willing to mentor junior employees and there several employee support groups.
cons: Chase is a large company and at times it is very bureaucratic. It's focus for the past few years has been on efficiency and reducing costs. As a result, the processes to prioritize initiatives. It is difficult to prototype or pilot concepts because manual processes are view unfavorably and IT systems are designed to handle the smallest of corner use cases.

advice: Don't take an Investment Management job unless you intend to stick around.  If you're the 4th or 5th Investment Manager in your position in the last three years, don't expect your FAs to immediately change the way they manage their books to conform to you new initiatives.  Demonstrate your staying power before you start shaking things up.
pros:
access to thousands of bank customer
prospects will take a call (or return a call) when it comes from their bank
ability to compensate bankers for referrals
tremendous flexibility of schedule
cons:
extraordinarily high turnover in management
low payout percentages and routine haircuts
high monthly revenue goals
disincentive to build book of managed money
equality of sales expectations, but great disparity in opportunity set (income potential dependent on affluence of customers in branch assignment - don't accept an offer if it's tied to a branch in a low-to-moderate income neighborhood... doomed to fail)

advice: To the abusive part of the management -- none. To the rest -- keep well and all the best.
pros: Some of my good colleagues were professional, smart and a pleasure to work with
cons:
Some of my other colleagues were difficult for various reasons. I noticed an alarming number of them were dispirited, and another alarming number of them were careerist. I'm yet to be convinced if anyone at all was there to actually do a good job and enjoy accomplishments. Perhaps due to an excessively rank-conscious culture, some of those with higher ranks were downright abusive, which I've had the good luck to not have encountered before this job. 

How the overall system worked there was Kafkaesque and frequently reminded me of Catch-22. I re-read Kafka and Catch-22 while on the job, just to have a laugh about it. Never had I felt so in touch with the "classical" American corporate culture.
