Despite my being an experienced professional, this job finally enabled me to understand shows like "The Office", "Enlightened" and appreciate Dilbert cartoons. 

Despite the advantages mentioned above, I'm very glad to have left. Feel sorry for my good colleagues who have to remain there and condition themselves to accept this as normal.

summary: Great Benefits, Poor middle Management - GTI
advice: They have to learn to become better mentors and understand that overloading is not the way to a quality product.
pros:
okay pay. 
great benefits.  
Work from home on occasion is not a problem with preapproval.  
4-weeks vacation to start. 
Pension, 401k with 100% match after a year; vest after three years.
State of the art Technologies
cons:
Work/life balance is poor due to the fact that they are understaffed, overloaded, and yet someone was just laid off.  So, the workload has only increased. I find myself working in the evening and weekends and yet still under water
Many managers do not speak much to their direct reports.  No Support is given by managers.  Its a sink or swim environment. 
Typically no raises, and bonuses don't necessarily increase so you may end up with the same total comp for years at a time

advice: Find more ways to help employee's because they are victims to customers accusations sometimes as well.
pros:
A great place to work temporarily, while in school or as a second job. 
Great benefits
Friendly Coworkers
Systematic tasks, you can't go wrong by following procedures in any situation!
cons: Have to learn everything on your own, little to no help from coworkers because they are busy or there is always still something to learn. You can't ever learn everything because the policies are always changing, you just have to keep up and learn on your own pace. Customers are quite rude at times but we must always have "customer obsession". They say you can advance after starting at chase in any position but anything besides a banker is hard to achieve because, they need at least 2-3yrs of experience which you don't have because we have worked at another position in Chase the entire time.

summary: Sound political parties working together to eat jpmorgan's wealth
advice: Go and join as Zomato delivery boys.
pros: Nothing to say about it
cons: Everything, dont join ,don't end your career

jobTitle: Global Finance and Business Management Analyst
advice:
EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE. Work on developing emotional intelligence, compassion, empathy etc. within your management-level employees. 

*Listen to employees' feedback about unpleasant managers, and make changes accordingly! Steer away from valuing the manager's comfort over addressing issues brought up by employees.
pros:
The GF&BM (Global Finance & Business Management) rotational program offers three different positions (one during internship, then first and second rotations) across finance and accounting roles -- which is helpful in gaining a range of experience in the financial services industry

I appreciated the formal feedback process that took place 2x each rotation, mid-way through and at the end of the role
cons:
While we were asked to submit our preferences for positions and sectors within the bank that we would like to work, the preferences are only taken into consideration to a certain extent. As expected, the business needs are the highest priority.

Management is hit or miss. I had one manager who I really respected and enjoyed working for, and another who drove me out of the company because I found them intolerable. Most employees are pretty pleasant to work with though, in my experience.

As of 2021, the compensation of this program is also not as competitive as I would expect.

advice: It’s not the managements fault, I’ve always had great managers it’s a company culture problem.
pros: It’s all the pros of working for a major company. You get pto, insurance and the hours aren’t bad considering you’re off every Sunday and are out of work Saturday by like 2.
cons: The pay is bad even with their announcement of a company wide raise, they essentially changed the responsibilities of the job role to make LAO’s, assistant branch managers (we’re even called that in the system) but won’t pay us an ABM wage, there operations system and ease of functionality across different departments is horrible I once had to talk to 11 different departments and 15 different people to solve 1 issue because Chase does not clearly make steps to resolve issues for us or clients. There is honestly so much more but I’ll leave it at that.

pros:
- Good Work Life Balance
- Allows for team mobility after a year of working
- Good benefits
- If you just want to get paid decently and just coast through life, this is a pretty good option.
cons:
- The development process is incredibly slow (as are most banks). It takes forever to make a change and get things out.
- They rely heavily on internal tooling and frameworks that are not transferrable to the outside world. So getting a job afterward is more difficult.
- Unless you're talking to a VP and up, a lot of people here aren't as competent with good developing practices.
- The amount of brown nosing that happens is really annoying
- Executives are always slow to adopt necessary tools and basically fish for praise when they implement a super simple idea that has already been around in the industry for years. They are also pretty detached from reality of everyday people.

summary: There are both pros and cons, but overall it's ok.
advice: Put an official mentoring program in place or provide direction for how to obtain one. Come up with a way to provide incentives (even if they're non-monetary) to those individuals/departments that "don't generate revenue for the company". We work just as hard as everyone else and still make valid contributions. Provide information that illustrates different career paths based on skills and current positions.
pros: Time-off policies... most employees got an additional week of paid vacation this year... I now have 4 weeks (5 yrs of total service). Leave policies are really accommodating. I received chemo and radiation following a breast cancer diagnosis, and the company has a policy that allowed me to receive my full salary as long as worked 60% of my regular schedule.. that was HUGE with the increased medical expenses.
cons: Since my department "doesn't generate revenue for the company", my co-workers and I aren't eligible for any type of bonus or incentive. There's no official mentoring program in place. Opportunities for career advancement aren't available in all areas of the company. Salary ranges are very broad and vary greatly within the same department. Management isn't able to help you define a career path or trajectory.

advice: Take efforts to set expectations for entering banking now that are realistic for today rather than how it was 10 years ago. Add at least some sales credit to the new responsibilities added to the associate banker position or pay higher base wages.
pros: Fantastic work culture, LGBTQ+ friendly, great benefits, and easy work. Chase makes sure to provide you with the tools and training to be successful. They provide a retirement fund as well as medical, dental, and vision insurance. They have a generous amount of PTO for all their employees. They take their mission statement of diversity and inclusion very seriously and take steps to ensure fair treatment for their employees.
cons: The company keeps adding responsibilities to the position without adding as much compensation. The role is changing quickly and while mobility is promised, trends in the industry make me very worried about advancement opportunities at the company.

advice: Appreciate your employees, show them that you care. There needs to be a better office culture, as I personally do not appreciate working with people are close-minded and racist.
pros: Chase Bank offers great training and it definitely a great place to get your feet wet in the financial industry.
cons:
The pay can definitely be improved, especially for all that you have to deal with. I personally had a terrible experience with JP Morgan Chase Bank, simply because they don't care about their employees. I was registered as a "part-time" employee, while working 40+ hours a week. Upon my graduation of college with a degree in Finance, I was looking to transition into a higher position; upon being told that they needed me as a teller and would not approve my request to transition, I began looking for another job. When I informed my upper management that I had found another job, they had me work all the way up until the day before my other position began. 

My management team also became very upset with my decision to leave the company; however if I am such an "asset" then help me transition. I didn't go to college for 4 years to be a bank teller.

summary: Too big but receptive to employee's concern.
advice: Create an online portal wherein employees can share what is really happening in their respective lines of businesses. Come up with an evaluation procedure/ process that will fit to the line of business candidate is applying for. Do not punish employee if his or her basic is already high, if he or she worked for that year and deserves a raise, then give it. Sick leave should be convertible to cash as an incentive for the employer to be always at best at work. Senior management should be visible and appreciate efforts of employees. Learn the culture of the employees.
pros: They take results of employee opinion surveys seriously.
cons: Unrealistic goals and if realistic, they are not being very transparent why goals should be that high. When you want to transfer to another line of business, they view your performance in your current role rather than come up with evaluation procedures that will fit to the line of business candidate is applying for. For you to get an increase, it should be exceed expectations. Sick leave is not convertible to cash. Senior management seem distant. Don't see any formal or streamlined culture.

advice: Nothing but great things to say here.  We were giving ample notice that our jobs were comig to an end.  We are given company resources to find another position with the company.  Unfortunately, it didn't happen for me.  My prior management continues to keep in touch with me to see how I am doing in my job search.  They are always asking if I need any help or if I want them to call other managers, inside AND outside Chase on my behalf.  I am humbled and very grateful for their continued assistance.
pros: Solid company.  Easy and beneficial to accumulate time on the job.  When a  position is eliminated they really try to find another position for you within the company.  Most managers that I've worked have been excellent and really care about their employees.
cons: You have to hold your breath every fall and be on the look out for end-of-year downsizing, but that is nothing new to the industry.  It is a little hard to move up on the pay scale.

advice: Listen better to your advisors, show the "care" factor.
pros: Many locations across the country, technologically well-equipped platform, good back office support, you can meet some good employees that can make your day better. Benefits are ok, although several years ago were much better.
cons: Base pay is somewhere between the lowest and avg in the industry, incentive plan continues to change for the worse (banking and brokerage), huge level of nepotism to older advisors (maybe 5% of all advisors on the platform) since their annual revenues are somewhat high, however, they have been with the company for 15+ years. You don't get a feeling that the management cares much, because you can't have real and honest conversations. If you are thinking about joining this firm, make sure you understand how politics work, fighting, literally fighting between the bank side and the brokerage side happens daily. Although it is one firm, it does feel like each department is on its own. Performance of their managed account is among the lowest in the industry, therefore there is a huge amount of outflows. Management tends to procrastinate any decision-making in a way of passing the responsibility to another executive, so not much gets done. Moral in the offices is at its lowest, many good bankers left to other banks and you are stuck with new bankers which expect you to train and often times have 0 financial services experience.

summary: Is there any green grass left?
advice: Take the same amount of money you spent on those beautiful, full-color booklets about company values and buy a copy of Leadership and Self Deception for each employee. After that, start enforcing your existing values on management at every single level. After that, I have a few more books for you to read.
pros:
- Good Health Benefits
- Generous Paid Time Off 
- Bonuses for employees* (see cons)
- Decent technology
cons:
- Corporate spends a good deal of time and money talking about values, but does not enforce them at the worker's level.
- There are not enough checks and balances for the every day worker's life, no one to go to if your manager is treating you unfairly or doing things incorrectly. For example, telling employees of their intent to fire someone once they fail their improvement plan (not to mention telling another employee that someone is on an improvement plan). This happened three times in one year in my department.
- Secrecy about pay keeps you from knowing if you're being fairly compensated
- * Bonuses are left to the discretion of individual managers. Unfortunately, if they don't like you personally, they can deny you a bonus, no matter what your review says.

advice: Pay better!
pros: Name recognition. History in the US.
cons: The firm does not pay well. Increase in base salary paltry. Bonus’s very small.

advice: In my experience, management caused unnecessary stress and pressure for the employees. Stop caring so much about your own bonus and "scorecard" and more about the well being and improvement of the employees.
pros: Great bank to work for if you're great at sales and relationship building. There are plenty of opportunities to make sales and earn commissions if you're in the right branch and have strong partners.
cons: A lot of red tape at this company. Management is only interested in their own agenda and what they get scored on. Company shifted into extreme micro managing, scrutinizing and focusing on mundane tasks and busy work, which didn't benefit clients. Not all markets and branches are the same, the only way to be successful in the retail bank is to be in a busy branch with a large D+I balance with good partners who show up to work.

advice: Need to be able to make quick but smart decisions, somthing Ive seen a lack of in the past 6 months.
pros: Managers treat all employees with fairness and respect.  Everyone's opinion counts.  Feedback on how you are doing is given when asked.  Anytime I have asked to take off it has been given to me, even during times there are "blackouts".  As long as you know ahead of time, they are pretty reasonable with work from home/time off.  Career opportunites to move laterally and up are out there, but they wont just be given to you, you must ask and work at getting offers for mobility throughout the company.  Benefits are some of the better ones I've seen, generous vacation is given as soon as you start.
cons: Compenstation seems to be on the lower side compared to the average.

summary: Stable place to work if you're content with very slow career growth.
advice: Focus more on employee satisfaction or you will continue to lose talented staff and be left with employees content on getting by doing the bare minimum. Both types of people seem to be rewarded equally here.
pros: 4 weeks vacaction is tough to beat. Also very flexible in getting time off as long as your work is completed. Good place to work if you're comfortable with just punching a time card and collecting a pay check, but not much hope for growth unless you are brought in at AVP level or above.
cons: Other than that everything here is dictated by politics and red tape. Because it is part of such a large corporation, tasks such as gaining access to an accounting database needed for daily work can take over a month. Salaries are low and bonuses are almost non-existent.

summary: Good Company bad management and review policies
pros:
Good company in terms of training and development as you will be expected to know your topic the best you possibly can.
Must be willing to be inquisitive in all meetings, a demand for engagement is something that is also looked for
cons:
Bad politics and management overall
Poor performance review procedures, they should model more on the job and immediate reviews as opposed to waiting at the end of the year to discuss past experiences - these reviews tend not be fair as they depend on your current manager and their opinion of what you deserve versus what you've actually worked for. Performance reviews in large companies are too important to not be revised at in terms of new ways to capture the true work on their employees

summary: This was the best institution I have ever had the pleasure of working with.
pros: Even though it's been a few years, I was extremely happy working with the team I was assigned to. My knowledge grew expeditiously due to the job responsibilities.  The Learning environment. I was assigned to the VP responsible for implementing new programs for the staff in various departments and I was required to critique them. I had never been involved with the creating process of a course and it was quite exciting.
cons: The only negative I came across was being dependent on other departments' staff members for the completion of some of our projects. I believe because we were a new department and didn't have the connections our projects were not expedited. Once we introduced ourselves and our mission this became a non-issue.

advice: Everything isn't always in a pretty box.  Innovation not only takes creativity and critical thinking, but it also takes courage.  Communicate with your people, really, not just in staged town halls.  Take the time to appreciate a subordinate and really open to new ideas, and not just the easy ones with very little risk or reward.  Need Technology to think and communicate a little more like Jamie.
pros: There are some of the greatest minds in regards to Technology, Engineering and Operations in this company.  Innovative and genious in some areas.
cons: If you work in some areas, well, think 1996.  I've been in technology for about 14 years and although technology has changed greatly, it's management (again in some areas) has not.  It's quite challenging to bring about change and new ideas in some areas.

pros:
* Good work/life balance (work 40 hours a week, period); this probably depends on your team
* Great videoconferencing; companies using Slack are cavemen by comparison
* Clear separation of responsibilities
* Interesting projects
cons:
* Lower compensation compared to other large firms
* Open floor plan; I can hear people from 3 rows of cubicles when attending technical meetings
* They are ridiculous about expenses. Example: mandatory trainings have a video component but my workstation has no sound. I've learned to read lips because to get headsets I would probably need approval from 4 managers (no joke)
* Takes 1 FULL YEAR before they match anything to your 401k (ridiculous)
* Healthcare plans are very expensive
* Career mobility is highly praised internally esp. by higher-ups but anyone trying to figure out how to get in on it realizes it's a cluster****

summary: If you're interested in finance technology, a good place to build a career
advice: Check in with your employees to make sure that they are not getting burnt out. That is a very common thing in JPMorgan but I will give them credit for trying to rectify that.
pros: When you get a good manager or a good team, you can really propel your career forward. Career is a big buzzword here at JPMorgan. They emphasize training, networking, and visibility to upper management. Plus mobility within the company is a very real thing
cons: With so many employees and so many various managers, there can be a decent chance you end up with one that does not suit you or is so caught up in their own career they don't feel like guiding yours. Sometimes dealing with legacy platforms can be a pain.

pros:
+ Supervisors were incredible, friendly, but still productive.
+ Flexible part-time hours
+ There weren't any unreasonable expectations set on anybody.
+ Very few surprises

The job was pretty much a cookie-cutter data entry position. They provided good accommodations for typists; good chairs, adjustable desks, standing desk options. Working with sensitive information requires a lot of precautions and regulations, and the supervisors did their best to mitigate them.
cons:
- No excitement/variance, though it's to be expected of a data entry position.
- Very strict breaks, lunch times. If you're not on break, you're glued to the keyboard.
- High security/lots of regulations. You pretty much can't take anything onto the floor except very specific music players. This just comes with the nature of the work, so I can't really blame the company/management.
- Keyboards were old and worn.

advice: I think everything would work better if the business really reflected and thought about business decisions and processes through the eyes of a customer a bit more; honestly I would never finance an automobile through chase or recommend anyone else do so.
pros: Good insurance and vacation benefits starting from day one outside of training. Training for position was adequate. Honestly, the customers were not that bad for the most part.
cons: Everything else. Bonuses were easy to loose, and I am aware it is just that a bonus, dress code was too strict for a call center and I was told that used to loosen up in the summer months, but not for the past two years, and felt like the longer I worked there I was doing more of another departments job on top of my departments job more often than not. I could go on and on.

summary: I have never worked in a more discriminatory workplace as an American.
advice: To Senior Management: Please have in person, thorough training to your VP's, ED's on unconscious bias, inclusiveness and anti-discriminatory behavior when working for a US company. Inclusion and acceptance of people from different backgrounds and ethnicities should be taken VERY seriously as a US company representing American workplace values. I have never worked in such a discriminatory workplace as an American.
pros: Good name until you find your next job.
cons:
There is very little growth here because career development is a highly political task based on the following reasons:

You don't have to be a decent colleague, person or good technically. Culture and treatment and opportunity is determined by your manager's  race to your race. 

My team has production issues left and right, yet people who are writing bad code claiming they have 10 years of experience that are still getting the exposure and visibility to leadership because they speak the same foreign language as their manager.

advice: Create a leadership rotation program to build bench strength and help fill gaps quickly as turnover occurs. Although there are a lot of opportunities; it's almost impossible to move from one LOB to another.  Stop new leaders from micro-managing -- provide structured leadership training/education. Revisit the policy/ idea of work from home as you are forcing people to take an entire day off vs. coming in late of leaving early for dr. appointments etc.
pros: Wonderful and talented group of people work at JPMC. Being a very large Company, there are a lot of opportunities in various lines of business.
cons: I don't see mid-level management walking the talk coming from the top; which is disheartening and caused a high turnover rate. It's very difficult to meet goals set forth while maintaining work/life balance.  JPMC doesn't allow people to work from home; which further decreases work/life balance.

advice: Communicate more often and be more blunt about expectations, deadlines, what you wish to see more of, etc. Provide individual criticism to help employees understand what they can do better and how they can move up.
pros:
- Lots of freedom, managers don't micromanage much
- The facilities are gorgeous and they have a Starbucks + 2 cafeterias inside + small snack shop
- The experience working here looks great on a resume
- Great benefits, bonuses are nice, referral bonuses can happen, there are a lot of ways to benefit from working here
- Many positions require late night calls because we work overseas. This can be exhausting and frustrating.
cons:
- Work is boring and generally unfulfilling
- I never feel like I matter here and cubicle work gets depressing
- It's a big company...if you like that kind of environment you'll love Chase, but it feels too big to me.

summary: Great place to work, if you have the right kind of leadership
advice: Consider truly having leaders in your branches, not managers, who don't know the first thing about their clients or their own employees. Pay more for talent.  work with your talent to promote them. currently your "managers" are not utilizing the talent they have access to on things that are best for the customer and the firm. They use the talent for self serving purposes.  Therefore you will always have an attrition problem
pros: Great benefits, products, socially responsible business
cons: too much  "management" not enough leadership.  Base salary could be higher. They pay you for sales, yet want you to focus on building a relationship, which would be fine if they didn't have a 30 day sales cycle in place.

summary: Great people, high turnover back in 2015
advice: When I left management was making an effort to change which I really appreciated. They took the time to listen to our concerns about whether things really changed when I left I'm not sure but it sure does feel good to be heard. I left because I was recruited by a V.C. with $20k increase in pay. I recommend reviewing base salary for admins.
pros: I loved the people who I supported genuine, caring, friendly and professional. I recommend JPM if you're looking for a place to grow in a fast-paced environment. I'm very thankful for my experience at JPM as an Executive Assistant.
cons: Turnover across the board. It was hard to keep up with the rate at which admins were leaving due to stress, long hours, and lower wages than other investment firms.

advice: Increase salaries, actually care about your employee's health. During covid times we we all still meeting clients without any shields at our desks. Management valued money over safety. The funniest thing is that they offered us a $400 "thank you" for working through covid but in order to get it you still needed to work the next 3 months. So if you got sick and had to stay out for 2 weeks, you would get nothing.  Think about your employees, during these times we want to be with our families but where were we? Outside working to 6pm.
pros: Easy to get promoted. Colleagues can be amazing.
cons: No care for employees health. Lousy salary for all the money one brings in. Sales pressure during covid times were through he roof.  Long hours. Healthcare is too expensive.

advice: Set up more locations
pros: The pay is great and everyone is pretty nice. The only down side so far is that the hours are really long but it goes by fast, you are always busy. They have a great system for when you put in overtime, you can order food easily and they pay for your cab ride home. Theres also a lot of discounts and benefits to being an employee.
cons: It can be hard to have a personal life at some points since work is so overwhelming but if you can manage your time and you like what you do then this is a great place to work. This might not be a downside to some people but I dont really like how frequent people have to travel, its alright if you are single but for a family it can get stressful.

summary: Pros and Cons or working at Chase
advice: Management has lost touch with retail employees a while back. Because they are so focused on showing good numbers, sometimes they forget they are dealing with human beings and not robots. I would advise them to consider a different approach that will not make people want to leave.
pros:
- Advance Technology, which makes doing things a lot easier
- Reputable name, which contributes in increased foot traffic in the branches
- 5% match to 401k contribution
- Tuition reimbursement
cons:
- Compare to other banks, base salary is ridiculously low (especially if you work in the branches)
- Recent change to incentive plan for branch bankers makes it harder for them to make decent money
- Ridiculous/unrealistic requirements from upper management that can bring about a serious level of stress
- Extremely hard to go from retail to corporate

advice: You are delusional about what goes on daily at the branch level. It is easy to make decisions from HQ. Pay serious attention to hard working employees and boost employee morale. Stop putting up a facade of caring for employee satisfaction when in reality, you are just blowing smoke.
pros:
Build great client relationships
Brand name recognition
Decent benefits/perks
Glass office
Working toilet
cons: Each year, the comp plan is getting cut. Funny how senior management always try to have you drink the kool-aid and say it is for the better. I am sick of hearing about "customer experience." The company does not give a crap about its employees. Retail employees are expected to take it in the ass from customers with a smile while collecting a below market salary. I feel overworked each and everyday while my pay is continuously getting cut.

summary: Too much bias in senior management.
advice: Give due credit to the actual employee who does the work instead of giving it to your "yes man".
pros: Good brand name to have on your resume. If you are targeting other big name companies, then it is a good name to have on your resume. I have heard back from companies like Google once I put their name on my resume.
cons: Biased management which will give credit for your work to their own "Yes Men". Horrible work/life balance missing something as basic as a library and charging you even for a simple water bottle. They will expect you to work beyond your 40 hours on weekends as well with no compensation or reward, however they will flag you on other days even if you are 10 minutes late.

summary: I worked for Chase for 9 years in equity, refinance and purchase loans.
advice: Researching a little further before making decisions.  Communication with the loan center management would allow decisions to be made and carried out in a more acceptable manner.   Work arounds for the software used are just one of the items where communication would make snap decisions more productive for the staff.
pros: The people make the job.  I had the best co-workers and even though I was on many different teams I was always able to have a well rounded team that worked together to get the job done.
cons: It is difficult working for a such a large organization as most decisions are made at the corporate level without any input from the management that works over the actual loan centers.

advice: Honor your employees and remember no person is perfect.  Take a look at your management team as the employees are uncomfortable that they too may be termed for simple mistakes that being documented lead to unfair termination.  The core of business is your employees and change needs to start with management.
pros: Ability to work in a professional environment. Can move up in the company.
cons: I have seen that in the contact center you could be released based on tenure and higher wages. Currently I have seen many tenured employees be termed based on so called company policy; however, when looking at the group that have been released, they have been with the company 15 plus years which have higher wages than incoming employees.  Attrition rates seem high.

summary: Like all of corp. America, nickel and diming. Highly rated managers have mastered the skill of avoiding collabaration
advice: As a too-big-to-fail institution, there is little incentive to do the right thing for customers. The lawyers and lobbyists are paid to keep you out trouble and they usually do. But this attitude poisons your long term prospects. If people can leave as customers or employees, they will.
pros: Salaries are on the rise. As long as you are entering the organization, they will compete. Individual departments can maintain team spirit. If you're working on a hot project, then you will be valued.
cons: Monstrous security bureaucracy (they kept promising fixes where on the way, maybe?). FUD is the main management tool. As in most corps, no loyalty given OR expected. Do what is best for you. Always!

summary: Fast paced customer idealized but shareholder centered
advice:
Ditch JP in CIB and allow the real managers there to work and make decisions.
Put the customer back into customer service after all, how much profit is enough.
pros:
Comfortable cubical farm call center environment, large desks and computers with dual monitors allowed you to multitask very efficiently. 
Speak very highly of customer satisfaction
Great pay, great pto, 401k and insurance package
International mobility
cons:
One up and coming Executive Director in CIB is consolidating his fiefdom through micromanagement and promises to upper eschelons of smaller staff more work means more money for shareholders.
Managers run around like chickens with heads cut off. 
There is constant cattiness and a game managers like to play called "throw someone under a bus"
More focused on shareholder profit than true customer service

summary: Decent employer... as long as you aren't fussed about achieving anything
advice: Empower your staff, treat them like the adults they are and listen to them. You have some very talented people working in this organization, stop overlooking them for external talent.
pros:
Good number of vacation days.
Personal days and bank holidays.
Friendly coworkers.
401k matching & pension.
cons:
Beurocracy makes it almost impossible to get anything done.
Decisions are made at the highest possible level with little interest in what those dealing with the task at hand have to say about the matter.
Antiquated approach to flexible working.
Office environment straight out of the 90's.
Senior Leadership seemingly have no idea what they're doing and everyone is pushing so hard for their piece of the pie and to be heard that nothing actually ends up happening.
Constant reorganizations (every 9 months or so).

advice: There is a lot of talent within the organization and it doesn't seem as if being promoted is not easy at this organization.  Also, this organization always promote family however very few lines employees does not have the ability to work from home,  especially if their children are home and have no one else to watch them.
pros: JPMorgan has great benefits for their employees and now have added 16 weeks for their maternity leave program so mothers can more bounding time with their newborn.
cons: I believe the biggest con for this organization is diversity.  I can count on one hand how many African American managers work at this company.  Another con is communication between some of the departments.  It seems one department procedures has something different than the partner department.

advice: Learn how to manage! You should care about your employees. And look at them as people. You should treat them with respect!
pros: None. This is the worst place place to work.
cons: This is the worst place to work! If your thinking of working here, look somewhere else. Upper management does not promote based on performance. They promote based on who they like. The majority of the managers do not know what they are doing. You can tell someone just handed them a promotion. The turn over rate is extremely high. They do a mass hiring and mass layoffs every year. They micromanage. They require you to work an excessive amount of hours. Upper management has such a lack of respect for employees. It was the same in every department. Working there was a nightmare and caused so much stress to their employees. And they don't seem to care. If I could give a negative star as a rating I would, for every category.

advice: You're doing great. Always listen to the employee specially the analyst bec they know how project is working. Give training to those leaders that was complained by employee for them to learn and grow more. They will be bad leaders now but through training they gonna be good at it.
pros:
A company that you can enjoy working. They took care the employee and gave training for individual growt. Salary is competitive, health insurance was great.
Most of the leaders were ok. Coworker is the best. Even if the work is challenging if you're sorrounded by supportive grouo it will gonna be easy.
cons: I think all company has a bad leader. And Chase was not exempted to that. In 7 years working with them I encountered 2 leaders that was not ready for their position.

advice:
Be more transparent with employees about changes in the company so that we are all on the same page. Sometimes information is held on to for months and we aren't aware of anything. Ask employees what they would like to see for the team, any room for improvements. Actually take information from the "anonymous" employee survey to change how things operate.

Stop pretending to care about diversity and actually do something about it.
pros: Good pay, people (depending on the team) are kind, a lot of room for growth in BRGs, there are sometimes opportunities for travel (depending on your team), work life balance is good (also...depending on your team)
cons: Poor communication, inconsistency from senior leaders, no transparency, not a lot of room for growth - some people will be entry level for 10 years

pros:
Pay and benefits are okay relative to what’s expected of you.  Easy interview process. If you are just looking for somewhere to be, it’s easy to get hired here.

The company promotes progressive values and inclusiveness.

If you can stick it out for a year you can change positions internally. Assuming you want to stay.
cons:
Too much siloing and bureaucracy. People tend to be unwilling to go beyond their silo to help. It takes a while to get to know people because of office culture.

Unless someone really needed a job, I wouldn’t recommend It.

You’re forced to take poorly designed training courses that are well intentioned but ultimately a waste of time.  I’m sure there are good compliance reasons behind them though.

I don’t get the sense that many people are actually happy here.

summary: Education and backround mean nothing to Chase.
advice: Train your entry level managers to understand that they have talent above even their own in many site locations due to the current employment market. Doing so will dramatically reduce turnover and make chase an employer experienced bankers would like to work for. Your loosing your talented staff to you competition due to your hiring criteria for managnment level staff. IE: high school diploma and 1 year management experience...its a joke. No wonder Chase has so many legal issues.
pros: Large stable employer, Reasonable training
cons:
Chase promotes a culture of micro management where even some of your peers try to exert power over you.
Chase takes full advantage of the current economic situation by placing people in positions that are entry level even though they have masters degrees and 15 years exoperience.
Chase does not value its human capital at all.

summary: JPMorgan Chase was a very professional place to work.  I worked with a lot of skilled and competent people.
pros: I worked with some very capable people who were open to discussions on how to improve processes or how to approach different exercises we worked.  I felt like my opinion mattered.
cons: The mortgage industry is going through a lot of changes and government oversight has increased which creates an enormous amount of work to meet compliance and reporting requirements.  Depending on what your job duties are you could be facing a lot of overtime - sometimes it is planned and sometimes it's not.  Delinquency rates are improving and foreclosures are decreasing which is great for the economy but not so great if your job happens to be in Mortgage Default.  Layoffs have been pretty constant and I met that fate.

advice: Too many acronyms, too many systems that don't talk to each other, and too much politics.
pros: Excellent benefits for employees in terms of Paid Time Off (4 weeks vacation, 9 Federal holidays, 3 Personal days, and 6 sick days), Maternity - Paternity leave ( Moms get 12 weeks paid maternity leave, Dads get 1 week at the time of birth).
cons: Too much politics inside the company. Internal job postings are plenty but you cannot even apply for them unless you inform your manager that you're looking. You getting or not getting the job completely depends on your current manager's feedback. Year end bonus and pay raises completely depends on your rating by your manager. The rating is finalized before you get to know. There is no discussion regarding the rating. Its more the management telling you the rating. If you're 'in the circle' then life's good.

advice: If it's not broken, then do not bother fixing it.
pros: You have a job.  Be thankful.  You have a great job.  Wash, rinse, and repeat and repeat some more.  You have a job.
cons: You leave dumber before you came into the company (brain drain).  PMC/Performance Management is a joke.  HR is a suicide prevention hotline.  A new fire drill to contend with every day.  Innovation is stifled.  People are not accountable for their actions and got away with being shluffs.  WM, CCB, and CIB were the worse people to work with.  When tempers flared, the CIO comes in on a chariot and calms the waters.  Extremely poor hiring practices.  Wrong people hired for jobs.  Company would put employees in a position so they would leave and not have to pay severance.  You are just a standard ID.  Run as fast as you can away from this place if you still work for it and don't look back.

advice: Learn to value your employees, they are the ones keeping this company going not the share holders.
pros: Good name recognition, get to work with some of the brightest minds in the business.
cons: Management is more concerned about short term gains over long term solutions due to a 6 month revolving door in middle management.  You get used to repeating the same tasks over and over which leads to very high turnover in the rank and file as people burn out and leave for greener pastures.  In order to tread water you quickly learn to play the same political games as everybody else.  No incentive to do more than the bare minimum, going above and beyond in your role is only worth an extra 0.5% raise on top of the already eager 1-2% raise you would get just for showing up.

summary: The company is obsessed with cutting costs
pros: 1. Industry leader; name recognition.
cons:
I can only speak from my own experience- I work specifically in the mutual fund operations side. The company is one of the top banks in the industry. But, our jobs are disposable, as is the people. They continuously cut, push more work, migrate and lay off, with no end in sight. Try having to train your own replacements from Manila and Mumbai. That's our reality. It's not getting any better. Morale is horrible. There are some good people but they too have been driven off by the toxic environment.
But it is what it is. The company is here to cut cost. Their long term goal is to automate to the point where everything will be done via technology and a global migration team. We are disposable. But hey, i guess that's capitalism for you.

advice: Management is great but you could be more understanding when it comes to the abusive callers
pros: Great benefits decent pay and great environment
cons: Carefully consider before accepting the job. I was so excited and proud to start this job. The management is great always trying to find ways to help BUT the customers for Chase sapphire are the absolute worst. Extremely rude. I've never been treated this way by a customer in my life. They put you down whine and complain and exspect you to make adjustments for every little thing. It's entirely to stressful for the pay that's offered. Everytime you turn around someone is out on a leave of absence because of the job. I had no choice but to leave because of the abuse from the customers drove me crazy.

advice: Give employees what they are worth. Especially your high meets/exceed employees who were rated this year after year after year. Play far! Allow people to feel rewarded for their hard work while on a team.
pros: Great company as for the benefits offered, they have a wide range of benefits for you and your family. Great work life balance if you are on the right team.
cons: They'd rather pay a new person coming in with 0 experience more than a seasoned individual moving up into a different role. I was heavenly tried by a hiring manager a few times when moving to a total different sector of the company with the lateral move talk. Luckily they wanted me bad enough to fix the issue but still very difficult to get what your worth if you've constantly moved up in the company.

advice: Stop taking responsibility away from bankers.  You are making them glorified customer service reps and customers see this.  It deteriorates their credibility when every time a customer has an issue you have to call somebody else to get it resolved.  I literally had a customer ask "so what exactly can you do?"
pros: Decent benefits, good upper management
cons: Local management is highly variable. Ability to hit sales goals is highly dictated by the branch location since bankers are told not to solicit business outside of the branch.  The position used to have more responsibility but over the years PCBs were forced to "outsource" almost every type of business except opening checking and savings accounts and credit cards (however you can't really service cc's).  You will work Saturdays often.

advice: Develop the communication and the way the managers treat the employers. Follow standard like Scrum agile and don't try to follow manager standard because when you change to work with different manager every manager can has his own standard.
pros: I am not sure, maybe the salary and the value to have on your resume
cons: The manager is God, and everything depends from the manager you have. Doesn't matter if he doesn't follow any standard, everything has to be as he said, if he said I want you to finish this by tomorrow you have to finish, even if you try to explain there is not possible, he doesn't heard nothing. This was the first time I don't want to wake up to work, your quality life is gone. They way the manager talk you is not professional, if you say you expect to complete a user story in one or two day he interrupt you and laugh about the time you estimate and he said "I can do this in 5 minutes"

advice: If teams are understaffed, people can't think clearly and important stuff gets missed. Hire workers who can solve problems not managers who just create more bureaucracy.
pros:
There are always great opportunities to network with colleagues and volunteer to help not-for-profit organizations. With your corporate ID, you also get in for free or reduced cost to many museums and cultural institutions. 

Many managers are open to your working from home when you need to (as long as you are completely connected).

After you've spent at least a year in one role, you can move to something else -- through mobility.
cons:
Long hours, high stress, overworked teams without enough members. 

The interranking process is painful and results in team members fighting against one another instead of working together to create a better organization.

Too many conference calls!

advice: I enjoyed working with my managers. As for higher management..... they need to have a full understanding of what each employees role is. Don't just assume positions can be combined or handled by a customer call center overseas or in a central locale. This does not work in all departments.
pros: Great insurance benefits. Good vacation and sick time. My managers were fair and provided assistance and support when needed.
cons:
After being a devoted and loyal employee for many years it began to feel as though the longer term employees were not appreciated as much as the employees with less tenure. 
As is common in banking, employees usually have to leave the company to be paid their true value. I stayed for many years because when looking at the big picture other things were more important to me.

advice: As one would expect, Chase is very a corporate environment.  Within the commercial Bank, decisions are made at an executive level of management.  Costs are driven down to low level cost centers.  Servicing and operations continues to move offshore leaving very little room for a control over US customer experience.
pros: Chase offers incentives based on performance.  Teams are rank down to the individual level.  If you have had  a year where you have exceeded expectations, you will be at the top of the list and receive compensation as anticipated.
cons: Performance ranking is subject allows for too much room as it relates to personal management discretion.  Team performance ranking must fit into a box of 20% exceeds expectations, 70% meets expectations and 10% needs improvement despite the actual performance of a team.

advice: widen the scope of duties, and have everyone rotate teams on a bi-monthly basis to gain more exposure to all forms of cases in the retail banking industry.    Swap teams with the brokerage and mortgage houses to build well rounded compliance professionals instead of mere investigators.
pros: It was very vet friendly,  as about 1/3rd of the analysts were military veterans or reservists when I joined.   Hours were somewhat flexible without needing to ask for each change, and there was good team espirit backed up by meals and parties
cons: Production based work, which grew more regimented as processes changed.    Due to the large size, teams specialized in case types which meant a "Small Aperture" approach to the subject, and less gain in skill.

summary: Chase is a great place to work
advice: Please try to find a way to keep your best employee's despite the downturn
pros: Many opprtunities for advancement, industry leader.  Pay is fair and job security is better than the other major banks.  Many different divisions to transfer into if you are concerned about your job security.  Training is provided to help you develope skills that can always help you in postions with other companies if you decide to leave.  It is one of the perceived winners in the financial meltdown
cons: Tough time to work in the banking industry.  It is a big organization so you can get lost in the shuffle if you do not proactively promote your work and achievements  Job losses are mounting in certain divisions

summary: JPMorgan is a great place to work, offers interesting, challenging work at competitive salaries
advice: JPMorgan should seriously consider revamping the performance review process, to make it less subjective and reliant on abilities of your own manager to present your case in an impactful way.
pros: From my experience, JPMorgan has many intelligent employees who are good to work with.  They also support mobility within the company.  A big bank like JPM has some of the biggest technology challenges, so therefore also interesting technology work.
cons: The huge size of the company can make people who aren't natural networkers not succeed as well as they might in a smaller place where their work is easier to recognize.  Also, the performance review and inter-ranking process is very tough as a manager, and can be unfair in some cases.

summary: business lending and relationship manager for larger small businesses.
advice: The regular retail branch business bankers should receive more training in credit and compliance.  You need to pick a priority that people should focus on and not always change it.
pros: I'm get along very well with all the members of my team and the management that I work for.  The systems are all very good and people are given the tools they need to succeed.
cons: I've heard that the compensation at other regional banks can be higher.  I haven't verified this or anything, just heard rumors about it from people who have left.  Having so many branches is great from a visibility perspective, but it makes it very difficult to attract new businesses since so many already bank with Chase or have in the past.

advice: Be more of a leader and not a boss.
pros: Learned alot about the industry.
cons: Worked to the the bone and had to work overtime just to get paid.  Allowed little to no breaks so you're constantley working in a high stress environment.  I was expected to be a machine and have zero errors.  Management would not give me a bonus for 4 minor errors from 3000 calls. Everyone hated their jobs which trickled down to new employees. High turnover.  Could never even network with collegues long enough before they were gone. Suppose to be a 52-week training program yet people would be there for years or leave the company. Very few would advance within the company. Also, there are so many policies and procedures that you have to walk on eggshells.

advice: In order to improve retention there should be more things done to show that the employees voices are being heard. Casual Fridays and other similar notions are weak attempts at creating a better office environment. There are no lounge areas and office space can be crowded since the company is in an expense cutting phase but I guess that can be expected with a finance company.
pros: JP Morgan roles offer exposure on the scale that few companies can match. They also offer at first glance attractive salary and vacation from entry-level through Officer level
cons: At the Delaware offices there was an extremely high turn over and little planning by management to help retention. Highly political office environment where you were expected to stay late even if your work was done, this differed depending on the team.

pros: Nice benifits      d                                 d
cons: Sometimes hectic                       d                                                 d                      d

advice: Good ideas do come from Columbus OH - we managed a successful regional bank out of Columbus for a long time before we became part of JPMorgan
pros: Salary, benefits, and interesting work. Versus other jobs in the financial industry in the area - great opportunities for self motivated people.  Career advancement and other opportunities within the firm are readily available, once you get your foot in the door, it becomes much easier to move around, and some movement is in fact encouraged to build well rounded employees.
cons: Large corporation, distance from NY offices where decision making is generally occurring.  With shifts in economy, generally a fairly decent sized purge of staff occurs every 3-5 years as new management changes the focues and priorities, and some areas are deemed less desireable.  Strong focus on cost cutting throughout the bank.

summary: WaMu WAS a great place to work.
advice: Senior Management should have used some common sense in the mortgage market.
pros: WaMu had a lot of great talent.  The company paid well for performance and did not give raises and bonuses to poor performers.  Achievements were publicly recognized, which is good, but too often those achievements were made possible by ignoring all policies and going full speed ahead.  The company should strive to recognize those that achieve great things while still following processes and policies.
cons:
The biggest downside is the company failure.  When WaMu was a going concern there was not enough accountability for poor performance.  Employees who did not perform well were never fired and were allowed to drift along.

Another downside was the lack of good training.  There were many online course offered but many things cannot be taught effectively in an online course.

summary: With the right opportunity, a great place to work!
advice: Make the tough decisions when evaluating staff for retention or promotion.  Often, the wrong person for the job is rewarded with the selection.
pros: In this economic environment, Jamie's fortress balance sheet can be extremely comforting.
cons:
The never ending mergers and acquisitions of other firms has resulted in a poorly defined and understood corporate culture.  If you are lucky, you will work with strong direct management  with a strategic vision to accomplish objectives.

In the current climate, mobility is an issue.  Although jobs are available, the numerous M&A's have resulted in decentralization of resouces.  If your willing to go to Columbus, Texas or the north-west, you may have an opportunity for mobility.  Forget it if  your tri-state based.

Carefully consider the compensation and benefits.  As with most companies, the overall package is becoming less attractive.

summary: The worst corporate culture I have ever experienced
advice: More than half of the management is redundant and serves only to protect itself and make life as difficult as possible for the employees - status calls, spreadsheets to track everything, dashboards, a giant waste of time.  This company could easily fire half of the people who are in management roles and have zero negative repercussions.
pros: Decent pay (but not best in class), and some degree of growth is possible if you play the political games and do whatever they ask you to do, no matter how stupid it is.
cons:
Routinely threatened to move to a "strategic" location (basically Ohio, Texas, Florida or NY/NJ).
No clue about letting people work from home, or other locations.
Micromanagement like crazy - managers demanding their employees get doctor appointments pre-approved before they make them.  
Constantly being told to do stupid and contradictory things.
Organization is completely broken due to processes and change controls, it can take months to do something as simple as setup a server in a datacenter or get access to login to a system.

advice: Stop the propaganda about promoting career-mobility if the senior managers wont let the employees go. People want to stay with the bank but not in the their current role
pros: unlimited overtime upto 6 months a year and good benefits
cons:
under-paid but you have the OT , peer group sucks - about 90% of the people complain but dont do anything about it. I was a part of a college group of 95 people and only 10% of the people are left after 4 years. People come and go all the time in this business specially with Chase. It depends if any money is the factor that drives you - this job isnt that bad but at the end of the day you will be soul-less. Management sucks - you always gotta be looking out for yourself. 
If you are 45+ and want a stable job till you retire: this place isnt that bad but if you are young and ambitious it will suck the soul out of you. Staying out of the corporate retail dept. is a good call.

advice: Make it worthwhile to keep your current employees, reward them with a substantial increase, develop training to keep them interested in staying with the company this would definitely help with turnover. Review why employees leave the company for other opportunities and see if there is a trend, then work on a course of action to remedy this situation.
pros:
Great place to climb the corporate ladder. 
My schedule works well for me being a single parent.
Promoted to another department with less than 2 years of being with the company.
Medical, vision, dental, 401K benefits are great.
cons:
Starting pay and increases are horrible. With the economy and profits being generated increases should not be less than $1.00 this would probably also aid in the high turnover.
Turnover is horrible by the time training is completed employees are leaving which means that the company has not benefited from hiring these employees.

advice: Focus on the talent that wants to be there and they won't leave
pros:
Looks great on resume but that is about it. 
Do not stick around for long if you care about your wallet and career growth
cons:
- Almost no room for growth (if at all)
- 2 years without a raise
- Stagnant Bonus
- What you know is irrelevant vs who you know
- Office politics play a massive role 
- Outdated mainframe system, poor tech investment, poor support
- Heavy outsourcing initiative, poor employee morale
- Layoffs and cost cutting makes you a dispensable worker
- Internal mobility CAN BE BLOCKED by your manager - shadiest tactic ever as it stunts your growth within and limits greatly your earnings potential.
- Low pay vs private institutions
- Mundane work with strict deadlines lead to a very stressful environment
- HORRIBLE job training - You are pretty much doing a lot self training
- High turnover rate

summary: Treated expendable and like a red headed step child. Operations
advice: Tell people what this job really is ahead of time. Will avoid the rapid and absurdly high turn over. It's a lame job and someone with only an associates degree can do it.
pros: Over time, if you want to waste your time. You are basically getting a paycheck to waste your time. It's only up from here, get an inside look at what the bottom and most thankless job in corporate banking is.
cons: Don't gain any skills. Don't get good raises or promotions. Operations get treated very poorly and nobody cares to make changes because you are just a number and an expense. Doesn't matter if you work 60hours a week, the only time you will get noticed is when an error happens and you get blamed. Avoid this job at all costs.

summary: Nearly 15 years with Chase and they laid me off and walked me out the door.
advice: Please practice what you preach!  I was told how valued I was as an employee (mostly during the EOS timeframe).  I started out as a rep and worked my way up to AVP.  Someone decided that the AVP role was not necessary and soon found myself on the outside looking in.  After nearly 15 years of dedication I was called into some snakes office and told I was being given a 45 day notice and was escorted off the premises like I had been fired!  I was not even permitted to return and pack up my belongings, I was humiliated.  I understand the financial aspects of the decision, but at least show your employees a little respect!
pros: Chase had excellent pay and benefits.
cons: Management in CBB, specifically in mortgage servicing and default are only concerned for themselves and their job security.  They constantly warn you that if you are not a top performer you wont be around long.

advice: Stop sweating the small stuff and focus more on leadership and technical training. Let people master what they already  know how to do, before introducing  changes. Changes tend to reflect a "flavor of the month" culture, whereby go-getter managers sign up for initiatives (to make themselves look good) and then delegate the actual work to employees.
pros: Employees and managers were sincerely helpful and forgiving of mistakes. Best new hire training, continuous training opportunities available which prepare you for success at other companies as well as Chase.
cons: Every typo or non-impactful mistake is documented regardless of overall performance, however, managers see this as "coaching." Regardless, this hurts team morale and comes across as petty and ridiculous. Often asked to do extra, unnecessary (flavor of the month) work by management as a result of managers advancing their own career agendas.

advice:
#1, QUIT OUTSOURCING.  Or get people who can actually speak English fluently.  
#2, direct managers need to start recognizing those who day in and day out give it their all.
#3, respect those who report to you and you will receive the same.
pros: Stable company.  Top level management appears to be leading the company in the right direction.  But this is wait and see.
cons: Current hiring freeze.  They are not replacing people who have left.  Puts more stress on current employees.  Senior management does not seem to care.  "Do more with less" attitude.  They recognize the wrong employees when others have bled their heart and soul into projects.  At times, direct managers treat their employees like they work at McDonalds.  Tons of "pissing matches" between groups in the same organization.  They outsource almost everything which causes a huge language barrier between off-shore and their U.S. employees.  Senior management allows managers reporting to them to perform badly too long before doing anything about it.

advice:
*Pay attention to suggestions made by the operations side.
*Keep close friends from working in Sr. Management together.
*Realize that working students are students who are working and scheduling them above and beyond what they were hired for will create problems.
*Keep branch associates motivated through regular contests backed with incentives.
*Do not hire unqualified employees due to an unexpected change in staffing.
*Seek and promote those employees who are loyal and add tremendous value to the company.
pros:
*Your resume will appear more presentable.  
*Opportunities for career advancement exists and there are training programs designed to help you get where you want to go.
cons:
*High turnover rate and staffing issues.
*It takes quite a bit of  time for your pay to change when you are cross-training for other positions.  Thus, the workload has increased without adequate compensation for up to a full year.

summary: WaMu swollowed up whole by JP Morgan Chase.
advice: Senior Management needs to take a closer look at driving efficiencies in all areas and at all levels of the enterprise.
pros: One of the few remaining banks with probably the most promising financial outlook. If you have a job that made through all the consolidations and transitions with Bear Stearns and Washington Mutual, you should have a secure and maybe even prosperous future at least through this challenging economic crisis.
cons: Huge corporation. Inefficient in many processes. At Washington Mutual we had focused to drive down costs in technology for the last 4 years without sacrificing customer service or quality. While challenging, I do think significant progress had been made. This became particularly visible when aqcuired by JP Morgan Chase where some of the organizational structures and technical strategies reflected the problems and issues WaMu had dealt with years earlier.

summary: Great financial institution to work for
advice: Assess what are the new working methodologies, tools and techniques that can be employed so that not only the company, but employees also gets benefited.
pros: Excellent work life balance, as there the work was not stressful and we could finish day's work in 8 hours. The management was also flexible regarding working hours. While the atmosphere was laid back, we could work on newer technologies at our own initiatives and also take up and accomplish side projects as we wish. The salary and bonus structure was also satisfactory, so was vacation, health beneits
cons:
Sometimes I felt that I am not working on cutting edge technologies and not in sync with the latest working methodologies and working style. The policies, processes, tools were still old fashioned with sseniority being one of major criterion for promotion. 
Other than that, I really cant think of any negative points.

advice: They should replace all of the management with better people. The management have been there for too long where they think they can get away with anything. Also they need to change their rating.review process where it is so unfair to the employee.
pros: It can be a pro if you're straight out of college and its your first professional job
cons:
Too many to mention...like other reviewers mentioned before a lot of red tape, political bureaucracy, offshoring our jobs away, bad management from top to bottom. There is no growth within the company unless you know people from the top..its all about who you know not how hard of a good employee you are which is a shame. There is no room for growth career wise. Once you believe it is time to go, listen to your gut and go, don't hesitate. 

The company treat their employees like child slaves in a sweat factory...all they care about is getting the work done and not about the well being of their employees.

DO NOT WORK HERE!!!

summary: JP Morgan Chase - Global Technology Management
advice: Realize that you can't keep cutting staff and still have a reasonable work life balance.
pros: Great Salary, Lots of responsibility, fast paced environment, leading edge technology
cons:
Long hours are expected. There were many weeks that I worked 60+ hours. It was needed to get the job done. 

They are constantly looking to cut cost and people is one way that they do that. Doing more with less it the common montra. 

I don't know if they still do, but they used to use a forced ranking system that demanded that 20% of the employees in a department were Exceptoinal, 70% were Acceptable and 10% were in need of improvement. This worked fine for a couple of years, but eventually good people were forced into a need improvement ranking because we had to meet the distribution curve.

advice: JPMorgan is focused on cost cutting and efficiency but sometimes sacrifices the human aspect of employees.  Please shift a bit more to caring about employees to maintain a balance.  Try to bring back the loyalty that it once was.
pros: Top benefits, great rewards for hard workers who come up with efficient methods and positive solutions.  Lots of lateral mobility.  Environment that encourages change and improvement.  If the culture of the firm suits you, then you will keep wanting to come back (if you ever do leave).  You get a feeling that you are working in a center of excellence.  Work from home opportunities are great!
cons: Not for those who are afraid of change.  Could be a lot of long hours if there is a new implementation or client.  This can interfere with work-life balance.

summary: Used to be so much better
advice: Stop chasing the almighty dollar and ignore obvious fragrant violations. All employees should be held to the same standards and not have an advantage when they are friends with upper management.
pros: Vacation days. The January of the next year when you are hired will give you 3 weeks of paid vacation days. In addition you also get one week of sick time and accrue floating holidays throughout the year.
cons: Too much politics. They have moved away from merit based promotion to unfortunately personal affiliation. They take a strong position that any employee can go to HR if they have any complaints or concern without any retaliation but this is simply not the case. If they brand you a troublemaker they will make your life a living hell and find a way to get rid of you.

summary: No surprises from a company this large
advice:
- Allow teams to fail and make mistakes. So much is learned from doing so.
- Humanize your managers. People shouldn't have to figure out how to move mountains because some executive read something in "Technology Today"
- You're not a technology company. Just because most of your business relies on technology doesn't mean you're a technology company. Stop claiming you are.
pros:
- Great experience working in a big corporate environment
- Tons of opportunity within the company
- Competitive pay and good benefits
cons:
- Innovation is only done by the business and never really from the technology side
- Not a place that tolerates mistakes or failures
- Extremely hierarchal. Everyone treats their managers as inhuman and never challenge their decisions.
- Everyone is always covering their rear ends. Working as a team is not part of the company culture even though they may claim it is.

advice: My suggestion  would be to have some of the employees that actually do the work to be involved in some of the decision making with upper management, as they do not have a glimmer of what is  actually going on for a specific project because they are not involved on a day-to-day basis.
pros: The people here are very nice, very respectful and make it a pleasure to come to the office each day.  We all worked very well together and always learn something new from someone else who has and put regularly. For such a big organization and the communication as well established
cons: The onboarding process is very tedious and not very well planned out.  Too many untrained individuals trying to get a new employee established when they really aren't aware of what the employee will be doing.  Took months.

pros: There are a lot of good people working there.  Overall, they try to promote you maintaining a good work/life balance.  I have been able on occasion to work from home but for the most part they like everyone in the office.
cons: The work pace can be heavy with a lot of expectations of overtime.  Although, that comes with our choosen field.  They don't have much of a culture of celebrating successes.  When, I first started here they seemed to try to promote an enviroment where people got to know people outside of just doing there job.  That has seemed to disolved.  More recently, they have been trying some new programs.  Perhaps, they have noticed this and are trying to change it.

summary: The people I worked with where great but the managers have no clue on how to manage people.
advice: Learn how to manage people!  Provide them feedback and goals so they can work to achieve them.  Meet with them regularly on their performance, and conduct weekly staff meetings.  Provide strategic vision to the team so they know where the ship is being steered!
pros: People are great to work with, helpful and friendly.  The pay is comparable, if not slightly better than industry standard.
cons: Management has no clue how to manage people.  Remote management never met with employees or held staff meetings.  The system's at Chase are legacy-based and ancient.  Company very slow and resistant to change management principles.  The political atmosphere outweighs people's work performance.

advice: Be competent. Learn the job from a technical aspect so that you can contribute and not just read spreadsheets and charts. Don't be afraid to promote top talent. At least you'll keep them in the bank and add some levels of competency to the bank. Otherwise the truly smart people will seek employment elsewhere.
pros: The company is large so there are lots of jobs posted and the opportunity to move around is there--it's not terribly difficult. The key is networking, which is abundant. Being internal gives you a better idea of the job titles and salary ranges available for various jobs. If you're applying from the outside it's an undecipherable corporate maze. There's lots of groups and internal resources. The company has some nice perks for events and activities in and around NYC. There are lots of JPMC office buildings and each has its own culture. The HQ at 270 Park Ave is super flashy (which some like and some don't) and has a nice employee cafeteria and an internal Starbucks. There are on site nurses, doctors, physical therapists and lots of other services available for employees. The culture of work/life balance and all other such things depends solely on the Line of Business (Commercial Bank, Investment Bank, Asset Management, etc). The Retail Bank is probably a standalone entity that cannot be compared to any of the other lines of business because it is incredibly different and distinct. Most people in Commercial Bank seem to be the happiest and most content with their colleagues even if they don't particularly care for their job. But that's what the internal job referral site is for. Move on! Move up!
cons: Large corporate maze. Moving around can be hard to do because corporate titles are hard to understand even internally. There are tens or even hundreds of thousands of people in some Lines of Business making it very hard to know what people really do. There are a TON...absolute TON of middle managers. Just managers in charge of other managers who really shouldn't be employed but were moved or shuffled from some other reorganized area and ended up being a manager of managers. Pay is not as high as the competitors like Goldman, but JPMC is so much larger that it wouldn't make economic sense for that to be he case (this doesn't apply to Investment Banking, as that is a different animal).

summary: Great Company, Bad Advancement and Compensation
advice: Talented people are leaving that want to stay because of bad promotion polices and being compensated way less than market. Adjust promotion and compensation policies.
pros:
There is a focus on Work/Life balance. 
20 paid vacation days, 6 paid sick days, and 2 personal days.
cons:
Corporate Policy is promotions only at the end of the year.
Had two advancement opportunities blocked 1. I couldn't go from an analyst to a manager because I had to be a senior analyst first even though the hiring manager felt I was the most qualified for the position. 2. Hiring freeze has stopped me from being promoted to a VP.
You can't be exceeds expectations two years in a row if you were promoted the year before.
Compensation is way below market.

advice: Bring in another VP who has actually been a documentation analyst.  Coaching is not sending an email.  Work to retain your best people.  When you have that strong a percentage of PiP's the problems are among your trainers and managers.
pros: Benefits were very nice.  The company in general is a great company to work for.
cons: Be cautious of new departments.  I worked in a new department after they closed this department in NY.  Manager did not understand our jobs,nor how to evaluate how we were doing.  Supervisors either didn't care or were on a power trip. More than half the department is on Pips and afraid of losing their jobs over small petty mistakes while others who make financial mistakes are being promoted.

advice: Engage more with the teams and create an inclusive work environment. Promoting individuals only based on time in line of business rather than potential candidates with well-verse backgrounds adding value to the organization and LOB to enhance overall performance to achieve stated outlined goals. With Managers, some that require guidance and mentoring, have been in their positions too long feeling a sense of stagnation and the lack of experience or motivation to achieve maximum potential in their career and the ability to influence others.
pros: Excellent Benefits and current stability of employment
cons: No career mobility. The management team only looks at length of time employed in the department at Chase rather than a comprehensive review of experience in management, operational production, Career Achievements, and abililty to mentor and motivate our teams.

summary: Opportunities are few and far between
advice: There need to be more ways for employees to get involved creatively and to voice when present managers are inefficient, incompetence or are otherwise using work time as personal time.
pros:
+ Huge global network with a quarter million employees worldwide
