+ Networking opportunities at NY HQs (270 Park & 373 Madison)
+ Tremendous opportunity to learn about an industry that fuels the growth of this city & country
cons:
- Very difficult to move into front office roles
- Wildly different cultural environments based on your line of business, department, and office
- Unless you're lucky, you need to "pay your dues" - being a standout employee isn't enough, you'll need to spend at least a few years in same role and at same pay grade before any sort of promotion happens

advice: Help out your team move to different roles, put out a good word for them, if they deserve it. Help them meet the right people not just advance in the department they are currently at.
pros: Great company with very generous PTO and 401K contributions. Culture is great, management is great. They keep you trained and up to date with what you need to succeed.
cons: Very difficult to move internally, even though they do promote career advancement. If you have the experience but not the right degree it will be very difficult to get considered for a different position yet alone get an interview. The positions that are available to you are more than likely lateral positions which provide you with a small to no raise in salary.

advice: Transparency for pay and everyone deserves inflation raises if nothing else for good performance.  I have seen them give people raises who didn’t even work but a couple months out of the year, managers don’t get to allocate raises, someone in HR does it.  There also not enough opportunities to work remotely or at least jobs that can be done from anywhere.  A company in Baltimore recently gave employees life changing bonuses, take notes and action Chase!
pros: Good culture where mild amount of pressure is present and if you are Managment you will get a very modest bonus.
cons: They pay to come in, but don’t expect a raise afterwards and if you get a promotion, don’t expect the raise till the next year in February if at all.

summary: Don't worry, you won't stay long
advice: Pay attention to how people are treated. Try to notice when people aren't happy. Do something about it. That's why you're paid the big bucks.
pros: To get experience right out of school. To learn how to navigate in a HUGE corporation--or--the military. As a stepping stone. Don't think these people are your friends--they're not.
cons: It's like working for the government. It's huge, bloated, slow and wasteful. They absorb other companies like a sponge. At least they have THAT down to a science.  Politics are INCREDIBLE there--never saw anything like it in over 15 yrs of working on Wall St. Too many complicated, useless systems in IT. Too much process--not enough content. That's what you get when you have 200,000 co-workers.

summary: A safe bet but you probably won't strike it rich.
advice: Stop outsourcing.
pros: Company is strong and growing.  Many opportunities to move laterally throughout the company and is a good place to start your career.   There is a job for every type of person here, from legal, to marketing, to computer science, to sales and trading.
cons: There is a lot of bureaucracy which can be frustrating although that is true for many large corporations.  Your bonus isn't as influeneced by your performance as much as your line of work.  There aren't as many fringe benefits as other large banks.  Getting harder to get in the door starting out as an analyst since they are hiring so many people in India to do the analyst jobs.

summary: A good job for the young & single.
advice: JPM has work/life policies their just not applied.
pros: Large network of diverse professionals provide for a longlasting relationships.  There are some good opportunities occasionally for advancement.  A good job for those able to sacrifice extra hours.  Some training and career development is provided.  The firm has a diverse business mix and many offices providing some flexibility in buiding a career.
cons: work/life balance sacrifice is needed to advance and often heavy hours are expected regardless.  cost cutting and layoffs happen regularly, often not publicly announced.   job security never really exists which seems to effect morale and teamwork..  pay, bonuses and resources seem constrained in a tight cost control environment.

summary: Looks good on a resume, but....
advice: Learn to show more respect to your people, realize that the high turnover rates actually end up costing you more in the long run.
pros: Pay is pretty good. Job can be interesting when you actually get to do something technical instead of fighting bureaucracy all the time. And when you decide to look for a new job, JP MORgan Chase looks good on a resume.
cons:
Management has no regard for work/life balance and thinks it's fine to have you work 60-80 hour weeks on a regular basis. 

The level of bureaucracy and red tape to get even the smallest thing done is astounding. Most of your day will be taken up by endless, mind numbing meetings where you go over the same things over and over every week.

advice: There is a direct correlation in how employees are treated  (employee satisfaction) and the level of customer service delivered.
pros: The salaries are competitive.  There are some mid-level managers who are glue of the company and are truly the unsung heros. The CEO Jamie Dimon is great.  He is a great leader.
cons: A very cold company to work for.  Managment by fear is used.  Forced stacked ranking (rank and yank) drives performance managment.  Forced stack ranking is held over employees heads as a threat.  10% of the workforce is managed out every year -- even if the employees areperforming .   It is certainly one way to keep salary expense down.  The work enviornment is poor .  Morale at this company is very low.

advice: JPMC seems to have a lot of duplicate work happening across all the lines of business.  If many of these tasks were consolidated then you would likely see some great synergy and reduction in costs.
pros: The pay as an intern is comparable to something you would expect in fulltime.  There was even a signing bonus for an internship.  Incredible.  The flex time was great.  The people are nice.  The cafeteria breakfast is cheap but the rest of the food is expensive.
cons: Too many people, kind of a depressing environment.  Very drab atmosphere and the building is setup like a sea of cubicles.  The work is very tedious and not very challenging.

advice: Force business heads to share leads or terminate them
pros: salary, experience, brand on resume, networking opportunities, some comraderie, sleep depervation training. It's a sales job and you will need to sell products that very few people need or understand because they are high margin products. The due diligence is poor. Portfolio managers are consolidated in Columbus and manage way too many accounts to truly be affective.
cons: vague expectations, throw the man next to you under the bus for promotion, stalinesque management. The culture makes the Marines look like the convent from the Flying Nun. The people you will work with are similar to JR Ewing but with less integrity. My advice is do it if for the resume but only if you can swallow the BS for a few years.

summary: JPMC is a strong company with top tier talent but
advice: JPMC needs to decrease bureaucracy to encourage a more innovative environment. Even though Jamie isn't leaving soon I'm worried about confidence in the company when he does go. Between now and then we need to get shareholders and employees comfortable with whoever the new CEO will be.
pros: Senior management makes a great effort to cultivate talent and encourages employees move around the company into different positions and lines of business.  The company is very strong and treats employees well.
cons: Hard to get a large increase in pay unless you get an outside offer that they have to match.  JPMC is a large organization so there are still bureaucratic issues and annoying red tape to deal with.

advice: Treat employees like professional adults, not grade school students.  No need to micro-manage if the employee is doing his/her work effectively.  Don't expect employees to be satisfied by increasing their responsibilities w/out it reflecting on their paycheck.
pros: Well known and respected company in the Financial Industry- looks good on resume
cons: Pay is average  compared to other financial institutions.  Difficult to move up the ladder unless you know the right people, managers expect too much of employees, constant changes add on to excessive workload, stressful environment, seems everyone working there is miserable.  Mid-year and end-of-year employee performance rating system is a joke (managers are told how many employees must fit a certain category- exceeds,  high meets expectations, low meets expectations, needs improvement.)

summary: Great firm to be a part of!
advice: Get in the trenches with your people- not only will they respect you more and want to win for you but it will keep your skill fresh and you will have a better team because it will help you manage them better.
pros: Solid work experience; those that want the opportunity to get ahead will get that opportunity to try. Top producers always highly compensated.
cons: Always peer ranked in bonus strucure so sometimes even though you worked really hard you may not get compensated for it. Not all positions allow work/life balance- most do not. There are a ton of career advancement opportunties if you decide to go one route but if not there really isn't a lot to choose from where you can advance.

summary: For a part-time job, it is definitely worth it.
pros: Part-time teller, when I worked for the company over a year ago, either worked 20 or 30 hours per week.  Being part-time you still get paid vacations days, paid sick days, the option to get health, vision and dental insurance.  Once you are vested with the company you have the option to get a 401K where the company matches up to 5%, a retirement plan and the option to buy stock.  You even get commission type things and possible bonuses at the end of the year.  Not too shabby.
cons: It is a major corporation so you have a lot of rules and a lot of management above you.

advice: Do not overhire the people when the times are good so that when the times are bad, you don't have to lay off people. I like the way the bank is so efficient in cost-cutting and that it has a clear idea of which direction it wants to take.
pros: Prestigious, big name company, everyone here is top-notch and very smart and you'll really benefit from learning from the brightest minds in the world.  There are also a lot of networking opportunities where you can meet and talk to people from the different lines of business. Mobility within the firm is also very good.
cons: long hours, and competition may get very intense.  It is also a huge company so it may get bureaucratic.

summary: Working as a Business Analyst at JPMorgan Chase
advice: Please try to be considerate toward the employees. They all work hard, and try to do their best. It would not hurt to let them know how good of a job they are doing. Provide some non-work activities to improve morale.
pros: Colleagues are friendly, and helpful. Lots of smart people that work very hard. Also, they are flexible about working from home, and taking time off.
cons: There is no real culture at JPMorgan. Everything is about meeting deadlines and getting the job  done. No much interaction outside of work. At the end of every year, the conversation tends to focus on the budget for next year, and whether there might be a reduction in headcount. Career mobility is hardly mentioned as an option.

advice: Keep the momentum going, but think about retention of junior employees and what it will take to improve the current stats. Clearly there are issues keeping talent in the pipeline as they progress towards senior management.
pros: I worked at JPMorgan as an IBD associate.  In terms of the company itself, it was well-run and it felt great to watch the other banks distinegrate while we remained intact- I would probably attribute this to the quality of leadership at the top.
cons: In terms of lifestyle, it's as bad as any investment bank, but anyone looking for work-life balance wouldn't be in the industry. Reorgs and layoffs happened seemingly at random and quite surgically as opposed to them staging mass-layoffs or dismissing entire groups, which was unnerving.

summary: It was a positive experience except for the Team Leaders.
advice: Open your eyes. There's a lot of fraternization going on amongst the managers and team leaders.
pros: The flexible work schedule, awesome benefits, a lot of great people work there, and the site in Lake Mary, FL is really nice and is in a great location.
cons: Many of the team leaders were promoted from within for reasons other than work performance. The team leaders value brown nosing more than performance. Many talented managers get passed over for promotions because they were busy developing their teams and achieving superior numbers consistently every month for those managers who's teams performed horribly but they were good at brown nosing. If performance were valued more, the company would be doing even better than it is.

summary: I have learned a lot from my experience with Chase, it has enabled me to move up the corporate ladder.
advice: Reward your internal employees who are talented enough for promotions by promoting them and most importantly rewarding them for these promotions.  Sometimes feel you are better off leaving the company if you are really looking for an appropriate pay raise.
pros:
Big company with lots of opportunity to gain knowledge for use both within and outside the company.
Jamie Dimon is one of the few bright spots in the financial industry over the last several years.
cons: Their compensation practices during promotions; they are unfair when it comes to compensation for internal promotions.  Someone coming from outside will get more money than someone getting promoted from within to the same position.

summary: Taking interest in the engine of your company
advice: setup controls to monitor how much care is to engine of the company(without the engine the car dies) in today's modern corporations there should be no room for discrimination  - top level management need to investigate because that very behavior because it will take jpmorgan down reputationally. 2.The Talent Re-assignment program should be a cost saving program but the managers are not utilizing the program to cut cost, every company is trying to retain there talent but the managers at chase are releasing and re-recruiting which make no sense, maximizing the potential of this program should make business sense!
pros: JPMorgan is a solid company that could be around for a long time with a few administrative changes
cons: The low level workers are mistreated

summary: so so company, stable but mediocre.
advice: pay the out performers more generously.   80% work done by 20%.  So should pay accordingly
pros: it is very stable, never heard any layoffs, at least in our department.   So a good place for your life before retirement
cons: more than half of people know nothing and do nothing.   I guess it is true for most giant firms.  So your pay gets diluted.  Even if you are a super star, does not make much difference.   after merger with Bear, you can tell the difference between Bear and JPM people.  The former are top notch for sure, far more knowledgeable and productive.  BTW, I am not ex-Bear.   Mediocre wins and management plays favorites.

pros: Great competitive atmosphere as well as incredibly smart coworkers.  The company holds very high expectations of each individual thus this job trains you well for others to come. You get to work with the top companies of each industry and it is a great experience as a result. Compensation is very competitive, but often times that is all that you can hold on to. The timely performance reviews also are helpful in keeping you on track.
cons: Life outside work is almost non-existent when a minimum work week requires 75 hours, and you are working 90+ hours during high season. When I was working there I would have all three meals by myself at the desk, and offices tend to be dead quiet so this isn't for everyone.

summary: Unpleasant work experience with no structure and organization
advice: Employee appreciation, morale and loyalty is needed & should be strived and reached.   Professionalism within upper management needs to be better displayed at all times and use of profanity should never be used or acceptable in the work environment.
pros: Good 401k and retirement options
cons: Inadequate new hire training  which doesn't provide the employee with the appropriate tools to do the job; poor communication & inadequate guidelines, department policy & procedures were outdated and consistently being changed, which meant that the employee and thw work suffered; favoritism very prevalent;  need clearer and precise guidelines before the department can effectively meet business objectives & goals; and department head consistently exhibited unprofessional and inappropriate behavior in and outside of the office.

advice: Slow down.  Look at the total picture.
pros: Great Benefits, Onsite Cafeteria, Decent people.  Flexibitliy with start time.  Lots of options for moving into different areas of company.
cons:
Way too many employees that you feel comfortable at times.

There are cliques and the in group everywhere.  Even poor performers are able to move into a different area if you're in the group.  If you're not in the group you get on a PIP plan.


They preach being personable to the group but when you do talk in the office it's brought up in your one on one that you talk to people as a negative

Expectations that new employees know the lingo should be scaled back.  Someone not from the industry doesn't understand everything.  Explanations should be given.

advice: You can be true to the client without being excessively restrictive to your employees. Learn to value them - and I don't mean with donuts and pizza and an annual favoritism contest.
pros: Pay is great, hours are okay, depending on what shift you get. If you are a permanent employee, the benefits are decent. During peak season, you have the opportunity to work overtime, and during low season you can take time off without pay if you'd like.
cons: In this small branch, there is little to no room for advancement. Management plays favorites big time, and if you're not on 1st shift, you don't hold a lot of sway. Rules for production are myriad and contradictory. They are very strict about electronics. If you are a temporary employee, during the low season you may be forced to take leave without pay.

advice: Get the branches better organized and everyone will make more money.
pros: It's what you make of it. You can wait for business to come to you and make your base pay and a little commission. Or you can be self-motivated and earn a lot.
cons: You have to be in a good branch in a good area to make $$$. I transferred to a branch with a lot of homeless and got bogged down with activities that didn't produce sales. They need more personal bankers and help on the teller line to allow the higher level bankers the time and room to focus on high net worth clients.  Also, if you are going to make bankers the Manager on Duty (MOD) you should actually give them a raise to compensate the operational activities.

advice: Don't offer networking events to employees if the networking doesn't work (and that is not just from me). We started with a group of 28 underwriters which now all are about gone due to not being able to move up or any other division at Chase.
pros: Great Work/Life Balance. Great Support by direct team leads and supervisors. Great training for the role you will do. Great place to start a career.
cons: Slow Movement upward. Hard to jump into other divisions of company. Consistent excuse of "we don't know you" although you meet the managers and others at corporate functions. No way to "prove yourself" for these other divisions - they believe you are only good at the job you currently do and do not believe you would be a good fit anywhere else. So, to move up, you must move out.

pros: The pros are that you are working for a great global firm in that the businesses are very successful and there is opportunity for a long and diverse career, if you are lucky.
cons: You have to play the corporate politics and game in order to be successful here. They talk a lot of talk but ultimately that is the name of the game to move up the ladder at JPMC. You can't just do great at your job and show that you are ready to move up; instead it's all in who you know if you really get the opportunity. There is a lot of great talent being missed because they aren't the type of people to run around networking instead they are the ones with their heads-down working actually getting things done.

summary: Interview the employer first… it’s retail.  Also it’s who you know there…
advice: If you didn’t do the job prior really well you probably won’t do the next level up role that well.  Your pushing the good people out.  Where have they all gone.
pros: This use to be the land of opportunity and growth for all individuals. They would tap you on the shoulder to promote you and you use to be able to make livable pay, kinda. You Must be PL1 or2. The JP Morgan name will bring in business and your as a bottom front line worker.
cons: You must understand how incentive/scorecard works in order to get paid a bonus if any at all. Then it will change the following year and most likely go against you. Different middle management every 1-3 years then you must prove yourself over again to the next girl.

pros: Working at JPM has lots of pros of course: great benefits, access to financial services, being constantly surrounded by very smart people and learning a lot about finance. i'm proud to work here. of course, it's very dependent on your team and manager. I'm lucky to have a really great manager who doesn't micromanage and a mostly great team. Pay is VERY good compared to skills needed. Management is very understanding of work/life balance and having a family and a "life" outside of work.
cons: growth can be tough because it's such a giant firm. you really have to push through but it can be done! again, since it's such a big firm, there are A LOT of bureaucracies in place that can be annoying but i think the pros outweigh the cons.

advice: Think about your employees. Stop cutting the incentive plan. Improve the pay. Stop lying about caring your clients when the company can not take care of employees
pros: You can have nice co worker and manager. 401k and time leave
cons: Low base pay. Not competitive compared to other banks. A great example of corporate greed. Commission structure gets cut all the time. Making harder and harder to earn every year. 40% bankers left. Imaging your pay gets cut 30-40%. They cut employees' commission to boost profits. Employees at the branches are over working. I have been working here for 3 years and have not seen employee satisfaction increase. Executives are great at talking motivation but lack of practical executions. Negative outlook. If you happen to be in good location, you will be ok. If not, good luck to make a living and move up.

advice: Work life balance does matter. This is not how it “used to be”, priorities have changed for most people in the world and family is as important as a job, if not more.
pros: Teamwork and atmosphere depends on which group you are a part. Make sure you ask lots of questions regarding your leadership and their style of leading.
cons: Flexibility has been limited recently with chairman’s decision of everyone coming back to office. Many of us in technology are working in hybrid - 1/2 time WFH and 1/2 time office. Team collaboration is still limited due to COVID restrictions while in the physical office, we question the value of being in the office.

advice: Reward people for the level of their performance rather than giving them a salary that seems appealing coming through the door. Try to keep talent rather than just acquiring it.
pros: The best reason to work for JP Morgan Chase would be the actual wor enviroment. You'll find the people to be intelligent and welcoming. Manager's aare understanding when it comes to life events within the lives of their employees. They truly have a human side
cons: Compensation and Benefits are poor compared to other organizations. The company asks its employees for a higher level of production while not allowing them to see the reward. There are no incentives to outperform peer. It appears that the only way to see financial rewardsis to leave the company then return to the bargaining table.

summary: Good Job to start or end career in.
advice: Pay community banking employees more if you would like better consuemr market results.
pros: I worked at JPMC for 3 years. I started this job at 19 and had it through college. It teaches you the basics of the professional world and looks great on a resume. Chase usually hires good people to work in the branches as well, most people I have met have been very nice. Good stability, Benefits and Co workers
cons:
actual job and expectations are not very desirable. It is basically summed up by the same saying. "Lots of work, not lots of pay".
The best thing to do was to get out of there once it started becoming soul-crushing for me personally. Others however who are satisfied with mundane work and low pay tend to stay because of the great stability, and benefits. and great co-workers.

summary: This is a great place for work / life balance
advice: Keep your eyes on the future. Don't be afraid to intelligently embrace the benefits that new technology offers.
pros: While JPMorgan Chase is a very big company, and managerial approaches differ, I have found that everywhere I have worked within the bank, the work / life balance has been very good. I have been able to take vacations, sick time, and other absentee days without being made to feel bad about it. Also, having the ability to work from home when necessary is a big plus as well. Although this would not apply to all positions in the bank.
cons: This is a very large company, and really good talent may be over looked for a while, and may take time to be recognized by upper management.

summary: The best of the financial services...
advice: If you truly want to jump ahead of the pack in the current market, understand what it means to develop "customer-centric" solutions. It means being more proactive about the client experience from the top down - integrating client experience methodologies into the org's DNA so that it's truly institutionalized in every aspect of the business. Create proactive, client-focused solutions built around actual client needs (and with client input), not driven by pre-determined release dates, politics or pre-existing frameworks.
pros: Given the current economic climate for FSI in 2008, Jamie Dimon has positioned JPMorgan Chase very well with a strong balance sheet. He's a highly engaging and inspiring leader who encourages the best out of his employees. I feel completely confident in his leadership.
cons: Like most of the financial services titans, JPMorgan Chase is well-intentioned but remains a big, slow-moving ship with regard to change.

advice: Objectivity is sorely missing in the workplace. The current appraisal process is not entirely based on metrics, but on "FaceTime" and not what you know but who you know. Work/Life balance is preached as a concept, but not practiced. Management has made it clear that 100% is not enough.
pros: Benefits including vacations and the ability to work from home are great. Salaried workers receive 4 weeks vacation at the time of hire (pro-rated). The locations in downtown Chicago are near the trains and easily accessible to commuters.
cons: Appraisals are based on a curve, which makes it extremely competitive and does not foster teamwork. For example, if there are 20 employees on a team at the same grade level, 3 will exceed expectations, 14 will meet expectations, and 3 will not meet expectations. This is when politics, nepotism, and cut throat behavior comes into play. Yes nepotism is alive and well at JPMC! Additionally, overtime is expected and evaluated on your performance.

summary: Was a good place to work until they laid off everyone...
advice: To be more open to all levels of the orginization.
pros: The card service division was once providian which had its up and downs over the years.  Then Washington Mutual took over providian.  There were many good coworkers and a very freindly enviroment.  The management was very different department to department and the Washington Mutual core values did not seem to be followed / valued by different parts of management.   This was a good place to work until they laid off everyone after the FDIC forced the sell of Wamu to JP Morgan Chase.  Since then everyone spends there remianing time searching for a new job and going to interviews.  Good by Wamu and the crazy commercials.
cons: Not the best communication from management.  No heads-up to upcoming changes.

advice: Get your employees some chairs!! And put them behind a bullet proof window please!!!
pros: I managed to get along with my bosses and my coworkers. I did like the benefits and all the employee discounts available.
cons: I hated the fact that as a teller you had to stand up. Our stations were setup like a cell phone store but worse because there was an area for the customers to look around on the screen as you processed their transactions. This was invasive and uncomfortable for the employee. Now that I think about it, this was dangerous given that anyone could come in and easily physically assault us since it was a bank after all. I felt like WAMU did not care about our safety. My legs would hurt after a long day of standing up.

summary: Training needs to be provided so everyone knows the credit policy.
advice: Upgrade systems, update credit policy. Also when employees leave the company that Managers should not bad mouth former employees which is against the law and can be held liable for not getting that job. Loan officers need to be trained correctly because they would mislead clients that there was no closing cost and the loan processor would be responsible for everything that went wrong on the file and should refund the loan processing fee to the client for misleading them.
pros: Learned something new. Good Pay. Great co-workers supportive with one another when management were unprofessional.
cons: Senior management and Team Leaders were aggressively verbally abusive even when employees let Upper Management know what was happening they did nothing. They should be sued for bullying their employees.

summary: This is a first-class, goal-oriented organization whose leadership has rightfully won accolades globally.
advice: Consider major urban locations outside New York as more than mere sales centers growing them into centers of operational and leadership excellence.
pros: I have never worked for such a sophisticated operation in my 40-year career since leaving college.  The environment is demanding yet rewarding.  Management is rock solid.  Employee relations and communications are first class.  Quality of work-life is appreciated.  It is a pleasure, a privlege and a source of professional pride to be associated with the JP Morgan Chase franchise.
cons: There is an East Coast bias (yes, okay, so New York City is the center of the universe financial and otherwise, but...) that does filter through leaving a sometime sour taste.  This bias has been noted in employee surveys but management response is inadequate.

summary: one year as a teller at JP Morgan Chase
pros: They will train new hires really good. I was working at a Chase branch in Indiana. They send me to Indianapolis regional headquarters for both personal banker and teller trainings. They booked me a 5 stars hotels every time they sent me to Indianapolis for the trainings. They also do care about customer experience.
cons: They are very aggressive at getting new customers or existing customers to open a new checking/ saving accounts or credit cards. In the morning before the branch opened the doors to the customers, the branch customers would tell bankers and tellers that he wanted 3 savings accounts and 5 credit cards opened at his branch today. I believe, both tellers and bankers ended up recommending customers new accounts they do not really need.

summary: A lot of bureaucracy with a corporate tech culture
pros:
If you like working at a large company in a very corporate environment, this may be the place for you. 

-Lots of opportunities to move around to different lines of business within the bank
-People in higher positions are very willing to talk to new employees just starting out
-People are generally friendly
cons:
If you are in tech and are looking for a culture with a more startup/relaxed feel, this is probably not the place for you

-There is no quality standardization to the development lifecycle process
-Quality of teams greatly varies, e.g. a lot of teams will have you doing mundane back office work, some managers aren't that great, ... it is very hit or miss
-General lack of openness to creativity given the nature of the business

summary: J.P. Morgan is the worst company to work with
advice: Treat human as human .... respect their effort and hard work....I curse JP morgan chase
pros: I felt worse whole year I worked there...I cannot even think one positive thing of JP...
cons: Employee are treated as like donkey... no work culture ..no cubical to sit..it is total mess... Managers acts so weird..no one will help ..not at all.. they discriminate if you are green card holder or citizen... means if manager is on h1b then she can make your life worse... all managers are so insecure... even my team mates used to look like as if they are coming from some death bed.... forget about growing... and salary increment. I worked there for an year and left .. and I am so happy here in my new company.... Later many people left... same issues same worse behavior ..JP is full of fools and insecure people.. I wish I never worked there ... such a shameeeeeeeeeeeeee on this earth!!!!!

pros: Great work environment. Flexibility to work remotely if necessary. Not a lot of micro-managing, despite the many layers of leadership. Lots of areas for growth and movement if you're in the right Line of Business (LoB). The is a REAL sense of commitment to diversity. They encourage volunteering and being a part of business resource groups. If you want to advance you have to get out and meet people. There's lot of opportunity but you have to be pro-active. All the people that know people move on and up often.
cons: Lot os managers, and managers managers. Not a lot of transparency with pay grades, bonuses, and what goes into that. Can be confusing to navigate if you're a new hire and trying to determine total compensation.

advice: "We are Chase" is not an answer to all question regarding bank shortcomings.
pros: I was attracted by the compensation. In a small market like Stockton, Sacramento, or Fresno CA, the salaries paid are higher than average and the benefits / commission structure appear good. However, smaller markets are not the company's focus.
cons: Management of Business Banking in California has a retail banking (not commercial banking) background. They are very grindy (ie... what have you done today). They have set up goals in buckets (loans, deposits, new relationships, cash management, etc...), and want you to fill the buckets equally. Goals in small markets are ridiculously high, especially when they have divided the market down to small sectors; only owner occupied, no non-profits, no agriculture.

advice: Consider giving junior people at least some work-life balance.
pros:
- Working with really smart people
- Steep learning curve in the first year, great exposure for someone fresh out of college
- Great platform with a lot of opportunities for transferring within the firm to other departments
cons:
- The hours.  Forget about weekends and friends.  You will be in the office all the time, and pulling all-nighters is nothing novel at the IBD
- When there is no deal flow, there will be a lot of pitch work to be done that most of the time will lead to no actual deals
- It's all about the money and not much else.  If that doesn't sound too bad to you, then it's a great place to be

advice: Work to eliminate the old-school hierarchy in order to promote a more collaborative and joyful office culture - especially to retain young talent
pros: High pay, great benefits, job security. 3 year defined program. Managers act as "coaches" to refine your communication skills. Access to large amounts of JPM proprietary market analyses.
cons: Long hours (6:45am-9:00pm); Private Bank is inundated with bankers/investors hired because they come from wealthy families and therefore have a network of wealthy friends who will invest their money at JPM; culture is extremely hierarchal (as an analyst you are expected to be the first in the office and the last to leave, even if you completed your work); daily work has shifted from analytical to monotonous paperwork as new banking regulations have tightened compliance standards

summary: It's a big and diversified company, yet sometimes too many hierarchies
advice: Try to cut the redundancy in the hierarchy and save firms efficiency
pros: Looks like you have a lot mobility opportunities in the firm, and overall it's stable and too big to fail so a good place for people that wants a stable job.
cons: You only serve a very tiny part on the whole chain and sometimes things get very repetitive. There are quite a few internal opportunities out there in the firm but when are really want to move its up to your direct management team whether they would support you for that. And the performance review in my team is not really very transparent. So good firm, but your experience depends on which group you are in.

summary: Poor middle management and no way around it
advice:
If you/your manager do not see eye to eye on items like work life balance, the availability of an agreed on solution is near 0.  Contact HR?  Yeah right, they'll contact manager 1st thing they get off the phone with you.  Contact skip-level manager?  Yeah right, put a "troublemaker" sign on your cube nameplate.  
Although I have seen a few occasions of mobility, the bottom-line is your manager sets your performance ratings, your potential new manager will see the ratings (and will have to decide to care what they are), your potential new manager can/will contact your current manager for feedback, and your old manager holds your release date - everytime I've seen this argued at executive director level (or above) with both HR sides involved.
Insight360 may hold the key with performance reviews (review manager->contributor and contributor->manager; and peer review).  However who is going to tell their boss they suck!  (Please read above on HR/management as a team).  Annual bonus raises need to shift to the real-time model to make the insight360 really work.
pros:
Great pay/benefits for IT work.  I appreciate the family programs and health rewards system.
Work with some of the best/smartest (some not so much, but alas its a big company; find the good ones and work with them)
cons:
Hard work and long hours is unrewarded, it is expected.  Often told "your standard workload done exceptionally is a meets, middle of the road performance".   Our team was small and had enough work for quadruple the size (which management is FINALLY putting into affect by off shoring).  So to accomplish the standard would require over 60+ hours a week for every individual.  No end in sight.  So I take on a huge project and work 80 hour weeks (3+ months); direct management barely responded with an email good job.
No work in team work, just pass the hard work and take credit for the "concept".  
Managers and HR are a team (as they should be), noone looks out for the individual contributor (you are alone).  No oversight/insight to a manager in the wrong role (my manager didn't know at a 10k ft level what swap or http vs. https (umm... we are a security first, devops team)), performing questionable (although not illegal) activities, especially with vendors.
Performance reviews are 1 way: down.  No way to effectively make a change, even if a written statement is proven inaccurate with other written documentation.  Email is the foundation of any written communication and only saved for 6 months.  Performance reviews are 6 months (a joke, only thing that matters is your rating, just a virtual signature effort) and 12 months.  Thereby everything is based on your written notes, any saved offline communications, OR what your management said happened.  Even if you have proven inaccuracies, there is no way to affect a change.

summary: Who you have as a boss matters......
advice: When a discrimination claim comes in, some one who is not affiliated in any way needs yo talk to the person.  You will continue getting class action law suits by assuming a person who has had basic training only can be effective in this situation. (HR) rep.
pros: I loved what I did for a living. I watched my employees grow and got to know customers. The days went by fast.
cons: There is no way to stop a bad boss. If you happen to get a boss that discriminates due to age there is no one who believes you.  Your on your own.  Human Resources takes the highest managers word even if you offer cold hard facts.

summary: Great place to work if you want stability and good work-life balance
advice: Diversity and inclusion can be improved. It should not be a slogan touted in certain times, but should be acted on with discipline. For example, managers should be measured by how well they create and foster an environment that values diversity and inclusion; how they manage unconscious biases; how they develop talents from different backgrounds / who look different from themselves; how they listen to voices that differ from their own...  Simply meeting quotas for hiring a few select races will not deliver the true benefits of D&I.
pros:
1) Good work-life balance;
2) Internal mobility
cons:
1) In big banks things move slowly;
2) Roles are narrow, so it can be hard to learn and grow fast.

summary: It all depends on your branch and team
advice: Care about more than just top performing clients.
pros: If you get a good branch this can be a very lucrative job, with six figure earning potential. There are a lot of great advisors and bankers in this organization to learn from. Chase has great benefits, and you start off with a decent amount of vacation.
cons: Coworkers and other branches can be pretty cutthroat and will steal leads that you are already working with. A lot of the top performers are "gifted" their leads from the advisors, and get credit for closing a lot of business when they don't actually do much work. While management frowns on gifting it's actually pretty rampant. Also, way to much emphasis is put on Salesforce metrics...

advice: Pay employees more, more remote abilities, and take employee feedback better. If I give feedback to my manager she starts nodding her head and rolling her eyes. She is already formulating a response in her head to respond. What I get is no understanding from her. Terrible middle management.
pros: mostly remote, easy procedures to navigate, the systems are easy to use.
cons: The job is stressful, alot of preasure from management, clients, and internal partners. Minimal pay increases, and you get more clients being added to your portfolio. If you mess up a little people will start complaining about you in all directions. Management is so greedy. They report billions in earnings and you get 0-3% raises.

summary: Typical bureaucracy for a large company
advice: Less is More.  Streamline the process and you could produce the same amount of work with a much smaller workforce.
pros: I make above market wage.  Job is relatively easy.
cons: Every process and procedure is way more complicated than it needs to be.  I have been doing the same job for about 18 years for different mortgage companies.  I currently produce about 1/2 the work I used to due to the complicated structure and unreliable computer systems they have.  Upper management rules from above and does not allow lower level managers to make any decisions.  They purposely chose weak people (mostly women) as lower level managers because they will be compliant and do what they are told.

summary: Client Processing Manager - Custody Middle Office
advice: Find Managers with experience within the scope of the department. People management skills are great but if you don't dominate the subject matter then you can't necessarily jump in when the fight starts.
pros: JPM is a phenomenal company to work for. The mobility within the company is second to none and salaries are very competitive if not beyond what other Financial Services shops offer. had the pleasure to work with a great group of people. Young and old, all energetic and willing to go the extra mile to get the job done.
cons: Long hours but that's true of any company today. Don't worry, if you are on the clock then you'll be making serious money at a young age.

summary: Spent too much of my energy with the company
advice: Learn to realize your colleagues are not just workers they are a human with other things going on with them. We will not just be overworked especially with our large workload because of COVID. They make you call customer all day and if you don’t meet your quota then you have to stay at work till you do meet the requirements.
pros: Chase banks are everywhere so it’s easy to work there however they pay you less than working at a fast food restaurant like In N Out
cons: They do not care about the workers the way they say they do. They do not pay for all the hard work people do. Will overwork you and not think twice about it.

advice: Focus on developing the talent you have in house and paying them market value
pros: Great benefits such as healthcare, vacation, 401k match, backup care for working parents, etc. very friendly coworkers, offices nationwide, there are managers that truly care about their employees and advocate for their reports, although this varies greatly
cons: front line employees are underpaid when compared to other banks, most managers are not interested in considering candidates that do not fit their "check list" or "box," which is why mobility between different lines of businesses is extremely difficult and opportunities to take on new roles for career development are rare, the bank prefers to hire outside candidates that require no training rather than developing employees interested in growth

advice: Good people are assets, not a cost. Respect their desires to work from home, especially when you have given 3%-4% increases during 10% inflation rates.
pros: Many opportunities to advance your career.
cons:
JPMC is forcing return to Office. It is currently set for 2 days in the office every week. Not as terrible as 5 days a week, but who's to say it won't increase in the future.
After a year of record profits, they have given a record lowest raise in wages and discontinued bonuses.
Punished for taking vacation as the work is piled on when you're away.
Work-Life balance is difficult to achieve as it seems all my waking days are centered around work -- and yes during weekends, too.

summary: This place kinda sucks for America’s largest bank
advice:
Start treating employees like adults and trust that the work will be completed. For the CCB team stop pressuring developers and ask every single person in CCB their opinion before you move offices on a whim or implement a new remote work schedule.

I’ll be leaving this company shortly.
pros: Projects are impactful and results matter
cons:
They don’t care about employees 

They lowball H1B and force us citizens to take the same salary, because It would cause pay gap.

They will move offices without asking employees on team how they feel about the move

They force you to come back to office even if you are more productive at home. They track when you are in office and hold it against you during year end review.

Managers put constant pressure on developers;

Developers need to manage so many non development tasks

I do not recommend CCB team.

advice: Honest and open communciations throughout the organization would be of tremendous value.  It would help to know what management is thinking at a tactical level so the entire organization can align with managment objectives.
pros: Very secure company with numerous opportunties for advancement.    With over 245K employees spanning a wide range of financial businesses there is something to do for everyone no matter what your education or past work experience.
cons: Very large organization, easy to get lost in buracracy.  It is difficult to demonstrate the value of your work in the context of the overall organization.  More often that not one finds that their own work is being duplicated in some other part of the organization.

advice: JP Morgan chase needs to know how to keep great employees.  Gave them flexibility, and incentives  before losing them just because you have to cut your budgets.  The company has to give loyalty to their loyal employees who worked hard for the company.
pros: You will have a lot of carrer opportunities in JP Morgan Chase.  Training is unlimited.  Benefits are competitive compare to other companies.  One of the top banks in the US.
cons: One of the reasons why I left JP Morgan Chase is I am required to work in Columbus, Ohio and I don't have any options to work remotely.  Another reason is they are starting to offshore IT jobs.

summary: Not as stellar as the name would suggest.
advice:
- The most aggressive people are not always the best managers.
- Build the company for the long haul, not for immediate P&L gains.
- Don't just talk about treating employees fairly.
- Think about the culture the managers are building in the company. I would not want my children to work in this company.
pros:
- company name recoginition
- stability of management
cons:
- Too big, employees become a cog in a great big factory
- Promotions and job opportunities at more senior level becomes a political game
- Compensation for non p&l related, i.e., non traders, non IBankers, etc, employees are below average for the industry.
- Once compensation reaches a certain level, it is capped there, unless one is on the fast track.

summary: Great place to work; supremely political
advice: It should be like bloomberg, there is something to be said about true meritocracy and it seems that JP doesnt really know the meaning of the word, the first thing i was taught when i came about was how to speak to senior people but of course this could be my desk
pros: Smart people; collegiate atmosphere; great positioning for an investment bank and amazing brand recognition; lot of avenues to grow; junior training is amazing
cons: politics between desks; favoritism for juniors from senior management regardless of ability is tiresome e.g. you need to play the game right, cant just work hard and expect to survive, you'll get laid off

pros: Health care benefits, you will have a job as long as you can manage the politics.  You get a 401K and a health savings account if you need to save your money pre-tax towards your health.
cons: Horrible work life balance, if you have a family you can forget about family time and definitely forget any dreams you may have of doing anything with your personal life.  I get up at 7 am to get to work and the branch closes at 6:10 pm by the time we are out 6:15 to 6:20 by the time I get home with traffic 7pm.  Monday through Friday and branch closes at 03:10 on saturday by the time you get out 3:20 to 3:25 get home 4:00 PM.  Say bye to your weekends.  More like your weekend day.

advice: There was a lot of micro management which was good and bad. The bi-annual and annual reviews were way to strict making it very difficult for anyone to get a raise.
pros: There are many pros when you work for the largest bank in the United States. They offered great training and I was well prepared to working in my first call center. They hourly pay was good and they also offer overtime to all employees which is a great way to make extra money. I was there for almost 2 years and received numerous awards, but was never promoted nor given a raise so I left the company.
cons: The reviews are very strict so one must make sure that he or she does everything the way they want you to or you will not get a raise.

advice: Try diversifying, try listening, try consensus-building, try learning with CAMs actually do.  Too many one-trick ponies taking a top-down approach.  Too many people getting promoted for being friends with the manager
pros: The brand. The breakfast at headquarters if you get to work there, but you won't in this position.
cons: No career path for CAMs.  The team does not have good standing with the Salespeople or other departments within the firm.  Lots of management shakeups and scandals in the last several years. Zero commitment to supporting team members' advancement.  Little to no incentives, low team morale.  Culture of constant remediation and reactiveness. It's not a think-tank so ideas are not really being generated and when they are they're not heard.  They find it hard to hire and promote minorities.  Not a great experience overall.

advice: Create a better mechanism to understand roles and responsibilities to that other may engage the right people quickly and effectively.
pros:
Great coming to work and talking with customers and having a great time with my teammates.
 i learned a lot with in my 4 years working at a great place, different investor. There no hardest part about the job, most enjoyable part is other co-workers and their ability to help each other.
cons: The  objectives were not cleared on how to accomplish daily or long term tasks. The company is a great but the team i worked with needs a lot of great leadership.. To many very long days and weekends. Managers micromanage you during a day, lack of opportunities to grow. Stressful environment, not able to clearly speak to upper management, not able to promote to different position.

advice: They should be looking to retain and find profitable revenue generating ways to engage their experienced staff in new careers. The mid life - mid career employees would appreciate that. Even on reduced base salaries.
pros: A good reputation with clients. J.P. Morgan brand benefitted from the Global Financial Crisis and continues to bank on that despite its best efforts to cut services to clients.
cons:
A hidden agenda of reducing experienced staff. Which ultimately is age discrimination. Horrible record of promoting women. That leads to enormous pressure to maintain older woman on their workforce at others expense. 
The company continues to cut benefits and comp for employees as well as staff in certain departments. Work harder ever year for less pay and benefits. 
Management is only worried about managing experienced and expensive employees out. Not true directional goals for business.

advice: Management never told me how to be a software developer, so I'll not tell them how to be managers.
pros: I worked at JP Morgan for 11 years.  It's a huge, global bank so your own experience will vary depending on where you work, what you kind of work you do, and most importantly who you work with.  Working for a huge company has its benefits.  There's good insurance, decent facilities and resources (usually), and corporate perks like legal assistance, adoption assistance, etc.
cons: Giant corporations like JPMC have so much red tape and hoops to jump through that one sometimes suspects they are actively trying to discourage any work getting done. This can be frustrating and it does wear on a person over the years and saps his enthusiasm.

advice: To Upper Upper Management, care about morale, pay your good people competitively and they will go above and beyond for you. Address known issues with employees directly instead of org wide.
pros: The CEO and company consistently focuses on socially important issues, diversity, and integrity. Most have the opportunity to work from home as needed.
cons: The management and lack of structure as you go down the chain. There is no leadership training here which allows for anyone to be selected to manage, many times over skilled knowledgeable, more capable employees. Dead end role. No room for advancement- the structure is not set up that way. Standard corporate 1-2% annual raises with the ask to constantly do more projects. 12 years of same. There is not a culture of transparency, instead there is alot of smoke & mirrors.

advice:
1. I would be very much happy if I could get an opportunity in my current location that would have avoided me coming out of the org.
2.  You are doing great!
pros:
Very Professional, a group of highly skilled people who develops great products. There won't be any blame game like " who did this" rather the discussion will be "what went wrong" and "how can this be fixed."

I am much happy that I could spend 4+ years in this amazing org. I quit because I need to relocate.
cons:
1. A little conservative in terms of adopting the latest tech stack. They do but at a slower pace than in other orgs.
2. Not many perks
3. Covid time bonuses are not super but I am completely ok that we are making great progress in terms of doing business.

advice:
You get what you pay for - You cannot have a great organization with mediocre people
See all the downsides above and work them out
pros:
Stability and job security
Better of the lot
cons:
It's an average Joe company.  If one is above the average, will get frustrated and leave.  Their performance evaluation is the same 20% Exceeds, 70% Meets, 10% Needs Improvement.

Very bureaucratic, change averse, cheap, employee insensitive

Glass ceilings - At least in chase card services there are very minimal chances of career progression if one is not a Caucasian male

One gets locked in at the salary they join the company.  Only way to improve pay is to leave

"Yes" men culture.  Difficult to challenge management.  HR is very ineffective and almost non-existent.

Very old technology at workspace, minimal facilities for employees at work

advice: Dont care much for your personal problems or needs. They are pushed to meet there metrics and then there for you are. You can even get written up if you consistantly can not meet the standards set by the company.
pros: Good Pay, and Decent Bonuses. Usually always friendly people and people to give advice and encourage you to make good numbers. Team incentives to spend money as a team every month on the team. Like ordering out food, or giving away gift cards.
cons: I feel the teams are to tightly wound and to stuck on beating the other team numbers and showing off employees with good numbers. While embarassing the ones without out good metrics. Not much room for advancement since they hire most team leaders from outside instead of recruiting from within.

pros:
Strong career development and internal mobility options for junior staff. 
Focus on quality customer service and regulatory compliance means you can work here knowing you are helping people - the company walks the walk when it comes to treating customers right, even if they mess up sometimes. 
If you are a scrum master, you can get a job very easily - they are desparate for them. Also for experience agile experts who can be coaches.
cons:
The majority of senior leadership is hired from outside the firm, especially in IT.  They say they are bringing in the best and brightest, but if the employees are so awesome, why can't you develop leaders internally? 
Chase is trying to do a lot of transformations, especially to become agile instead of waterfall. Poor business engagement for the first 2 years meant only dev teams changed and the surrounding and support processes didn't (no product owners in business). Now the business is on board, but there is little visible progress.  Some of the most senior IT leaders have announced that the PM, BA and QA job roles will be eliminated, but what happens to those employees is unclear. Between this and the various business changes happening, there is a general feeling of anxiety and instability.

advice: Top performers don't necessarily make the best managers. Take a look at all employees as some will surprise you with their leadership / management skills. Good motivators and "teachers" make the best managers in my experience. Make it a level playing field for all employees. Compensation and goal system based on tier system of branches not what it currently is which if you are in a "slow performing branch" will make it almost impossible for you to stand out. A tier system would show you a more accurate look and make it a level playing field for all. Some adjustments to compensation plan have been for the better but always room for improvement.
pros: Great company to work for. Great culture, great benefits, good pay. Very smart CEO running our company.
cons: Maybe take a look at internal politics from preventing talented individuals from reaching their potential. Let employees transfer after a set time frame at current position to let them grow into other possible positions within the company making them more valuable not only to the company but to themselves and open up available positions to the interview process to all applicants instead of saying that certain positions are open and then not letting everyone have a fair shot at the so called available position.

summary: Your happiness can vary depending on location
advice: In short, a lot varies by where you are located. One branch in your area my have a much better culture and work environment than another location just a few miles away. Management plays a huge role in this. Poor management will equal a poor sense of fulfillment and you can get burnt out. If you feel appreciated and rewarded then it is much easier to push through the lows of the job. I was happy most of the time as long as I encouraged myself and did what I needed to do in order to take care of my family first and JPMC second.
pros: Benefits, career growth and opportunities, decent bonus opportunity, great place to network as well.
cons: As a banker it can be very difficult to get time needed (not wanted) time off. Some locations require you to work weekends and depending on location they may only approved one person to be off on any given day (so good luck if you are competing with senior bankers for a day off in December.) Your overall happiness depends on management and it's difficult to know their management style until you've already been placed at a branch. Transfers can be a little tricky to achieve at times as well.

pros: Nothing I hate this place
cons: Worst comp and work life balance and no one knows what they are doing

advice: NA
pros: Slightly better than its peers
cons: Office politics, average pay, poor work life balance, too much micromanagement and zero work flexibility

pros:
Bonus are good for employees
Salary is competitive
cons:

No proper trainings
