advice: Continue employee focus. Remind employees to feel empowered to tell people when they’re becoming abusive.
pros:
This is a really good company to work for if you’re looking into retail banking. Pay is competitive when you take benefits packages into consideration. 
The atmosphere in most branches is pleasant. Direct management can be a hit or a miss. 
If you’re willing to fight for a career you can have one there, just have to be willing to work for it. 
Major company focus on employee happiness. 

The shift in community banking the last couple years has emphasized self service banking. This is a huge plus considering the staffing being so limited. A lot of what is done in branch has self service options to where clients don’t even have to leave the comforts of their own homes.
cons:
As I stated above management is a hit or miss. Depending on the area Chase has been looking outside the company for management and many times the folks they hire have no banking experience. That makes it difficult for branch employees because then it’s a lot of babysitting. 
Client obsession can make it a little difficult when dealing with not so nice people. Feels like we have to just suck it up and take it.

summary: Amazing benefits and good place to work overall.
advice: Chase prides on career mobility but several times I've overheard how opening positions were being given to friends and acquittances of whoever was hiring. The job posting will still be posted but very few candidates were called for an interview. I know this because of highly qualified coworkers who never got called for an interview. We would later find out someone outside of Chase would get hired for the job who were coincidentally acquainted to the hiring manager.  My advice would be to have a third party hiring person who would do interviews with the hiring managers to make it fair. There is a lot of favoritism.
pros: Great benefits, great people to work with, career/ life balance support. Fair starting wage.
cons:
I had a vey incompetent boss who was cheating with another woman in the department and everybody knew about it. He was very hard and uncomfortable to work with. He was also unfair, hard to communicate with and had anger issues. HR couldn't do anything about it despite multiple complaints until one day they finally laid him off for unrelated reasons. 
Also gossip, from day one everybody was talking crap behind everybody's back including the trainers, it is so unprofessional.

summary: Excellent company to work for.  My position as a Senior Loan Consultant afforded me unlimited income potential.
advice: Stop emailing so many memos!!  Just have a weekly sales meeting / call from immediate supervisor to inform loan originators of policy changes.  If it is so important that everyone must be informed that same day - then blast an email as "priority".  Commissioned reps have more on their mind then to constantly check their email from corporate (expecially when they get several per day).
pros: They provided a monthly draw against my unlimited income as a commissioned employee (about $3,000/month).  Annual trips for achieving Presidents Club - all expenses paid including exceptionally gorgeous hotels (upscall Hyatt / Marriott) usually at tropical destinations like Hawaii.  Awards and recognitions at the annual banquet.
cons: Be at quota and everyone will be happy.  Even if you are not at quota they will support you any way they can in order to achieve that goal.  401k contribution was 10% up to the 10,000 mark annually.  Guaranteed rate of return on same.  Golden parachute after 5 years which was 10% of your annual income they they simply "gave" to you in an account that they held and managed until you left.

advice: Pay your notaries that you abuse as an institution, this is a service they are giving to your clients.  A manager stated that as a notary your acting like you are doing them a favor...you are since there is no benefit to you, just the benefit of client satisfaction.  Pay me the 8k for my notary service at $2 per notary minimum please!!!
pros: Stability of low income...potential for ok/good commissions to pay the prior months bills when you had a bad month
cons: Low salary, and then they give you 3 weeks vacation that you don't want to take because you can't earn commission when your not there.  Management is good and bad...depending on location.  If your not in a good busy branch, potential for increased income decreases dramatically.  When you become a notary, you become the team, not a team player.  In the past three years I must have done over 4000 notaries, this is not an exaggeration.  And the best part is you don't get paid for it!!!  They tell you to drink the juice and it's an opportunity to meet people, yet while your stuck doing the notaries your missing opportunity for walk in business that you would get paid for.

summary: Good firm but nobody is safe in Spring
advice: Don't underpay or hire grocery store clerks and pay them more than experienced AML Investigators! Fire incompetent middle management when they repeatedly fail instead of moving them to another department only to destroy morale and the department like they always do.
pros: Good firm with good benefits
cons: Massive layoffs every spring with no rhyme or reason. No bonuses in years of record banking profits. When moving internally, I was told it was a lateral transfer. My new manager informed me that I was underpaid vs base salary/my peers by $10,000.00. 2 years of fighting with a "powerless" upper management chain and no resolve. They will absolutely hire outsiders with no experience and gladly pay them more than experienced in-house candidates. And yes, that is all 100% true.

advice: Play it fair and give bankers their fair share of floor traffic. Help the team out more with day to day instead of just making outrageous demands to boost productivity which can never be met. Also outbound phone call quota can get ridiculous with bankers make 100+ calls a week.
pros: Commission is fair, you can make an extra couple thousand a month if you're in the right area and work really hard to cross sell a lot. Mortgages, investments and business loans have great commissions.
cons: Some bankers can be spiteful and not take floor traffic so that they only focus on customers they can make money from. Other bankers suffer from this. Management does not care for this and often do nothing about it. Some managers are under-qualified and just out right questionable as to how they became managers.

summary: Need to work on promoting from within
advice: Promote from within. Need to review management. Nepotism has got to stop that’s why there are so many incompetent people in crucial company roles.
pros:
Good benefits 
Hours are okay
cons: Chase never seems to want to promote from within. They will always seem to go with external hires with less experience about 8 times out of 10. Only get one chance a year for a raise and if you get one it’s usually $0.05-$0.25 but most bankers haven’t seen raises in years. Tend to keep Latinos are low income branches and they make less money but refuse to move them because they cannot find a sufficient bilingual replacement. Lots of nepotism, and favoritism. There are managers that work 10-20 hours a week and leave their branches hanging but are somehow favorites with upper management.

summary: Work hard, but make sure someone knows about it.
advice: Keep employees happy and work on developing realistic project deadlines.
pros: JPMorgan Chase has great benefits.  Salaried workers have twenty days of vacation.  Career opportunities are plentiful if you are willing to learn new things and fit into the role.  Great people to work with for the most part.  Managers believe in the idea of work smarter not harder which is great.  Communication is great, any concerns are handled by immediate manager, but having an open door policy is a great plus as well.  Very knowledgeable workers makes working here easier and helps when trying to pitch new technologies or solutions as people are willing to try new things.  Overall great company to work at.
cons: Politics do come into play just like in any other work.

summary: Good place to start your career, but need to get out before they deem you "expendable"
advice: Am ok with Jamie Dimon. It's the next level down that I feel are incompetent and don't care about their employees
pros: One of the few banks still around. When you start your career here, it's great because you will learn a lot. The bank is humongous so you can leverage many resources the company has. People you work with are very good at teaching you the ropes. You are judged against very high standards, so you end up working very hard.
cons: Too big; easy to get lost in the shuffle. When the round of layoffs came, the process was very political. If you were aligned with certain MDs or EDs that got let go, you were also in trouble. It was less based on your performance.

advice: In card services, the management that I have is excellent for the nature of the work. I doubt you could find a better call center to work at.
pros: Great communication from everyone in the team. I honestly hate my job because it's a call center and that is just the nature of things, but this really is a good org to work for. I have a degree and am stuck at the call center level but that is just the way any large corp. works. They are flexible about time off and you really have to try hard to get fired.
cons: Just the basic "Office Space" factor that is really inescapable in the modern work world. If you don't want that, start a business or be really brilliant, in which case you are probably not reading this.

summary: Fine company, but I can find something better that values me more
advice: Be more flexible in terms of training, education, and the career aspirations of employees.
pros: It is a huge company so there a lot of people to meet and places to work. You can work with different people not just all over the U.S. but also the entire world. Also, you can most likely find something that sparks your interest and network to put yourself in a better position to obtain your goals.
cons: It's a lot harder to get the salary you should be paid if you only move within the company. They value talent that comes from outside the company much more and definitely show it in how they pay outside managers versus internal. If you start here, and like it, it's much better to leave and come back later.

advice: People are not numbers.  Treat them and their families with respect in regards to the decisions being made that affect them.  Update the computers and work equipment.  Allow flexible work schedules and encourage work from home.
pros:
Diversity include racial, lgbt and gender populations
Corporate benefits like 5% match on 401k 
Expensive but valued healthcare including mental health.
Vacation and sick time.  Maternity/Paternity leave.
Local footprint
cons:
Executive level management has zero connect to base employee.  Senior VP level and above. 
Pay is between 10%-25% lower than competing financial institutions (BoA, PNC, TelOhio).
Work conditions and equipment are 5+ years behind.  Some Systems have not been updated since the 90's (not exaggerating) 
Poor communication between departments.
As with most every cubicle job it is WHO you know not what you know.  This cliche is firm within this firm.

advice: company is in a death spiral, you are listening to, and valuing, the wrong people.  You don't want to hear the truth.
pros: Large, diverse corporation with many opportunities across many diverse areas.  Many opportunities for entry level employees to gain experience.  Chance to meet people from all different backgrounds.
cons: Very slowly moving, has a difficult time reacting to change, let alone being proactive to change.  Managers have very little say in developing their employees, everything is driven from the top and passed through multiple layers to the bottom.  Very little chance of having ideas heard or accomplishing anything innovative.  Focus on cost cutting is mind numbing, talent leaving.  Once experience is gained it is best to move along.  Huge discrepancy regarding CEO pay versus the average worker.

advice: Put a greater focus on technology, work cooperatively instead of against each other.
pros:
- Safe job - even in re-orgs or when your team gets removed there is plenty of opportunity to move around within the company
- The cafeteria at the Dallas location was great
cons:
Not an ideal environment for the software engineering career...
- Very difficult to do your job due to: no admin access on computer, limited access to technologies and internet
- Developers are generally not passionate, the firm does not generally encourage using new technologies and tools or "hacking" new ideas
- Continuous learning was limited to very basic (and poor) internal training videos. Very few teams had funds to send developers to conferences, etc...
- Many employees (especially on prod support) had to work long hours, my team's work-life balance was fine. Normal hours.

advice:
Take a hard look at incentives as people are being  rewarded for actions that actually detract from profits and also don't really benefit customers either.  
Provide real leadership/management training to the supervisors and senior managers.  They usually know the technical details of the job but lack the skills to effectively build and lead teams.
pros:
Decent benefit package (health, 401K, 20 days vacation, 10 holidays).
Free coffee/tea in breakroom.
Generally competent and friendly team members.
Large enough so that it can weather economic ups and downs.
Actively working towards a more diverse and accepting workplace.
Tolerant of flexible work in many business units.
cons:
Benefits getting very expensive.
Many layers of senior management.
Business units sometimes seem to be competing against each other rather than cooperating.
Culture varies a lot between lines of business.
Multiple legacy systems to deal with.
Many support functions are outsourced/offshored.

advice: I would cut some areas to the bone. Many functions are completely useless if not harmful to the  company. Also the review system is completely flawed. I expect that if things continue like this, the company will lose its appeal to super-smart people.
pros: Pay is good. This is perhaps the best thing about JPM. Benefits are also OK. Some of the people working there are very smart (unfortunately not in my group).
cons:
The company is immensely bloated. Layer over layers of management. For every minor decision, you must go up 2-3 levels. It's the worse work experience I had in Finance. It seems that the strategy has been to hire people without regard to management structure (or quality). 
Smart people keep coming and going after they get the point about what's going on.

advice: CEO mentions customers, employees & profits are given equal importance, try to keep that promise about employees.
pros: Good benefits, stability, decent pay. Company makes tons of profit. Good long term outlook.
cons: Very conservative towards change, new development mostly fueled by regulatory restrictions rather than need for improvement. New requirements handled in an ad-hoc manner without much plan or thought on the current workload, Agile means, keep changing the requirement until the day of release. New product development is rare, even that does not start on a clean sheet due to tight coupling with other systems. Mobility is said to be encouraged, however the selection/rejection is not very transparent. Poor work-life balance. All depends on whether you have a good manager and a great team with great projects.

advice: Continue to make your junior level employees happy and appreciated. The movement to improve the Junior initiatives for work-life balance are great.  A premium shop should also focus on premium compensation, which it currently does.  But it's always something to be cognizant of and encouraging and supporting lateral movements internally and externally.
pros: The global platform, quality and variety of resources, and most importantly the quality of employees at this firm provide an amazing experience and opportunity for growth and to learn.  With that attracts some of the most interesting and best clients and transactions to work on.
cons: Highly demanding environment given the responsibilities we must take on since we're dealing with some of the largest clients in the world and among the most complex transactions.

advice: Put less pressure on sales, more on relationship building. Share the wealth, no need for the executives to make multiple millions and hard-working bankers in the trenches have to be on Medicaid and Food Stamps to supplement their income. Raise the banker base salary to $55,000 and pay out more on incentives, (you can afford it), then you would lower your banker turnover and burn-out rate. If a banker doesn't perform then you cut them, but for the median bankers that consistently produce, they should  be able to earn six figure salaries.
pros: Great starting incentives to get you going. Book of business in place.
cons: Cut annual bonus, raised the bar on incentive payouts, archaic promotion process, it' s liking pulling teeth to get established clients to invest with you.

advice: Don't lose sight of junior employees that are willing to invest in this LOB and asking to take on more work.
pros: The network you develop at JPMorgan is amazing but if you aren't willing to do your job and then 10 other things you will not be able to push through to the next level. If put in the right situation with a team or mentor that is willing to teach you are going to succeed. The exposure to senior management in this LOB is fantastic and if given an opportunity to prove yourself you must take it.
cons: The size of the firm can lead to feeling lost. Trying to compare yourself to others is difficult when it comes to trying to advance. Waiting for a raise is a process that requires tremendous patience.

summary: Got to write a review to access glassdoor website
pros:
- benefits (401k, bonus to 401K, health/vision/dental insurance)
- paid vacation
- paid sick time
cons:
- salary $18/h. If you want to make more as a banker you are on commission but since we turn every customer away due to understaffing and new technologies, it's not worth it.
- understaffed all the time
- always asking to turn customers away to direct them to new technologies or just because we don't have enough staffing
- customers (I'd say that half of the people going inside the bank are going in with issues, so half of the time you get yelled at by angry customers)
- schedules (always have to work on Saturdays, and workday end at 6:30pm)
- rules and restrictions from the bank which unable the staff to provide great service and makes customer mad

advice: Given the firm's size, one of the biggest challenges for senior management is to be able to really be on top of what is happening at the lower levels of the organization.
pros: Well-run business; strong and deep platform. One of the survivors who will come out with a stronger market position out of the downturn. From a prestige standpoint, continues to rise and is now clearly in the top 3 overall, and continues to gain momentum. Jamie Dimon is one of the best leaders in financial services, and in business in general.
cons: Can get lost in the shuffle -- there are many, many cogs in the wheel. Like any investment bank, there are long hours involved and high demands in short timeframes. While generally very professional, it is nonetheless more of an up or out culture.

summary: Good company, decent pay, good place to start a career
advice: Make staff feel like they are in control of their careers. This is partially the responsibility of the employee, of course, and subject to the conditions in the department, but I had some colleagues who had leadership potential that was not recognized, and this was an arbitrary circumstance more often than not.
pros: Rotational Program is very useful for starting career, but not sure if I would want to stay at this location long-term if looking to expand skillset. Utilize contacts in NY if at all possible to move into more challenging role.
cons: Pay is not particularly great relative to peers - since the company has such a strong name recognition and reputation, does not need to pay as much/more than peers in order to retain staff.

summary: Chase is a good company to work for.  I would work there again
advice:
Put people in management positions that add value to the organization not just because they have a military background. 
Pay bonus's or commissions to positions that generate the most revenue.
pros:
Great people, Very supportive ( in my experience) They gave me lots of resources, 

I was very happy with the training I received and continued improvement they stressed,
cons:
The pay was just not enough for me to support myself.  I was making 13.50 in a collections job.  
There are not enough opportunities for advancement.  They might have 50 people that are looking for one position internally. That does not include the outside candidates.  
They are focused too much on filling positions with military people.

summary: Job security, great benefits, decent pay,  work environment may varry.
pros: For the first few years of my career, I felt I was compensated fairly. I then learned that new employees were being hired at higher pay than existing employees with tenure. I had amazing managers and coworkers but like any call center or office, there were other managers that were very strict and showed a lot of favoritism. There is typically a lot of overtime available in the call centers. I like that OT is never mandatory and you can schedule your own hours.
cons: Working in a fast paced call center environment can be mentally exhausting, even for those of us that are seasoned. I worked as a Supervisor in escalations and the clients were extremely hostile and abusive. Most of us have been called every name in the book.

advice:
Increase salaries for all employees not just new hires but a large pay bump for everyone especially employees who have been with the firm for many, many years
Encourage open discussion about pay and benefits with employees and between employees
Stop making these kinds of conversations seem dangerous or forbidden for employees to have
pros:
Benefits package is outstanding (health insurance, employee stock, pension)
Health and wellness center on site
Day care on site
A lot of talk of inclusiveness and culture building
Business Resource Groups for all kinds of people is nice
cons:
After 8 years my pay seems stagnant and I do not have much upward mobility anymore
Seem stuck and unable to move anywhere else in the company
Salary seems to be less than competitors pay
There seems to be a culture of salary discussions being forbidden or not allowed between employees

summary: Was a great company until forcing people back into the office
advice: You continue having your most profitable years ever but you only offer competitive pay to new employees. Stop giving out mediocre comp adjustments and bonuses or you will continue to experience chaotic turnover in your employee base. Also, the resistance to Work From Home and the premature removal of social distancing policies in the workplace in February 2022 is disgusting. Everyone knows that the changes you are making are purely to enhance surveillance on who is in the office for how many hours. The company could be so much better if you embraced working from home and stopped putting your employees health at risk.
pros: Work/life balance, benefits, training resources
cons: Pay is lower than competitors, regressive ideas and behaviors from management

summary: External new hires are more appreciated than their tenures employees.
advice: Take care of your tenured reps that put in the work and show it with their performance not promote just because they say yes to projects just to get out of making calls. A lot of good reps are being passed up on because of the popularity games played.
pros: The only good thing about the department I work in is my supervisor and few long lasting relationships built throughout the 3 years I’ve been here.
cons: Tenured are not appreciated as much as external new hires. Been with this department for years and people that started months ago are paid just as much as I am with no experience. They make it hard to move up and if you want to move you you basically have to be a yes person. Work ethic and skill don’t mean anything. You have people in higher positions that are lousy and lazy at their job but got there because they said yes to a project.

advice: Think about your employees and do the right thing instead of the cheap thing.  Starting with Jamie Dimon who needs to get his priorities straight.
pros: Solid pay and benefits plan
cons: Worked hard for 8 years there - was rated 'exceeds expectations' for 5 years in a row.  Was the first to be laid off because I made too much money.  Peers rated 'Needs Improvement' are still there because they made less money.  The 'speak' was "if your score card is good, you have nothing to worry about."  Couldn't have been further from the truth.  Chase is completely greedy company that doesn't care about its employees, but only seeks to make a buck - from any source - whether that means raping customers with fees or getting rid of GREAT employees who make too much money.  Jamie Dimon is a great leader only from the stock-holder perspective, but he couldn't care less about employees or customers.   DREADFUL change from Bill to Jamie

summary: Great company---Culture was very good, but failure at senior levels ran the Bank into the ground.
advice: I think the Bank could have remained a strong and solid Bank if it wasn't for the loosing of lending guidlines and a "race to the bottom" to approve any and all loan applications.  Housing prices, borrow incomes, and FICO scores,  are always a snap shot in time---and while that is how all loans are u/w placing more conservative guidelines could have made all the difference!
pros: Good pay, benefits, culture.  Support in-house promotion vs. outside hiring unless.  Excellent stock options and benefits made this a good place to work.
cons: Failure to see that risky lending practices and a greed for money took over vs. doing the right thing for the customer and the employees ended in the Bank failing.

summary: It is a great company to work for.
pros: The people I worked with were very helpful in training. Management was fair a treated us well. I learned a lot at JP Morgan Chase. Management was flexible with time off and vacation request. They were very understanding when there was a family emergency. When we were getting laid off, they did give us notice and help with finding a new job. I don't know of any other company that would do that. I am very grateful for all they did for us.
cons: They at time overlooked the really good workers for promotions. They did not train us as well as they could have. But later they did start introducing more training. We were high producers in our office, but our office was closed. Very unfortunate for us and the company.

summary: Good stable company, but bureaucratic environment puts a large weighting on politics
advice: Attempt to assess employee contributions by evaluating accomplishments on an ongoing basis rather than once a year through the overly simplified employee review system as it seems is currently done.
pros: JPMorgan is a secure and stable place to work. Great for recent grads as the companies rigid framework is well defined creating well defined roles among superiors and peers. Extremely large company is great for networking. JPM brand name looks great on a resume.
cons: Not bad for everyone, but strict bureaucratic policies makes career advancement difficult without a focus on politics. Merit based accomplishments tend to go unnoticed without campaigning yourself. This is usually fine, but can be extremely impeding if you have an indifferent or lazy superior. Company attempts to standardize most business processes creating a mundane environment.

summary: Working at J.P. Morgan has been a great experience and has offered unparalleled training.
advice:
-Spend time streamlining and standardizing processes to eliminate inefficiencies in the pitch/deal process
-Identify bankers with leadership ability early on and foster this
pros:
-Phenomenal job training through the initial structured training program, continued learning opportunities and the opportunity to work with so many other talented individuals
-Excellent compensation
-Great access to senior bankers
-Given a large amount of responsibility even as an analyst
cons:
-Senior bankers are promoted solely based on ability to bring in revenue, not on actual leadership ability or managerial skill which tends to translate into work processes being inefficient (Maybe not specific to the firm, seems to be an issue in IB anywhere)
-Work/life balance is nonexistent (again, generally an issue in IB at any firm)
-Colleagues are hypercompetitive to an alarming degree

summary: So glad I am not there anymore
advice: No work life-balance, although management constantly preaches how important it is.  Complete boys club mentality and that needs to go if you want any kind of real progress forward.
pros: Perfect for someone who wants to work 10 hour minimum days, come home depressed, tired and hungry.  Some people love that kind of grind, and if you do, JP Morgan is your place.  Decent/good base salary and a pretty good bonus, but not worth the constant state of depression at the end of each day.  4 weeks vacation but no chance you'll ever get to use it all.
cons: Where do I start?  It's like a bunch of chickens running around with their heads cut off at all times.  Constantly trying to keep your head above water as the work keeps piling up and never stops.  If you don't drink the kool-aid, they will let you go quickly. Do yourself a favor and just don't bother working here.

summary: All that glitters is not gold
advice: Be blunt, be transparant, give people enough information to make decisions in their own best interests before its too late.
pros: There is a certain prestige working for a recognizable global brand. This can work to your benefit in some circles. Good "3rd" company to work for (i.e. work at JPM, then leave, then perhaps return to JPM with a better sense of market value)
cons: Since everyone is clamoring to get in and work for a recognizable global brand, they're (aware or not) willing to forgo much more competitive compensation. Base pay is stingy; "meritocracy" is not what it seems, and you have no leverage as an individual to take anything other than whatever is given to you. Don't get too comfortable, 2-3 years tops and then leave to sell your self to a higher market-value bidder.

advice: Please pay this position more. There are people in this role who stay in the role for 4, 5, even 7 years because there is no career path except to go into a sales route via a personal banker position. It's disappointing how much responsibility you have in this role and how little you will be appreciated, and paid.
pros: Great benefits, 3 weeks PTO. as well as paid personal and Sick leave and paid holidays. Excellent training program and good learning to apply in your role or outside of the company.
cons:
Zero opportunity for career advancement in an Operations role, you are forced into a Banker or other sales role
Perform all the functions and responsibilities of a Service Manager at Wells or an Assistant Branch Manager at other Banks, but get paid $10-15k a year less

summary: Love the company, can't stand current trend for branches.
advice: Stop cutting corners, your small branches are drowning with zero support.
pros: Great benefits, paid holidays, vacation time.
cons: Giving more access to tellers (associate bankers) and then cuting staff making it impossible to cover teller line while having to sit down at desks to solve complex needs. Bare minimum staffing makes call offs/vacation time a nightmare. Tellers now expected to open personal and business accounts with no incentive. Also call centers are pure chaos, it's russian roulette that you'll get a rep who actually knows what they're doing - and most things require a phone call do to no access at branch level. All other branch positions are either sales or management, and with no work from home opportunities you have to go to the city - currently looking outside of the company for new work opportunities.

advice: Not much.  Most are gone.
pros: There is a lot of freedom to do your job and not micromanaged.  the people you work with are nice in the branches.  The WAS a unique culture atmosphere here, but that has gone along with the company.  There are not many other reasons.  It was a good place to start.  but there is not much left and much uncertainty about Chase now.
cons: The unknown of what will happen when chase takes over!  Also, there is a serious disconnect between yourself and the backoffice.  Everyone seems to be working against each other instead of against.  Also, there is a genuine heiarchy going on here.  Nobody moves up around here.  Everyone just stays stuck.  Except for the upper maangement, they change around all the time.

advice: Learn from the success of the larger banks like BofA, JP morgan chase.
pros: I think it all depends on the branch your working at and who your regional manager is.  Overall, from my experience i think its a fun place to work.  Before the seizure and buy out, Wamu had competitive products which made selling a lot easier.  They stressed the idea of having customers into the branches, so you would get a lot of opportunity to sell.   I also think the compensation/bonus is much higher compared to other banks.  I like the idea the bonus is not capped
cons: Most of the new accounts reps or personal financial reps get paid more than assistant mangers and branch managers.  Branch mangers were paid on a profit model of the branch, therefore working short staffed meant more bonus.

summary: Satisfying place to work w plenty of potential
advice: Listen to your employees, they have the insight and knowledge of how things work and should be done.  I know that organization is under pressure to cut costs, but some departments should really remain in house, not outsourced.
pros: Very generous benefits package for entry level management and above; 4 weeks of vacation plus personal time.  Senior management at this location was very aware of the work / life balance and open to time off requests.
cons: JPMorgan is an example of an organization that has gotten too big.  The simplest task would take several weeks and phone calls to accomplish.  IT was a perfect example, with support locations all throughout the world nothing was ever easy.

jobTitle: Customer Service Representative @ Chase Investment Services Corp
summary: The best place for your career to grow as long as you suck up to the right person.
advice: Look at the talent that you have within instead of hiring some kid out of college with no experience because you can pay less.  Have employees provide feedback about management and TAKE it into consideration.
pros: Large company in which you will be able to network and be able to obtain a better position at another firm.
cons: Very difficult to transfer to different departments.  Working mandatory overtime.  Managers retaliate if they feel the slightest push-back or disagreement.  Best way to move up is by sucking up to the right people and not by the quality of work.  They prefer quantity over quality, but punish you for complaints.  High stress job, not enough pay.  No set policies and procedures, so more room for error and more reason to not qualify for bonus.   We received an email stating we could not use the restroom if there were calls in queue.

summary: Ok for about 2 years, then move on
advice: Move into the 21st century.
pros: Depends wildly on your team. I've found there is a strong focus on learning which is nice, as well as maintaining relationships. Decent work/life balance. Work can either be interesting or extremely aggravating.
cons: No real room for advancement unless you happen to be the lucky few to latch onto a senior executive. Salaries are below industry average and they will string you along if you ask for more without committing. Too many managers. The closer technical management gets to the front office the more childlike they behave - there is no unity in technologies across even very related parts of the firm because each manager treats their product like an individual product in an open market that must be preserved and advertised over other, similar systems; little cooperation.

summary: On their way to another multi-billion outsourcing deal
advice: Try doing something besides "managing up." It leaves the people who report to you feeling like you don't care about them at all when the only people you respond to are those "above" you.
pros: They're always hiring, and they're not very picky.
cons:
Old, sometimes ancient technology, e.g., Solaris, NetBackup, SVM, ...
Onboarding is your responsibility; do not expect anything at all in this area.
Current model features four days on, three days off, no choice, you work holidays and you are paid by the hour. You'll be promised overtime pay, but this requires paperwork that most managers do not know how to do. Mine just put it off until I quit.

No non-management bonuses for IT personnel.

Worst moment: Learning that I'd be working on Labor Day on the Sunday before Labor Day:

Me: So what are you doing for Labor Day?
Co-worker: Working in the office, same as you.
Me: We have to work Labor Day????
Co-worker: You work your four days in a row, no matter what.
Me: Wow.
Co-worker: Well, we are working on Sunday.

summary: You start making too much money they will let you go!
advice: Don't get rid of people because of their salary - they have worked hard and long for your company to earn that salary. give raises based on merits not favorites, or sex.
pros: If you make more than your peers - they will give you less of a raise so they can give people who make less more.. Managers - give raises to favorites - not the hard working ones.
cons: I was with the company for 10 years in the IT department - I was making the most money because I was there the longest, so I got laid off, but then they hired 2 people who were making the equivalent to my salary.. so basically  they said lets get rid of her and we can hire  2 people

summary: Good People, good group, maybe less $$ than some competitors
advice: Too much politics, old corporate environment. Consider having younger people in senior position and foster a more creative environment.
pros: I was working full time in quantitative research in the NY headquarters. The group was very relaxed, incredibly smart and supporting people, inspiring boss. Work life balance was OK.
cons: We (quantitave researchers) were given no real responsibility of the algorithms and models we created. Our job was basically and internal consulting to the managements. All business decisions (involving our work) were done by senior managers who had no knowledge of the advance math and engineering we were using. If you are a talented quantitative person and want to do "real work" consider joining a quant hedge fund instead.

advice: Present your support staff with growth opportunities to move into different areas.
pros: JPMorgan creates a huge safety net for all of its employees. It's an extremely safe place to work for and the job security is always there. Grade A benefits, tuition reimbursement, company stock, and the name opens up many doors.
cons: For a support staff member you will quickly learn that you will be very limited as to what you can do and how far you can go. They want you to stay put and not really expand. The salary raises are extremely low and bonuses, at best, are mediocre. Administrative salaries are also capped. It's easy to get comfortable but being stagnant will only get you but so far.

advice: Management need to put themselves into their employees shoes (even though they may not be able to help every one) they should at least try to help one. For example, many employees want to go back to school, but they cannot afford to because they have children that they can hardly feed.  There should be a full scholarship funding to at least one employee for outstanding customer service over a given period of time.
pros: Assistant Branch Manager was great with staff and customers alike. She would ensure that all tellers cash boxes are to the "t" while she is on duty. She was very prompt with feedbacks to customers.
cons: Most employees were demotivated and only came to work because they need to pay their bills.

advice: Find other ways to motivate your employees, especially in the slower branches that don't have individuals always wanting new services or that only have regulars.
pros: If you hustle and work hard at it, you can make good money. Everyone I worked for was very friendly and encouraging. It's a big company that is well known.
cons:
The salary (not commissions) is pretty low. 
You don't necessarily make "cold calls",  but you do call existing customers to offer additional services with little to no incentive to the customer.  For example: you could be asked to call a 90 year old person that once had a mortgage with chase to convince them to bring over $100,000 to savings all for a $500 incentive for the customer.

advice: It all comes from above. A hugh fear mongering angry place to work, The mistakes management makes are attricious but never see them getting fired. I could tell some real horror stories but I won't, They have enough legal prolems. My story would result in billions of $$'s in fines
pros: Name recognition - deep pockets
cons: The most disorganized inefficient compant that I have ever worked for an there are many, Way too uptight, Way too paranoid.  Too big way way way too big. Team managers to be leaders; to be motivational, not demeaning; to be transformational, not transactional; to be respectful.
ACTUALLY be open to innovative ideas, strategy, re-engineering -- don't just throw these words around because they're "hip"

Located in/around NYC
Decent pay and "extracurricular" benefits (i.e. museum passes, botanical gardens, etc.)

Managers, not leaders

-uncomfortable work environment because of the above

advice: To stop letting go of qualified internal talent due to HR policies of not promoting employees
pros: Good medical Benefits and 401 with profit sharing. Can work from home. It’s a good starting company for college candidates.
cons: No raises, no internal mobility or promotion. If you are an associate and there is a position you are qualified for but is a level up (avp) HR won’t let the hiring manager make you an offer. They do not promote from within regardless their mobility campaign. Employees can only move on lateral positions. They only go outside the firm to fill positions and dismiss internal qualified candidates. Employees have to be 4 to 5 years on a position in order to apply to the next level but salaries a below market

summary: Stable company; great if you're in tech or tech-adjacent, not so much if you're anybody else
advice: Operations leadership needs to be straight with staff about the firm's priorities.  Technology staff should partner with the business vs. push "good enough (but not really)" solutions.  Work/Life balance is preached, but not allowed to be practiced.
pros: Leadership is strong overall. Strategy is clear at top, and priorities are articulated well. Firm is diversified and market position is strong, so firm avoids mass layoffs. Good culture of controls and thoughfulness.
cons: Tech is ascendant--it's necessary, but sometimes it's the tail wagging the dog. Tech investments overrule investments in other areas, and the priorities of ops, marketing, and non-tech in general are secondary. Firm avoids mass layoffs, but performs smaller periodic reductions. Poor work/life balance.

pros: Stable company, moving towards newer technologies will allow to learn new tools as Chase implements them in the company. Heavily works with AWS (Chase specific) and kubernetes. Moving internally is easy and if you don't like your team, Chase has one to fit your skillset or what you want to do. Chase also has a great entry level (college graduate) software engineering program (SEP), which will place you on a team that best fits your interests and skillset.
cons: Almost everything is "Chase specific", nearly 35-40% of what I learned while at this company cannot be carried over outside of Chase. Cyber regulations don't stop for applications that are external facing and even for internal facing applications it can be difficult and time consuming to comply with the restrictions.

summary: Some Good People, some not so good people
advice: If you ask for feedback, use it. Don't just ignore almost all of it and pretend that because you asked for feedback, there's been some actual change.
pros: Good starting hourly pay, decent benefits, easy overall work. You can just turn your brain most of the way off and listen to whatever you like on an appropriate MP3 player. Employment is about to be contingent on full vaccination, finally.

Management will constantly pretend that they care about your feedback. Weird hours (for now?), four ten hour work days or nights. Current (November 2021) expansion construction is disruptive.

advice: I think that the company cares about its people, but upper management needs to be realistic when it comes to objectives and handle times/the bottom line. They expect perfection; robotic yet human, in a very small amount of time, which is IMPOSSIBLE. We cannot predict how long the caller/customer will take w/ explaining or venting their issues.

cons: Unrealistic goals from upper management; it was not fair that one has to meet ALL of the goals in order to be considered for a promotion. A person can be capable and ready for management or a promotion, despite their handle time, etc.

pros: Great job, with a work/life balance. Working as a back off analyst, is the perfect job for me, and there are decent benefits.

Friendly coworkers
Most Internal Systems work well and and up to date
Easy to move around internally - can gain lots of experience in different areas
cons:
Management can be horrid
The culture is mean and competitive

Pressure from Management

pros:
- name recognition
- 401(k)

summary: A pretty good place to work
advice: Keep the focus on conservative risk management and maintaining high ethic standards.
pros: JPMorgan Chase has strong executive management and it has been able to maintain a high level of ethics relative to financial services companies in general.  Most of the people I work with are able to log into the network and work from home when necessary.  For those that need to work from home on occasion it's a nice option.  It's not hard to keep a reasonable balance between one's work life and personal life.  Compensation is reasonable.  The scale I've seen on this site appears a little low.
cons: If you're not willing/able to live in Chicago or New York then your career opportunities are more limited.

advice: Encourage your direct reports to achieve their goals and instruct them to do the same with their reports as well. Not everyone is out to take your job, there is plenty of pie to go around.
pros: The business structure at Chase was great. Bankers are well trained and given the tools to succeed. There are opportunities at all levels of the organization for hard workers.
cons: In my experience management was very lacking in basic business skills. The path from banker to manager might as well be a Ponzi scheme sometimes. Aspiring managers or those looking to transition from a retail to a corporate role beware, your efforts may not be met with the enthusiasm and support you've been hoping for.

summary: Big, Dumb and Slow-- but trying to improve
advice:
Strive to speed up the pace of change, by creating additional feedback loops and increasing their frequency. With today's IT tools, every employee could answer a three or four question survey once a month, on happiness with job, immediate manager, managing director, and the firm.  "Hot spots" of unhappiness would likely be a leading indicator of problems.

Mandate that "exit interviews" actually be performed.
pros:
JP Morgan Chase is huge, and the employee experience varies tremendously from one Line Of Business to another. The executive leadership at JPMC, starting with Jamie Dimon and on down, is attempting to continuously improve the performance and the culture of the organization.  (Jamie and his direct reports are commonly referred to as "the Operating Committee".)

And, as with any company, the employee experience is determined 90% by their immediate manager. As a mid-level manager, I was able to create great working conditions for my teams of employees. They were happy and productive. The teams were recognized for their achievements, and employee turnover was low.  My methods were aligned with the new culture of Servant-Leadership which the Operating Committee has been trying to foster, and my team members were recognized, rewarded, and promoted.

The firm encourages internal mobility, and there are many opportunities to move around from department to department (however, rarely with increase in compensation). And, the package offered during layoffs is also moderately generous (based on time with the firm).
cons:
On the positive side, I was given a "free hand" to operate my teams based on my best judgement. The problem is, so were my colleagues and my managers (and their managers). And, there are only the poorest of feedback loops established for monitoring the health of the culture and the happiness of team members.  The big reform during my decade at JPMC: We went to an employee "pulse" survey every year, instead of every three years.
The scale and tradition of JPMC is both a strength and a weakness. During my years there, I came to admire the resilience of an organization which has lasted over two centuries. A colleague's retort stuck with me: "Big, dumb and slow worked for the dinosaurs, too."

There is a tremendous amount of waste at JPMC, at both small and large scales. Much of the wasted effort, including failed IT projects amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars, is due to failures in communication and coordination. The Operating Committee recognizes this and is trying to change the firm's culture. However, the culture is very resistant. 

My favorite story of the resistance of the culture is the young woman who explained to me that she used to be a business analyst who wrote 200-page requirement documents for a development team. But three years ago, she proclaimed proudly, she became a Scrum Master for an Agile Team. I asked about her job responsibilities as a Scrum Master: "I run a daily meeting, and I write 200-page requirement documents."

summary: Good people but poor Commission and Pay
advice: My advice is to the executives at the top of consumer banking. If us bankers just made the most ever last quarter in D & I. You probably shouldn't cut our commision in half. This will cause in my opinion a massive loss of talented bankers.
pros: The people i work with are awesome and supportive.
cons: when I was hired they said that the commision earned ws steady and that they rarely change the way they pay the bankers. They just effectively cut 1/3 of my commission check because of new limits on how much we can make. Corporate does not care about their employees and I will be leaving the company ASAP for better pay.

summary: Decent place to work despite everyone's whining here.
advice: Try to give your employees a little bit more recognition for their hardwork.
pros: They offer greats benefits just as everyone has said.  I've also received good personal recognition for my work.
cons: I can't really say that there wasn't opportunity to grow but that was because of the position I was in.  There might be other opportunities elsewhere in the company but as for the type of work I was doing, that's since been outsourced to India.  Not only that but it's such a huge corporation and any ideas you may have to improve the processes there just gets tossed aside or will take so long to implement that you'll never see it put in place in your lifetime.

summary: Overall satisfied with my time at Chase.
advice: To upper management: taking the time to truly understand what the worker bees are really doing (not just reading charts) would serve you, the company and employees far better in the long run. Take some cues from middle management, they’re stuck in a huge gap and not given appropriate credit or authority.
pros: Diversity. Fair treatment for employees. Benefits and many other employee perks. Great immediate level support. Encouraging atmosphere to nurture teamwork mentality. Learning and educational options. Community minded environment. Salary ranges. Flexibility and accommodations for employees.
cons: For such a massive company, there should be much more reality to opportunities within Chase, especially for displacement situations. A lot of touting, little action.

pros: Chase is a bank, it is a large employer - it comes with all the associated pros and cons. Some of the pros from my experience: Lot of flexibility for lateral movement. Stable employer, is able to work its way through market cycles without much impact. Good retirement benefits like pension plan, ESPP. Average healthcare benefits with rising premiums.
cons: Tons of bureaucracy. Enough processes, audit trails, and other useless tasks to tire down the most energetic workers. Well behind the curve to adopt to new tech. Super low compensation compared to market. Very limited growth prospects for upward movement (impossible to go beyond VP) - unless you fall into one of the special categories that public companies are looking to promote. Management keeps shuffling all the time.

summary: Washington Mutual was a great place to work...until the end
advice: They're all gone, for the most part...I guess in the future, don't put all of your eggs in the same (mortgage) basket and listen to the FDIC, Fed, and Treasury when they tell you to sell...even if you think they're wrong.
pros: I felt like I worked with my extended family and I was able to chart my own course in a big way.
cons: The end, when the bank literally failed (or was allowed to fail, unlike the other "big banks"), was rough. Seeing stock gains vanish into thin air was tough to take, plus being acquired for next to nothing by Chase was hard to swallow. After the take over, all of the good reasons for working there disappeared.

advice: Adhere to the policies and philosophies that Chase professesses to subscribe to. Some departments / management take to heart what employees learn in the compliance courses (eg, Fairness and treating employees with respect, etc) while others like to talk the talk but not walk the walk.
pros: Benefits are reasonably good compared to other big banks.
cons: It's a hit or a miss as far as whether or not you get a manager who will support you. I unfortunately didn't have that. It's nice getting the 4 weeks vacation that comes with working for a big bank but when you're working during all your vacations, it kind of defeats the idea behind vacations. Work load was way too much. Too much nepotism, clicks and back stabbing.

advice: Better pay for high performers and get rid of the slackers. People are really pissed if their colleagues change jobs and get 40%+ pay raise.
pros:
- A well known company that provides good exit opportunity
- Good internal mobility in the institutional side as lots of people move around AM / CB / IB / TSS
- Lots of networking opportunities and people are eager to share their experiences.
cons:
- Low moral due to below market compensation and long hours
- Poor perks when comparing with its peers
- Big firm means lots of bureaucracy. Even a simple request can take days to completed 
- Infrastructure requires lots of improvement. The 1 Gb ram Pentium 4 desktop couldn't run more than 5 programs at a time

advice: Ensure managers chosen for interns actually care about the interns. Performance reviews are usually biased based upon how much the manager likes the intern as opposed to the quality of their work or workload.
pros: It is only a 10 week period but you stand to learn a good amount at a pretty decent salary as an intern. Most interns gain lots of positive support from managers as well as interesting work. No traffic in Columbus. JPMorgan has effectively come through the financial crisis and appears to be increasing steam.
cons: Manager satisfaction varies greatly by which manager you have. Some are extremely good, others are horrible and treat interns poorly. Columbus is an extremely boring city. HR very territorial so do not expect to move around.

summary: Overall, a good place to work at ...
advice: Create incentives for various areas of the company to work together.  The incentives given to various areas don't really allow for these areas to work for the best interest of the company.
pros: JPMorgan is a pretty good company to work for.  So far, I have encountered really nice and smart individuals within my department.  There is a lot of opportunity to try out different roles and grow your career.
cons: Like most large companies, JPMorgan has too many layers of management and there is a lot of disorganization in terms of getting some things done and avoiding the typical big company politics.  The salary and bonus numbers are not too great here as compared with other companies.

advice: Stop changing everything on an annual basis.  I had 4 different performance management systems, over 5 different financial reporting platforms and 5 different sets of goals and platforms to measure them in 5 years.  Make a change to an area needing improvement then do not change that area again for at least 3 years so the business can run without having to figure out how to rebuild the car each and every year.
pros: Highly capable people across the organization. Strong ethics and integrity. Client centric.
cons: Investment banking personnel and management taking over the middle market area. Oversegmenting and overcomplicating the business. Appears to be little thought to how these changed impact the people in the business.

advice:
-streamline training and internally hire job-specific trainers, that way we can ensure they know what they're talking about.
-compensate employees that do more for the company (peer coaches get bas pay and often miss out on the chance to bonus, usually resulting in the new hires getting more pay than them)
pros:
-Very competitive benefits packages
-A lot of paid vacation time, even for new employees
-tuition reimbursement after working for the company for 1 year
cons:
-Management tends to tow the company line, specifically when it comes to policy that doesn't make sense 
-grading for quality standards vary from manager to manager
-training is not very good. peer coaching is excellent, but peer coaches are not adequately compensated so most stop assisting new hires after a week or so

advice: Internal hiring! Look at the strengths you have and allow people to move and grow. I shouldn't be still on the phone after completing a bachelor's degree and half of a masters degree however every position I apply for, I get a decline to interview letter.
pros:
My manager is fantastic!
New benefits package is really great. Hearing aid coverage.. which anyone who has them will realize is a huge thing for a company to cover.
cons:
Schedule flexibility is essentially non-existent
Plenty of sick days however unless you have FML status you get docked for using them
Advancement can be tough... hard to move between lines of business for example

advice: Be a bit more flexible on WFH and adjust salaries to meet market conditions
pros: Great company good perks and benefits. Challenging job but try and promote work life flexibility. Try and be social responsible promote diversity and fair hiring working practices. Seem clued into what is going on in world and environment on that front
cons: Since Covid significant attrition and salary’s have not adjusted to current market conditions (review as of 5/2022). Also been steadfast in making folks come back to work at minimum 50%. These two factors causing attrition

pros:
Great Company, nice working environment, employees are friendly and helpful.
Great compensation
Good name to put on your resume.
cons:
No room for career growth, yearly reviews are based on a quota or something like that so less than 3% of people will get Exceed performance rating and get promoted while the rest will range from meet to meet+. No matter how hard you work or what your accomplishments are you might get a mediocre performance review if you don't have he right connections and play politics.

I've seen a lot of people leaves JP after getting disappointed with the yearly performance review!! Their yearly salary raise is 2-3% and sometimes they don't even do it (Last year there was no salary raise for anybody in JP).

summary: Good job stability/security but red tape, old-school corporate culture, and questionable pay
pros:
- Good job stability; there's always work that needs to be done
- Very strong company (Industry leader)
- Get to work on projects that impact the global economy at both macro and micro level (e.g. retail and wholesale technologies)
cons:
- Stressful environment driven by deadlines instead of actual capacity, budgeting, resources, people
- They don't keep up with the market rate of salary growth or reward backend technologies with compensation (especially if you stay too long)
- Slow pace of change due to bureaucracy 
- The usual cons of banking corporations: you're just a number/resource, lot of red tape/policies that restrict personal and salary growth, old-school culture and mentality.

summary: Lot of potential but bad management
advice: Only by fixing the lines of communication can the team progress. Just having a leadership position and addressing the wider (200+) team as a family is not going to change how the business runs. In the long run, stuff will collapse miserably as the foundations are shaky.
pros:
* Good tech stack (depends from team to team)
* Interesting work with private cloud
* Opportunities to learn AWS and work on it
cons:
* Too much politics at the management level in the Corporate Technology line of business directly impacting product direction and day-to-day work
* Broken lines of communication leading to duplicate products being developed, eventually leading to the collapse of some products and thus teams losing jobs 
* Poor compensation (realized much after quitting)

summary: Maybe the Consumer Card Side is Better Than the Commercial Card Side...
advice: Don't expect morale to be good when your employees are drowning in work and customer complaints are non-stop due to poor executive decision making.  Staff your teams appropriately and listen to what your employees are saying.  They need to know that they are more than just numbers contributing to your performance score.
pros:
Benefits are good- 401k, insurance, PTO.

Can meet and work with some lovely people.
cons:
Management is a mess.  This department is always looking to 'cut corners' to save themselves money; they put shareholders before employees, thus putting increased workload on the client-facing teams with no extra compensation.

Internal career mobility is too nit-picky and doesn't always result in a just pay increase.

advice: Rework the insurance plan!
pros: The company is very pro growth opportunity.  Mobility is big and is seen as a plus.   It's very multi-cultural and tolerant of differences.  It celebrates it in fact.  Literally.  I love the fact that I work at a company as diverse as this.  And not only that, but I work with people located all around the world.
cons:
Some managers need to work on giving feedback throughout the year instead of just during review time.

The health insurance is not great.  Maybe all companies are suffering due to Obama Care.  But my family deductible is $3k which is obscene.  If you don't get sick, it's great.

summary: Heavy Red Tape, not much common sense
advice: Allow feedback to influence planning, do not be deadset on an idea from the start and never change it.
pros:
- very little pressure short or long term
- Randstad offers certification training reimbursement/incentive
- some remote work available during COVID
cons:
- you will be bored 95% of the time, there is almost no work to do and when there is large projects they hire out
- Except when they don't, and then you're doing heavy physical labor you're not supposed to be doing.
- There is no specialized industry knowledge to be gained in this role (aside for excel opportunities)
- Feedback not asked for or considered by management during planning, and the final plans never make much sense.

summary: Strong organization, with the expected bureaucracy associated with its size
advice: continue to strive to act like a small, nimble organization
pros: JPMorgan is a strong, stable financial institution with a proven track record and positive opportunities given the current state of financial markets.  The senior management is intelligent and engaged on the important issues, with the necessary attention to detail.
cons: It is a large, bureaucratic organization with the expected difficulty in navigating the organization for both business initiatives and personal questions.  Despite the expected rhetoric, it is a siloed organization where products / lines of business are given incentives to act in their personal interest, rather in the overall interest of the company.  In short, JP Morgan is product-focused as opposed to client-focused

summary: WaMu employees mostly happy with JP Morgan Chase.
advice: To the new Chase management: It's ok to keep tabs on production and customer service, but please recognize results and improvement when you see it. Also, your communication with employees has decreased since the merger. WaMu employees were very impressed with your extensive communication in September, don't let that fade away!
pros: Good benefits, tons of information and resources. Also, Chase is coming to town! Mostly everyone is really happy that JP Morgan Chase bought WaMu. But it's sad for those who are losing their jobs, good luck to you all.
cons: Way too much micro-management. There's a right way to do it, but the way it's done here doesn't account for results. It's micro-management with no follow-up on results.

advice: Relax HR rules around promotion, enable internal candidates to get the salary and title of new positions on start date.
pros: Great working environment, ample opportunities for growth, one of the most respectable companies to work at, access to senior management, great pay, meritocracy.
cons: Internal moves are lateral even if you are moving to a higher level, you get more responsibility, maybe more hours, but same pay same title (Officer, AVP, Assoc. VP, ED) until you are recommended for a promotion. HR policies make promoting people an uphill battle. External candidates get the Title and Salary of the position posted (unlike internal candidates, but internal candidates have preferred status, followed by JPMC Alumns)

summary: Great Company - If You Get a Good Manager
advice:
Management who only sees the numbers in the reports should really put in the actual work and you would see why numbers and productivity over quality become quite stressful
Managers (all levels) should be required to Take Mgmt 101 (and others) courses. Especially with COVID, communication changes and there will always be demand for improvement on all ends.
pros:
Great Pay
Time Off
Benefits
Values
Company Employee Appreciation Days can be fun
cons:
Raise Rates
Sometimes Numbers seem like the only thing that matter that can really deplete morale
Some Managers are either too busy or come across as condescending and will not try to help you succeed (this is rare from my experience, but I had the experience)

advice: Encourage some common culture. Encourage team work and prevent constant reinventing of the wheel by enforcing  unified BPM. And please, ease up on reorgs every 6 months.
pros: Solid, stable. Myriad of business lines and locations to choose from. Reasonable work/life balance. Surprisingly by 6pm office is almost empty. Flex work arranegments are allowed. Top global name, well respected in the industry.
cons: There is still huge overhang from all the past mergers. It is extremely ciloed, and every manager may impose their own view and philosophy, that may completely contradict the previous one, which becomes disorienting during frequent reorgs. Very political. Decisions are made not based on merits of proposal, but mainly from self-serving motivations. Constant positioning and jockeying for power among line managers.

summary: One of the greatest companies to work for with the culture, the atmosphere, and the ability to grow.
pros: The ability to grow within the company and the massive amounts of opportunities are what make JPMorgan Chase & Co. a great company to work for. The people you spend your career with become life long friends and it makes every day fruitful. The knowledge you will receive and be trained on will be a step above any other company. If you like the idea of coming to the office and striving to be the best, this is the company for you.
cons: Too many times I would have to discuss life issues with people who couldn't leave it at the door. I believe this is at any company.

advice:
Not sure why but you're dropping top talent like flies the last 2 years or so. Hope you're recruiting top talent just as fast.

To management: You're playing the infinite game prepare for like it's an infinite game. Stay hydrated, happy etc. the numbers will always go up and down.
pros: Great place to work. It's large so if you don't like the team/leadership just move to another Team and leave feedback while you're leaving lol
cons:
It can take a while to get recognized and promoted especially if you're not extremely intentional about it.

Also, the salary bumps are not high so you better walk in at a super high level or just leave after 2 years.

summary: I never thought I'd be a banker
advice: I'm not a big fan of Mr. Dimon or some of the shenanigans that Chase has gotten up to on a global level. That being said, I think Chase is a well managed company.
pros: After 4 years I'm surprisingly satisfied with my job at Chase. I've worked in technology for a long time and while there are no free meals, or even free coffee, Chase treats its people well and the people treat eachother well. This is the most collegial, collaborative environment I've ever worked in and I'm very glad to be here.
cons: It's taken time to adjust to the pace of working in a regulated environment. Things happen very slowly compared to the average technology company.

advice: do not ignore your junior employees, because for the most part they do the real work, everybody else bs their way through work. Be appreciative of peoples effort, and only offer constructive criticism.
pros: the salaries are competitive if you bargain right, it is a huge firm so you are assured of career stability if that is what you are looking for. They give back to society a lot and there is a lot of room for growth and challenging opportunities.
cons: There is less career mobility though the company makes a not of noise about it. there is hardly work life balance, another thing they make a lot of noise about, and the culture is a throat-cutting, backstabbing one.

summary: JP Morgan Chase - Don't join this firm
advice: Change your middle management or make them more effective. Provide opportunities for people to grow. Remove the rule that there will be no change in position or salary if you move across departments. People move for growth. Would you rather a valuable employee move to a competitor? Provide a clear career growth path and direction for people. Make your HR more responsive. In Asset management, the HR needs improvement. Pay per market standards.
pros:
- Great work life balance
- Decent benefits
- 22 days of time off
- Big brand name
cons:
- Very Bureaucratic environment. Takes forever to get anything done
- Responsibility without authority
- Promotions are adhoc and not based on experience or skill sets or value addition
- Worst HR that I have ever seen. Does not get back to you if you have any queries
- Pay is below industry standard
- Run like a government organization

summary: Hard work, not the best pay, big name, lots to learn and keep you busy
advice: Be more flexible - know the value of your employees and understand the amount of investment that goes into learning how these incredibly complicated systems work.  If you find a talented, knowledgeable employee KEEP HIM/HER.
pros: Talented coworkers, a lot to learn, decent mobility within the organization, and it's generally a well-run place considering the huge volume of everything they do (though I would say less so during recent lean years).
cons: Very hierarchical and political.  Negotiate hard before you start because you won't get a raise, and bonuses can be laughable.  Generally fairly stable work if not the best-paying.

summary: Mr. Dimon does a tremendous job leading the company and the industry.
advice: Spend more time getting direct feedback from more than 2 levels down and ensure that the actions of those 2 levels are having the intended impact of the productivity and health of the organization.
pros: A well managed company with strong vision and leadership at the top of the house and a strong performing dedicated workforce. Problems are addressed early and decisively. Customer focus is very strong. Worklife balance and diversity are top priorities across the company.
cons: Organizational change is rapid and not always well controlled or communicated. There is a persistent disconnect between the vision and values espoused by senior management and the way they are acted on by middle management.

summary: A Good But Not a Great Place to Work
advice: This company tries to be a leader among banks when it comes to doing the right thing. Now be a leader in resurrecting America's middle class and bump up pay for your lower middle class workers. Stop paying the least you can get away with like other banks and instead be the bank that pays the most and attracts the best.
pros: JP Morgan Chase attempts to help employees develop their careers and provides decent benefits and vacation allotment.
cons: The pay is underwhelming. While there is opportunity for upward mobility, almost all of it is in management so if you are not excited about the prospect of managing people, you will be out of luck.

advice: Management should give out better compensation packages to retain top talent and should discourage junior management from cutting corners in order to supposedly meet deadlines.
pros: JPMorgan IFAS Dallas was and is a great place to get to understand from an observer point of view as an accountant the field of pension fund investing.  The benefits package is good and the HR policies of JPMorgan are beneficial for the employee.
cons: The compensation in JPMorgan IFAS is subpar to what one might expect working as a fund accountant for an investment manager.  Furthermore, it is easy if you are not proactive in learning to not really know how the entire fund accounting process at JPMorgan works.

advice: Practice what you preach
pros: JP Morgan is a large company making it easy to bounce from job to job. It's easy to have many careers with in this company.  Benefits are also good.
cons: Many terrible managers.  The company preaches the importance of good fair management practices but only promotes people that lead by fear and intimidation.  It's odd to see a manager stay for more than 2 years and turn over is a very large problem. Layoffs and restructuring is common place and led to my title of 18 managers in 5 years.  There are pockets of good people but most are negative and disgruntled just trying to get through the day.

summary: Lead a team of experienced and highly skilled customer service specialists
advice:
Be consistent and work for your employees
Keep the team leaders in mind and know that they have the biggest impact to your front line agents as they are in direct contact with them 8 hours a day.
pros:
Benefits provided: matching 401k, vacation time provided, flexibility with the schedule, medical/dental/vision insurance
Ability to work with some great individuals and a chance to help people grow within the company and fulfill their dreams and/or start their career
cons:
Inconsistent management

Not enough focus on the team leader level and the employee experience that is being provided there. More focus on this level is needed as they have a direct impact on the first level employees

advice: Focus on leading and not simply managing what you can control. You have been placed in a position to develop the future of the company. Allow for autonomy and become a leader
pros: Aligned with current medical, dental, and vision benefit plans. One of the few companies left that offer a pension plan.
cons: Network type of company. It's who you know not what you know. Too many managers and not enough leaders in positions of influence. Too much outdated management where seasoned management unable to adapt to change and new approaches to lead people. Upper management view talent and leadership from a direct report as a threat.  All resulting in minimal to no career growth opportunities

advice: Better communication between all levels of employees and better promotional advancement opportunities along with action on diversity, not just rhetoric.
pros: Large network of employees with various careers and interests make it a great place  to meet people.  Internal mobility is possible but only through meeting the right people and networking due to the size of the company. The company has great brand recognition which is helpful when networking for external opportunities.
cons: Salary and bonuses could be better and also seem to be unequal across teams. The process of telecommuting and flexible work arrangements are not enforced equally amongst teams and lead to employees being hesitant about inquiring about such policies that could improve work/life balance.

advice: Be fair, do not talk about staff members outside of the team because the impacted people will be told what you have said about them, learn to find a way to equally divide the work for the team,  when members leave the team and their function is critical please replace faster and not take up to a year to replace.  Managers should be coached and trained on how to do theirbjobs,  HR when the turns over twice in 3 years maybe should investigate.
pros: I had the opportunity to learn a lot over a 20 year career
cons: Long hours with no compensation, poor and unprofessional managers, discrimination if not indian or asian, managers aloud to be verbally abusive, constant doing more with less so teams are not appropriately staffed,  off shoring does not work especially when US based workers are expected to pick up the slack

advice: More flexibility, more responsibility to junior staff
pros: Great benefits, pay, reputation, culture. If you're looking to work in an investment bank -- especially one in a bulge bank , there aren't that many left.
