pros: Fair compensation, lots of very smart people to learn from, my longest-run manager was tough but fair. I found work-location options to be fair. In my role, I found it IMPOSSIBLE to cross over into other fields of interest.
cons: Management decisions from 2+ levels up seem short-sighted. New tools brought in from outside vendor felt like someone's wink-wink-nudge-nudge deal. Some management behaviours smack of intimidation. My last manager was absolutely focused on 1 senior staffer, while ignoring 3 others.

summary: Consumer Loan Doc Specialist: NO Training, Mean Supervisor, YOU get fired for their BAD management
advice: Provide training to your employees and calm down, be patient with people who u KNOW don't have experience! Employers are SO lazy now, no one wants to train anyone anymore! You have to be born with experience to do anything now!
pros: great pay for the area, cool facility (A/C), sit down all day except to turn in complete files. I see constant of these positions listed on: careerbuilder, integrity staffing, roberthalf, kforce, randstad, etc.
cons: Supervisor was a jerk. i asked him could he repeat the password and he got smart with me! They didn't provide training to the new employees until they realized i was getting files wrong and i asked about training. That training lasted 2 day! I DIDN'T learn anything about the job. That so called training didn't give us step by step of what we should be doing.

advice: Eliminate both layers of the management and the fire drill mentality. People are overworked by the need to run every decision by committee after committee to gain total and complete alignment. Additionally, decisions on what to focus on are often driven by the desire to please a senior leader and not what is good for the business.
pros: HR at all levels has a tremendous focus on the employee experience, ensuring that pay for entry level employees is fair and equitable, and the latest technology is available to support networking and collaboration.
cons: The organization, despite a strong desire to adapt to the marketplace is weighed down by its "collaborative" culture and inability to formally set a strategic direction and prioritise.

advice: Listen to your employees.  Don't try to spin things when you take away benefits, titles, work from home, increase premiums/deductibles, keep raises/bonuses flat when profits continue to be record breaking every year.  You say employees are important, but you don't walk the walk. Don't promote yourself as a green company if you're not going to allow employees to work from home to save  resources.
pros: They do have health benefits, although they're anywhere as good as they used to be.  Their 401K matching is good.  They have a small pension fund.
cons: Promotions are almost non-existent.  If you want any kind of significant raise or promotion, you will need to leave the company and/or leave the company and come back.

summary: A very good company, but a difficult environment for software development
advice: Have IT groups report directly to business units instead of in a parallel org chart.
pros:
Great people who are willing to help across business lines.  People make time to try to help others from any group.
Competitive compensation.
Good benefits and work-life balance.
Good mid-town NY locations.
cons: Too many layer of approval needed to make changes to any business process. This leads to many changes building up waiting for approvals, so when the changes are finally made they're more stressful and error-prone than would have been the case had a sequence of small changes been allowed.  This makes development work frustrating.

advice: Keep up the good work but pay your people more!
pros: Great benefits, resources and people. Focuses on customers and value. Great work life balance, although pipeline is always back of mind. Great company strategy. Good hours.
cons: The incentive plan is set up so that the more you make, the more you make, and the less you make, the less you make. As much as you want to be consistent or hard working, deals either close or they don’t. Sometimes you get paid with out any effort (right place right time) and sometimes you go the extra smile and don’t get a penny. Also, not being able to wear your own ties and dress shirts is not allowed. Must be chase branded.

summary: No work life balance for overworked employees
advice: Stop being dismissive to employees.
pros: Part time employees can get benefits. Corporate discounts on travel.
cons: I work full-time but I was contractually hired as a part time employee so I only qualify for part time benefits. We are always short staffed for being a busy branch. Tellers are gaining banker responsibilities with no pay increase or incentives. Personal banker positions are being removed, and they have only been given the two options of becoming tellers or Relationship Bankers which they need to get licensed to work. Relationship Bankers are overwhelmed and over booked with appointments. Internal promotion is almost impossible even when you meet most of the qualifications and have contacts in that current position vouching for you to work there, something about "HR Politics". JPMC had their highest earnings in the first quarter of this year and their employees got a congratulatory E-mail for all our hard work.

summary: Good Company for this who like slow paced environments
advice: management kill young developers dreams as they don't care about anything but their promotion.
pros:
- salary is decent
- workload can sometimes be minimal to nothing
- work/life balance
- managers tend to be very understanding
- 401k matching up to 10%
- free chase premiere accounts
cons:
- no real benefits. No stock options, health plan is not that great
- bonuses are not based on performance
- too slow paced
- too much bureaucracy at all levels
- there is very little opportunity for new ideas and innovation
- not recommended for young and talented people
- environment can be toxic given that the only reason to do things is for the purpose of being promoted

advice: Listen to your employees and concerns to help improve the business. Learn to love your job and not look at as just a “check”.
pros: Great pay, loved the environment and my coworkers. Certain managers truly care about the employees and their job. Only a couple would help to improve productivity.
cons: Unfortunately the rest management was prone to ignoring its employees and being lazy. Most didn’t care for the job and only looked at it as “check”. COVID really set the company back and made management content with how they handled business. Turn over rate was extremely high. I witnessed 50 people leave in a span of 3 months. Upper management would purposely seek out the most minut detail to fire someone.

advice: The numbers themselves should not be the only decisive reason for somebody to get promoted to be a manager.
pros:
Company's name recognized everywhere, prestigious. The biggest bank in the World. 
I did have some very nice coworkers who eventually became my friends.
cons:
Chase bankers generate the majority of the revenue for the bank but they make the least amount of salary. and they are not well treated or respected either inside the bank. Investment banking generates considerably less (compare that it was the main revenue source for the bank back in the days) and they make the most and they are well respected. 
The most dishonest, low emotional intelligent, crooked sociopaths are getting promoted at Chase. Some of the employees are getting hired off the street without any education or some relevant meaning job (
For instance, I had a couple of managers/employees ended up in jail because of stealing clients' money.

summary: A strong sense of self is a must. Favoritism by Race
advice: Let everyone earn their way.
pros:
Best Training if you are new to the field of customer service/ call center
Great benefits
Vacation available beginning of the year
cons:
Work load as Collections SPECIALIST I or II is overload

Racism rampant and the Tempe office at Discovery Center favored a particular race I er others.

People who were supposed to have TL and DL position, who earned it, did not get it.

They bought in a guy from India who also favored a particular race. 

I heard a DL offer to raise an agent pay so he could get an even higher pay offer to another department. Talk about using one's authority. Position are not always earned.

summary: Chase as a company A++  my dept eh
advice: MAKE SURE you know how your trainers coaches and management of training staff are doing the right thing and not being BULLIES
pros: Chase is a wonderful place to work for. Corporate is amazing. They are just AMAZING AS A COMPANY! I love everything we do and how we help people get back on track with their finances.
cons: You are marked from the day 1 of training. If someone don't like your (for any reason) they all gossip like little girls and mark your name and the chances of your getting out of that dept is hard. 1 lady wasn't even included in our graduation from training photo! They literally cut her out and made it seem like uh she looks like this coach so I thought she was in it. Even though I was right behind them when they were laughing about it saying just cut her out anyway XX looks like her. Felt so horrible not saying anything and not sticking up for her but I didn't want to end up on that side of the fence either cause how bad they make it.

summary: Great place to work if in Investment Bank or if in New York; otherwise pass.
advice:
-The VPs are the problem: they're trying to save their little kingdoms, rather than do the right thing for the firm, employees, or otherwise.
-Communication takes a long, long time to happen.
-People are afraid for their jobs
pros:
-Name recognition: everyone knows the firm
-Solid benefits program, including Tuition Assistance, pension, Health/Dependent Care Reimbursement Accounts, Parking Reimbursement Accounts, etc.
cons:
-If you're not in New York, Columbus, or Tampa, you're part of a future cost save.
-High voltage politics
-Great deal of churn around project funding requests: 6-9 month process with a gazillion revisions to the plan.
-Lifer employees who are more interested in holding on to their jobs than moving the business forward

summary: Great experience - learned a lot about the industry and met amazing people at JPM.
advice: Start entry level workers at a slightly higher salary and make them exempt. This will help you retain top talent and help limit frustration of mid level employees due to entry level workers getting paid more than themselves and help low level employees become less reluctant to take a promotion as they won't be losing money.
pros: Great opportunity to learn and good firm culture.  Very good work environment that allows the opportunity for career advancement. Great dental and vision insurance.
cons: Very long hours and bad bonus / salary structure  The company starts recent college graduates out at non exempt and due to the long hours they are able to rack up overtime which bumps them up to mid level pay (salary + 30-40 hrs OT / month at 1.5x pay). Then after a year or two they get promoted and lose overtime for a small increase in salary which results in a pay cut. Promotions should not result in pay cuts in any way shape or form. This is not a good way to retain talent.

advice: Surround yourself with people who know how to deal with a crisis and can do it quickly - while at the same time not upsetting the regulators.
pros: Like most companies, there are good managers and bad managers and WaMu was no different.  I was fortunate to work for good managers -- people who cared about doing a good job and doing the right things.  I had several great opportunities while I was there for promotion and recognition.
cons: Response time from senior management was slow and indirect.  When we could have and should have been dealing with customer and employee fears and concerns, you could hear crickets from the upper floors.  It was a shame...

advice: If you're going to move people into various positions, then recognize and act upon when people are failing in their new roles and don't just keep dead weight around because they have seniority.
pros: They do go out of their way to move you to a new position if your current position has been eliminated.  The benefits are pretty good.  I was personally lucky enough to have two great managers - I'm still formulating an opinion on my new current manager.
cons: Because they go out of their way to move displaced workers, people are sometimes moved into positions where they are either incapable of, or don't care to do their best.  If you have experience in whatever business they move you to, you may very well be answering to someone who has zero experience in the department that they are in charge of.  Not to mention that the most inept employees can be making considerably more than someone with experience, due to the fact that their previous position had a higher salary which they got to take with them when they got moved into their current role.

summary: A Great Place to Learn and Establish a Career Path
pros: JPMorgan Chase provides an opportunity to obtain experience in a broad number of financial services and technology disciplines.  WIth global exposure, an abundance of subject matter experts and plenty of in-house training and funding for external courses, one can reap great benefits if aggressive and eager to learn.
cons: As with many large financial institutions that have ability to impact the markets, caution leads to beaucracy that can make it difficult to get things done and frustrate those who are results-driven and seeking instant gratification.  Also, while the firm has fared better than most competitors through the economic downturn, success has come at the expense of signinficantly reduced employee benefits.

summary: Good salary and benefits but layers of bureaucracy are stifling
advice: Lighten up a bit with some of the security paranoia.  Break down some of the layers of management.
pros: Good salary and benefits.  Management seems open and fair and strictly adheres to firm-wide policies.  In this global mega-corporation you can easily move to other jobs within the firm.
cons:
Super-paranoid and extremely risk-adverse. If you are doing software development,  you will be hindered by the fact that all the hardware is strictly locked down and access tightly controlled. Getting almost anything done, no matter how trivial, requires a formal electronic request that must be approved by several layers of management. There is a Risk organization that constantly comes up with new restrictions they can put into a place that end up making your job more difficult. (e. g., recycling bins were removed from everywhere because of the risk that someone might throw confidential docments into the recycling rather than the shredder, forcing everyone to dispose of all recycling in the shredder.

Work/life balance doesn't appear to one of the firm's principles.  You are expected to make yourself available at all times.

summary: It has been a huge blessing in more ways than one. I've grown considerably!! Thank you.
advice: JPMorgan Funds is wise to implement the Client Services & Business Administration Competency Pyramid. Something expected of all employess. Examined deficiencies become classes which set aright all misconception in your targeted area requiring improvement.
pros: Brand recognition amongst peers fascilitates a positive rapport. I'm in a position where, if I plot my course very carefully, my full-potential will blossom. JPMorgan has given me transferable skills.
cons: Given that JPMorgan is in a highly competive market - the much welcomed  'laissez-faire' approach, is slowly becoming a thing of the past. Professionalism is sometimes given too much precedent, making a simple exchange - something like wrestling with a strained anaconda.

advice: Cut the red tape for developers.  It is too hard to learn new techniques and software practices during work hours because the common desktop prevents software found from trusted partners to be installed without elevated access rights.  I'm sorry, but your internal training doesn't have the all of the answers and is too slow to adopt new ones.
pros:
You have the chance to play with some good tools and experience good projects
Rollout of updated software is quicker than some companies
Benefits are fairly generous
cons:
Too much red tape to get to the tools you need.
Lack of focus on the developer environment and too much focus on a common environment for all.
In some areas outsourcing developers is the rule.

summary: Incompetent and Untruthful Managers, Highly Political, Unstable Infrastructure, Low Morale
advice: Managers need to stop behaving selfishly and promote a more collaborative work environment. There's a lot of politics and backstabbing among employees. I got the impression you need to suck up big time to your superiors in order to move ahead. The work environment literally resembles elementary school due to the rampant gossiping and superficial and snitching employees.
pros: Cafeteria is decent. Some intelligent people and drinks are paid for at social events. Good technology and IT systems.
cons: The managers for the most part are horrible, tend to overly micromanage, and lack the aptitude to motivate employees as they are mostly concerned about themselves. Management definitely needs to take some classes on organizational behavior as the environment is chaotic and disorganized. High turnover rate as they literally work you to death and it's mostly about who you know and not what you know. Very political and there's a lot of backstabbing among other team members. Employees for the most part are viewed as expandable as they use the JPMorgan name to bully and intimidate employees. Also, the buildings, desks, and furniture are very old and you feel as if you are working at a prison. I would suggest you only consider a job here if you have absolutely nothing else on the horizon.

advice: If hiring a manager that had been downsized in the past, take a look at his/her entire resume, How did they treat those under them, Do they value the knowlege of the people working for them, should that manager be allowed to put her sexual orientation on display then assume you have a problem with it? Should she be able to make racial jokes and lie on revirews? After notifying Human resources, this manager was allowed to continue to bully and block raises.
pros: Compensation is no where it was when I began in 1997 but the work life program is great
cons: Managing Directors that know nothing of the business but base your knowledge on your skin color.

advice: Need a legitimate way for middle management to escalate without reprisal to top of firm.  While direct management may not be involved in an issue/complaint often they themselves don't or won't verbalize an issue with the next tier management or higher up the chain.
pros: Good company overall, great benefits including MED, DENTAL, LIFE, SUPPLEMENTAL LIFE, VISION, ELDER CARE, LONG-TERM CARE.  All/Most at substantial cost reduction compared to normal market cost.  They even pay in full for some benefits.  Stock/401k Plans/Employee discounts.  Perks like free Checking/Savings.  Company uses meritocracy in determining raises, promotions and anyone with a good work ethic can succeed and have an awarding career.
cons: Like all big banks and large corporations/companies bottom line is always driven by share holders results.  Extreme pressure put on its middle managers.  Buck stops with you in regards all things.  Company talks a great deal about transparency and escalation and fighting bureaucracy but its all smoke and mirrors because if you complain you will be targeted.  Like all management positions and any company if you can play the game you can succeed.

pros: JPMorgan offers a wide range of opportunities, career advancement, and wide exposure to several technologies. I worked in the Investment Bank and the pace was significantly faster than the Retail side. The benefits are comparable to other Fortune 100s; however the health plans continue to place more of a burden on the employee through higher deductibles and premiums.
cons: With respect to the IB, there is a limited number of upper management roles in the Houston area. The worklife balance can tip unfavorably depending on which team you belong to. There is relatively constant pressure to reduce costs, specifically headcount. The year interranking process rewards the top performers well but can be brutal for those at the opposite end.

summary: Bad employee morale in certain businesses
advice: This company is too top heavy and too lean at the bottom.  Don't turn labor to a sweat shop environment, your security layer depends on competent and happy workers.  Too many workers get shafted by bad management and leave gaping holes in your security and business processes.  You want to prevent getting hacked?  Hire and protect workers then they will show their appreciation.
pros: Lots of initiatives and tons of internal opportunities.
cons: Lots of useless re-orgs and putting morale down the toilet.  Managers governed by different set of rules, often managers crosses the line and gets away and workers with gets mistreated either pack up and leave if they're good or if they're not good treated like worn old shoes.  Culture can be downright toxic and unproductive as often asking for help is like asking people to donate money.  Too much contractors and too no ownership.  The company is over-ran by talent-less people at the least productive layers.  Often nothing gets done because resources are dried when there's hiring freezes or a request for service gets red taped to death.

summary: They helped me prep for grad school
advice: Take the feedback process to heart and really help your groups succeed in their career paths.  It will only help you in yours.
pros: Swing shift was difficult to find, so I appreciated that.  Also, you cannot find many companies with so many great benefits! Medical, Dental, Vision, Health assessments and perks, smoking cessation program, cell discounts, car discounts.
cons: The company has a silo mentality.  With such an involved CEO, one would think he would also promote a true environment of mentorship and promoting from within.  Well, those promoted from within were usually friends with someone in management.  There were definitely great managers, but they were not rewarded for their hard work.

advice: I was employed at Chase for 5 years and the first 2 years were great! It was so much fun! Every month or so, there was something going on and food for the employees ordered as a reward for our hard work.  The work atmosphere was amazing! There was a general camaraderie and you could tell that there was feeling of general happiness to work for a great company. There was a lot of team recognition and competition, it made work fun and enjoyable. About two years in, everything changed. The recognition dried up, the competition stopped, and job satisfaction was really low. You could tell the difference. I think Chase should go back to caring for their employees, yes the bottom line is improtant but so is the health and welfare of your employees.
pros:
Great insurance benefits
Variety of schedules
Vacation and time off are really good
cons:
If you get ill, as per most companies you must be approved, however if your not ready to return to work do to said injuries, regardless of how sick you are, back to work you go.
Can be extremely stressful

advice: Tighten up risk management. Revamp the way business is done in certain areas. May be get rid of them
pros: Take care of employees extremely well. Nice work place environment. Have a well established infrastruture but seems like lot of it has not been used effectively. An effective and efficient management team will have its hands full in coming up with veariuos ways to put the company's resources into great use and bring it back to profitability.
cons:
Unstable business
weak managemnt
Mismanaged operations/ expenses. Often one wonders as how so many ppl are at a mid level mgmnt position and what work they must be doing. The operational expenses must be too high for this company. The company has literally put itself in the buyer's market and has eventually sold itself to JPM. There are lots and lots of great talented ppl in the company but one believes if it comes with too many unneccessary baggage, meaning lot of redundancy. On top of all the top level mgmt have misguided the company into dire straits. One main reson could be too much optimism with inexperience at the top level.

summary: Chase has been a great opportunity to expand my PM skills and learn new technologies.
advice: Promote within the company when warranted versus looking outside.  While it is excellent approach to get fresh views into the company, it is a better strategy to carefully balance the new hires with internal promotions.
pros: Ability to move around and gain a greater breath of business acumen.  Exposure to cutting edge technologies and work life balance add to the benefits.
cons: Promotional opportunities are limited but ability to lateral is encouraged. The parking is very limited in the Polaris campus creating a culture of eating at desks for lunch since it is too difficult to leave for lunch.

summary: Average to say the least.  Salary extremely lower than industry average.
advice: Hire competent managers.  Don't make the ability to move up incredibly difficult for the employee.
pros: The referral opportunity in the bank channel offers a great ability to succeed.  You work with partner within the branch ie business banker, mortgage personnel, bankers, and managers to acquire business opportunities.  You have full access to the book of business from the bank side to call and sell.
cons: If your placed in the wrong branch/location/demographics the ability to succeed is difficult.  If you enter with the intention of moving up it might be harder than they like to make it appear.  You are golden if your the guy who slings all of your clients into the inappropriate investment making tons of money.  If you are the ethical advisor that does the 'right thing' for your client you are left behind to say the least.  Compensation works when you sell your clients that things that don't work for them.  They pitch you on a book of business that you walk into but the residual it typically pittens.

pros: I am very appreciative of having the opportunity to work at JP Morgan.  Both my coworkers and management are very supportive of one another, and management is supportive of career growth.  The office culture in my position can be laid back when things slow down, and we all feel like a bi family, but everybody knows how to put their nose to the grindstone when necessary.  Workload can at times be a lot, but so are the rewards.
cons: Some positions can be hard to move out of and into other areas.  The various technology systems that the bank utilizes do not always work together as smoothly as one would hope.

summary: Great ceo but concerned about moving too many functions to India
advice: Cost saves in moving functions to India needs to be carefully reviewed. You get what you pay for. Some functions can be moved to India but do we really want critical functions like risk management and compliance there?
pros: Great ceo in Jamie and encourages people to speak up to reduce bureaucracy.
cons: Moving way too many functions and staff to India. Chase has over 40k employees in India now and growing there and shrinking in US. India shift looks good on paper but will hurt firm in long run! Benefits not as good compared to other banks especially for mid level managers. Once your cash comp is over $250k, no 401k match.

advice: Mentor incoming talent, provide upward growth possibilities, change the culture to one that more accurately resembles JPM as a whole.
pros: JP Morgan has a very strong network of intellectual people with a high degree of conviction in becoming the best player on the street and doing so in unison as a team. Unfortunately, the credit risk center in Columbus, Ohio, is a completely different environment which does not allow for upward mobility and senior management is the worst many tenured employees have encountered.
cons: No leaders, just managers. No upward mobility nor descent salary raises. The work environment is not interactive and everyone seems to be dissatisfied with the overall culture and senior leaders. More operational work rather than fundamental financial analysis.

advice: Live your values.  Be honest about what is happening in the bank - especially when the news is very bad.  Work on communication.
pros: Interesting industry - Banking right now is very volatile and newsworthy  Working at WaMu when the bank failed and was siezed by the FDIC and sold to JPMC was a great learning experience.  Great people - A lot of the employees live the WaMu values of fair, caring, human.  The workforce is very diverse.
cons: Poor communication - Information did not flow down from top leadership.  A lot of unnecessary "What?  It's due tomorrow? Why didn't anyone tell us?" type remarks.  Information about terminations and information sources was also very poor.

summary: Good Place to Learn, Promotions/Mobility can be Difficult
pros:
JPM invests very heavily in technology, so their platforms and integrated functionalities  are often best in class.

Very mature governance structure: management has an excellent, structured approach to managing change across the business, with standardized best practices for nearly every process.
cons:
Goal setting for employees can often be too vague to be helpful

Criteria for promotion is not clearly defined, and in some cases, not communicated explicitly--which can be frustrating.

Internal transfers can be extremely difficult.  In my experience I have twice applied for positions in other departments, only to learn that I was not offered the position on account of my current management team refusing to let me out of my current role.

advice: Consider paying people based on current work production and not past. Pay should not fluctuate by only 10%, if a person  is exceeding all expectations and producing work that is deserving of the top 10% of peers then pay that person accordingly.
pros: Strong big bank, with opportunity to grow if you live in certain areas of the country. PTO was inline with other banks.
cons:
With Big bank comes the chances of layoffs.
 The compensation program started strong with achievable goals and the opportunity to bonus monthly and annually, then it was changed to only hourly pay which was based on your past 18 months production, for some this was welcomed, for others who just stared it a shot to the wallet.

advice: Decrease the fear culture to have trusting and hardworking employees and be welcoming of better work-life balance not just when employees go out for "suggested" happy hours.
pros:
- Well Known financial institution so it looks good on your resume
- It's a Large Bank &  there are opportunities for mobility if you put in effort Early on
cons:
- You will succeed only if you play the game and accept office politics
- Managers are allowed to do & say whatever they want to their employees and Senior Managers allow it - borderline bullying
- Faux diversity, almost all of the promotions go to Caucasian men
- They push out whoever "doesn't fit in" either through blatant firing or constructive discharge

advice: Truly help staff to accomplish what they want to do. Not everyone wants to be in management nor are they good at it.  The firm tends to promote only 'yes' people at the sacrafice of solid workers
pros: Benefits, salary in some areas
cons: Very political and management always focused on how to fill their bank accounts with money at the demise of the people who actually do the work. A significant amount of staff layoffs where management is rewarded for the down sizing and staff are left hanging to find new opportunities.  Management always focused on pushing staff to move to next step up at the sacrafice of the workers.

advice: Make sure that ALL mangers are trained on how to work the teller window if there is a rush of customers.
pros: Fun people (depending on the branch), Team oriented (depending on the branch), Great training program for retail banking.
cons: In the retail side there is a lot of standing around depending on the type of branch. High turnover rate in teller position so there is a lot of working full time type hours for part time wage. Constant movement from branch to branch because you go wherever you are needed even throughout the work day. Training is done in branch while trying to help customers so there's really only time to review if branch is slow. Slow movement through corporate ladder.

summary: Used to be one of the best places to work
advice: I don't see how replacing our team of 6 US developers with 12 offshore developers and 4 H1B visa workers truly saved money.  Even if there were wage savings, the efficiency and quality of the work suffered.
pros:
- Large company with lots of opportunities
- Good 401K with match and they still have a pension
- Employee perks
cons:
- Most IT jobs have been (or are in the process of being) outsourced
- LOTS of red tape to get anything done
- The large bureaucracy creates lots of bottle necks and extra work
- I was logging over 60 hours a week with the included weeknights and weekend deployments

summary: Great Benefits, Communication Gaps, Management does not relate to employees
advice: Walk in the shoes of the employees before instituting changes.  The change might look good from the outside but how is it going to affect the employees that will have to endure the change and pass that information along.
pros: Chase has some of the best benefits around.  From health insurance, to paid time off, flexible schedules in some instances
cons: There are many communication gaps.  You generally have to dig to find information or plead with senior management to be able to discuss certain things with employees.  Its always a better experience if you are up front and honest with employees no matter how good or bad the news might be.

pros:
A place where you get to practice your interpersonal skills a lot by reaching out to clients and discover their financial needs, whether it's business lending, mortgage or investment advisory. Cold-calling is a significant part of the work and getting to engage with potential clients while helping them can be very satisfying. 

However, for those who concern for a higher purpose in their work. We might have doubts as we're recommending mutual fund products that might not be the best investment vehicles customers need.
cons:
For those who work in this job to make money: please find a promising branch location, as it plays the biggest difference in your performances. 


Career opportunities can be limited to 2 directions:
become a higher level banker, then become a financial advisor. Mobility to move across the company in other directions can be just as challenging as applying externally.

pros: Work/life balance can be decent depending on the team / management you are apart of.
cons:
My group was infested by micromanagers, making it very difficult to do the right thing and to do it well.

Vacation is technically accrued. The tracking system does not show this (shows total vacation for the year) and was not told this when I hired on. And management talks as if the vacation is all available Jan 1. This all works out until you quit. You actually accrue 1/12 of total vacation days on the last day of the month. So, if you take more vacation days than you've "accrued" in the month you resign, it is a salary advance and will be deducted from your final pay. Stop telling people you get 20 vacation days and instead tell them you accrue 1.66 days on the last day of the month.

summary: If you get a chance with Chase, don't pass it up.
advice: Don't ever forget your current mind set of keeping your employees first.  Your sucess is based on their happieness as you more than prove every day
pros: Definitely a great place to work.  Pay and benefits are based on other major companies.   They do not try to make you believe that the industry base is lower than what it truely is.  No micromanagement and you are evaluated on your performance and knowledge.  They willingly get you classes to improve your ability to succed for both yourself and the company in a whole.
cons: The only down side is that you have to work anyway for a living.  Although you would probably be bored of that after a while.  The only other down side would be that you don't already have a job there.

summary: Nice place to work in a troubled economy...
advice:
1. Increase head count where required
2. Treat people as employees not resources
3. Better compensation - salary may not be the only factor to boost employee morale...
4. Outsourcing is ok but look at the quality of people we are adding - we end up with more problems than what we can solve on account of outsourcing (and I'm an immigrant!)
pros:
1. Stable bank in an unstable economy
2. Complex environment (IT wise) - nice place to pick up skills in a short time 'baptism by fire'
3. IT Management has some of the best in breed people
cons:
1. Too much work, too few people
2. Outsourced like crazy - get people who can speak the language
3. Timelines stuffed down the throat of middle - everything needs to be done in 2 weeks - no matter how big or how small

summary: If you like being a puppet slave, welcome aboard.

summary: How to make JPMorgan a better company
advice:
I’d like to start by saying that I’ve been with the company for many years and am a very loyal employee who genuinely cares about the firm. It is a great organization and I believe we have the best CEO on the street.  I’m using this forum in the hope that senior JPMorgan colleagues read it and maybe take note of some of the points. I would not be able to do this via an internal route as it could be seen as bad for my career, even though they are all points aimed at helping the firm.

People:

Hiring – We often hire people from outside the firm and bring them in on higher salaries and grades than people who are currently doing the same job who have been with  the company over many years. If you work with someone for several years then you know their strengths etc, but hiring someone based on a one hour interview is a big risk. Very often the people who have given their heart and soul to JPMorgan and who are very good at their job are left demotivated and disillusioned. I’ve seen many colleagues leave the firm or department in these situations. The new hire has not always performed well. The importance of years of systems knowledge, experience in a role, internal networking, dedication etc. is often underestimated.

Quality of staff – JPMorgan has some really great people, however we also have many poor performers. When someone is bad at their job and we want to replace them, it is nearly impossible to do this. Instead of seeking the very best people, we end up with departments full of people who are just not that good, and they will be there for years. This causes so much damage to the firm.

Promotions – JPMorgan has a policy of only promoting people once per year. So, if your job changes in February and you have much more responsibility etc, you will not receive your grade change until January next year. However, an external person can be hired at any grade at any time.  Again, this demotivates people who have been loyal and worked hard for the company.

Grading consistency – Ok, this is one that I really have trouble getting my head around. You have two people doing exactly the same job, same number of years with the company, same performance level, responsibility etc, but they work in two different JPMorgan offices. One person could be a Vice President and the other could be a senior clerk.  This inconsistency again causes employees to be disillusioned (if you are the clerk) and makes no sense.   

Expenses:

Energy – We promote ourselves as a green company and are spending millions of dollars upgrading buildings and telling the media that we care about the environment etc. What I have never understood, and have tried to raise many times over the years is that in all the JPMorgan offices I have seen, we burn lights overnight and at weekends when the offices are empty, and many colleagues leave their PC’s on standby mode when not in use. We could dramatically cut our energy use and costs with minimal effort, but I have never seen any focus placed on this.

Employment agencies – The economy is in a bad state, millions are out of work, people are desperate for a job, yet we use the most expensive way there is to find people to hire – agencies. In NYC, we pay 30% of someone’s annual salary as a finder’s fee. This must cost us millions of dollars each year. An agency is no guarantee of getting the best person either. On many occasions, we have been disappointed, and the person has left or we have asked them to leave. There must be less expensive ways to find people.

Overtime – You have two clerks working in the same team doing the same job. One is very quick, efficient, performs to a high standard etc. The other makes constant mistakes, is always taking coffee / cigarette breaks, works slowly etc. Guess which one gets paid more? That’s right – the poor performer. This is due to the overtime system, which rewards people for being in the office longer than their required hours. This is extremely abused within JPMorgan and costs the bank tens of millions of dollars a year. People know that they can sit at their desk over lunch, come in early or stay late and can greatly increase their earnings this way. In my mind this is theft, pure and simple.  I’d like to see management stop paying overtime in locations where it is not required by law, and effectively manage it in other locations.

Travel and entertainment – I’ve saved the best ‘til last. This is my number one area of abuse and excessive spending at JPMorgan. Rather than talk through the issues, I have outlined some real life examples:

1 – A colleague travels often around the US to visit clients. The firm has a $65 allowance for meals when you travel on business. My colleague will go to an expensive restaurant on his own every evening he is away and spend the entire $65. If the allowance was $100, then he would make sure he spent the whole $100. Now, I’ve never been anywhere in the US where you can’t get a decent meal for less than $20. Why are we letting employees waste money like this? 

2 – Two colleagues live very close to each other just outside of NY. They are traveling together to a meeting with a client in another city. They will take the same flights there and back. Their schedules are identical. You would think that to spend a little less of the firm’s money they would share a ride to and from the airport, but no, they decide to book a limo each. The round trip is approx $200 per limo ($400 in total).  So, JPMorgan was charged an extra $200 because two colleagues didn’t think to share a car for the same journey and had no incentive to do this.

3 – We have an approved list of hotels that we are told to use. They are usually the most expensive hotels in any town. For example, in Dallas, we use the Marriott, which is ½ mile from the office and costs over $200 per night. There is a good hotel over the road from our office which is $50 per night. Even though it is closer to work, cheaper etc, we are not permitted to use it. 

4 – I visited a client in another city a few months ago. One of my colleagues who lives on the other side of the country said he wanted to come with me. I was surprised that he asked this, as he didn’t really know the client, and had limited interaction on their account. He came along and when we were walking to the client’s office I asked why he wanted to join me. His answer was “Air miles”. So, he had just spent over $1000 of the company’s money so he could save a little when he took his family on vacation. I know that this is a widespread abuse. If JPMorgan banned employees from collecting air miles on business trips, we would see flight requests drop like a rock. The cost savings from these unnecessary trips would be enormous.

5 – Business class is considerably more expensive than economy, but our people only use business class for trans-Atlantic flights. I’ve traveled that route many times in economy (even on a business trip), and see no reason to pay an extra $1,000 or more to sit it a bigger seat for 7 hours. I’d like to see an incentive for making our people use economy. This would save millions of dollars each year.

6 - Each department is given a travel budget. Managers are told they have to use it up or they will get marked down in their review for not predicting budgets accurately. This results in managers rushing to spend any remaining monies close to year end on unnecessary trips. I've seen tens of thousands of dollars wasted this way just for one department. Shouldn't we be rewarding managers for coming in under budget, not punishing them?

advice: Please try not to refer to people who work for you as "resources".  It is generally not nice to compare people to cattle, even in Texas.
pros: JPMC survived the financial crisis as arguably world's top investment bank and all-around financial services company, stronger and more respectable than before - while its stock price barely rippled thru the market turmoils.  This will tell you a lot about the company culture.  The company captains battle the storms, while you only need to focus on rowing the ship and carrying out the orders.  Company policies and culture are well-established, while compensation packages are generous - pension, legal plan, and support for domestic partners.  You work on systems that support millions of trades, billions of capital, and business around the world.  Opportunities for internal openings are many, and each department can work on a different set of architecture and technology.
cons:
Flip side of a Fortune-100 behemoth - things move slowly and it's easy to lose your place in the giant machine.  For the relative job security, you will not see the mind-blowing bonuses at some of the Wall St. rock stars.  You are more likely to be working with mature mainstream technologies rather than the hot up-to-the-minute tech fad - although at a massive scale.  In addition, you are expected to support company deadlines and production issues like a good soldier - weekends or holidays.  Projects are often committed, before the schedule and resources are worked out in reverse.  Then people start scrambling to meet the deadline.

There's quite a bit of politics like in most large organizations.  In addition, you'll often feel like you are in Bangalore or Singapore, with people chatting and even working in Asian languages.

summary: OK to start, not the best place to make money...

advice: Be careful.  Cost cutting is great, and has been proven to work at JPMorgan very well.  But it comes at a price, and that price is your good staff.
pros: There are many opportunities at JPMorgan if you want to work hard.  If you don't want to work hard and compete with your peers, then it's pretty tough.  The benefits are okay, and there is a pension plan.
cons: Too much focus on relentless cost cutting.  There are targets given out, and you must hit them.  The targets aren't based on improvements (thus being able to realize efficiencies); rather, you are given a target and just have to do it, regardless of the outcome.

advice: Allow remote workstations. Productivity will increase with the flexibility to work from a company laptop at home when convenient.  It is easier for us to maintain motivation when we are able to focus time with our family (especially children) as well as get work done. A test run once or twice a week for a month, comparing the productivity levels, would be a good way to gauge the pros/cons.
pros: Team oriented, good benefits, opportunity for advancement, low stress, entry level positions with great pay, positive environment, appears to have good job security
cons: Workload, expectations for first year+ isn't measured properly, bonuses and salary don't seem to be competitive with other companies in the same position.

summary: Review as a Teller at JP Morgan Chase
advice: I would prefer a higher wage as a teller. Being a teller is not always easy, and it can be a stressful and demanding job.  This position requires a high level of responsibility.  There are other companies that pay the same as Chase, and the positions are easier and less stressful.
pros: This company provides good benefits, including a surprising amount of vacation time for part - time employees. Chase also guarantees a set amount of hours and a consistent schedule.
cons: There are other banks that pay their tellers a higher wage.  Also, company employs uniforms, which can be annoying and pricy. This bank is not always closed on all holidays.

advice: Be more pro active in pointing out your employee's  strengths. Find better ways to move talented employees into positions that are better suited to their strengths. Actually make it an internal company priority to provide the "Platinum Rule" .
pros: good pay and benefits decent schedule options.
cons:
Hard to get promoted. There is a pool of team leads who cycle through the company, so it is difficult to break into a managerial position.

Highly stressful environment

While there is a claim to focus on Customer Satisfaction, there is not real incentive to be as great with customers as they claim to want you to be. 

Feedback from management is mostly negative, with a "no news is good news" attitude.

advice: Identity your talent better and promote and reward those who are doing well. Meager raises when you hire outside people at full market value really decreases morale and forces people to leave.
pros: Very stable company with decent benefits. Many extremely smart people to work with and learn from. Good career opportunities.
cons: Poor work/life balance - have to work a lot of hours. Practically impossible to get any real raise from what you started with the firm with. It is common for people to leave for a year or two to another bank and come back so they actually get their market value raise that they deserve.

advice: Stop playing games with employees and clients.  It's degrading to both.
pros: Well known brand name in the marketplace.
cons: When I heard about the Wells Fargo employees opening fake accounts and numerous family accounts, it reminded me of Chase.  The unrealistic goals in the branch caused many employees to open numerous friend and family accounts to real their goals.  After a couple of years of clients complaining that they were "harassed" to open new accounts, Chase switched gears and emphasized 5 Star customer service.  Then we had to worry about receiving the highest ratings possible from client surveys.  We used to remind our clients all the time to rate us a 5.

summary: Easy to get caught in politics but there's good career potential.
pros: Good people, focus on technology, definitely attempting to innovate. Lots of good perks like competitive salary, retirement plans, pension, and ability to work remote if your group is open to that.
cons: Management is luck of the draw, you can easily end up in a good group with terrible leadership and it will be a dead end. Open seating (unassigned spaces) is bad if you ever want to have a private conversation or even personalize your workspace as the next day someone else can be sitting there. Political moves are everywhere so if you don't want to play that game this isn't the place for you.

advice: Be more disciplined with your business plans and give more career growth opportunities to people who are already with the organization
pros:
-Base salary is high vs. industry average
-Great place to start your career at (training, learning opportunities)
-Pretty good culture vs. other main industry players
cons:
-Bonus is too subjective and depends on many unpredictable factors
-Hours are long vs. industry average (11-12 per day for Associates; and higher for Analysts). You work like IB but get paid like PB.
-Too many politics involved instead of focusing on meritocracy; also, Management changes pretty often and each new manager wants to change something in order to leave his/her mark, which may not necessarily end up in a better outcome

advice: The "worker bees" work so hard but are paid so little, salaries have not increased but profits have - its time to do the right thing and pay everyone fairly according to their efforts & worth.
pros: Pension, 401k matching, PTO. Upper management does listen and care about customer issues, and will make changes accordingly - that isn't always the case with other companies.
cons: Executives are greedy, the worker bees receive hardly any bonus's, very small raises, and there's no profit sharing. It's evident all over, Men make more than women for the same level of experience, education & background

advice: Try to pay talent what they are worth instead of being limited by HR % based caps on compensation raises
pros:
Vacation Policy - 4 weeks; Generous Sick/Personal  Days 
401k Match @5%
Ability to work from home, as needed (although most people don’t bother coming into office on Fridays)
cons:
- Tons of dead weight who have been doing their same jobs for 15+ years and have no adaptability to change
- Changing / Improving a process doesn’t always get welcomed with open arms
- Hard to get recognized, move up in corporate ladder, even if you are identified as “high performer”
- Tons is corporate politics 
- Yearly guidance on raises ~ 3%

summary: Great Company to work for and grow
advice: Pay internal transfers the same market rate you would offer to an external applicant. The salary they make now should not be used a guideline for what they could make in the new role. Look at the LOB's that practice this and change it to enhance employee moral.
pros: Jamie Dimon has streamlined the company and set direction with his values that trickles down
cons: While there are numerous options to move around in the company and management supports it, there are certain lines of business that will not increase the salary when making those moves. they are looked upon as lateral moves. This does not happen in all LOB's

summary: Fast paced, well run business model
advice: With significant workloads consider: in house gyms or alternative programs,  more work life flexibility.
pros: Learn a lot as they are always changing to “take things up a notch”, ethical, diverse employee population, good healthcare package, amazing “employee appreciation week,” and I have absolute confidence in senior leadership to weather any economic storm.
cons: Limited remote flexibility and many employees have very challenging workloads, pay scale lower than competitors(BOA, Barclays etc). Also, most competitors offer on site gyms, or partner with local fitness centers etc. The amount of time people work at JPMC, need to stay healthy and fit.

summary: They Know How to Treat People to Keep People
advice: Connect smaller offices with larger offices in more and better ways. Don't forget about small office comforts.
pros: Often a great work/life balance, even during intense project periods. Nice facility locations. Excellent tech and tools. They make every effort to make the massive company feel smaller and more intimate, and it works to an impressive extent.
cons: Despite many locations, it really feels like there are a few main offices, and career growth in smaller locations feels limited. Healthcare benefits don't stack up well compared to other companies in this class. The need for absolute security can make the pace feel slow sometimes.

advice: Work on better code reviews to ensure better code and try to make sure that when young new developers are coming in they get utilized properly and now thrown into non-dev roles
pros: Great 401k, Health, Perks, Discounts, Mobility and decent pay for the area that we live in. Some teams are very progressive and have great development enviorments.
cons: The teams that have good development work are few and far between. On bad teams applivation development work can be poorly reviewed and written causing a bad learning experience for younger developers . Some projects and paths invested in are very misdirected and poorly decided on.

advice: For the decent managers, sorry you have to deal with the insanity. Keep fighting the good fight (or) run for the hills and watch from afar.
pros: Great brand name,  a well respected CEO, decent work-life-balance for some, loads of valuable training available for you to partake in your spare time and inapplicable mandatory training also, tech certification programs, solid work opportunities in the robotics space, ability to join new projects, and loads of opportunity to move around if you are lucky enough to get into the right cliche.   Even though the company is not leading the industry in salaries, the pay/benefits are not bad  and they have programs to  support education, new mothers, etc.
cons: After you get past the cool building amenities, hand crafted job titles that misrepresent the actual job, meaningless HR surveys, beautifully packaged propaganda about training and supporting employee development, diversity, and doing the right thing.... well there's not much substance to it all... like eating a Twinkle. It looks good, taste good, but there's little nutritional value.  There's an unsettling amount of organizational changes, more than a reasonable amount and with little notice and no explanation.  The internal pay/promotion structure is a Rubik's Cube that tilts slightly left of reasonable and is shrouded in secrecy, despite the masses repeatedly asking for the full picture. Basically the company is made of  various groups and levels of management  either doing their best to do what they think is right, doing what they think makes them look good, or doing what they want because there's little  accountability for bad behavior or poor performance in management.  There are good managers there, you just have to find them and hold on so if you just want a job or a resume builder,  this should work.

advice: You are entrusted with Trillions of dollars, you treat your workforce with a great deal of professionalism and respect.  Now challenge yourself to better manage your “own” labor budget, your are better than your current norm!  You have no idea what your EOY layoffs do to your employee loyalty.
pros:
Salary:
Very well compensating company

Environment:
The all around best company I have ever worked for.  This company does not play the “blame-game” and they are sincerely focused on learning, from the good and bad and progressing forward.

CEO:
Absolutely the best I have seen and JP Morgan cannot let this one go!
cons: Embarrassingly layoffs at the end of every year to “make the numbers”

advice: Management knows the difference between easy accounts and the more difficult accounts that are more detailed and time consuming. It would make more sense to pay employees accordingly to the kind of accounts they are given. I know there is a system in place that gives you a little more time to process, but that's not good enough.  As a former employee I would have liked to get better pay instead.
pros: Work independently, fast paced environment, so time goes by quickly, lots of overtime available, mostly friendly people to work with, flexible shifts, good benefits and annual bonuses
cons: Fast-paced environment so it's very easy to make errors, constant changes on job specifications only adds more to the work load but not the pay, speaking of pay, it is not that great, also, some managers are very fake and play favorites

summary: Really depends on the group you're in
advice: All managers need to take some course on management training. I think it should be mandatory, without having to make a complaint to HR.
pros: I've been with JPM for almost 5 years, in several different roles. Every group is different - workload, managers. You definitely get to work with a lot of smart people. Health benefits are good and PTO is sufficient. Lots of opportunities for internal mobility.
cons: Merit is standard, bonuses are average. Depending on what team you're in, you'll either enjoy it or hate it. I've been on both sides of the spectrum.

advice: Hang in there managers... Actually, jump ship before the kiosks and techies take ur jobs!
pros: Technology, management, and benefits. I was a Macy's sales associate when a Chase manager approached me with a job offer on the sales floor of the men's dept. I said, YES. Within four years, I went from a teller to a banker, to a business banker, to a licensed banker! If you want it and work hard, they'll supply the training and tools to help you build a career. Now I have experience, a securities license, and a ton of reco's. By the way, some college no degree.
cons: It's a mega corporation. That being said, there are often times when you feel forgotten or unappreciated. Remember, the botten line is profits. It's not about you, it's about making people rich.

advice: Invest more in promoting people who currently work at the company (so they don’t leave for more money elsewhere or a better title). Most of the time they do a great job AND contribute to the overall well being of the brand. D&I contribution is important as well (meaning how much are people engaging diverse groups, ERGs, etc)
pros: Great company culture. I can ask for help, never feel like I’m being micromanaged, and they really see the importance of workplace equality.
cons: Sometimes you’ll need to spend a lot of your own time to learn new technologies. Not enough on-site trainings. Promotions can be very hard.

advice: When looking to promote someone, make sure skillset as well as personality combined are a good fit. It should be of equal value, not one or the other.  Would like to have seen more diversity in leadership roles-minorities especially since the company advertises it. Stay true to embracing all cultures and ethnicities in leadership as these individuals are just as talented and smart and can lead successfully in your organization.
pros: Great benefits start first day of hire, pay varies depending on Dept and band level, company promotes wellness & has onsite nurses
cons: Company provides only 6 sick days to earn annually. You can work a lot of hours-over 40hrs can be of norm, seems more opportunity & exposure to other depts is at downtown location where executives work. Downtown location and atmosphere is more corporate than other locations.

advice: Don’t misguide young talent just because of the JPMorgan brand. Let these kids know they are doing BACK OFFICE jobs. If you end up switching the program to salary, you will lose talent.
pros: Rotational, OT Eligible, Program Management
cons:
Don’t do CADP. Molded with Operation Analyst Program. Went from 4, 6 month rotations to 3, 8 month rotations. All of the high quality analyst network for front office jobs. The rotations are ABSOLUTELY TERRIBLE. Post program opportunities are terrible. Starting Associate through CADP is starting Analyst pay for front office (sometimes even lower). Back office jobs. Do this if you aren’t into
Finance finance. Once you figure it out, it’s too late.

summary: It was one of the worst work experiences I have had in my 8 years of professional career.
advice: Teams need to be diversified. I mean this to extend to teams with a huge majority of only one minority group. My horrendous work experience at JPMC was not because there were not enough diversity as a whole. It was that my team and a pattern of many many other teams that have minority groups that hold the majority in their respective teams were profoundly discriminatory toward the minorities outside of the majority group. It was utterly the worst experience I have ever faced, I know professionalism in the American workplace does not tolerate this kind of workplace behavior.
pros: Fortune 500 company on your resume is a positive.
cons: Work place was toxic, absolutely zero emphasis on psychological safety. There were all sorts of discrimination.

summary: Good company but could be great.
advice:
Remember to praise your employees when they do well and appreciate them for their hard work. Good employees are hard to find. If you take the time to appreciate your employees, they will be loyal and work hard for you.

Branch Managers need to lead by example and be more present.

Senior Management needs to be more visable and appreciate the employees.
pros: Great benefits for employees and nice annual bonuses. Many opportunities for advancement and wonderful training programs.
cons: Chase used to be very customer focused but  over the years the company and culture shifted.  Senior  management is mediocre and should be more understanding of each individual branch. Not all branches have the same clientele and traffic therefore management should not treat all branches the same.  They should cater to the demographics of the local area.

advice: Recognize your employees!!  Encourage them!! When making changes to company policies regarding vacations and tenure take in to account the effect you are having on your long term employees.
pros: Chase has a great health and investment plan for its employees.  They had just increased vacation time for new employees and celebrations of anniversaries.  They will work with an employee who goes to school, has children or parents they take care of.  It was wonderful working for this company.
cons: Chase did not give raises easily.  Raises and bonuses were based on a branch profitability not on individual performance.  It can be discouraging to employees when CEO receives a $29.5 million salary (not even POTUS gets a salary like that).  When policies change regarding employees and long term employees feelings are not taken in to consideration.

summary: Good atmosphere, good pay, but cumbersome bueraucracy
advice: Work to streamline organizational structures, try to reduce the number of Chief to Indian ratio.
pros: Great pay and you get to work with some outstanding people. The environment is friendly and contractors are treated with respect unlike in many organizations. The company (at least in my division) seems to understand that IT brings value and is not just overhead.
cons: It can often be hard to get things done due to a massive Corporate Bueraucracy. Even small changes to systems and network resqources can take weeks or months to get done due to cumbersome procedures and a staggering list of stakeholders that all have to be consulted.

summary: JP Morgan Chase is a great company to work for overall.
advice: I encourage management to do a better job of communicating changes and to plan appropriately before cutting staff as a result of location strategy.  As a worker of 5 years with remote working experience, I was able to perform my role from my locations however, I was let go using the location strategy excuse.
pros:
1) Good pay and benefits
2) Upward mobility is good in some areas
3) Overall culture is open and progressive with a strong push for equality and fairness
4) Flexible work arrangements are available to some roles and departments
cons:
1) While mobility is good, there is also an underlying level of competition that can be somewhat cut-throat
2) Because of the corporate nature of JPMC, dollars are the bottom line and it is not uncommon to reduce force to save $

advice: Be more risk averse.
pros: There really are none since the company no longer exists.
cons:
Almost everything about the company is poor.  The culture is born of a CYA mentality.  People are more concerned with making sure they aren't to blame instead of focusing on the end result.  Communication between senior management and staff is apalling.  Rarely any communication is sent or spoken, and when it is, it is vague and strained.  The benefits, while plentiful, are expensive.  The 401k choices are really bad; whoever picked those funds to invest in should've done more research.

That being said, the people that work there are great and friendly.

summary: Enjoyed my time, but advancement limited where I live
pros: Had a good crew to work with besides one particular person. Hours were very flexible with a ton of PTO right off the bat. Other benefits were awesome as well.
cons: The one person that made the entire team miserable including the managing staff still works there. No way to fire them due to 'good numbers.' Employee moral took second fiddle compared to numbers' effectiveness. Working weekends and late days sucked. Lots of training that was superficial at best. The branch I was located at did not have the advancement opportunities that I was looking for. If you wanted to work up as a banker, then there were options but top spots were limited to 1-2 with every other banker in the area pining for them. Everything else was lower end positions with minimal pay.

summary: I loved my job, but I can't take it with me.
advice: If it wasn't too late, I would suggest that they consider seeking moderate success over the long term rather than short-term gains at the expense of customer loyalty and sustainable profitability.
pros: We have a very collaborative atmosphere where mutual respect is key to the strive for success.  People take pride in their work and participate in projects as team players.  In the majority of instances, project goals and deadlines are reasonable and attainable.  Issues are addressed as opportunities for process improvement, rather than finger-pointing escapades.
cons: Lay offs and the fact that JP Morgan Chase has WaMu operations in run-off.

advice: The little people matter. Employee happiness directly correlates with productivity and motivation to do well.
pros:
-Software Engineering Program is well built out and helpful in actually training and preparing incoming employees for their position
- Competitive Pay
- MANY opportunities - JPMC is both a consumer and investment bank. there are endless opportunities and typically is a place described as 'being able to have many different careers at one place'
cons:
- JPMC is a financial institution at the end of the day, not a technology company so working in tech for a bank you realize they are not as fast/up to date as other tech companies
- upper management = business politics , there were many times I felt like just a number or my opinion and ideas were undermined by my (less experienced in engineering) manager

summary: Be good in sales or you better invest your time in gaining valuable high paid skills
advice: Investigate your managers and their work, sometimes you can find a lot of interesting stuff..
pros: If you work hard, have good relationship with your manager and your team besides being good in sales this position is for you
cons: Favoritism, As far as commission may be even over 50-70% of your salary taking a vacation might be a hit for your pocket. If the manager doesn't like more likely you can get fired within 6months or even less. you better take the notes for every interaction with your manager regarding your performance or other job related issues.talking to hr shortly after might lead to corrective actions, so try to resolve your issue either with your manager or above, involve HR when communication to management doesn't lead to any results

advice: Make sure annual reviews are based on title level and not expectation. For example,I've been performing at a VP level for several years. My managers and peers expect a certain level of quality that I know is above my pay grade and title. But my reputation is stellar. So I deliver. Still I'll get a review based on these standards, which should be a pay grade higher than where I am.
pros: Opportunities Internally and Externally with experience working with such a large corporation.
cons: Competitive. You've got to take the highs with the lows when it comes to promotions, layoffs, org shifts and overall dynamic of a world facing business. Professionalism and resiliency is at the top of my list when thinking of very basic attributes required to work for a company of this scale.

advice: Transparency is important. If you are managing a team and trying to make numbers or projects look/sound better than they actually are, you only  put your team and the firm at a disadvantage. Stay honest. Do your best.
pros:
Excellent benefits for the area
Great compensation
Lots of opportunity
The company is committed to changing with the times
cons: It really just depends on the team you end up with as to whether your experience will be good or not. Sometimes you may have to move around a bit to get a good fit. Some managers are still managing in the old ways but the company is pushing management to learn to adopt better policies.

summary: Solid company, be careful not to get complacent
advice: Need to lean out a bit in the senior management.  Foster real creativity internally.  Developers are held back and get complacent in their roles. Top levels get paid a ton compared to some other firms and given the environment that wasn't a good look.
pros: Stable, Good Benefits, Easy to move internally, Good bonus, Employee discounts
cons: Pay was low for the position level, Stock discount was weak, political to move up to Executive Director, no clear compensation package changes, no RSUs or stock grants even though I held a high management position, terrible (and I mean terrible) employee appreciate awards and gifts.

pros: Chase offers positions to people straight out of high school, up to the highest executive level. There are literally positions for everyone and anyone. My department provided yearly bonuses and raises. Good benefits. Office cafeteria offers healthy options at low cost (healthy meals $2-3). Free food sometimes. Wish the pay increased more to match inflation but there are other jobs that don't give raises at all, so its hard to complain. There are temporary overtime allotments when the company needs it, then drops back down to 40 hrs max during slower times (can differ depending on department)
cons: Not as flexible when it comes to working in office or working from home.

summary: Terrible pay for back/middle office positions. Office politics is uncontrollable
advice: Change your team's culture. Listen to the people. Promote an environment where everyone can speak freely without fear of being hammered by their managers if you want to make any positive change.
pros: None besides having the name on your resume even if you're not in an IB role.
cons: Raise and bonuses for middle office is laughable that it is better to jump ship than to stay and accept your comps given how high inflation is right now. Technology is so behind it doesn't feel like they are catching up with their competitors. If you don't know how to butter up your managers prepare to find yourself in a difficult position from time to time and don't expect to get promoted. Also diversity here is laughable. Managers only hire those who share the same demographics as they do.

advice: Managers  know how to work well with their teams. Most people love their managers. My advice would be for executives. Please read the room. I have witness some inconsiderate conversations and comments.
pros: It’s okay pay. Not leading but not falling behind.
cons: Training is terrible. One of the world largest banks that lacks real integrity for their employees. They don’t really care but they put on a good act. Every idea you give them that they literally ask you for is turned down but they tell you they are listening and respect your ideas. You will not have access to your manager because they are always on a call and in a meeting.

advice: I would say that you always a voice to speak with management or even HR if you have an issue, but that not true. I overheard a call where managers were literally laughing at the idea of firing people to inflate their numbers and HR did nothing. As soon as they realized no laws were being broken they looked the other way.  So when you hear the jargon of an open and honest workspace....they're lying.
pros: Decent pay, Good benefits, Schedule Flexibility
cons:
Managers spend way too much time preaching policy and work culture that they ultimately never follow.
They hire metric based employees to supervisor roles with zero people skills and its awful.

summary: A fair & stable place to work
advice: Work to achieve stronger technical proficiency. Listen to your employees.
pros: the place offers great job safety. It's very easy to be lost in a large company and most people have the sort of job where they need not be bothered. This is the sort of place where you don't have to try very hard to do ok.
cons: It's very easy to be lost in a large company and most people have the sort of job where they need not be bothered. I have met VERY few people that of technical proficiency levels past high school. I left immediately because there was no advancement opportunities here.

summary: Bogged down in politics and fear of new media channels and ignorance of the changing market dynamics.
advice: Trust your employees more.
pros:
Experienced professionals in the card industry
Great vacation time!
"Banking hours"
Great location, easy access to train or bus to NYC or DC.
Decent pay.
Good place to get a varied set of experiences in the industry.
Good health benefits.
Large budgets to work with.
Very "team" oriented approach to work, requiring buy in from lots of people (if you like that sort of thing)
cons:
Silo approach to product segmentation
Lots of politics, with constant battles for prioritization.
Excessive amounts of time spent managing up, managing emails, and managing meetings.
Meetings, meetings, meetings...
Old-fashioned management with major risk-aversion issues.
Lots of bureaucracy and VERY top-heavy org-chart.

summary: Great bank and opportunity, depending on your position
pros:
Focus on work-life balance
Young company, with most employees in the 18-45 age range
Good benefits
Frequent 1:1 meetings with management
Lots of communication
cons:
Performance reviews and expectations not in line with those advertized.
Performance reviews were changed so that the vast majority of employees received a "3" out of 5, which meant doing your job well, but not enough for even a cost of living raise.
Salaries for employees varied widely and sometimes had jumps of up to 50% of base salaries.
Salaries are not in line with corporate standards for areas with higher cost of living.
Frequent micromanagement
No margin for any error, which was, of course impossible, even 97% was not good enough.

summary: JPMC has a lot of opportunities for growth; network with your managers!
advice: For non-sales employees, management tends to overlook their needs, but does give a good focus on promoting those that do well.  In order to keep those talents, and ultimately increase sales, there should be a little more focus on keeping them happy.
pros: Knowedgable people, great support system, many opportunities to advance.  For those that work hard this is a great place to advance your career.
cons: Every office has its problems.  If you feel stagnant in your career, talk to your manager.  If that isn't helping, you have a whole host of resources at your disposal at JPMC.

summary: My experience with JP Morgan was not so good.
