advice: Stop laying people off.  Conduct your business in a manner that does not require constantly laying people off to remain profitable.  Treat people like people instead of cattle.
pros: Benefits are generous and pay was not bad.  These are the only good things I remember.
cons: Leadership throughout the company leaves a lot to be desired.  The company presents an image of compassion towards people but the leadership doesn't seem to fall in line with that philosophy.  The number of people laid off by this company is staggering...  The work environment becomes very depressing after you watch one person after another being laid off.  Because of the total lack of job security with JP Morgan I would not ever consider going back and I would not recommend them to anyone else.

advice: Have a clear division of responsibilities.  Are teams governed by LOB alignment, technical function, region, or some combo?  Pick one and stick to it.  Inevitably, no matter your choice, this will involve compromise and coordination.  So you need to actively incentivize cross-group collaboration, not just hope individuals all do the right thing, else you are de facto incentivizing ICs to pass the buck.
pros: Opportunities for improvement & impact.  Competitive comp (in the strategic areas, at least).  People management is very supportive.
cons: Operational and technical management. are disorganized, burdensome, and overall not very effective.  Many (too many!) try to steer the huge ship; none succeed.

advice: Define a career path for your employees otherwise they will continue to search and leave for other opportunities.
pros: Great Benefits, 5% matching 401k, 4 weeks time off per year which is increased after 5 years of service.  One of the few companies that still utilizes both a 401k and pension plan.  Plenty of opportunity  for over time and movement from within.  Job security for AML related positions.
cons: No defined promotion or career path.  Too much emphasis on micromanaging of each employee's daily work.  Not flexible with work life balance although they claim it to be one of their top priorities.

advice: Overall I think mgmt is doing great in regards to ensuring all admins have the proper and adequate necessities to provide great support to our teams. Again, just know we work extremely hard to keep our team on track and the factor of overtime pay shouldn't be an issue.
pros: Excellent competitive company with room for salary advancement.
cons: Work can be tedious for Admins and managers want the admins to take an hour unpaid lunch. Many times we don't have the time to step away and we shouldn't be questioned or feel forced to step away unpaid when there's tons of work to be done.

summary: Great place to start a career
advice: Build a personal connection with each of your team members & take the time to truly get to know everyone. Treat people fairly & be patient with them. Own your part in employee development.
pros: Excellent training & systems. Benefits are decent.  Most of the managers are fit to lead & treat employees fairly. Lots of opportunity for advancement.
cons: In my opinion the salary should be higher and they need more staffing in their branches. They did away with assistant branch managers & reduced the number of tellers in their branches which leaves managers less time to properly train & coach their employees to build a successful team.

advice: Employees dont leave  bad jobs they leave bad managers. There is a difference between managers and leaders. Flexibility goes a long way.
pros:
Benefits are great. Lots of time off. Always a chance to get involved in volunteer events.  Endless opportunities if you network, be present. 
Compensation is great for some positions.
cons:
Hard to advance unless you are liked
Career movement is hard because Grade Bands are so important when applying for positions. 
Management needs improvement and there is no work life balance. Not centrally located since they opened a new campus that is huge commute. Now willing to work with you on flexible work arrangements. Career Development is a joke.

advice: Promote entrepreneurship & reward those who are driven to produce results. Your technology organization is riddled with red tape & the firm would never get its bang for the buck or be a market leader until some flab is cut.
pros:
Stable job in technology if you are half witty & opportunity to work with few brilliant minds provided the size of organization.

There are programs like expert engineers & firm devotes a considerable amount of money on such initiatives.
cons:
Growth is not driven my meritocracy but being in the good books of right management. 
The firm wants to project an image of gender & race inclusion but that’s a lip service by any measure.

advice: Pay your dedicated employees so they won’t leave. You make Billions every quarter, you can spare some to the employees & middle managers that make the firm operate.
pros: JPMC picks from the most experienced in the field so your co-workers & middle managers are talented & competent (usually). Egos do clash & there is a “get-the-job-done at all costs” that bonds teams & makes it competitive. Great, if you know how to handle office politics and climb career ladders.
cons: Stress levels are high because of the competitive nature of the firm. Somewhat poor work-life balance (it is sometime mitigated). Poor career advancement (all sizzle, no steak), even poorer compensation increases & bonuses.

summary: Encourages and stimulates technical and professional growth
advice: Ensure directs are engaged and actively working on their technical and professional skills outside of BAU work
pros: Stable benefits, Large range of software/projects to work on across firm, mobility culture, promotes technical and professional growth, prefers soft skills rather than technical skills in entry-level positions out of university
cons: Very large firm, easy to feel swallowed up or purpose-less. Managers vary across the firm, sometimes feels like a lottery if you land a good one. Salary + Benefits are average. The firm likes to call itself a tech company but as a bank there's a lot of governance and red tape that stalls innovation and the start-up mentality.

advice: Learn to respect the individual. It just seems like chase is one of thoss go ol boy clubs. Hopefully things change for the better in the future but i doubt it. Quit promoting hateful managers to vp level, it doesnt help your mission be diverse and inclusive.
pros:
Good pay and benefits.
Ping pong table
cons:
Management doesnt do enough for their employees and are too busy playing politics.

Lack of job stability(people are always being let go). They dont care about your current financial situation and would quickly get rid of you. If you are working for another company and youve already established yourself there then do yourself a favor and avoid this company at all cost.

No sign on bonuses for the people hired during the underrepresented minority hiring event( im sure their other previous employees received bonuses but they didnt offer any to me)

advice: Keep the hybrid working schedule or wfh permanent. Enforce rule to keep people out of the office with a cough. Too many people feeling upper management pressure and coming in sick. Stop making departments lay blame on each other. It's why we don't act like one Chase. We always have to find who is at fault and it makes teams defensive.
pros:
-PTO average is 29 days broken up into sick time, vacation, personal days
-Banking holidays
-Healthy/positive team culture with strong work ethic
-colleagues care about their work
-Health insurance is average. Ohio is specifically on an odd plan.
-some on-site health centers. Wonderful in a pinch.
cons:
-Doesn't do market adjustments for salary
-No corporate laptop for majority of employees. If given a laptop constantly at risk to lose it for cost cutting measures.
-IT and several departments are known for high stress environment

advice: Pay more, hire more, give people a chance to excel
pros: JPMC has excellent an excellent benefits package.  Everything imaginable is covered at a reasonable cost.  There are lot's of opportunities to pick up and learn a variety of skills (if you don't mind transferring departments on a regular basis.  Although such transfers frequently require relocating to OH, TX, or AZ.  There isn't much room to move upwards but you can make your way if your careful & patient.
cons: JPMC has a frustrating amount of bureaucracy and despite policies meant to do otherwise; there is a formidable glass ceiling; good luck getting past lower/mid level management if you're a minority.  The pay is mediocre especially when compared to other financial firms and recently the frequent job cuts have made for a very demoralized environment

summary: You don't know what you've got til it's gone.
advice: I used to think you were too conservative but now I'm comparing the value of my JPMC stock with the value of my current bank employer's stock and I miss you, Jamie Dimon!
pros: Good salary, benefit package, coworkers.  Pretty good work/life balance.  Company name recognition is valuable.  If you can get in at one of the hubs, you'll have much more opportunity.
cons:
It's a bank.  These days, that's not a good thing.  Like lots of other folks, I got laid off.  I'd go back in a minute, if I had the opportunity. 

Limited openings in my city meant limited advancement potential and even less chance of being rehired once you're gone.  Difficulty in getting training approved when you're out of the loop.

summary: Waiting to see what working for JPMC will bring...
advice: Please be very clear as soon as you can about what current efforts are going to be cancelled so that we can plan for the future as best as we can.
pros: Not a lot of good reasons right now.  With JPMC at the reins, there's no guarantees anyone will have a job.  Besides this, the people all are very dedicated to doing a good job.  It's amazing that there are so many who are continuing to do "business as usual" when clearly this is a wasted effort.
cons: There is very little job security here now.  The people are getting rather depressed as there is so little information about our fate.  Also, with the JPMC acquisition, it appears that our pensions and any stock grants will be wiped out without compensaton.

summary: Utilize the ability to move around and move to new opertunites, get your foot in the door and move on and up.
advice: Utilize the qualified people and get them more involved with the day to day.  Meet with your people and let them know about changes before they happen instead of when they happen.  Back your people up, and stand up and dont allow other areas to dictate how you operate
pros: Great opertunities to move within the company once you take a job.
cons: Depending on the area you work in promotions are based on time and likeability and not ability and compentency.  Management does not utilize the qualified people and distribute the work load properly.  The good people in my area end up leaving because they get bogged down with work and there is no room for advancement.

advice: Career development for employees does not happen by having them fill out an online form listing goals for the year. Development happens when you encourage employees and help them attain those goals and move forward - and that makes management look good.
pros:
Employee perks/benefits are decent
Good name to have on resume
cons:
No room for growth/ promotion opportunities non-existant 
Very poor management - no care taken in communicating/encouraging employees
No logic to hiring/what level new hires are brought in at (i.e. new hires with little experience brought in at a higher level than existing employees with years of experience)
Very low morale/ low level of professionalism
Workload is huge and broken down to the point where you are just doing one task over and over as part of an assembly line
Technology is behind compared to other firms
Jersey City office feels very isolated from New York

advice: You don't always get what you pay for when moving jobs to lower paying regions. Paying somebody in another country $10,000 to do a job formerly on American soil I believe is short sighted and you will always lose out on some quality. All the big banks are going through this though. Being a big bank has its pros and cons. I moved on to a much smaller firm and am much better compensated for doing similar work that I did at JPM. I still think JPM is a great form and great place to kick off your career but I recommend exploring other options after a few years to see what else out there may better suit you.
pros: Overall great company. Great CEO. Many opportunities.
cons: Average compensation. Large company means jobs are silo'ed. Constant risk of outsourcing.

summary: Unfair Treatment towards Women and Minorities
advice: when you rescind an offer on a former rehireable employee, make sure you have a legitimate reason that doesn't conflict with FCRA or EEOC.
pros: In 2010, when I started with this company, the culture was all about family, growth, and it was truly an exciting place to work until the OCC Consent Order.
cons:
*Removed the Job Coach/MIT role which provided excellent mentor ship to those seeking growth into management 

*Too many people in positions lacking the experience. I personally experienced a lady with no mortgage experience be promoted to a Supervisor after 1.5 years, then AVP 6 months after. All because her father was friends with a SVP. In a nutshell, their requirements for requisitions hold no weight as they hire based on "Likes" and not true qualifications. 

*Lack of Experienced Leadership

advice:
Dont fire us just to save money.
We would work better if you gave us more ways to actually help customers. I cant even offer a late fee waiver unless they ask
Build a better training class around development focused around knowledge and pay us better for the bonus incentive you took away that makes going the extra mile for you worth it.
pros:
Health insurance
3 weeks paid vacation, which you may have to pay back if they lay you off before you earned the time.
40 hours sick time
3 days personal
cons:
Layoffs..
Bonus and ot taken away
Supervisors that dont want to work and only care about saving their skin
Bad upper management that treats emplyoees like slaves. You should be here to work and nothing else.
Micromanagement
Performance reviews about your profitability when you were trained with a emphasis on customer service and doing whats right for the customer.
Having to show up whenever they need you. They constantly change your work schedule. You may sign up for nights and then be forced to take a day shift or vice versa

summary: The best job I’ve ever had.
pros: Working here brought a huge change into my life. I started as an intern and was able to progress quickly. My managers have been supportive and consistent with feedback. Through the 2020 pandemic I’ve been granted plenty of time to take care of situations outside of work. Thanks to Chase I was able to go back to business school and still keep my role while balancing home life.
cons: Feedback I would provide to Chase is that we recognize employees with mental health obstacles. We are granted plenty of entitlements to cover time off, however I believe Chase should have an extended amount of time or a leave of some sort for those who have been diagnosed with mental illnesses. If such a thing exists, it does need to be brought to the light more often.

summary: Rapidly turning into a white collar sweatshop
advice: You hired the cream of the crop.. the best in class.  Treat them as such and show them their value.   Stop micromanaging and let them do what they do best, and trust them when they want something more.
pros: Name on your resume especially if you’re a new grad.  It pays the rent.  Many of your co-workers will be fun and helpful and you may get some good contacts.  Because there are so many lines of business within the organization you can actually see what areas within the industry you like best.
cons:
They’ll make your first six months or so amazing to hook you, but it can only go downhill from there.  The work is pretty soul crushing, while working hard and the quality of your work will mean nothing to your manager, even if they do compliment you or tell you how exceptional your work has been.  (Remember:  They’re paid to do that.)  I guess I can only speak for the AM side of the business but since most of the work is process based.. your manager will make sure they make it obvious you can be replaced.  Not to mention you’ll know how menial your job is.  Performance reviews are garbage and treated as such.  Promotions / bonuses / transfers are all about who you know and what they think about you aka what you’ve done for them lately.  They keep hiring from outside of the firm as if they have no one within the firm that can do said job.  The name on your resume is greattt but you definitely have to leave the firm to really get anywhere in your career.  Everything is completely controlled and it can be pretty hard to move around so once you feel the urge to do something new, get out.  You already have the name on your resume and (hopefully) connections in your pocket. Most of the new managers aren’t really trained or expected to know anything about the group or how to manage people – just how to manage senior management’s expectations.  I bought into that whole work/life balance stuff when I first started but I can assure you they’re saying it to convince themselves more than they are you.  Speaking as an analyst who is pretty well connected around the organization, I can tell you that most of the analysts around my year were pretty miserable and just biding their time until they paid their dues.  Most of my group from analysts to VPs has had one foot out at all times.  I’m pretty sure they “lifers” actually got the few good managers right out of the gate or just love telling their friends and family that they work for JP Morgan and that they’re “important.”

YESS its true that the company feels it can pay you significantly less than the market just because its JP Morgan.  Benefits, employee discounts, etc aren’t all that great either.

advice: It takes longer to learn how to work at JPMC - the JPMC way - than most companies, that is time spent not being productive, innovative or engaged. Integration of experienced hires is pathetic.
pros: Fair Compensation and exposure to a large and complex multinational. Employees have many options to move between lines of business and take on different roles.
cons: Management is rude, unprofessional, as a VP, my boss and 2 peers do not even have a college degree, a very closed culture which promotes from within and avoids addressing valid concerns.  A high degree of bureaucracy which can be annoying and stifling.

summary: Reason not to work for JP Morgan securities
advice: Hire people who know what they are doing, not accidental mangers, pay people more. The salary should be a salary. Measure performance based on the branches the FA are assigned. Account assignment should be done by someone neutral. The market managers feed those they favor.
pros: Managers who are clueless. a salary that is a draw. Paid less on mutual funds and insurance proucdcs than at comparable firms. They push managed money but what they don't tell you is that you get paid 3 months later and it does not count towards the grid or production. A performance rating systems that measures performance of an FA with a $200MM branch with an FA with a $60MM branch as the same. They expect the same resut from the two.
cons: The JP Morgan name still has mileage

summary: HFS a few years behind the rest of the market in terms of hedge fund admin providers but moving in right direction
advice: Get rid of all the checklists for checklists and all of the daily/weekly spreadsheets that add no value, but detract from value adding elsewhere
pros:
Growing hedge fund services space equals growth potential but plenty of pain points in the interim.
Huge company, plenty of room for internal mobility.
cons:
Need to be in a role minimum 3 years for promotion.
Starting to get pretty top heaving at the upper management levels.
Roles between operational groups not clearly defined, neither are the SLAs
Staff have very mixed backgrounds and not all are knowledgeable

summary: If you are motivated the opportunity for advancement is endless!
advice: There are too many roadblocks when trying to work between different lines of Business. Do everything you can to remove unnecessary policies and procedures so employees can be more productive. Continue to seek out and develop top tallent. I have been promoted twice since I started two years ago. It is so wonderful to work for a company that does not place a glass ceiling on employees!
pros: Excellent benefits,  great work life balance, great room for advancement if you take initiative.
cons: There is a lot of red tape when trying toget big projects done.

summary: My experience with the company started off Great, it ended on being about who you know, not what you know!
advice: Manage your people . Not work against them . your team and their spirit or moral is reflective of your management style!
pros: Consistent Benefits, decent pay, retail side has great incentives. overall GREAT BENEFITS. Company so Large you can move to almost anywhere and still work with the bank.
cons: Company is to large to focus on problems within a smaller division or area of the Bank. Some operate by the rules and some do not. Having one bad experience with a manager/superviosr could honeslty affect your position or status within the company.

advice: Show Client Service Associates that you actually care about keeping them here instead of letting them jump ship and replacing them with new hires with no experience.
pros: Laid back atmosphere and nice office location.
cons:
Pay is well below average and there is a big problem with retention. Most people are able to leave and get 15-20% more at other banks for the same position.

There are clearly favorites of managers. Promotions are few and far between and based on who a manager likes more.

My initial training class of 14 when i was hired 3 years ago has dwindled down to 3 people remaining.

advice: no advice
pros:
The HR Department is very well structured and does not judge you from a personal stance but from a policy stance. 

As you network you have management that will give you advice and are very approachable.

Leadership was great, a lot of mentors and managers who wanted to push you to become a better person
cons:
From my experience they train you very heavily for the position its up to the individual how much they would like to succeed. Time off they let you the policy in advance.  I had a great office experience. 
If your manager was approachable and easy going then your office experience went well.

summary: Who your manager is makes all the difference in the world
advice: Train your managers to be professional and respectful, not only to the clients but to your employees. Working at chase reminds me of a retail store that constantly lose and refill there staff.
pros: Possible advancement within company, team value is a plus,  Great benefits for health plans for individuals or families.  Good environment
cons: Nothing matters unless your manager is good. If you have a crappy manager that could make or break your whole experience while at Chase. The retail portion is really hectic depending what branch you work in. Unless you have a high banker position, nothing else matters.

summary: Didn't live up to my expectations.
advice: Provide a development program for employees interested in other areas or moving up and go through to get some experience. It's easy to get stuck in the corporate office due to not enough experience; you literally have to go outside the company to get the experience because they don't seem to want to move employees up (in corporate, not sure about the branches).
pros: Having 2 weeks of vacation starting off as well as the employee benefit websites for discounts.
cons: The pay is low, you have to take a whole week off at one time even if you don't want to, and there isn't much room for growth.

advice: Better communication is very necessary, listen to your employees, and stop with the politics.
pros: One of the leading financial organizations  who pride themselves on their overall good reputation and leadership across the globe.
cons: In the specific division that I was in, management was like a revolving door.  While they all meant well, there just wasn't enough organization and communication within the prepaid division and this ultimately led to the firm's decision to eliminate prepaid entirely.  Additionally, there were some who liked to play favorites because they had personal relationships with one another thus preventing deserving individuals from being properly rewarded for their efforts.

summary: The bigger the company got, the less personal it became.
advice: Hope managers respect their staff and find ways to inspire them rather than rule by fear and nit pick. Encourage employees to have a work-life balance rather than frequently require them to work nights/weekends.
pros: Large company, multiple roles, worldwide footprint, stable pay, descent technology and employee discounts (admissions to museums, etc). Occasional work-from-home permitted.
cons: Poor work-life balance, difficult to get promoted, more and more roles are pigeonholed, frequent re-org, bad managers, force ranking when it comes to employee evaluations, unhealthy work environment (very stressful). There are some departments that are well run and have good manages. But that is not the norm.

advice: Do an across the board salary review and bring current employees up to your competitors wages and make sure there is not such a disparity between your employees in the same department.
pros: Chase offers great time off with vacation, sick time and personal days. You can move around to different areas to gain exposure to different departments.
cons: Raises are incredibly disappointing. Someone that gets hired from outside the company will make more than people that are doing the same thing because the raises are so small every year. Work/personal life is never in balance, it's not uncommon for people to work 60 hrs or more every week.

advice: It isn't really the management's fault. It is the job itself.
pros: Benefits. Lots of vacation and sick time. Although it is impossible to request those vacation time off. Sick time can be used at anytime.
cons: Everything. The call center is 24/7 so days are long and customers are rude. It is impossible to request days off. They get denied immediately. So many rules to follow exactly by the books. You're required to be on the phones all day. If you're a minute late from break then it effects your adherence time which then effects your scorecard. The atmosphere is bad. Everyone there is miserable and it is greatly underpaid.

advice: Listen to your subordinates when they have a concern. Top level management needs to understand  and listen to retail level employees.
pros: Tremendous benefits with perks. Great benefits like 401k, health plans, tuition reimbursement. The company culture is great, easy going and a friendly atmosphere. If you are in sales, the sky is the limit. Managers always want to help. Stress level is very low because someone is always there to mentor you.
cons: Very hard to move up unless you are in the top 10 percentile. Most employees have been in the same position for many years.

advice: Put more accountability onto specialists and team leaders.  Review the customer service that's be provided to card-members and re-evaluate what type of experience you're providing.
pros: A reputable firm known as being a leader in the financial industry.  They focus on employees and create a relaxed and friendly environment.  Many of the supervisors I had were receptive to feedback and had an open-door policy.
cons: Similar to many other large companies, implementing changes can be difficult due to an excessive amount of management levels.  Allow more subtle changes at a team level so long as they don't affect Code of Conduct and Policy and Procedure.

advice: Listen every now and then. Be open to be ideas.
pros: Pay and Benefits.   Large company with many resources.  Investments in technology.  I can't really think of anything else at this point.
cons: Management constantly changes. I had 6 managers in 8 months.  Work life balance is not very good in my department. I'm sure it varies greatly depending on what department you work in. Hours in the office, whether productive or not is valued. Politics and favoritism in my department. At times it felt like I was in a high school cafeteria due to all the gossiping.  Expected more from this company but not impressed.

advice: eliminating bureaucracy needs to come from top. Many junior members have no voice.
pros: Great company with great benefits, strong balance sheet and reputation
cons: slow to change with too many redundancy. Many smart people and many underperformer as well.  Senior management brags about career mobility, but in reality this is extremely hard to achieve because hiring managers in each team are reluctant to be open minded about internal candidates with "non traditional" backgrounds. For internal candidates, we need to prioritize individual talents and potentials, not what functions their current role holds, what's more important is what have they done on top of their day to day responsibilities.

advice: I would say just keep doing a good job. You somehow manage to keep balance between keeping employees happy and hitting department goals.
pros: The culture is very positive, all of management that I've met is super supportive. Upper level management actually listens to our concerns and does their best to accommodate us. Our director drops in from time to time and have focus groups and personally meet with us. The pay is not bad, the job is not stressful. Overall its a great department to be in.
cons: There isn't much room for growth in the department itself as of now. But that could change in the future.

summary: Hard to find a better employer than JPMorgan Chase
advice: Reward accuracy and attendance more, metrics less.  Have more helpers or ITLs on the floor for support.
pros: Excellent pay and benefits, 401k matching, insurance, 4 weeks paid vacation, 48 hrs sick, 72 hours holidays and 24 hours personal time (not 100% sure on amount).  Maternal and paternal time off, 4 months paid.  Great people to work with and customers.
cons: Stressful job,  traveling to and from work in bad weather conditions,   Hard to get days off that you want.  Unrealistic handle time.   Its phone based work mostly, very few jobs off the phone.

advice: the firm definitely needs more investment in technology - new computers, monitors, as well as business applications, also need to consolidate help desk/technology support for better response time. generally the firm (JPMorgan investment bank) is known as a good place to start and prove yourself before leaving for better pay somewhere else, so the average person here tends to be young (average age is under 27).
pros:
good training programs
people are generally more laid back and not as arrogant as those at other firms on the street
diverse work place
cons:
technology and resources - takes forever to request new hardware and software, need greater investment in newer technology
compensation - lags behind other firms

summary: Although a well known company JP Morgan Chase is not a good company to work for.
advice: Provide more training and knowledge transfer so that the employees are able to reach their full potential. Keeping the employees up to date on the company news since they don't want to be caught off guard. Please ensure you are fully aware of the process before taking on the management roll.
pros:
Benefits provided are better than normal
Stable company regardless of the state of the economy.
Fast pace working environment.
cons:
Opportunities for advancement are not readily available.
Cross training or knowledge sharing is not provided.
Extremely competitive environment.
Information on company status or changes are not provided until the day of the change.

summary: Support positions are made to feel like second class citizens
advice:
Ugh, where to begin
-JD, quit it with the outsourcing. It is coming back to bite the company in the ass.
-Promote from within!!!  I dont want to see a job posting on the internet for a role that is right above me!!  Give people a chance to try and fail.  That how it used to work in the old days.
-Dont nickel and dime long time employees.  Longevity should have its benefits.  Make people in support postions feel more valuable, if by no other means than giving them a few extra thousand if they deserve it.  It means so little to the company, and so much to individual.
-Have managers take classes on how to manage-just because someone is smart doesnt mean they know how to manage people.  This is RAMPANT at the company.  Have them make their staff feel more important.  Have them take every employees performace review with the greatest level of professionalism and attention it deserves.  A once a year review should be taken seriously.
pros:
-Good benefits
-A fair amount of friendly people going throught the same grind as you
-One of the better banks in terms of layoffs, have not been as quick to reduce headcount
cons:
Many
-Pay is below average-I reiterate what others have said that the only leverage you have on salary is during the hiring stage.  Once you are in, forget it, unless you are really tight with your manager.  My raises/bonuses never exceded 10%, and that was in stellar years, figure 5% on average for support positions, and thats for TOP performers!
-Unless you have a manager willing to really go to bat for you, you will never be promoted.  Doing a good job is not enough, you have to be an all-star.  I have heard of people who had to leave the company, and then come back to get to a higher level.    
-Spoiled front office personnel-rich pricks that are upset they spend their whole lives in the office.  They make millions, and its never enough.  Young analyts/associates driven purely by greed.  
-Finally, as the title says, unless you are in the "front" you are in the "rear".  Support personel, ie those that dont generate revenues for the company, are an expense, and you are treated as such.  Accounting is typically seen as a profession, not here.  Very clear line between who is valued and who isnt.

summary: Poor Leadership in training, procedures department
advice: Leadership is lacking, they post they empower, move people up the ladder, listen to the associates wants and needs. Start to practice - walk the talk! Remove the leaders who think they can get the work done by making associates feel afraid.
pros: Excellent amount of time off - 4 weeks vac time, personal, sick days too.
cons: I left after a year. Its amazing to me the lack of tools meaning software programs, laptops, to actually do the job. No one wants to hear ideas to make things better or change. When I provided my 2 week notice. Leadership barely acknowledged and I was rated well on my performance reviews! My last day no one conducted an exit interview, walked me out, I had to contact HR and turn in my badge to the guard. What the heck is this?

summary: Global firm with constant change in organization
advice: I would suggest putting more emphasis on enhancing service to client firms and what it takes to accomplish this understanding that efficiency opportunities should always be explored.  Just as important, decrease the amount of "teeth pulling" the present staff are subjected to in striving to meet management requests and dictates.
pros: Plenty of hard working, smart and dedicated teams working to achieve targets
cons: Emphasis on headcount tracking, staffing requests and movements between groups to the nth degree in my division consumes entirely too much time in my opinion. Managers can't get attrition replaced, staff runs short handed constantly and stress is the result.

summary: It is nice company to work for, but development and growth is not a priority.
advice: Listen to employee input more. Develop employees so they can grow instead of taking away from there development by limiting what they can do. Every year there is something new that a position is no longer allowed to do. That is backwards. Movement throughout company is extremely streamlined by department. (Once in retail, stuck in retail)
pros: Their benefits and HR services are outstanding. Management is easily accessible. Very diverse company as well. Sales commissions are decent.
cons: Career development is very minimal. Political work environment. Salary portion of pay is low. Personal growth is extremely limited.

summary: Get what you can on the way in!!
advice: We should increase the relationship between the less senior staff and senior staff to open dialog to creative new ideas to resolve lingering issues. We should also make sure we compensate our talent appropriately l.
pros: Great for developing your skills, lots of potential exposure, and looks great on paper for future opportunities
cons: Lack of appreciation for employees, senior staff typically alienate themselves from less senior staff, lack culture building environment, pay sucks after you get in due to lateral moves which keeps your pay the same with more responsibilities, not very open to new ideas and always a new lawsuit which effect lower staff pay incentives

summary: Nice company with a frustrating bureaucracy
advice: Empower the management to remove individuals who do not contribute and actually hold everyone to the same standards.
pros: JP Morgan goes out of its way to hire individuals from diverse backgrounds and is a well known and well respected employer. Work is rewarding and the majority of people are friendly and easy to work with.
cons: Too much bureaucracy and no effective control measures to ensure people actually work.  Long time employess come in late, leave early, do sub-par work and feel entitled to management roles.  Level of professionalism that is accepted is also quite suprising for such a big company.

advice: Upper management should talk to employees to find out how things are going in the office, it's not all about numbers/ dollars
pros: Decent benefits, if you're lucky enough to have a good manager who truly cares about their employees, than its a good place to work at
cons: Long hours, constant changes in the schedule due to lack of respect of your time from management, it doesn't matter how good of an employee you are, they have their favorites, those people can come and go as they please, had to deal with racist remarks from co workers, HR doesn't do a thing about it, I left after 15 years, very disappointing

advice: Please be clear to potential employees what the nature of the position will be.  It does no one any good to hire employees who are significantly over qualified for a position unless you are going to present them with advancement opportunities.
pros:
Prestigious Employer
Decent Pay
Solid Benefits
Good Opportunity for Veterans without much other experience, especially if they lack a solid education
Minimal Education Required
Informal Dress Code
cons:
An AML/KYC Officer position at JP Morgan is heavily geared towards junior enlisted veterans who have just left the military.  I would strongly advise against the position if you have a prestigious education or other qualifications.  This job is an easy enough job, but offers little potential for growth.
Job was pitched as 9-5, but the expected hours as necessary to support the bankers.  Compensation did not meet hours expectations.
Health insurance is expensive and not particularly good.

advice: Offer more amenities and salary to obtain better quality workers. Stop outsourcing.
pros:
I landed in a good team at the company. JP is constantly shifting and new projects are opening and closing, offering lots of opportunities.

> Great place to start career.
> Good work / life balance. 
> Decent pay.
> Great benefits.
cons:
> Tech dinosaurs that joined 20 years ago and are stuck in the past. (Lots of dead weight)
> Office amenities are rare and cafeteria options are expensive.
> Very slow to adopt new tech.
> Way too much outsourcing and offshore hiring to keep salaries low.
> Hard to find quality leadership/coworkers in the software development roles.

summary: Too big with silos and poor leadership
advice: Focus on giving everyone a voice and collaborate
pros:
Have money to spend on campus programs 
Looks great on your resume if you can handle it
cons:
Top-down approach with no collaboration 
Business out of the loop with 0 partnership 
Don’t know how to strategize - very task oriented/reactive 
Leadership micromanages 
So big to the point where you have no voice in anything or even no what’s going on 
Turn and burn model with lack of candidate focused experience 
Perks are terrible with under performing benefits 
They don’t issue laptops or company phones
Their systems are very slow and freeze up consistently 
Seem to still be very old school in their ways
Lack of respect for people with rude NYers 
If you are desperate for a job, I’d say take it until you find something else

pros: Stable well run organization. It is a durable company
cons: It is a big bank and a big organization and therefore has the associated bureaucracy

summary: Good name, the rest is a struggle
advice: They make enough money to ignore any of my suggestions
pros:
J.P. Morgan is a great name for the resume (although this has begun to change with the current market shift towards tech/startups/thinkers)
Had a fantastic boss for a short spell of my career here, so there are some great people
Well-oiled machine that prints money - lot of expertise
cons:
Return to office despite no interaction with anyone outside of zoom
Health insurance options leave much to be desired
Many are super proud/prickish about being at such an elite firm - it becomes their identity 
Fight for every inch of pay outside of IB/Markets
Communication could be improved from mgmt

pros: Good place to grow and learn. The size of the firm and complexity provides good experience if you choose to work hard and participate. After succesfully making some participation, it will certainly add good value to your resume and will become easier to get new employers' attention.
cons:
- Merging within the firm between various different groups frequently happens and this could impact you unfavorable way 
- Somehow the management pushed NYC metroploitan area employees to come back to the office during 2020 summer, when pandemic was still a real threat. That was madness. Still don't understand what that was about.

summary: Research Department decent for internship but no long term prospect
advice: Top tier management is handling the financial crisis well and steering the company in the right direction, however departmental managers need to tell employees the truth.
pros: Well run summer internship program with Blueprint speaker series featuring top tier management. Experience provides great introduction to the firm culture and the financial industry. Great name on resume with decent skills development under a good manager and great associates.
cons: Unstable working environment in research with 2 rounds of layoffs in 2 months in summer 2008 and hence no prospect for job offers. Management maintains commitment to research division in words only.

summary: Jamie rocks. Working for the IB… not so much.
advice: Treat people better. Provide better work/life balance. More comp for top performers. Be transparent.
pros:
- Name recognition/strong brand
- Stability
- Excellent benefits
- A lot happening right now
cons:
- Not at the top of the industrycompensation scale. Probably towards the bottom.
- No transparency. In anything.
- They make a lot of terrible hires, who suck up the compensation/bonus pool without providing any benefit to the tea.
- Way too much in-fighting between LOBs
- The firm does almost everything its own way, which is often interesting. To say the least. 
- They say that comp/promotion is merit based. That is a lie.

summary: Great Company to work for. Not much room for advancement though. Be happy in your position.
advice: Give the little guys a chance once in a while you will be surprised!
pros: Great benefits, great people to work with. Getting to know the clients is fun as well.
cons: No room for career advancement. I was there for 6 years, while I was going to school. Finished school and after a year and a half of trying to move up or be promoted I never got the chance. So many people are fighting for the same position, it is IMPOSSIBLE to get what you want/deserve unless you know the "right" person.

advice: If you are promoting that you hire veterans of armed services, don't screw them over by luring them in with high salaries just to let them go or cut their salaries once you get your tax break from hiring VETS.
pros: Seeing this company's name on your resume looks good , good training programs, can network.. Located worldwide so good transfer options.  Able to work in several different departments in less than a year(that could be a con also)
cons: Don't value employees. Came in starting at a comfortable salary, seven months later salary was cut 75% and  sent to a commission based role which I had no previous experience in nor did anyone want to be in. Was able to leave that position( had four different positions in less than two years) but never got my initial salary back.

summary: Solid company with plenty of opportunity
advice: Figure out how to leverage top performers regardless of their physical location.
pros: Excellent experience working in a world class, global organization.  If you are willing to apply yourself there is a great deal to be learned at the firm.  Excellent business and technology opportunities.
cons: There are benefits to being in the right locations.  The firm has a bias toward providing opportunity in New York, London and a few key other locations.  It's not clear if this is on purpose or if the firm has not figured out how to fully leverage top notch talent irregardless of physical location.

jobTitle: Vice President, User Experience Design Lead
summary: Great place to learn and grow
advice: - Change things up.  Technology (dev) should not be driving user experience.  There needs to be more transparency and involvement of design and ux teams
pros:
- Great place to learn as JPMorgan Chase offers plenty of courses, classes and other resources.  In particular programs to continue growing
- Ability to work closely with dedicated research teams
- Ability to cross pollinate to other lines of business projects
cons:
- Can be a bit bureaucratic  and political with lots of in-fighting
- Technology tends to drive decision making.  Too often UX design is not involved early enough

summary: You are in charge of your career
advice: More in-place promotions for those who have stretched themselves in their current role.  Many times people move around due to new recruits moving in above them which leaves them feeling overlooked.
pros: There are so many opportunities at JP Morgan Chase including a broad array Training classes, Lateral Moves to increase your knowledge and perspectives, and networking opportunities.  You can take control of your career and make it what you want it to be.
cons: With so many areas of such a large company, it can be overwhelming to find the next opportunity for your career.  Networking is important.

advice: My manager and market director are great.
pros: The company goes above and beyond for their employees. They invest in their own and actively promote from within. Incentive plan allows you to make pretty decent money right away if you are consistent. I make probably 50% more than another RB at our branch.
cons: Banks have regulars that can be a pain. You’ll spend a good portion of each day digging people out of holes who are habitually irresponsible with their finances. Also elderly / technology resistant people are the worst. They “don’t trust the internet” and make you run around for them as a result.

summary: Pros and cons of being a banker for Chase.
advice: unless you are working less than 50hrs a week and making 6 figures, get out.  The mental stress is not worth it.
pros: job stability, many locations and possibly one close to home, 401k.
cons: You have to be an aggressive sales person to thrive here. Company is changing its incentive plant almost quarterly and is usually more and more hurdles to reach thresholds which are also always changing. If you work in a working class neighborhood you sell your self as a guide and counselor but in reality you are just another sales guy/gal working to meet a quota.

summary: Push to find mentors because group culture does not promote it
advice: Push for mentorship and intangibles development even if analyst turnover is high. The positive impressions from actually investing in their growth will lead to a positive feedback loop in recruiting.
pros:
Brand name and general reputation underlying the experience
Hard-working, like-minded peers to bond over the difficult hours
cons:
- No real emphasis on mentorship and development (especially soft skills and leadership) due to the known high turnover amongst analysts
- High turnover driven by long hours and seniors who view you as a resource above all else
- Difficult to stamp out any personal time when work demands are around the clock

advice: Listen to your employees.
pros: Good job security. Mediocre works well here.  The days when Google was the coolest place in the world to work are gone. Google is deteriorating at the edges. Many managers at Google got their jobs just by having low employee numbers and are otherwise unqualified.
cons: Low technical proficiency. Few advancement opportunities here.  Very long hours, and at times when work just piled on (Summer credit crunch) it seems that no one was really able to take a break. Some of the trading and marketing desks seemed to be understaffed as they would almost always have to work over 14

advice: All the managers I worked with were great!  Job training could have been a little bit more organized -- most of us were trained by shadowing other employees who'd started just a few days earlier.
pros: Friendly, laid back managers.  Good hourly compensation, with breaks.  I wouldn't call the work interesting, but it required enough concentration to make the time go by quickly.
cons: Computer systems are a mess -- we couldn't do any real work for the first three days, and for the last hour of every day the computer systems shut down so we got paid to surf the internet.

summary: Great experience and career building company
advice: Before JPMorgan merged with Chase, it was the greatest place to work.  The culture and how talent is retained has changed drastically.  Many top talent leave or have left because of this.  In short, if management wants to keep great talent, they need to pay them at the level on the street.
pros: Senior level managers know their stuff and majority are great managers to work for and work with.
cons: In order to get promoted to VP level, you have to give your blood or really get on someone's good side to get promoted to the next level.

advice: Remember to stay out of the way of people getting the work done.  The "organizational announcement" emails about people doing abstract things at way above our pay levels gets old really quick and makes me think layers of bureaucracy are growing above my head faster than I can possibly climb.
pros: Solid, dependable bank.  Good management inside the investment bank even in a tough year. Compensation is higher with less deferred than some other banks.
cons: It is a big bank with a big bureaucracy to feed and support.  There are some annoyances associated with that (stupid, poorly enforced rules for example).

summary: Decent company, was micromanaged, stuck in dept
advice: You can go overboard with the micromanagement
pros: Paid decently but I was overpaid. Good culture.
cons: Chase laid off our entire department due to business changes. They flagged everyone in our department so the only positions we could apply for are customer service and collections. We were denied for other jobs that we qualified for. Even a supervisor admitted on our last day that we were flagged because we were overpaid. HR denies that any flags are placed on profiles, however one re recruiter admitted it via e-mail. Very few, even top performers were promoted in this department.

summary: Overall a Decent Company To Work For
advice: Hire a more educated employees.  Require more than a high school diploma and be willing to train.
pros: It's about the same as working for any other company.  The benefits are comparable.  There are huge variances in culture depending on what part line of business and department you work for.
cons: In many of the larger Ops centers, it's a toss up as to what kind of manager you'll have. Managers aren't well trained, which is a huge issue.  Chase doesn't have a standard manager training, which makes it challenging for new manager.

summary: A good place to work in the short term and settle in the long term.
pros: Good compensation package, benefits, and flexibility. Good working atmosphere and coworkers. There are a lot of opportunities for mobility within the firm. There are a lot of projects to improve the various businesses. The company treats employees well.
cons: Very large corporation. Changes come slowly due to tight regulation, and a lot of networking is required to make the mobility work for you. It's easy to get stuck in the same old ways with all the same people and processes.

summary: Good place to work in need of some modernization
advice:
Cut the red tape while preserving the controls
Attract good people in infrastructure services to make the work life of all employees more interesting and your operations more streamlined
Reduce the sycophancy and encourage people to produce constructive criticisms
pros:
Good work life balance
People are friendly and open
A lot of possibilities to grow as a developer
cons:
JP Morgan is a bank, it has change management and infrastructure deployment systems which are geared towards fulfilling audit requirements. Continuous delivery is difficult.
It is easier to create software that rocks here than to make sure that this software actually gets deployed to production

summary: Great experience with a lot of resources made available to you.
advice: Overall management is effective and supportive. As anywhere some individuals have a hard time letting go and truly empowering lower level managers and staff.
pros:
Excellent systems, technology, and support staff. 
Company tries to listen to employees and effect change. Relatively nimble for a large corporation. 
Middle Management is effective.
cons:
Middle management can be over-bearing. 
By nature of the position schedule flexibility is difficult to achieve. Company has attempted to remedy, but it's retail with specific hours.
Limited growth in the retail environment for those outside of major hubs that have support staff and other job lines.

advice: With so much restructuring you are starting to lose some of your top talent. Do not forget, you are only as strong as the people you employ.
pros: J.P. Morgan’s Corporate & Investment Bank is a global leader across banking, markets and investor services. The world’s most important corporations, governments and institutions entrust us with their business in more than 100 countries. With $18 trillion of assets under custody and $393 billion in deposits, the Corporate & Investment Bank provides strategic advice, raises capital, manages risk and extends liquidity in markets around the world
cons: Profits are a must, if you don't produce, you are replaced

advice: While politics are a part of any workplace, I found it excessive at times in JPMC and would suggest that some level of performance measurement for collaborative activities is implemented.
pros: There were several long time subject mater experts in the risk area who at times were willing to share and develop staff and teach approaches to risk and new methodoligy
cons: Corporate politics, lack of growth opportunities, and favoritism in both opportunities and growth.   Peers rarely shared information and environment was not always collaborative.    Information was used by peers against you if they could use it in such a fashion.

advice: (CCB) Invest in the resources required to get things done, i.e. Engineering and Technology - both staff and technology, don't make it more difficult  for me to make a small change that makes sense, i.e. InStream prioritization.
pros: Opportunities for advancement, fantastic benefits, love the culture and people I work with, satisfied with compensation, focus on employee satisfaction.
cons: Systems are antiquated for what you would expect at a multi-billion dollar company, resources are spread thin and the proverbial "red tape" makes it harder for employees to do their job ... great company but sometimes the size of this great organization is it's downfall.

advice: Learn to do your job before you try to tell someone else how to do theirs.  Quit constantly changing policies and provide more incentives to the employees.
pros: Great benefits, friendly and helpful co-workers, many perks and good pay for the industry, flexible hours, promotes from within and allows transfers to other locations.
cons: Management most of the time has no idea what they are doing.  Most are not qualified for the position but our hired based on length of employment.  A lot of corporate politics and backstabbing with middle management. Raises are very small and for and few in between.

advice: Invest in better technology. With a better network, you would not need that same headcount. Also, seek out ways to reduce the number of intermediate managers between senior management and folks who actually do the day-to-day client work.
pros: I've generally found it to be a pretty collaborative environment among my immediate colleagues. People are willing to help each other out with their assigned clients. Also, mobility within the company is encouraged/supported.
cons: The org structure is very hierarchical to a point that does not make a lot of sense. The technology is really poor, and compromises your ability to do your job on a day to day basis.

advice:
Get a backbone and have ability to protect YOUR team.
Set realistic goals.
pros:
A lot of different departments that you can transfer to.
Some people on my floor were very cool.
cons:
Too big of a firm where they pay less than smaller banks because they know there is a line of 100 people around the block waiting to get your spot and that JPMorgan name on the resume.

In my specific department, management needed to get a backbone and know when to push back to other departments so we do not get overloaded.

Making up unrealistic number to accomplish.

summary: Great Place to be an Advisor
advice: Keep advancing technology and product set. Increase compensation packages for bankers and branch managers to keep teams assembled.
pros: Client accumulation engine by banker referrals other firms can’t offer. Great leadership. Fair compensation plan with monthly commission and annual bonuses. Just added a longevity stock bonus as well. Advisory solutions are robust and expanding. Technology has significantly improved over the past two years as well
cons: All dependent on the banking team that is assembled around you. Some locations might require more client sourcing than your branch. With any big company, turnover within leadership and the branch will happen as well.

summary: Great company & perks, OK pay, OK Benefits
advice: Keep being amazing and working hard for your employees. Continue to listen to the feedback provided, while also providing a balance for more career growth, training, and access to networking opportunities.
pros:
Work here for a year and you can go anywhere
On-site daycare so you can bring kids to work
On-site chefs to cook food for you
Great people
cons:
Have to work a year at current position before you can move
Benefits are good upfront (no payments) but there are multiple deductibles
You start off not making much, and it takes a couple promotions to really start making money here (outside of sales)

advice: To be fair and train managers to be better leaders
pros:
-Great company benefits
-401 match and stock options
-continuous learning new skills, programs, systems, tools
-exposure with all levels of the organization
-security for the most part
cons:
-Takes a while to be promoted and it all depends on what team you are at
-Managers I have great ones and terrible ones, who mainly are after themselves succeeding but not to inspire and be leaders and promote their staff
-salary if you started low, you won´t get a fair paid compared to someone new entering the company making more then you. 
- Long hours, so work life balance almost non-existent

pros: Really affordable life insurance. This company is too big to fail.

summary: Good people, smart leadership, great company.
advice:
Hire externally more often, and stop offshoring so much.  There's a tremendous number of highly talented, creative, and passionate individuals here in Columbus and other US cities looking for work.

Build more custom solutions (and support existing ones) rather than buying big turnkey packages that are a pain to customize and don't really fit anyone's needs in the end.

Adopt emerging and alternative technologies much more quickly.  We certainly have hopped aboard the Linux bandwagon, but the lack of enthusiasm for other very popular, successful new tools and products is disheartening.

Finally, I'll give the same advice I'd give to any corporate leader:  Innovation (real innovation) in a company like this happens in only one way: the work of a technologist inspires an artist, who, in turn asks for more from the technologist, who improves the technology... and it repeats in a wonderful loop.  The fact is, this cycle tends to just *happen* -- independently of other processes -- when you hire good people.  It not only needs to exist, but it must also be supported and encouraged.  The amazing products you've seen on the cover of tech magazines didn't come from the executive team, middle management, or even product owners.  Those killer apps came from engineers and designers, and were ever-so-delicately transitioned into the formal product development process -- mostly unadulterated -- and supported from the bottom up.
pros:
The financial industry isn't exactly the most stable place to be right now, but JPMorgan Chase has made good decisions in rocky times.  They're in a better situation than their competitors, to the point where they can actually bail out other failing firms.  The majority of my co-workers have been here for well over a decade, and that's nice to see in a time where job security seems to be a thing of the past.

There's always something new to work on at JPMC (new applications, technologies, mergers and acquisitions, etc.), and no shortage of ways to grow within your own role, or shift to a new one.  People make lateral and vertical moves here all the time, so moving to a position that better fits your skills is much easier than other places I've worked in the past.

Senior management here is pretty darned smart.  It's not the kind of place where you might look a few levels up the chain and think, "Sheesh, I could do their job."  Here, it's pretty obvious that you couldn't.  Their salaries are well earned; and throughout the firm, the distribution of compensation, responsibility, and appreciation is much more even than most companies for which I've worked.  Across all the many lines of business, good people are appreciated, treated well, and paid well, here.
cons:
As a designer, I'm used to a more laid-back feel where dress code is concerned.  However, this is a bank, and perception is always important.  There are plenty of folks wearing jeans and polos in lower-level roles, but if your job falls a little further up the org chart, you'll do well to trade up for collared shirts, slacks, and smart shoes.  T-shirts and shorts are right out.  Fridays are definitely more casual, so save the jeans for the end of the week.

Don't expect swanky offices, the newest hardware, myriad fringe benefits, or subsidized snacks.  Jamie Dimon's philosophy for this company is to do more with less.  Your computer might be a couple of years old when you start.  The cafeterias are kind of expensive compared to other companies.  Contractors sometimes have to pay to attend division functions.  They may seem downright cheap at times, but here we stand, doing well enough (in a very rough economy) to acquire other highly-regarded firms.  How can you argue with that?

IT policies are also kind of annoying.  It's a bank, so security is paramount.  They don't limit Internet usage to a list of approved sites, but they do block a whole bunch of them.  Don't expect to be checking your personal email, webmail, or social networking (LinkedIn is permitted) while at work... those ports and sites are locked out.  The hypocrisy can be a bit annoying, though:  they'll force certain software to be uninstalled, lock out flash drive use, or remove admin privileges en masse for "security reasons", and yet the company's standard web browser is (a fairly old version of) Internet Explorer.  Nice.  When you're one big exploit away from doom, who cares if you're using iTunes?

summary: If you want to work in the financial sector, JPMorgan Chase is a good choice, but it definitely comes with frustrations.

When times get tough for your customers, then times are tough for your employees as well. When my job gets more difficult, as it has in the past few months due to market movement, then I need encouragement, not more micro-management.

And in reality, my area of work and my experience thus far (a year and a half) has been greatly shaped by my immediate boss(es). We have, as a result of guidance at the VERY top (CEO, Jamie Dimon), done very well in the financial crisis. Everyday when I deal with customers/clients they realize they are banking with a stable company. It is rewarding to be a financial advisor because I act as a guide during difficult times. I am heavily relied upon by hundreds of families and that is the most important part of what I do. I spend a lot of time taking something very complicated and explaining it to clients of all different backgrounds and different financial literacy levels. It can as well be financially rewarding as well, the top advisors will make more than 300k.
