SIZE: When problems arise, the company is SO huge that finding the right answers can be difficult. Sometimes tracking down parties responsible for errors is impossible.
MID-MANAGEMENT: Very little concern of, or desire for, employee feedback. Prefer we put very little thought into our work and follow the company line. Of course I understand this is necessary to an extent, but they have taken it too far. The middle-management group are pros at CYA and not listening— whataya gonna do there? And my particular bosses have perfected micromanagement...it's almost embarrassing.
SALES: my biggest frustration is not specific to JPMorgan Chase, but it is definitely prevalent here. My role as a financial advisor is, at the end of the day, a sales job. I act as a guide and all like I said above, but I'm only paid to sell new investments, not manage them well.

advice: Don't do subprime lending. Oops. Too Late.
pros: It used to be a great company but that company no longer exists.
cons:
Company is bankrupted. Layoff of all Seattle HQ employees are imminent. "We hope to do to this industry what Wal-Mart did to theirs, Starbucks did to theirs, Costco did to theirs and Lowe's-Home Depot did to their industry. And I think if we've done our job, five years from now you're not going to call us a bank."
Kerry Killinger
WaMu chief executive, 2003
During Killinger's tenure, WaMu pressed sales agents to pump out loans while disregarding borrowers' incomes and assets, according to former employees. The bank set up what insiders described as a system that enabled real-estate agents to collect fees of more than $10,000 for bringing in borrowers, sometimes making the agents more beholden to WaMu than they were to their clients.

summary: A great place to work in a fast-paced environment.
advice: HIre more people to do the job, rather than overload the current employees.  The client is the person to ultimately suffer.
pros: The best part of working for JPMorgan Chase is that you are given a lot of responsibility immediately and the pay and benefits are good.  The atmosphere is very professional and the people are friendly.
cons: The workload is excessive and the computer systems are counter-intuitive.  It is not uncommon to work six days a week and 50-70 hours a week, outside of tax season.  During tax season, we worked 12-14 hours a day six days a week.

summary: Great ability to leverage the power of Chase in building an Investment portfolio.
advice: Reward employees for their success through Continued education, bonuses, or access to career advancement.
pros: Great retirement benefits.  Though payouts are lower than a smaller firm, the ability to leverage Chase's resources (current clients, brand name) to build an Investment portfolio are excellent.  Products are very competitive with other firms and research is superior.
cons: Lower payouts.  Ability to access other career positions within the JPMorgan Chase family are difficult.  Once you get into a Financial Advisor position, your next move is staying longterm or moving into management.

pros: Great benefits and work/life balance. Lots of job flexibility. Its an easy company to move up in and work your way towards the management level. The company encourages employees to stick with Chase because there is lots of room for growth and opportunities to transfer departments.
cons: Very easy to get laid off. Very policy driven company. Everything you do has to be up to standard otherwise it isn't good enough. Very low pay. Employees who have a college education shouldn't be making less than people who don't. Managers are there for the experience to get in and to get out. Very high turn over.

advice: Better at making schedules and also to provide a quicker way to move up in the company. To not over hire in the work place.
pros: Overall easy job not too hard to do a good starting pay for someone going to college with a bit of a flexible schedule so can work around your class also the ability to move up is there but does take some time.
cons: Some days customers will mess up your day and although you can move up it can be a long process and you might get overlooked. Although schedule is flexible some times schedule can be all over the place.

summary: Talk about a joke of a company
advice: HR is should be an employee advocate, not a shield for MD's. As a manager having to call HR to report issues with associates HR reps are 1000% for the manager, yet when you get the same HR rep and are voicing a problem with HR about a higher level employee you become the problem.
pros: They know how to through a party
cons: Its very very clique, if your not part of the in crowd you never will be and they will find some lame reason to get rid of you. I seen it done, I reported it, did everything I was suppose to do and it got me kicked out of the club and I could tell every day that they were looking for some reason to get rid of me.

advice: Bring back the PB role. Licensed bankers are hard to find and this would also provide a path from teller to banker.
pros: The company values diversity. Good benefits and the company contributes more for lower-wage workers. Many opportunities to connect with other employees via networking vehicles.
cons: Short-staffed branches make work/life balance difficult. Long branch hours. People in sales roles (banker roles are sales roles) are under near constant pressure to call clients when they are not working with customers. The company just spent a lot of money on a Salesforce client tracking system and rely heavily on its use.

summary: ALWAYS adding to the plate....and everything is the most important thing
advice: Please focus on simplifying the BM role....you've added far too much and its hurting your managers!
pros: Excellent brand and solutions, compensation can be strong for branch managers contingent on your performance
cons: Additional tasks, pilot programs, extra tracking is always being added and nothing is ever simplified. There is always a new flavor of the week as senior leadership attempts to reinvent the wheel over and over. This takes BMs away from their teams and clients and ultimately hurts the business. Focus on taking these barriers away so BMs can really coach and facilitate the sales process!

advice: Inform managers that rank and file employees voice matters since we are the front liners. We face clients and angry customers everyday. They should know how to respect our opinions and views and should not in anyway retaliate.
pros: JPMC Manila Corp Center has an extensive benefits for its employees like healthcare. They promote diversity and respect cultures, backgrounds of their employees.
cons: Salary is not that good especially if you're only a rank and file employee. Managers tend to limit salary increase if they don't like you. Managers needs more training in terms of handling workplace conflicts and issues and should not retaliate if escalated.

summary: Competitive pay. Didn't enjoy the work environment
advice: Take the time out to properly train staff more and answer their questions and concerns. Look to improve teamwork as everyone was looking out for only themselves.
pros:
Competitive pay for entry level work.
Hard working people
Decent management communication
cons:
Work-life balance wasn't the best because of work hours for this position especially for management.
Technology is very behind as most people used Windows 7 and Excel version fluctuates between different computers which made certain macros/programs work on certain computers.
SOP wasn't clear, however, they are working to improve it.
Workload gets very heavy.
Not the best teamwork, everyone is looking out for themselves, not the team.

advice: I understand that clients make the company, upper management face these big clients and control the mass of employees. I just wish they'd take care more of the front-line employees who are facing the regular consumers and clients each and everyday. Jamie Dimon receives such a big cut every year and yet cost cut on bonuses for the lower ones advising it's already part of their salary. I understand he keeps the company afloat but it does leave a very bad taste for normal everyday employees.
pros:
-Outstanding Career Progression
I started as a fraud specialist, moved to auto financial service advisor, then recruitment sr. specialist until finally I became a Reference Data Analyst which is really a Project Management Role. This all happened in a span of 5 years. If you're interested of growing your career and really moving up the corporate ladder, this is really a great company for that.
-Teaches you the importance of finances
Before this company, I hated credit cards, loans, and vehicles in general. They gave me the financial knowledge to understand how to manage this privileges to bring me to the next level. At the age of 29, I already have a condo, a wife, and a car without the help of relatives or parents. I'm not even earning that much!
cons:
-Old culture
There will be a road block someday as people tend to see years of experience is better than a yuppy who has a heart. You just have to really prove them wrong.
-No nonsense work environment. I actualy like this but I'm certain some others won't.
-Love of frugality
Love it or hate it. This is the reason why the company is striving against the others. Upper management does get mores bonuses than the little one and hey I'm getting some of the benefits since I'm in the middle. I do see how sad it is at the bottom.

summary: Not the company it once was
advice: Pay your employees who kept your doors open during COVID. If we were struggling as a company, why is it that our CEO’s compensation had no change?
pros:
•Decent vacation package 
•Pension (No longer offered to new employees)
•MRA funds
•Tuition reimbursement (to be paid back if one departs within two year of completion)
cons:
•Base pay is low and about half of what you can get at other banks 
•Commissions are cut yearly to make sure bankers work like animals to meet sales goals
•Constantly overworked and understaffed
•Bad morale throughout company…many bankers interviewing and planning to leave to competitors
•30 minute lunch
•Doors never closed during COVID and company risked the lives of employees while other banks protected their staff
•Bankers are expected to be telemarketers and call the same clients over and over

pros:
The team I was placed on started a new project in the beginning of 2021, and because of that we have a very modern tech stack. 
Good work life balance
Company culture is good, people are willing to help each other out
cons:
When there is work to be done, there is work to be done. Sometimes there's weeks where you're not doing much, and then other times( rarely) you're working on a Saturday to get something done.
I have also heard that promotions are pretty mediocre, significant increases in compensation usually only happen in promotions( which only happen every 3 or more years)

summary: Can make decent money but via long hours with terrible benefits and a tough culture
advice: This kind of pure shareholders focus is why people are voting for crazy presidential candidates. Stop investing hundreds of millions in Detroit, and treat your own employees with some respect and dignity.
pros:
Big company name brand
Probably pays better than a lot of other jobs, but less than some direct competitors
cons:
Treated like factory workers with assembly line office seating, one on top of the other
Health care benefits are awful
Constant threat of layoffs or "proposed" (forced) relocation
Corporate people move jobs every 2 years or so
40% or something of tellers turnover every year
Always reducing benefits (pension, vesting, etc.)

summary: The Feudal System Still Exists - Slavery Is Legal Here
advice: Accept that people need their downtime and don't discriminate against those who disallow themselves to be suffocated or stifled by your current feudal environment.
pros: Some work from home, but only because you are expected to work crazy hours in addition to the basic 40 hours a week.  Good 401K program.  Has talent reassignment programs for soon-to-be displaced employees.  Has short-term disability programs which finally gives a work life balance to employees receiving cancer treatments.
cons: Too much out-sourcing.  No respect for employees, bullying and verbal abuse from upper management, no work life balance.  No recognition for good performance if you don't put your life on hold for this company.  You will become ill due to the work schedule expected of you, and maybe even mocked for your physical weaknesses.

advice: It is ironic that the firm recruits the absolute best and brightest on an entry post-college and MBA level but once you get to mid-level management, it is a Roman empire of average intelligence but politically internally savvy bankers, protecting their turf (and outsized bonuses vs the no rocket science work they do)
pros: Well trained, intelligence workforce and overall more gentle environment that other Wall Street Investment Banks
cons: Very political and bureaucratic. Nepotism is wide spread where proteges of bosses are the ones given the opportunity and generally, ending running the teams under these bosses. Generally, not the best and brightest but the most politically savvy.

advice: Quit treating your people like galley slaves.
pros: Worked with some of the smartest people I've ever met.  Decent pay, 4 weeks paid time off, all holidays and good health benefits.
cons: 90% of Dilbert cartoon material comes directly from JP Morgan.  Without embellishment.  Had to endure some of the most miserable backstabbing management on the face of the planet.  Your co-workers value your contribution. Management is rewarded by climbing the pile of the bodies of their slain underlings. Your peers recognize your effort.  Management treats you like an expendable commodity.   Most of the smart people I worked with ended up quitting for better opportunities.

advice: Be more forthcoming and honest with your staff and don't make them promises you know you do not intent to keep. Stop dangling the carrot as a manipulation tool. Pay more attention to the intangibles.
pros: JPMC provides many different opportunities if you are willing to move from department to department. Decent pay & benefits. They do actually reward good effort. Good people for the most part.
cons: Not as flexible with schedules as they say they are. There's a low ceiling for upward mobility (plenty of lateral mobility). People that have been there a long time tend to get stuck in status quo mode and are not open to new ideas.

advice: Work on ensuring EVERYONE has a means of developing a long term career path - saw a lot of great talent leave as they couldn't retain good skilled people.
pros: I thought the individuals that worked there were fantastic, and a lot of people went out of their way to try and help my career development.
cons: However, in a big bank or any large financial institution, it's quite difficult dealing with red tape and human resource structures that can sometimes work against individuals careers. While there were a number of great people pulling for me to make career advances on their own teams, HR rejected on numerous occasions.

summary: Given too many roles too soon without the proper support
advice: There should be more on-boarding tolerance and patience, especially for those who have graciously agreed to take on additional roles at management's request.
pros: Great benefits, fun co-workers, many opportunities to do different things in different roles, geographic transfer potential...
cons: I was given too many roles at one time (Relationship Banker and Small Business Specialist) and didn't get enough support at the beginning while trying to absorb both roles. I was ultimately let go due to procedural issues with account openings with business accounts. There were other more seasoned bankers in the branch who declined the offer to be the Small Business Specialist. I know now why.

summary: Only if you really need a salary
advice: Replace the employees you fired or lost through natural attrition, the workload exceeds our capacity and the rest of the team is ready to quit from being overworked for over a year. Also, develop a path for growth and development, this role has no future and we get stuck with unwanted skill sets for other hiring managers.
pros: Great benefits as an employee, many opportunities to be involved with the company outside your scope of work.
cons: Our team has been neglected by senior management for over a year, with increasing responsibilities, fewer resources to accomplish them and no plan to make improvements in an impactful way.

summary: Great place to work if  work-life balance is a priority
advice:
Review process - often, it's pre-determined and just a formality for the sake of completing annually.
Most of the managers are not proactive in nurturing the growth of an employee.
Hiring managers are reluctant in hiring internal employees trained with new technology; rather they prefer to hire people outside.
pros:
Great Culture
Work-life balance
Good blend of Technology & financial services
Job Security
Mobility
cons:
Promotion policy
Salary increase
Career Progression/promotions 
Scope of learning something new & accepted by the hiring managers
Review process - often, it's pre-determined and just a formality for the sake of completing annually.
Most of the managers are not proactive in nurturing the growth of an employee.

summary: Overall positive but it seems there are barricades to advancement
advice: Create a better career path for Private Client Bankers to progress into advisory roles or into JPM.
pros: I enjoy my uncapped commission, team based sales approach, differentiated product offering, and work life balance.  For most career paths there are many ways to advance and many opportunities.
cons: As a Private Client Banker my options for advancement are limited. I work through Chase Private Client and seemingly have nowhere else to go. J.P. Morgan seems to blacklist employees from the Chase side of the firm and the Private Client Advisor jobs tend to be filled externally by experienced advisors who can bring in outside books.

summary: Aggressively cut commission structure. Bankers are leaving
pros: You are lucky if working in a good branch. coworkers can be nice. great management
cons: commissions get cut aggressively from bankers to offset salary raise for everyone. bankers are leaving. becoming a call center selling investments and mortgage. It is even worse if you work in a branch with lazy and unmotivated financial advisors who can not close deals. I make great referrals but advisors suck. No incentives for opening new account. They want to you to make call to sell expensive investments and uncompetitive mortgage. The bank put more restrictions on what you can get commission from while executives and CEO get raise to 35 mil salary. Please find yourself a career that you can build experience and feel valued. They want to squeeze you out and their vision is to get rid of bankers.

summary: Great entry-level corporate opportunity for anyone looking to gain advancement in the finance world.
advice: Listen to your employees concerns, no matter how big or small they may seem to you at the time, because regardless of the importance of the matter at hand, if it matters to them, then it should matter to you. Afterall, without employees who feel that their concerns matter, you cannot expect to have a successful and profitable branch.
pros: Company offers great health benefits and gives plenty of opportunity for career advancement.
cons: Not all branches are staffed with experienced and knowledgable management, which can create challenges for employees looking to grow in their position or quickly advance to another position.

advice: Train your team as you expect them to be top preformers and offer support in any way you can.
pros: The only pro is that Chase is a very reputable company with excellent medical benefits.
cons: In my current role there is no real life work-life balance. They act as if they care however, you can be on call depending on what type of project you're working or if there is a system issue in the middle of the night. Please keep in mind that this isn't disclosed during the interview. Also, there is absolutely no real training. As a result you're constantly tired and stressed with no real support.

summary: Great People, Hours what you would expect
advice: The people you have working already for you need to be valued better. Encourage career development and mobility - get your talented employees to stick around longer than 1-3 years.
pros: Awesome people - i work with a talented team. It's a well-known and respected company. The work is interesting and challenging.
cons: Hours are what you would expect from a large bank - and pay is not competitive compared to smaller institutions. Turnover is high and layoffs are not uncommon. Management is not focused on development and refuses to invest in the people they currently have working for them. Culture is very polarizing in some areas of the business.

pros:
Name brand for the resume.
Some teams make use of cutting-edge technology stacks.
cons:
Poor gender diversity — Low women's representation within management makes it difficult for women to advance. 

Rigid culture — The culture is very rigid and far too traditional for the current time. Politics makes the job difficult.

Poor compensation — The compensation is low and they don’t care to fix it. There are no incentives for taking on additional responsibilities.

Poor benefits — No free food or snacks in the office. I had to pay for everything except coffee and water. I was required to install 3 apps to login into their systems and check my emails, yet they didn’t give me a work phone or offer to pay my phone bill, which is typical in most companies. Health insurance can also be better compared to what other companies offer.

pros:
- Good experience
- Good benefits
- Nice coworkers
- Many resources to advance within the firm
cons:
As like most positions in services or production, it's quite unrewarding. I rarely, if every see someone who is getting paid a living wage, even though it's 50-100% higher than minimum wage.

They limit you to 35 hours, so you won't be considered a full-time employee, which limits your benefits to half. Essentially, there is no room for growth. You can maybe become a team lead, but that's marginally better than a team member. Your only chance at a future in Chase is make use of the career tools available to all employees and get out of production.

advice: The environment is very political, engineering minds are not very appreciated. People are promoted based on loyalty. I would encourage to reduce number of virtual communication, embrace new technologies. Less town halls, less speaking about how great things are.
pros: A very generous mentor-ship culture. Variety of training. There are many interesting people who work for JPMC and the institution encourages internal networking. Good paid time off compensation.
cons: JPMC users a variety of very obsolete technologies, massive lay-offs for the past 2 years. Virtual meeting take up to 50% of time daily. Process overhead is tremendous, a lot of paperwork, hollow meetings. There are too many town halls and cynical speeches about good and great.

summary: A great company for people who want a comfortable lifestyle
advice: Shake up middle management.  Move more towards a meritocracy rather than a tenure based bureacracy.
pros: The best reasons to work at JPM are that you have the comfort of a large corporation with a fairly stable workplace.  You work reasonable hours for reasonable compensation.  The benefits are good and most of the people are pleasant.
cons: Its a huge company that moves at a glacial pace.  The bureacracy is mind blowing and sometimes people focus on the policy and rules rather than doing what is best for the business, customers or employees.  Sometimes people forget to think.

summary: Good salary is possible but beware.
advice: the amount of cronyism must end.  too many good employees are leaving the company due to hopelessness that can occurr.
pros: No cap on comissions.  Vast network of branches.  Training is provided.  Marketing department does a fine job of driving in business.  Base is low compared to competition, however total compensation is higher than other banks.
cons: The amount of office politics and favoritism is rampant.  Too many incompetent persons are promoted bypassing more knowledgeable employees.  Getting along with your regional manager seems to be key to advance in the company.  Knowledge and hard-work on brings envy from co-workers.

summary: A good place to work with smart people.
pros: Good benefits, vacation policy, managers and staff treat you well. They are very diligent about following policies and treating everyone equally.
cons:
Pay increases in technology are very small to non-existent for bonuses. Have barely had a raise in bonus in last ten years. And base salary increases are usually no more than 2 or 3 percent. Other people had bonuses decimated due to a single low performance rating and they have never gone back up again even with high ratings.
Promotions to levels above vice president are very hard to get. It is easier to quit and get rehired at a higher level.

advice: Checks and balances are critical but shouldn't be overwhelming. Risk management is a necessary tool but needs to be employed holistically.
pros: A large, well-rated bank with a big balance sheet, engaged in diversified banking sectors. Lots of sharp people who know their business.
cons: Too scared of its own shadow. The bureaucracy is staggering even if a huge institution. Too many committees and too many people who have an opinion who don't deserve one.  Lack of intelligent decision-making processes make it too easy for people to say no to deals.  The bank is too big to manage intelligently. Banking is changing.........

summary: Great for career advancement; bad for collaboration
advice: Work better at communicating across teams and being open and honest about the communication. Stop finger pointing and make it a more collaborative and positive work environment where people aren't afraid to share ideas/information or be chastised while trying to understand an issue.
pros:
1. Career Mobility/Development (great opportunities for upward mobility)
2. Vacation time - 4 weeks for salaried employees
3. Programs/fun events for employees, including family events
cons:
1. Communication and collaboration between teams and similar departments within the bank
2. Work/life balance can absolutely be a challenge depending on which department you are in.
3. Not a positive work environment.

advice: Get educated, get to know your people who have sacrificed many long nights get where they are
pros: Coworkers, cafeteria, flex work schedule, benefits, 4 weeks of paid vacation, 3 personal days, 6 sick days
cons:
Constant change leadership,  many of whom have no real talent, experience in the related field or possess any formal education and are proud of it. reckless changes in performance
Metrics after most of the year is over along with job roles rhat change often usually in favor of the inept leadership cronies'  unrealistic quotas for production, lots of pressure to produce, worse than sales. Better off somewhere else

advice: Listen closely to the rumblings in the ground or on the street. When people have concerns, please do listen to them. Not everything is about cost savings, the employees there love what they are doing and serving the customers. Be transparent to them about everything.
pros: Lots (and I do mean LOTS) of things to learn and at first glance, the company is indeed big. You can easily spot various and several areas for improvement and if given the opportunity, you are allowed to tweak them in order to adapt to the signs of the times. Also, you can get to be selected, if not volunteered, to be the champion of your respective domain if you are a performer (lots of them there).  Pay is good; benefits are so-so. Lots of supportive folks who will help you along the way. A lot of managers take care of their own and stick to their guns and principles. Some will even go the extra mile to fight for you and your accomplishments and value to the team, if not to the business.
cons: Ever heard of office politics (a lot of people keep score especially if you put them on the spot and make them seem to lose face; once had a manager who even questioned the feedback received and why such was given. Ever heard of free speech?)? When put on the spot, some people go up the chain (aka their boss) to fight for them, if not clean up their mess). Red tape (would you believe calling up the help desk just to raise a legitimate issue ticket will take you several minutes even for an urgent one when the business is already getting calls from customers)? Bureaucracy (classic case of too-many-cooks-will-spoil-the-broth)? Throw in stagnation (two words: dead end), favoritism (I've worked with a team from different locations and guess which one always gets the early worm despite their tardiness and poor performance), finger pointing (lots of this so HEADS UP and this is the norm by the way), throwing under the bus (also, another one of those "part of the norm" things), ego and power tripping (yep, the moment you meet people who suddenly become leads or managers? oh boy, you're in for a long day), etc. Quality of work? Just a buzz word and the "in thing" is statistics and metrics. Don't get me wrong, but if you managed to latch on to a group with good managers (dwindling number, sad to say and as the saying goes, how come the good ones always get to leave) then you're in good hands. Otherwise, good luck. Things change fast so be on your feet ALL OF THE TIME. One must have a ton of patience, perseverance, guts, and a very thick skin if you want to work for a long time in this company.  Business partners? Good luck as well! Depending on the group and location, some folks tend to be territorial of what they do specifically. Like most companies, everything is a touch move, has to have confirmation, etc. Depending on function/location again, some tend to sleep-walk on the job (you know, going through the motions like a bot, a program), job abandonment despite the fact that they're taking looooong breaks even when it is past the 15 minute or 1-hr mark. You'd be surprised when you get to meet people who are oh-so unqualified for the position (I hate to say this, but again, LOTS of them). Oh, did I mention people also like to cry wolf? or like to press the panic button as if the "world is always on fire?" Your past accomplishments and experience? Throw them out the window and you won't get recognized for having those under your belt. You have to beg the "gods" if you want to take a leave or ask for considerations, etc. and a lot of managers there prefer to impress upper management instead of taking care of their people.  Great discrepancy of work among locations (contrary to the equality value they "try" to espouse). Not being a sour grape, but after a few months on the job, you'll get to see the "real" deal and what you signed up for.

summary: WaMu was a good place to work, I hope it stays that way when it becomes Chase
advice: Instead of losing people through attrition please just give the people you want to lose a severance package and get on with it. It is disappointing to hear Scott Powell degrade management team's performance and cut their bonuses due to lack of preparation on his end.
pros: the work environment is inviting. it feels like family here. There are a lot of changes taking place right now with Chase buying us out, not sure what will happen next.
cons: you hear news about the stutus of your employer through the news, rather than senior management. Communication is low.

summary: Great experience and room to move.
advice: My advice to management would be to provide more in terms of compensation to people who aren't necessarily generating revenue.  That is a personal bias, though.
pros: They provide a great benefits package, vacation, competitive salary, and you work with friendly people.  Managers provide a review of your progress and are willing to help you  move around the firm.
cons: JPMorgan may not provide the top level salaries in the industry, but the firm is managed better than the rest, and given the current economy there is not much else you could ask.  Job security is solid, especially if you're not in the IB.

advice: Be more involved with customer facing employees, check the work of the employees who aren’t... stop playing on your phone!
pros: They spend a lot of money developing their tech, which made my life a lot easier. The double edged sword was their youth, while it made some interactions more pleasant and streamlined, I often dealt with employees who should have had more professional, personal, and emotional experience before working in an office.
cons: Generally, employees are straight out of college or high school, which makes it difficult to delegate for a manager.

summary: Chase is what matters... Not the employees
advice: Cancel all of your meetings and re-join the teams that you lead.
pros:
Great work experience to start a career.
Benefits and employee discounts are solid.
Lot's of vacation time.
Branding yourself as a JPMorgan employee.
cons:
No training.  No career coaching. No life outside of work.

Pay is the worst--seems that is is tenure, and not performance based.  Compensation is decided behind closed doors by people who may not even be familiar with your work. 
The only rewards are more and more responsibility.

Too many people doing too many things; there isn't the capacity to implement all of the ideas.
"Try to keep talent rather than just acquiring it."

advice: Mangers should be reined more often. Senior management should do more skip meetings , meaning meet with the managers team. Understand the team moral. Most managers are not managing , just managing up
pros:
Many different areas to choose from. 
If you can navigate, and make good connections you can get to a particular specialty that interest you
cons: Very large place. You need to do a lot of navigating on your own. Your boss is not advocating for you. The culture is you present to senior management, however if your not on some big projects, not much to present about

summary: a dysfunctional mess of overlapping reorganization, GTI as service LOB is terrible
advice: be honest with employees, manage Business-as-usual vs project work,  All project work creates more Business-as-usual, retain people by bringing new business to team not reduction of costs and labor, let immediate managers manage
pros: Various LOB and technologies,  good 401k match, budget will be provided on popular projects
cons: Business case approvals are joke,  GTI force ratings is popularity contest between manager on your performance, always be nice to managers (or they will stab you in back),  managers have wrong skillset for business,  too many bankers managing technology without clue to functionality, No raises are causing forced attrition, secret layoffs

summary: Competitive. One must be enduring and hardworking to succeed
advice: The managers are too focused on just trying to get the work done and ignored other things such as the employees supporting them. Managers should not lose sight of the people around him are important as well.
pros:
There are a lot of compensation benefits such as help in housing, medical, paid trips and so on.
There are a lot of amazing people too and if you can identify them and form a network, your future will be very promising
cons:
bearsterns people helping their own kin
political
Too much employees
Too little synergy
Control systems are not effective
Managers too focused on doing their own work

meaningless 5AM meetings and bs status reports

summary: A good culture and a good company
pros:
- It's the largest bank in the US, so any projects you work on are bound to be significant, both from the perspective of your time and the broader society
- It's got a solid culture with a lot of good people
- People care about doing good work and doing work that benefits the broader society, so it is an energizing place to work
cons:
- It is hyper bureaucratic, so it can be frustrating trying to communicate across teams or bring people together
- It's a big institution, so a lot of business processes are very manual and inefficient

summary: It's easy to get lost in such a HUGE company
advice: Invest in people management; provide proper training to the new hire to enable them to make contribution;
pros: With the right manger who is willing to spend time to bring you up to speed and put you in the right position to excel, this is a great place to work; good for your resume
cons: Very top down management style; hard to get notice as the company is so big; benefits is not as good as it should be; compensation for most of the employees are down from years in the past while senior management continues to take home the big bonus checks.

advice: People Managers should be hold accountable for bad hiring and firing people who earned an M+ rating in previous years! I'm sure fixing this would itself bring least 2% saving in global hiring practices cost.
pros: Good Infrastructure, Lot of Growth Potential
cons: Keeping resource like commodities, fire them even after 2 years, once the project/initiative is completed, transitioning from 1 role to another, one BU to another is so ineffective, won't be surprised if Sr Mgrs runs the scam of making extra money through hiring FTE from agencies rather then giving weightage to internal resource or hiring through company career tool.

summary: A tough place for mid-career hires to start
advice: Put people (clients, employees) first.  Put technology and systems in the service of people.  The firm has grown  so fast it is the other way around now.
pros: Amazing firm and resources, terrific product offerings for clients, smart hardworking people.
cons: Accessing those resources is very tough when you join as an experienced hire.  You'd better be supremely self confident, phenomenally resilient, impervious to threats and fear mongering, and very hard working and effective. You;ll get next to no feedback or guidance.  The regulators are all over the firm, which has added to stress and a bad mood among employees.

summary: Its a wonderful company to work for!
advice: Positive environment keeps everyone happy, wanting to produce quality work, and prevents great employees from leaving the company.
pros: My management was awesome. I had wfh one day a week, great benefits, and health plan.
cons: I worked in the corporate office in Lewisville. Initially the environment was great, everyone were friends and we did alot of pot lucks. Then layoffs started and the employee moral had decreased. The team members were given more work and were appreciated less. We did less team building activities too. It became a work-only type of environment in which people just came in, did their 8-5 shift (sometimes overtime), and went home.

pros: JP Morgan is a machine, it has a lot of money to throw at its biggest problems and will not hesitate to hire the best people to do the job it needs.
cons: For management, it’s a revolving door. New hires are given the hardest jobs, expected to fail after a period and discarded as and when it happens. Often senior people brought into roles that 3-4 people are already responsible for in other areas in the firm. Be sure to enter at a high comp level, it often stagnates once your through the door and comp is targeted at the junior levels.

summary: Good Company to work as a Developer
advice: please be transparent to the employees and re-evaluate the managers attitude towards employees.
pros:
great company to start with for developers
slowly migrating towards latest technology stack
good benifits
fast growth till you reach the max that you could in a position (then becomes stagnent)
cons:
no transperancy in filing citizenship and lot of other things as well
could get political pretty quickly
few mangers attitude is very bad (like I pay - I can fire you anytime!!!)
lot of bureaucracy, not employee friendly.
managers expect too many after work hours and weekend work. 
lot of calls involving people with less or no knowledge about an issue

advice: I would be surprised if management listens to any reviews. Even being with the company, management didn't even listen to employees, let alone former employees.
pros: Learned a great deal of the finance world, met a lot of people with all walks of life. Great opportunity to learn if you put yourself out there and meet your clients
cons: A lot of politics, manager would only show up 2-3 days out of the week and expect everyone to be on top of things when leadership is barely a presence. Upper management doesn't even care, regional management is the same. It trickles from the top.

advice: Be consistent in what you ask for. Be realistic with sales expectations (though you are governed by your bosses, who are governed by higher up bosses - so suggestions to reexamine areas are very difficult to have heard by anyone with power to actually do something.) Encourage your staff, commend them for successes. Be open to conversation with and suggestions from your staff. Do not belittle your employees.
pros: Opportunity to interact with customers and see the impact that you have on them. Some opportunities to work across sectors with other specialists to diversify knowledge and understanding.
cons: Very bureaucratic system in which it was hard to get noticed or heard or ahead. Chase did not evaluate markets individually to set sales expectations accordingly - same expectations applied whether your branch was located in a very wealthy area or a very impoverished area.

summary: Great co-workers, firm does not compensate internals
advice: Be proactive in employee retention. Don't pay external hires with less experience higher salaries than present employees with high ratings. Reward the valuable employees you have so they stay with the firm. Offer greater flexibility and reward people for doing their jobs well and going the extra mile.
pros: Fantastic group of people, very knowledgeable, helpful and hard working. Department has many programs and initiatives meant to enhance the processes and employee experience.
cons: JP Morgan does not compensate internal employees and will hire external candidates at higher salaries than current employees in higher levels. Pay and bonus inequities are great and no recourse is available

advice: Know your job, promote on merit, stop putting unnecessary pressure on your subordinates, and motivate your people. There are still many who belive in the company.
pros: The healthcare benefits, period! So many people have made reasonable improvements to themselves without an extreme amount of debt being incurred. There are some people in leadership who will still recognize what employees do well. Rapport between employees can be memorable.
cons: The culture is very unprofessional and cut throat. The people are unexposed or desensitized to real life events. The rudimentary nature stagnates anyone with ambition. You have to be strong to have any chance of gaining tenure.

advice: Stop micro-managing and value the loyal employees who have been there through all the merges and has always been loyal.  If you want employees to be loyal to you then you (management) needs to be loyal to their employees. It really is a shame, because Chase was once an awesome company to work for.
pros: I worked for the company for almost 20 years and for 14 years I really enjoyed working there. Management cared about work life balance and I always received exceeds on my performance reviews because I cared about what my responsibilities were. The company seemed to really care and you felt valued until the merge with Bank One and the Chase adopted their philosophy.
cons: After the merge, my department was being centralized so I transferred to another department and that was a huge mistake. I transferred into the Loan Integrity Operations Dept and the Senior Manager is a HUGE micro-manager and he could care less about his employees. If you are tired after working 60 plus hours a week,  he expects you to come in on weekends or "they can find someone else to replace you".  After almost 20 years of service with the company - I got laid off and from what I hear from my friends who are still there, it has gotten worse. In fact they are all posting out or going out on medical leave for health issues. The stress is just not worth the pay. Yes they give you 4 weeks vacation, 6 sick leave & 2 personal days, but if you take them you get grieve from upper management. You are actually looked down on if you take all of your time. I would rather work for a company that cares about me as an individual an get only 2 weeks vacation, a few personal days and even receive less pay then to deal with the stress.

advice: Salaries should match the employees worth, knowledge, experience in order to retain great employees.
pros: The company offers great benefits with Vacation, Sick, Floating holidays and Personal allowances.  401K, Medical, Dental and Vision are also provided along with other insurance policies and resources made available.
cons: Positions in lower management and below are grossly underpaid compared to other companies for all lines of business of Chase.  The state of mind is if you leave Chase and return you will be paid more than you would with promotions or internal transfers.  The Credit Card division has the lowest amount of career opportunities with the Mortgage banking side having the most.

pros: Lots of opportunity for mobility within the company if the person is qualified. An employee's experience at JPMC  really depends on their group and manager. That makes a world of difference. I really appreciate the business groups that throw great events and tackle challenges employee may face. JPMC has tons of resources for people who take advantage. I have no complaints about the pay.
cons: A person's experience really depends on which group they are in. Each line of business has their own culture. Managers have a huge influence on an employee's experience. JPMC is making an effort to cut out some of the bureaucracy

advice: Be open minded about moving VP's to Director status with more frequency.  Some directors were definitely out of touch with new technology and new business cultures.
pros: Really good salary.  Good work conditions unless you work in operate or incident management - outages can get very hectic and tempers tend to flare up.
cons: Long work weeks, regularly 50 to 60 hrs.  Very clickish, more difficult to move between groups than it should be.  Directors tend to take their loyal employees with them from group to group.  More who you know than what you know.

advice: If you want to keep people in their roles provide proper training without continuous rapid change of processes. Also, hire more people to keep up with the workload so your process doesn't get vastly hung up waiting on three people to churn out an impossible amount of oversight and approval. Perhaps, add more time in the beginning to allow for hold ups later.  Do not promote managers who are performing poorly simply because you are short staffed.
pros:
It's a secure large bank who is performing well/ Job security
As with every corporation you have great people working there and difficult personalities
cons:
- Benefits are terrible: very high deductibles and only two plans to choose from which have a lot of gaps in coverage
- Disorganized
- Rapid turnover
- Rate of change too rapid for new employees to keep up
- Stressful environment

summary: A Great Place for Growth if You Can Network Properly
advice: I’ve had some really great managers and some that needed much improvement. To the ones who need improvement, try to be present more and be engaged as well as knowledgeable in your team’s daily functions.
pros:
Great Pay
Lots of PTO
Important Job Titles 
Multiple Opportunities to Get Involved 
Awesome Senior Management Team w/ 90% being very personable.
cons:
Lots of Favoritism regarding promotions. It’s not at all about what you know, but who you know. Within a 6 year period, I faced lay-off 3 times. Others may be compensated significantly more than you do in the same position based on favoritism. 
Lots of gossip

summary: Lack of Emotional intelligence at Management /  Kindergarten / Chase Bank
advice: Treat everybody under you the way you would like to be treated even so if the costumer experience number is not 9 or 10. Do not blame any employee for your lack of emotional intelligence and management skills. Should not live or die by the company's policy. Use one of the 5 star (common sense) with the employees.
pros: Great benefits, health insurance and other perks
cons: Everybody is for themselves no matter what it cost. Lack of Emotional Intelligence from the management even if Jamie Dimon supposedly values the most. Everything became a numbers rating game regarding the costumers experience.

advice: Get rid of Dimon and clean up the rotten culture. Stop selling fake news.
pros: The company tries hard to lead in tech but the leadership is totally incompetent.  I can’t say much in this section since all that needs to be known is known. Same old stuff.
cons: Technical leadership is worthless and innovation is practically nonexistent. When comes down to internal mobility it’s all a fraud. Once you get into a department you’re never getting out.  Don’t listen to all the fake news. The culture that Jamie Dimond put together is really toxic and not constructive. Which makes him one of those leaders that already needs to go. Looks elsewhere!

advice: Hire Team Managers that will be leaders.  Just because a representative sounds great on the phone doesn't qualify them to be in management.
pros: OK pay and benefits. There is opportunity to move to different areas of the Company.
cons: Its a call center.  You're tied to a phone, no opportunity to make friends with co workers.  The Management lacks leadership skills.  My manager couldn't provide a crucial conversation to save his life and the only feedback I get from my Team Leader is when she growls at me in passing in the hallway. They have no idea how to keep employees engaged.

advice: Restructure the Private Client division, PCB should not be standing at the ATM showing people how to use it, we should service just our book of business.
pros: You have a well established company, and technology is industry best.  Chase is convenient since they are everywhere you do get time to study for your series 6 and 63
cons: You have to buy expensive Chase clothes and are poor quality.  I was told in my interview that I would help with high net worth clients.  All you are is a glorified, under paid, personal banker, who prints debit cards, and take customers to their safe box.ant

pros:
Amazing program, if given the opportunity definitely take it! 
Great pay
Good work/life balance
Numerous events & opportunities to get to know the other interns in the program, from areas all over the globe!
Amazing managers. Everyone is so helpful and make a big effort to make interns feel welcome 
Terrific Learning Opportunity
cons:
How they choose who gets the job after the internship is unorthodox
Once you are in the program you do not get to choose what area in the company you will be working in. I worked in an area almost completely unrelated to my major

advice: Hire more staff. So much money is lost due to not having enough people in a bank. Thousands of potential dollars walk in, cannot be serviced quickly and become irate and leave for a different bank.
pros: District Manager and Branch Manager were awesome. Benefits are amazing even for part time. 3 Weeks Paid Vacation. Great Free Employee Bank Package. Banking made convenient.
cons: Some District Managers and Branch Managers can be bad. Customers can be extremely rude. Their Policies and Procedures guide is very vague and never up to date. You have to remember thousands of Policies that you will never use in your job career.

advice: Let people eat lunch and take the personal time required by law. This only leads to many of the workers becoming overweight, unhealthy, alcoholics and in many cases even drug users!
pros: Great benefits and cool people to work with. Learn a lot. Technology is great! Room for growth for those that work hard. Hard meaning you are in top 10 percent.
cons: No respect for people's lives. They could care less if you have a family, need vacation (although it is due to you) or need flex time for personal matters (beyond 2 personal days per year, which have to be scheduled according to the banks needs, not yours.

summary: "Great place to work if you like finance"
advice: Consolidate effort to remove unnecessary bureaucracy and reporting. Integrate better with other LOBs. Offer better tuition reimbursement options.
pros: JPMorgan's asset management business is a fantastic place to work if you love finance. The people are very bright and they compensate you well. It is easy to be proud that you work at JPM.
cons: Great deal of bureaucracy. The organization is so large it's easy to feel like you're lost or like you're not having a real impact on the business. Distinction between "front office" and "middle office" or "back office" makes those not in "front office" feel like second class citizens.

advice: As an Employee, there has been an incredible amount of bureaucracy that has been created in the past 5 years.  It makes it incredibly hard to get things accomplished.  Procedures need to be simplified.
pros:
JPMorgan is an Industry leader
Jamie Dimon is down to earth and gets it.
The people for the most part are really good
Innovative
cons: Slow to market - It's tough to move things along quickly.  Processes are good, but sometimes its is overkill.  Technology is good, but unless you get a live body on the phone or know someone in technology - it may take you a while to get technology issues resolved.

advice: People are your greatest asset. Recruiting for the part of the bank I was working at was incredibly difficult, yet there was not a single initiative to retain talented individuals. When you're spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on recruitment. Perhaps paying even at market rate for your engineers could help with keeping them. If a bank can't even compete in compensation, I don't see why engineers would want to work there over a technology company.
pros: Opportunities if you seek, driven people, intelligent peers.
cons: Culture, coworker interaction, scale. Below market PAY for engineers if starting your career here.

summary: Good company that is trying to do things the right way
pros: The company has a strong commitment and investment in technology. It values the people that work for it and often gives back to the community.  It also has a surprising level of morality for a bank. Though competitive, I enjoy working here and the culture is generally very good.
cons: Sometimes too many projects going on at the same time and resources get stained trying to keep up with them.  Being a global company, some meetings can take place outside of normal working hours, but that really depends on ones role.

advice: I guarantee you JP Morgan could not care less about my advice.
pros: Big company with all the perks that come from that. However the companies are very separate and that could cause a lack of exposure for crossover opportunities.
cons: You can do everything right and succeed in every job performance category and still wake up to jump on a call that tells you you are laid off. Also a very homogenized culture that still is trying to understand how minorities fit in. Extremely poor work life balance. Zero defect environment creates intense negative office politics. Senior Management is not to be trusted.

advice: Take a honest look at employee surveys and talk to employees. Your metrics reports are ridiculously skewed. Instead of just looking for good reports, look for the truth.
pros: Good pay and benefits. Good work life balance
cons: Many layers of management that only know most employees as a row on a report. There is a tickets quota to meet and it is very easy for techs to close tickets without actually resolving issues to inflate their numbers. If you take pride in helping people you'll be constantly frustrated cleaning up after1st level help desk. Always feel like you are just an expense to be reduced or eliminated

pros: Working at a large financial foundation provides exposure to various different teams and departments. Specifically for product controllers, it is a great way to build computer skills (Excel) which becomes something you can take with you no matter where your career takes you. The company as a whole focuses heavily on process improvement and efficiency which is also always appreciated. Internal opportunities is great given the size of the firm and the positions available.
cons: While working at a large financial institution is great to build exposure, it can also mean that the work that you do can be extremely narrow/specialized as well as being repetitive.

pros: JPMorgan has been consistently wonderful in providing a great work/life balance, allowing time off on short notice, understanding of family situations, and allowing work to be completed on a schedule that is best for me. JPM is also the most diverse workplace I've experienced.
cons: Compensation is considerably lower than other banks; raises can be small or nonexistent, and bonuses are discretionary. If you are hired at a lower salary it is very difficult to achieve higher salary levels in your role's compensation band. Additionally, health insurance offers a decent range of doctors but deductibles are high and non-deductible, non-covered out of pocket expenses can be significant.

advice: Value juniors' time and understand that the best associate and VPs are A2A promotes. With the status quo, no one will stay and you will continue to have headcount issues at the executive director and down levels.
pros: Rigorous experience that teaches you a lot about working as a professional in finance. Technical work experience and ability to take ownership early on.
cons: Poor group culture. This is entirely group-specific, but the FIG team and specifically the Insurance vertical have a very poor culture / high turnover for junior team members. In-part because of a lack of focus or care on retention and understanding that the job is commoditized.

summary: They tell you you're doing one thing, and you end up doing another
pros: It's client facing, and at least you can do some maintenance on customers' accounts. I love helping clients in that respect.
cons: I was told I wouldn't be spending too much time on the teller side, when literally I guess Chase is making associate BANKERS be tellers from now on. I left my job at BofA as a teller there to come here and be a "banker" and open accounts, which they told me I would be during the interview (just with not as much access as the RBs), and I'm relegated to be a teller. So, Chase basically lied.

summary: Decent first job, would never make my career here
pros:
don't have to work over 40hrs (sometimes its needed but so rarely)
competitive pay
depending on the team your work environment can be really great
cons:
No 401k match for the first year
Policies are old fashioned - very little flexibility to work from home, most other companies wine and dine their engineers but its not like that here. We are an expense, the bankers make the money.
My direct manager lies, manipulates, and threatens to fire everyone on our team on a regular basis. Its definitely an isolated issue and most aren't like that.

summary: OK place if you can deal with the egos.
advice: Don't just use "team work" as a catch phrase.  Promote it, reward it, and make it part of the corporate culture to leave egos at the door.  We'd get more accomplished and the quality would be higher.
pros:
-great benefits
- decent hours
- immediate manager very good
- flex time ability varies too much from department to department - needs to be consistent.
cons:
- lack of budget to do great creative work
- egos are rampant at all levels, so it's a bit cut-throat
- no advancement opportunities in staff positions
- it's a bank...and we know how people think of banks these days!

advice: Recommend to HR, Legal and Compliance a deep-dive into how each Not for Profit LoB is handling Reduction in Workforce termination cases.
pros: Ability to leverage exceptionally brilliant, well educated, connected resources throughout Investment, Asset Management, Corporate Finance, Legal & Compliance, Treasury Businesses. Superior Brand. Heritage JPMorgan, Chase as well as Citi Leaders remain in charge of running Investment, Asset Management, Corporate Finance, Treasury, Global Technology, Businesses
cons: Less qualified Bank One resources selected to run several not for profit Lines of Businesses. Outsourcing results, overspending initial budgeted projections. Those Not for profit Lines of Businesses starting to regularly apply performance results as justification to terrminate employees, vs. Severance Payout.

summary: A stepping stone to another position that gave me insight into Corporate America.
advice: Focus not only in promoting not only those individuals who perform at sales but those who show natural leadership qualities that other employees would be willing and eager to follow and perform for.
pros: Many of the employees who work there are friendly and interested in helping you develop as an employee. The benefits and reward perks for employees are great.
cons: Many within the management tier were promoted due to popularity and performance not on skills and ethics, which made working for these managers very challenging. Ethics and company protocol say one thing and the managers say another.

advice: Although there is much government over-site occurring because of the economic issues, management should provide more training on working in the new environment.
pros:
Number one - variety of job opportunities. I have done many jobs here, and for the most part have enjoyed doing them all.
Work/Life balance - Not just banker hours, but also a supportive management group.
Benefits - best health care in industry and some flexibility in scheduling.
cons:
Mid range of salaries within industry, and some what below for same job outside of industry.
With advancement the quality of life sometimes sacrificed.
Government regulation, which is necessary, can often slow down the process of doing the right thing.

advice: Keep up the good work. Listen more to the employee surveys. Also meet your direct reports -1 once in a while.
pros: Director Board and Operating committee sets clear directions. So you are well aware of company goals. Great mobility opportunities. Great leaders. Great learning opportunity.
cons: I don't see anything I didn't observe outside of this company. If you have a career plan and work towards it, chase does their best to help you. Mobility can be hard at times if your appraisals were bad and your Manager can sabotage your career by giving a bad rating.

summary: Not a bad place to work right out of school.
pros:
Large company so there are many different areas and services to work in. 
Looks good on a resume. 
Fairly diverse work force.
Lots of opportunities for advancement if in the right line of work.
cons:
Huge company, so while many opportunities exist for growth and advancement, it can be hard to meet the right people you need to meet in order to advance. 
Can be hard to find where you fit in.
Does not always seem like a very personable place since it is so big and involved in so many different lines of work.

summary: You make your money walking in the door, don't expect a lot of career growth.
advice: Learn that 60hr weeks are not productive and when someone goes above and beyond normal efforts not expected efforts reward it with more than a pat on the back and a meaningless title.
pros: Great learning experiences and education opportunities and good people to work with lots of opportunities for varied experience the staff are very helpful with assisting you on your career
cons: Degrees mean nothing, long hours are expected, technology is at least 10 years behind and management is pretty disconnected from the working staff

summary: It's a very high pace and high performance environment
advice: Successful managers are those that practice the company values and commitment to employees.  Managers that just process numbers and ignore the employees, will create short wins at the expense of losing top talent.
pros: You will work with some of the best technology specialist.  Your opinion is valued and you will move up if you are one that steps up to challenges and corrects/recommends solutions to existing problems.
cons: With such a high pace, you can get burnt out and if you don't manage your work life balance you will not have one.

advice:
Please focus hard on employee satisfaction to keep morale high and promote a better culture of collaboration.
The low ranking employees are the most over worked without commensurate compensation.
pros: You get to benefit of working on some large scale projects with focus on minimizing down time and upkeep.
cons:
Due to the large size of the company and the many levels of hierarchies it is not very easy to advance your career. Projects gets delayed far too often and are shut down as priorities often change.
Hardly any employment benefits apart from 401K and average health benefits.

pros: Excellent pay and benefits for banking.  Good growth opportunities...........if you're in the right line of business in the right location!
cons: Very intense and stressful work.  Always seemed like we had a deadline of yesterday.  Changes priorities and direction too quickly in too many areas all at the same time.  Poor at rehiring and talent reassignment i.e. more rhetoric than true action.   Laid off 09/2013.  Applied for 24 positions from 06/2013 to 07/2014.  Had 2 interviews and got 24 rejections!

summary: Good place to work if you don't mind a large corporate feel
advice: Make sure you treat your employees with respect.  Do your best to provide career and development opportunities.  Take personal interest in your employees.
pros: The work was consistent.  There's always checks to cash and applications to process.  There are some good corporate perks through Chase and other various programs.
cons: The company is so large there isn't really a personal touch.  You're basically a number who performs various functions on numbers.  But if you don't mind just showing up and doing your work it's a good job.

summary: true life: behind the scenes of pledging blue
advice: its not just about customer experince but also employee experience. Happy employees will be able to provide happy customers. Incentives shoudl be better structured & defined managers discretion isnt consistent & every manager thruout same districts define incentive differently.
pros: Security & Insurance. Having such a big presence your branches will always have traffic & the insurance is great.
cons: work & life balance does not exist. you will never have a set schedule, therefore never having time for a life outside of work. Incentives keep getting smaller & smaller & your workload is more & more.

advice: The biggest hurt to employee morale since 2004 has been the hiring of former colleagues by MD levels, as a preferred method of filling roles, over the promotion of those who have spent years with the firm and who have better qualifications.  This has been a very big issue for quite a number of people who have seen their careers stagnate or had to take lateral moves.  Further, touting those lateral moves as "mobility opportunities" in cases where they truly were not, has eroded senior management credibility.   Everyone has a lot of good things to say about the firm.  The method in which desirable roles are filled is not included in the list of good things.   More must be done to truly understand the capabilities that each person brings to the table.
pros:
Exposure to very large, complex, operations and/or technology
Leadership can be very strong, depending upon the senior manager
Benefits package is better than most
Flexibility to manage work/life demands through remote technology
You will be pushed to continuously raise the bar on your performance
cons:
Size and complexity feed bureaucracy that is resistant to change, despite management efforts
There are more weak leaders than strong
MD level managers will hire their colleagues from former firms before promoting from within
Many jobs moved to Asia Pacific
Your starting salary and bonus will very much dictate your progression through the years.   Big bumps do not happen for the greater majority.
Promotion process is now committee driven which drives fairness; however, if you are not well known by those on the committee, your chances of promotion to VP or ED can be negatively impacted.
Work/life balance can be non-existent, depending upon the role, program or current business requirements.  Expect 50+ hours/week as a minimum.  Don't be surprised when 60-80 hours/week becomes the norm.

advice: none
pros: Lots of opportunity for growth and variety of new projects you can throw yourself into.
cons: Depending on the project and the management of that project, the hours can be crazy.  I worked on a project that was high profile and it required lots of travelling and they wanted us to work Saturdays, Sundays, and some of the grill holidays to attempt to meet project deadlines.  There were a few times where we were just going through the motions of being there to look good while we were waiting for a vendor to develop bug fix patches.

summary: Great people, but management is draining
advice: Stop making everyone a one trick pony.  It's impossible to figure out how to get things done because tasks are so specialized.
pros: Plenty of room for career advancement, but be prepared to put in 50-60 hours per week of work to have a chance to do so.  Great benefits and the majority of people whom I've worked with there are great to be around.
cons: The more work you do, the more that gets asked of you.  Management is in no short supply and there are plenty of people looking to get the monkey off of their backs and onto yours.

advice: If your employees are doing a good job.. let them know.  don't just point out the bad stuff.  Moral is very important in high stress environments.
pros: Great company to work for benefit wise, Paid time off, sick days great health insurance, dental and vision, as well as STD and LTD.
cons: Very stressful environment.  constantly changing. if you can't adjust quickly might not be good fit.  My job with same team of coworkers changed several times in 2 years,  I actually got two new job titles in one day.. in the middle of training for it.

advice: It was fun while it lasted. Thanks for the good times. Standing on the stage with like-minded producing peers was definitely rewarding. It meant a lot to me.
pros: The people that worked there were the best! The experience was enlightening and I am glad it was part of my tenure.
cons: Management knew only one thing and that was make money at all costs, which eventually, lead to their own implosion. In spite of tremendous "in-the-door" volume, the compensation plan was diminished at best and completely geared toward 'Super-Producers'. No front or back-end points. I made more once I left to become a Mortgage Banker.

advice: Project goals and priorities and stick to them.  Often the focus changes and this effect employee experience as well as customer experience.
pros: JP Morgan Chase is a global company which offers extensive opportunities everywhere.  If you are looking for mobility this is the place to be.
cons: Retail Banking changes focus often.  If there is one consistent message at Chase that would be change.  Chase is a performance based company meaning if you out perform your peers you will be rewarded.  However, if you are average or underperform you will not make as much as you could at other banks.

advice: Management needs to communicate better on the employees and avoid relying too much on own decisions to avoid conflicts and escalations on the process and the organization morale.
pros:
Compensation - While not at the top of the financial shared services industry in terms of basic pay, they make up for Night Differential (covers entire shift worked) and Holiday Premium. There are 15 Vacation Leaves and 9 Sick Leaves for Team Leads and below. Not much but adequate. These empty pretty fast in a span of one year.

Benefits - Their HMO is relatively extensive and covers an additional number of dependents.

Infrastructure and Location - Their building is located closer to the main road (EDSA). More accessible for many living in the north and western side of Metro Manila. Clinic is round-the-clock operational. Also has a 24 hour cafeteria serving passable and very reasonable meals which many other companies don't offer.

Internal Mobility - IJP (Internal hiring) is strongly present here and this gives staff the opportunities to look for  which role suits him/her best.
cons:
Politics - This is the main root cause of the high attrition and less-than-satisfactory scorecards for certain processes. As long as you're currying the favor of the upper management, you will have no problems in the risk of being reprimanded or given a disciplinary case despite breaching company rules and policies (e.g. no completing the 9 hour shift, leaving work undone). Hence, some of the main contributors of the process are left out.

Performance Management Not Objective Enough - Depending on the team, despite the highly complex level of performance metrics given, what is written on the evaluation does not reflect on accomplishment of the employee. In short, the objectives are not followed completely and ratings could be factored on the general impression of the management towards the individual. This can affect the promotion of the employees since on some teams promotions can take very long or even not at all.

Work-Life Balance - Again, depending on your team, working at an average of 15 hours per day is needlessly terrible for your physical, mental and emotional health. If you're unlucky enough, work days of 22 hours for five straight business days are not unheard of. The obsession of FTE Saves by the upper management should be stopped or lessened since this is taking the toll of their employees' well-being. To make matters worse, Infrastructure cost reduction is attained through hotdesking, where worstations are shared by at least two people with different shifts. Hence, when one is rendering overtime, he/she should move to the overtime work area to give way to the next user. Quite a hassle considering overtime is the norm here.

Process Improvement - The amount of time for one process improvement to migrate is incredibly slow. It goes into several bureaucratic issues before being approved. Too many shifts available are on WHEM (graveyard). Morning shifts are on the rare side. If other shared services can make the WHEM processes do on morning shift, why can't JPMC?

Hiring Strategy - For the lowest ranked employees (Team Members), they have a soft spot for fresh graduates since the salary offered is on entry level. For those with experience however, they are reluctant to hire one due to the possibility of asking a much higher rate. Hence, the external hiring of Senior Team Members are less common now. Most are through level promotions (which can be slow).

summary: Ok place...make lemonade out of lemons...Strictly Newark, DE Operations - Tax

pros:
Great benefits package
Plenty of opportunity to expand your knowledge and learn across groups.
cons:
This review is strictly for the Newark, DE Tax Operations group.It is only fair to add that the group I am reviewing only make up a small portion of the company and do not reflect the overall culture at J.P. Morgan.

The culture in tax requires an individual with a thick skin. In my personal experience I have seen a huge turn over. I believe the excuse of its tax and people don’t like the hours is management in denial. The hours and work in tax are not bad at all. Yes, you have your busy season for 3 months, but then it's very slow the remainder of the year. Although each individual who left may have their own reasons, the overall consensus is that the tax operations department in Newark,DE requires stronger management. This is due to the fact that the culture there allows employees to behave in a child like / high school manner. Although this speaks to a select amount. The way people interacted with each other was childish. I’ve seen staff and management, yell, curse, and back talk to each other daily. Employees are openly disrespectful towards one another and management seemed powerless to be able to take action. I say that with the knowledge that there were a few managers whom have stepped up and tried to do the right thing but were shut down by higher management. In one instance, the response received was to retain those employees and find more "fun" work for them. To me that was a sad response. I believe we are all adults and should conduct ourselves with respect towards each other. In addition, no one is responsible for you to have "fun" at work. Each of us owns our career, The reason you were hired is to help the organization reach its goals. If you refuse the job then no problem best of luck to you. Someone who is willing to do it will come take your place. This type of behavior caused more work for other employees who decided to be a team player and help with work others were refusing. The employees who chose to stay professional, eventually had enough of the environment and left. You can work here and make friends, but be prepared to deal with a individuals who do as they please without any repercussion. My advice is to learn as much as you can and move to a more professional environment where everyone is a bit more civil.
