summary: Be very careful about the position you are offered. If you have multiple opportunites, strongly consider others.
advice: To anyone looking at Chase for a job:  Please strongly consider working elsewhere.  If you receive an offer and have the luxury to compare against other companies, you must research the best you can on who you will be working for and the projects you will be involved in.  This company is so big with so many regulations and controls that you are very likely to experience a high degree of job dissatisfaction.  For most people, there are about 10 to 12 levels of management above them.  This unusually top heavy hierarchy causes huge communication gaps between senior leaders and ground level employees.  My experience is limited to a group in the mortgage space at the Irving (Ridge point) location.  The benefits are standard faire compared to other companies but the real issue is compensation.  Time and time again I saw wonderful employees accept promotions only to not get compensated for an average of six months to a year and in many cases, they never saw what was promised to them.  It’s truly sickening to witness this in such a large and prominent company like Chase.  Nearly all talent gets fed up with this and leaves.  To be fair, there are some amazing managers that do make differences but they are rare.  Low performers are commonplace and never seem to get fired or held accountable for their poor performance/actions.  Chase culture is highly reactionary in everything they do.  A negative story hit the newsstands and all hell breaks loose internally with no plan or direction.  The company literally lives day to day with no sound technologies in place to protect itself.  The servicing systems are extremely outdated and very few people understand them.  I often heard the phrase, “It’s amazing this place makes money given all the system problems”.  This cycle just keeps going and going.  There is a ton of money pumped into the PR department so that “reputational risk” is minimized at all times.  I have to say, the PR department has built an effective Chase image and facade that keeps other bigger issues well hidden from public view.  If the public knew about some of the day to day issues, Chase would be in big trouble.  I’m very serious in saying that.  This place is a true house of cards.  Work life balance is horrible in all of the IT and MIS groups in Mortgage Banking.  I’d say the average time worked by most good employees is well over 60 hours per week.  Most managers even expect you to work long hours because everyone is so short staffed with no reprieve in sight.  I heard for two years, “we should all step up during these challenging times” but yet we were recording stronger profits quarter after quarter.  Trust me when I tell you that this is a VERY hard company to work for if you are an IT or MIS person.  If you need to have a sense of accomplishment at your job, this is not the company for you.  There are so many other companies that have better values and know how to maintain an effective workforce.  Just please do your research and be informed by talking to whoever you can before you trap yourself.  Best wishes and good luck!

The problem is that we also claim to be a tech company, which means we are also competing for talent with other tech companies. It is no wonder why you can't hire and retain tech talent when they are receiving other offers for 6-figure salaries and permanent work-from-home. You need to start looking at other tech companies as competition too. You also need to start listening to the feedback you are collecting.

While we are hybrid right now, their ultimate goal as stated many times is to return 100% to office, which is the exact opposite of most other tech companies. They are also continuing to loose top talent and now there are many positions open across the firm that can't be filled, mostly due to the salary and RTTO decisions. Management recognizes this exodus of talent as a major problem and have hosted sessions which they called "feedback circles" in order to figure out why this is happening. Other employees have mentioned salary and RTTO countless times during these feedback sessions and it continues to go unaddressed. I also want to point out that salary does not improve that much with a promotion. I have colleagues who have left because they were promoted but didn't get the bump that they really wanted.

cons: The company is very large and although they try to create transparency between divisions, it is not as clear as I would have liked.

summary: not a great bank brokerage program, very limited product, lousy grid....not annuity friendly
advice: be a real brokerage firm. Trust your advisors. offer desired products. Offer all products but require certification rather than just pulling product to protect clients from a few foolish advisors.
pros: great brand. Nice facilities, strong company. Strong brand recognition and access to lots of client funds. Open access to client info which is really helpful. Far more open than BOA or Wachovia.
cons: limited product for bank brokers, long branch hours, micro managing at times. HO compliance is ridiculous, local management is green and not  real experienced.

summary: Relatively Speaking, Nice Place to Work
advice: Layoff some of the excess layers of senior management and hire more people who actual produce something instead of create busy work.
pros: Most of the people are smart and treat each other with respect.  Jamie Dimon is impressive and navigated the firm well in the downturn.
cons: It is on the cheaper side of places to work when looking at Wall Street Firms but I think they are all cutting out the perks so this may be the norm.  There are way too many layers of senior management.

summary: I was happy to work there for 21 years.  I wish my department had not been outsourced.
pros: Decent salary and an excellent benefits package.  Good corporate culture.  A great place to work until the last few years, when the layoffs, outsourcing and offshoring began.  Good severance package though.
cons: During my last few years at Chase an ever-increasing drive for efficiency led to large scale reductions in IT staffing, with ever fewer employees expected to carry heavier workloads.  My department was eventually outsourced.

advice: When an employee goes above and beyond for the company and deserves a promotion, give it to them! Having empowered employees is a priceless asset for any company. An employee's salary is how they know they are a valued part of the company so show some appreciation and reward those who deserve it!
pros: Global company offers endless opportunities anywhere you can imagine. Decent benefits.
cons: Promotions are hard to come by and even once you get the opportunity it takes an extremely long period of time to get the salary increase (typically 6-12 months but occasionally longer).

advice: Don't let "Greed" be the driving emotion. Don't try to play up the profits for the stock markets.
pros: Work life balance is great. You work around a great set of people. They have a volunteer program that lets you take 12 hours of paid time off each quarter - how great is that. I used to use it to volunteer at the local school. At least my immediate manager was super-effective and really helped me progress in my career. At least my department was very good with getting communication down from the leadership to all the employees.
cons: Senior management rode us to the ground :-(

advice: Decisions need to be made in a more timely fashion and decision makers need to get closer to the staff that understands the details.
pros: A challenging work environment where an intelligent, hard working employee can always find opportunities to extend themselves (though you have to be willing to seek out the opportunities yourself, don't wait on management to find you).
cons: The company is too big.  Decision makers are far removed from the actual operations.  Getting approvals to initiate a project or spend any sum of money takes months and people with the knowledge necessary to make decisions have little to no access to the decision makers.

summary: One of the most dynamic, fast paced and creative segments of this world class organization
advice: Think about the benefits of rehiring some retirees to help rekindle some of the culture of the various organizations that are now part of the world class J.P.Morgan Chase organization.
pros: The opportunity to be a part of one of the best organizations and asset managers in the world. The organization provides all the requisite tools to be a success.
cons: It is not a 9 to 5 job. It is a challenge and demands an individual's attention. You are expected to perform and if you do not, it can be very difficult.

advice: Leadership, what leadership.  All the managers did was come in early before the main boss and leave late after the boss left.  All day long they were either in meetings or talking just to be heard.  No trainging or career coaching.  Everyone was on their own and just took care of themselves.
pros: The only  good reason to work in the job that I had was that I got to work 4 10 hour days.
cons: The working environment was really bad.  My co-workers treated each other like dirt and me also.  No one would help me and everyone who had any experience would only give out information that they thought would not threaten their position.  In 30 years of work, I have never worked in a worse environment.

summary: Good place to start a career
advice: Improvement is needed in the training of new employees to understand the overview of the bank and how and the progression path of their career.
pros: They offer very nice benefits such as discounts on many stores and items, 401K, health and dental insurances. The company has many job opportunities depending on your career path. This company has a very good work and life balance.
cons: Transitioning into a new role is a bit difficult and requires a lot of effort. You need approval on some ways you want to invest your  own money.

summary: Decent paycheck.  Soul-sucking experience with little gained.
advice: Be a human being to your employees.  Don't lie to them.  Be on *their* side.  Don't trade them between departments like interchangeable cogs.  My managers lied to me on several huge departmental changes, and it shattered my work ethic.  The CEO, Jame Dimon, used to send out newsletters that said stuff like "our company has almost no debt! we're awesome!"  All I had to do was look up Chase's SEC filings to find that 94% of the company was in the 'liabilities' column of the balance sheet.  Propaganda?  Really?
pros: Pay was adequate, schedule flexibility/time off good.  Management really did not seem to care, so it was easy to come and go as one pleased.  This had the advantage of making it easy to leave early for something and stay extra the next day.  Obvious disadvantage is that some people worked roughly 2 hours a day.  This was a disadvantage to me because when fellow employees underperformed management would just reallocate their work load.
cons: Incompetent management.  Infinite red tape - corporate bureaucracy at its most insane.  The HR department insulated horrible coworkers from getting fired/transferred/demoted/etc.  Intra-office politics controlled promotions (and therefore raises) as opposed to work ethic, fresh ideas, and motivation.  If any thing, these latter categories were frowned upon because in order to implement good ideas then things would change.  If things changed, then the day-to-day become more efficient and transparent.  If that happens, then the management has to ask others to change what they do.  People from generation X and up hate to change stuff.  They get angry.  Even if it is something like "rather than printing everything out, save it as a pdf on the network drive."  They foam at the mouth and yell at you.  It was insane.  I attribute all of this to the corporate culture there.  I've worked at other places where everyone expects changes to happen and everyone welcomes greater efficiency and transparency and motivation.  The culture there was like a 1960s, protestant, stubborn, selfish, I'm-just-doing-what-I'm-told, deference to protocol/policy, bureaucratic, litigious, and terrible.  Furthermore, from a practical stand point, there weren't enough rest rooms.  It was god awful.  I don't believe that the company doesn't care about its employees.  I just think that the concept of *considering* your employees has never crossed their mind.  They employ you, give you a cubicle, your manager gives you work to do, and that's it.  So, they don't purposely do this... but it is b/c that company is exactly the mega-corporate giant you see in movies like hudsucker proxy or something.  Unreal.

summary: Opportunity to build a career by gaining valuable experience and become marketable in the workforce.
advice: Listen to your business analysts (SMEs) before making changes. Consider periodic aptitude tests for employees for better placement
pros: Many benefits and opportunities to grow as a professional. Open to considering people with transferable skills. An entry level employee has a lot of resources to gain knowledge and exposure within the company. The company places a lot of value on training, coaching and employee feedback.
cons: It's a business, therefore layoffs or reassignment are almost inevitable at some point in time. There is a lot of opportunity to improve how changes are implemented.

summary: Don't buy in to the propaganda!
pros: Great benefits, large stable company
cons:
Poor Salary:  As an experienced PM in their Wilmington, DE office, I was making at least 15k less than cities less than an hour away like DC, Phiily, NYC.
Productivity is mired in burocracy and process.  Easily 50% of my time was spent in "process" work.
Poor advancement:  If you;re not a part of the boys club, you're not going anywhere.  It's not about gender.  It's about blathering on about the sports or your golf game.
After 6mo.  I had enough.  It wans't the worst job I ever had.  But it's a close #2 to EDS.

advice: Help the people who help you.  No overtime pay and a lack of advancement opportunities leads to most top talent leaving for more competitive offers outside of the firm.  I watched a team of just less than 20 people have 100% turnover in less than a year, but management sees no problem.
pros:
Company as a whole has good values and excellent stability.
Vacation and time off is very generous.
cons:
Management is a mess; not receptive to change like many large companies.
Limited promotional opportunities. 
For the hours worked, pay is not very competitive even for associates. No overtime compensation.
Financial Analyst Development Program is poorly run.

advice: Be available to help your employees with their needs and weaker areas as opposed to focusing on every tiny detail without recognizing the employees progress and helping to further their success.
pros: Job is relatively simple, as far as what you need to do in terms of actual work. Working for the company provides countless benefits that are pretty necessary in life.
cons: Customers frequently have poor attitudes and are difficult to deal with, but keep in mind that now-a-days most people only come into the bank if they have a problem. Sometimes it is difficult to deal with micro-managing and drama, but it is all about the mindset you go to work with.

summary: Great company due to resources, professional experience, exposure to management. Inconsistent upper management, bad pay.
advice: As the leader in the banking industry compensate your employees accordingly from top to bottom and treat them well by not overworking them with understaffed branches and you won't have such a high employee turnover. Make it easier for employees to transition from retail to corporate side if desired and qualified.
pros: Perks such as free banking accounts, free passes to museums, events, etc. strong management, great technology, software systems, CRM
cons: Executive level management team, switching corporate strategy/culture every 1 or 2 years makes mid and lower level management seem inconsistent and like hypocrites

advice: Manage your employees better so you do not have to lay off so many people.
pros: Good PTO and salary and I had a great boss.
cons: They do layoffs all year long. You dont see them announced as the other big banks do since they do them all the time. You will see people who have been there from 20 years to 1 year and whole departments being laid off. Then they go and hire them back in either other positions or the same position. Development does not work as a team with the other groups so the whole process was not as smooth as when everyone is working together.

summary: Very demanding corporation to work for as they want the most out of their employees, but offer mediocre compensation.
pros: The possibility of moving up in the ranks and seeing the fruits of your labor. The love to offer their employees plenty of incentives for working with the company.
cons: Lack of upward mobility, management tries to keep you in your normal BAU role. Managers speak highly of you furthering your education, but it actually challenges the status quo. The company can post record profits, however the bonuses are not guaranteed for individuals that are not either a VP, Executive Director, Managing Director, and/or executive board member.

summary: Excellent benefits & career options make up for a lack of transparancy
advice: Need more transparency around organization changes, career mobility, compensation, and promotion opportunities
pros:
Excellent vacation benefits (3-4 weeks for new employees)
Fair compensation and above average health benefits
Excellent career mobility options if you are able to find them yourself or have a manger to vouch for you
Opportunity to receive senior management exposure often early in your career
cons: Impersonal environment, HR is extremely disorganized (also lack of transparency in compensation, promotion opportunities, and career mobility options), teams are typically fairly siloed, a work/life balance varies drastically depending on your manager and what organization you are in.

summary: jpmorgan chase is not a bad place to work if you work in a bigger branch. the opportunities you will get there is muc
advice: There are ways to advance to management but unfortunately working in a small location it becomes almost impossible.  they do recognize good work but not with the advancement to management.
pros: one of the best things about chase is the hours and the locations. they are everywhere and it is not hard to transfer to other locations.
cons: their process of advancement is not the best.  working for this company is great but if you would like to advance you will have to know the right people

advice: Listen to employees more often. There is room for change but no one wants to listen because "this is how its always been done." When there is a problem - don't just hire more people - try and solve it.
pros: Good benefits and decent salary - there is a good amount of networking opportunities and a decent amount of opportunities to be more mobile within the firm as well.
cons: management needs work and there is a lack of structure. there is a lot of politics but this is expected in such a big company. Everyone plays the blame game and doesn't want to take ownership of mistakes.

summary: Great mobility and great to work
advice: Things dont have to be 9-5 but be reasonable in your approach to how people should manage their work-life balance.  People have families and want to have a real life too.
pros: They offered me a lot of room to grow, and really work in a process I could define at first.  They also offered me mobility to move around to different groups and even through different positions (I started as QA)
cons: Over time process became more rigid.  While not strictly enforced, the work life balance clearly favors those who put in excessive hours.

advice: Take the time to really gather information about employees before making rash decisions. Can be very short sighted.
pros: Great Firm, Great People, Complex and interesting deal flow. You will learn a lot just being here. Many other financial firms want to hire officers trained at JPM.
cons: Big, factory like atmosphere by growing every year. No loyalty by Senior Management and despite how much value you add, this is not the priority. Support jobs i.e. Credit, Risk are seen as expense driven only and there is a movement to rid the firm of seasoned experienced folks in favor of cheaper junior folks.

advice: Keep your employees happy and you will avoid turn-over.
pros: The option to have a flexible work arrangement is a huge plus for me. They offer beneficial training that helps broaden your knowledge and career.
cons: Things have gotten worse over the last few years I have worked here. You may get a promotion and move up, but the raise associated with it does not match the work that you are doing. They seem to be taking care of their interns and young out of college new hires in stead of those that are seasoned. It ends up being the seasoned ones that end of leaving.

advice: Retain your people, treat with equality, if you have an issue don't lose talent, expand upon it.  And understand that there will always be people you are losing that you should be retaining because of your poor management decisions.
pros: Decent pay, good benefits, there are good people outside of NYC and Scotland,
cons: They are brutal, getting rid of people whose pay is in a range of not quite VP but at the top of the grid.  They are not good about listening to people who are not in New York/New Jersey.  Anyone outside of that area is a second class citizen.

advice: Have trainers that are focused on training, not on applying for another position within the company which causes them to be distracted and out of the training class frequently. Also, make sure team are aligned prior to new employees going to the floor and having several TL's over a short period of time,
pros: Chase hires on at very competitive salaries. Benefits are incredible as well as the vacation/sick days/personal days. Great work environment.
cons: Training is thorough, but they tend to focus on some aspects of the job that aren't as important as others. Should have a more focused training staff.

advice: Executive team should engage line level staff to understand the impact of decisions made at the middle management level. Management is out of touch and overly concerned with meeting deadlines instead of setting realistic goals and taking time to do it right the first time
pros: Large company with a variety of opportunities and great benefits. Lots of great people trying to do the right thing.
cons: Constant restructuring that tends to be counter productive. Poor communication between management and employees. Unrealistic workload and very little recognition. Turning into a company that just wants to get it done now and clean up the mess later.

summary: More stability than working direct for a fund manager
pros: I much preferred the formal corporate structure to being at the mercy of egotistical executives who’d built their company from scratch and could be terrifying to work for. It was much more controlled and structured, which I found refreshing, though obviously that can have down sides if you’re looking to make your mark on the world (which I wasn’t).
cons: The health benefits were rubbish. Other than that, it was fine. I was well treated and felt valued - right up until a department head in another country made me redundant.

advice: Don't micromanage the analysts.
pros: There is an excellent culture at JPMC. It is not as cutthroat and competitive as some other BBs but it is still an excellent learning environment. They actually care about their analysts and want them to learn as much as possible.
cons: Once you get a job at JPMC it is rare that you are fired and for that reason there are some people in lower management that are not that great at their jobs.  One of my supervisors knew little about the subject manner of the projects we were working on but still tried to micromanage.

summary: JPMorgan Chase - Good for the investors and fat cats; not so much for the person-on-the-street
advice: Seek more input from employees on the front lines--and not just those in the large cities such as NY, Chicago, Indianapolis, etc.  There's a lot of wealth out there in the other front offices, yet no one asks us to participate in input on new systems, policies, etc.  We end up with too many policies and procedures that then have to be retracted because someone didn't even try to see the whole picture.
pros: Flextime as a corporate institution--but subject to individual managers' whims; benefits coverage for domestic partners of both sexes; generally good communication about the "big picture" in the company; salary competitive and bonuses available for jobs well done; good technology (although sometimes cumbersome); benefits include so-so visual, so-so dental, good medical, health care and dependent care accounts, parking accounts (pre-tax); 401K with 100% match of first 5% of salary;
cons: Outsourcing of jobs that should be done locally to Mumbai, India (e.g., court accountings to be filed in county courts are done in India!  The courts are very specific about their rules.  How will Mumbai know those rules?); centralization of other functions such as Tax Units, etc.  Elitist attitude about clients--"We only want clients with $5M+ in assets"; There are many clients out there with "only" $3M or $1M who may grow to $5M.  Shortsighted  management in terms of policies, etc., and not receiving input from employees who are on the front lines.  Technology is good in terms of having it, but much of it is not user-friendly to employees, and it takes at least 50% more time to use the systems while trying to help a client.  It's frustrating and demoralizing.  JPMorgan sees itself as a saviour of Wall Street (which, perhaps it was), but it's to the detriment of employees and customers/clients.  The corporate culture is not an inclusive one.  If it's not done in NY, it's not done in OH, or WV, or KY or any of the other states far-removed from NY.

summary: Great place to work, but not for a long period of time
advice: This business is run well. Many of my managers have been hands off, and I have seen this style work well for teams in the past. Keep this up. When a tenured employee takes on a new role, if you truly like this employee pay him or her what you would pay someone from the outside. I would think it would be good to keep your best and brightest.
pros: My Schedule here has always been very flexible. This is for me a very large pro. In all my years, I have typically been in charge of my own day to day business. Very little management oversight when you show responsibility. Chase is spending a good amount of money to try and make this a great place to work. There are activities from exercise classes to community events that Chase participates in. They have event days in the office for Hispanic month or breast cancer awareness. Often times this means bringing in food. They attempt to provide everyone with a nice Christmas party.
cons: Chase will try very hard to keep you from earning more money. It is very common to apply for a new position that is clearly a higher grade and not be offered a higher salary. I have received an increase in the past for getting a higher grade, but I have also not received one. For the most part, people are not getting higher salary for higher jobs requiring more skills, experience, and responsibility. When a new employee joins your team from a different company, they will almost certainly make more than you. People who take higher positions outside the company will almost always earn more. Then if you look for a job at Chase again, you will be able to get a higher salary because you will be from outside.

summary: The potential of Chase's shrewd financial management record is largely unfulfilled due to poor interdepartmental coop.
advice: Eliminate top-down mgmt dogma, encourage employee creativity by releasing stranglehold on daily schedule (especially on West Coast, where Big Brother corporate micromanagement clashes with other more successful models), and take employees out of their silos, in particular in tech support.
pros: Good compensation relative to other firms in industry. Aggressive in the desire to expand into new markets.
cons: Left ring finger ever knows what the left punitive is doing and only has a vague concept of what the rest of the body is doing. Result: waste, waste, waste.

summary: AWM Technology at JP Morgan Chase
advice: Read 360 feedback carefully to gleam any patterns of bad management reported by team and take appropriate action.
pros: Great bank to work for with latest technologies and support for mobility within the firm. Emphasis on diversity.
cons: Managers working in different locations  from their Managing Directors  can run their organizations with little oversight from Senior Executives as long as deliverables are met. Emphasis on diversity but more work needed to ensure experienced employees drop behavours associated with  bias against women. Pay inequality between sexes is still very much present.

summary: Crazy place to work; must have high tolerance for pain
advice: Get your head out of the sand and wake up to what is really happening on the floor of your departments; understand the true need to value employees, train employees, and reduce overtime to achieve some work life balance
pros: Lots of work; endless change; lots of needs and challenges for people who want to extremely over achieve
cons:
top down dictatorship
Under staffed departments
Under funded important projects
disorganized executive management only focused on immediate short term fixes to problems so numbers looked good at the sacrifice of a better long term vision and structure
Overworked and under valued

summary: What to expect when working with JPMorganChase
advice: I would tell them to pay more attention to the senior management that you bring on board.  There are alot that just surf the web and do nothing at all.  If your paying them these six figure salary they should be contributing.  Senior mgmt should consider doing 180 degree performance evaluation.  But you should do in a way, that lower ranking staff are not afraid to tell you the truth.  Base on personal experience, i have seen mgmt serve the web 5 times a day and click alt +tab.  In the end of the day, if your paying mgmt a 6 figure salary and they are busy surfing web-it is a waste of money.
pros: It's currently doing well in comparison to it's competitors.  It's a huge company, if you can figure out how to navigate and build the right contacts, then your opportunities are unlimited. On good years, if you are bonus eligible you can get a pretty decent bonus.
cons: There's alot of lousy managers.  They might be smart, but they are completely clueless on how to manage.I had alot of experiences where I would bring issues to a manager and they would do absolutely nothing.  In the end of the day, Sh** will fall down.  If your at the bottom of the totempole, then you will probably get screwed when it comes to your performance evaluation.  It's hard to cya if your at the bottom so it's very easy for mgmt to get away with bullying you around.  Note, hr isn't set up to protect employees.  They are set up for the company.  The mgmt culture and goals are to get as much out of their employees as possible while paying the least amount.  If you choose to work there, you have the best bargaining power once you get an offer.  If your in the door, it's hard to bargain or negotiate for a better compensation package.  Also, there is no work/life balance.  They usually don't tell you the truth when you are interviewing.  Training is very poor.  Processes are very antiquated.  The company has went through many mergers which means the processes are very convoluted.  Imagine a machine broken and you keep on putting a band aid on it.  Also, the company goes through alot of reorgs, and change of management.  So end of the day when you get hired don't walk in with any expectation because it's subject to change by management.  In addition, you don't always feel like they appreciate your work, therefore when working for JPMorganChase, you need to have a mindset that you are here to collect a paycheck to just do a good job.

advice: Employees recognize that evolution and change within any business is inevitable.  Companies providing an open dialogue with employees provides a highly productive work environment where the constant worry of job security is not an issue.
pros: Motivates and encourages employee advancement.  Provides career development opportunities for all employees regardless of race, age or gender.  Provides a great environment for all to succeed.
cons: As with most large companies especially Financial institution, corporate bureaucracy along with stringent government regulations frequently places undue burdens on efficient product development,

summary: Exercise Caution: Not a place for those with career passions or ethical integrity
advice: Overhaul your review process. You cannot have incompetent managers scape-goat veteran employees and expect to continue to attract/maintain professional talent.
pros:
*Great benefits.

*Many great people to work with.

*Good opportunities if you know the right people.

*Competent CEO - Jamie Dimon is sharp guy.
cons:
*Chicago offices are ruled by good-ole boy mob of middle managers.

*Sacrifices and substantive contributions are nothing compared with covering the mistakes of middle-management and making them look good before their superiors.

*Work-life balance a joke to middle-management seeking fame and glory.

*Software engineers beware - business and management married to waterfall mentality.

advice: Nurture relationships with good employees. Show genuine appreciation. Coach effectively. Sometimes that means changing managers. Many of them are terrible.  Stop micro managing
pros: The company itself is great. Many different lines of business to choose from. Commission structure is about average for the industry.
cons: Micro Managing is at an all time high.  Low Base Salary. Management needs to be evaluated. Some of the technology is slacking compared to other banks. Too much pressure on sales.  Most support numbers we have to call are with outsourced employees.

summary: Great Overall Firm, unless your in Retail Financial Services
advice:
Stop treating Retail Financial Services as your red headed step child.  We contribute almost one quarter of company revenues, yet have none of the same prestige as commercial or investment bank, not to mention any of the same perks: Expense account, sporting event tickets, discounts on certain products, etc…

Put managers in place who have real world experience in that particular field.  I don’t mind taking my lead from someone who understands the difference between what is taught in training versus the applicability in real life.  I want a leader who has walked a mile in my shoes.

Understand with deepening of client relationships come referrals, more assets, better client service and retention, etc…  How can we honestly expect people to bring us all their assets and referrals of friends and family if we are talking to them, like they are just a number?

Raise the bar on hiring standards and we will have less employee turnover.  In Retail Financial Services, the requirements are sales experience and a GED.  Which means you cannot finish high school, have worked as used car salesman, have a pulse and you’re hired.  Whether this skill set translates into a long term career is a different story.  Yet this is another objection you must overcome when talking to a client whose last account officer messed their account up due to incompetence.
pros:
Excellent name and Reputation.  With all the problems most financial institutions have had, people recognize JPM Chase as best of the best

Excellent, Pay and Benefits package

Huge market share, access to existing client base.

Worldwide operations, spanning many countries.  Opportunities for advancement and transfer across lines of business are endless.
cons:
Aggressive Sales Techniques:  Managers telling you that if you work at a bank long enough you will eventually have a compliant filed against you.  You are encouraged to tell clients one thing to get them to move assets over to JPM Chase and then do something different once the assets get under our control.

Unrealistic sales goals:  Sales goals are based on National not regional averages.  Which means what is low to mid in NYC, is high in Texas.  In addition select people who are mediocre/average hang around long enough and are able to accumulate assets through others leaving, after a while this person is held up as a shining example for producing revenue and bringing in clients over a 5-10 year basis.

Building client relationships is a no-no:  We are not allowed to communicate with clients by cell phone and not encouraged to communicate by email.  Appointments are encouraged to last less than 45 minutes, with 2-4 minutes of rapport building.  

Managers have no experience in your field:  Many of the managers have 10 years+ experience, with 3-5 in management, but none in your field.  So they lead you in theory and by what they read in a book or what they learned in a week long training class.  Not actual job experience.  That’s akin to a recent political science graduate from Harvard, telling Karl Rove or David Plouffe (both college dropouts with real world experience) how to run a presidential campaign.  Who would you listen to?

advice: You don't need three project managers on one project. If you are going to keep three project managers on one project, then you should not switch them out every other release.
pros: Competitive salary and decent benefits as with any large financial corporation. You can quickly sneak through the cracks and do as little work as you'd like.
cons: Leadership is non-existent in IT. Management is usually coming from the business with no IT experience. Zero work/life balance. Burn out is very quick. Lots of people on all levels get "sick" just to get a day off.

advice: Either lower tuition assistance requirements or create a 30-hour teller position.
pros: They work with you, decent base pay at $15/hr minimum compared to other similar jobs such as cashier. Great benefits.
cons: Some branches you can get extra hours, others you are either strictly a 20 or 40 hour teller. Tuition starts at 30 hrs a week, almost no branch will give you that average. You are typically either a 20 or 40 hour teller, and it is almost impossible to go to school as a 40 hour teller at a University due to schedule conflicts.

summary: Great professional development, lousy life style
advice: Improve culture to value face time less, encourage working from home on the weekends more, etc.   Also, more frequent feedback / review sessions would be great.
pros: Great training and professional development, especially for employees recently out of school.  NO other job better prepares you and teaches important skill sets  so quickly.
cons: Work/life balance was terrible.  Face time is a problem here just like at any other big bank.  The satellite offices felt out of touch with the energy and activities happening in the NY headquarters.

summary: Fullfilling work in a collegial atmosphere.
advice: Balance the bottom line with foresite of opportunity to grow and create an atmosphere of excitement about  new business and new markets rather than a focus on managing and maintaining what is in place.
pros: Excellent managment direction and creative approach to problem solving on the job.  Appreciative of the work done and effort spent on completing tasks.
cons: Large organization with typical structural issues and "feeling like a number' sometimes.  Top management at times exhibited a singular purpose to the bottom line of the co without regard to effect on work force.

advice: Remember you need people to run your business.  Treat them like you appreciate them, not scare them, and you will get more out of them.
pros: Great Benefits, Still has a pension, Great Product, Great for customers, Very good sales systems!
cons: Only 33% of Employees would recommend working here per last employee survey.  They have so many things going for them, but can't treat their people right.  Turnover in all job families is high and lots of down sizing going on at the moment. Management creates a fear based atmosphere.  They make sure you know you are replaceable.

summary: Stable for the banking industry, great people, about average for pay and benefits
advice: If you want to remain competitive, get with the times as far as flexible work arrangements.   We live in the age of technology and are a global company, so recognize that employees can be productive from home computers.
pros:
Certain benefits are great by comparison.  4 weeks paid vacation, 2 personal days and 6 sick days are standard for salaried employees.  The company also provides a small pension in addition to 401k matching.   Performance bonuses are just that...based on performance.  Onsite backup daycare is provided at no cost for 10 days a year, which is a great fallback for emergencies.  Maternity leave is paid for 12 weeks.  

Mobility within the organization is encouraged.   The employee is expected to be in charge of his/her own career path, and (most) managers embrace assisting employees get where they want to go.    There is a wealth of career development training, networking and mentoring available.  (Although finding the hours is sometimes a challenge!)  

The environment is casual, people are generally happy and friendly.

The company name is great on a resume.
cons:
This feedback is specific to Information Technology areas. The company is huge and there is a TON of bureaucracy, so if you want to be on the cutting edge of fast moving change, this is not the place for you.  

Pay is average.  Once you are in the door, it is difficult to get a substantial increase.  Internal moves to other roles do not translate to pay increases, even if then new role has more responsibility.  

Health Insurance is below average.  The company offers only two plans to US-based employees, and both have very high deductibles before they pay for anything other than a primary care vist.  ($3000 or $5000 for family plans.)  The deductibles are offset by a company-provided medical reimbursement account; which can be anywhere from about $500-$1200.  The insurance benefits are probably fine as long as you aren't prone to sports injuries or have young children.

Although the company touts flexible work options, they are not widely supported by management.   JP Morgan Chase lags behind its competitors in embracing telecommuting as a way to keep employees happy and productive.

advice: Managment should listen to and ACTION the concerns of employees if they want to retain top talent.

Morale tends to be low in most groups; everyone that I speak with does not like working here for various reasons.

summary: Good overall culture, stability and good benefits, but inconsistent leadership and a few pockets of malignant idiocy.
advice:
Be more prepared, know what you are doing, don't be afraid to take a healthy risk, and spend less time covering your butt and more time serving your customers.  Too many managing sycophant busy-bodies that act like they are busy and confident but lack critical thinking and independent thinking.

And when you tell people the direction to go is the direction things are already heading, you can't say you have vision.

Thanks for keeping things stable, despite the issues a big company has.

Keep up the firm-wide enterprise architecture initiatives.  Could have happened sooner, but better late than never.

Manage internal information better, make it searchable, accessible.
pros:
Overall Software Development and Technology within JPMC is improving company-wide, after years of not having a firm-wide vision.  It's still like living out a Dilbert cartoon, though.

If you are in a good organization, you can really make a huge difference have a lot of fun.  These pockets of greatness make the company that customers like.

The facilities are great.

A huge push to raise customer satisfaction, which may fix some other issues internally.

advice:

- Extremely helpful employees. Even if your manager is not helpful, there will always be someone on your team that will help you out.

advice:
Loosen the purse strings and properly compensate the AVP and VP level employees.  

Align women's salaries with their male peers. 

Understand that the focus on regulators and compliance issues is not working.  Departments are slapping on a bandage and telling regulators and auditors what they want to hear, and process testing is a joke.  Testers are taught to get to the right outcome, but are not following actual processes and procedures. 

Technology is antiquated and in some departments cannot cover the basic needs much less be improved to satisfy regulators.  

At Chase no matter what level you are, you will always be just a cog in the wheel. You have to leave to get ahead.  As I did. Some of our very best employees and managers work at other banks now.  Chase lets the top performers become their competitors best employees.  No attempt to retain and promote key players.

After 20+ years, it was easy to walk away from a career I once loved.  I no longer felt I had value.  My value is very clear and appreciated at my new employer.  I just wish I had left two years sooner.
pros: Was able to work at a job I loved for over 20 years, and progress to a senior management level.
cons:
The past year or two have been the worst in my over 20 year career. Upper level mgmt does not care about employees, only the regulators and compliance issues.  As a senior level manager, there is  way to promote or compensate staff to be at the level they deserve. Constant reorg of job titles, pay alignment and job grades has benefitted low level staff, but has almost penalized AVP and VP employees.  Sr. managers are handcuffed by "do more with less" and it is hard to provide an environment that supports work/life balance that the corporation preaches about. Chase seems to have gotten too big. As it grew, the employees became less of a focus, which is a shame, because there are some pretty incredible employees in my former team. 

The level of stress is overwhelming from the lowest level employee on up.  The environment is hostile and has become a horrible place to work.  No matter what you do, it is not enough.  No matter how well your team does, they are expected to do more, with no additional support or compensation.

advice:
- Be authentic, or just don't say anything at all: When I started, there was a lot of talk about "endless possibilities" and how one person started from the bottom and moved their way up. Then you realize that was just a single antidote story and the truth is that you are confined that department, they don't care so much about your ideas, or your potential. Company makes a push to community engagement, but does not allow you schedule time off to attend any volunteer events. 

- Localize HR again: Since I've been there, I have not had contact with a HR person. You are expected to call a hotline where you are bounced around group to group... those reps have no incentive to help you because they are told to focus on their handle time. I'm McKinsey & Company sold the current process as a great idea for business... but its bad on the human level. 

- I know efficiency is important and helps save money. But when you implement a plan, look at the whole picture and not department by department. For example: Customer calls into telephone banking... the employees job is to "handle" the situation in the lowest amount of time... this causes employee to give only partial answer for the sake of time. Customer then becomes upset when the issue isn't resolved fully. They go to a branch to complain, and correct the issue taking away resources, branch employee then calls various support areas to resolve the issue which takes even more time--- this issue would not have happened if employees were not encouraged to keep their AHT low. Point is, when one area of the business tries to create an efficient process for their benefit, the Firm should how that impacts other areas of the business.

- Teams: I don't know what to say... are we in middle school or working adults? Its hard going into a office of 100 cubicles, white walls, no sunlight, stress... and then being told to "cut a piece of paper and write your superhero on it" we are adults in our 20's, 30's and 40's how ridiculous does that sound?! Team building and encouragement is hard, but we need to figure out a way to be more authentic. Maybe look at some of the newer research on this subject? (any no cookie cutters implementation, please)

Overall, I really love the company as a whole, I've declined job offers because I thought I could contribute in a meaningful way but even after I put some time in, I have yet to see any commitment from my LOB/department's part to really develop people before they burn out. I guess its because they can just replace me with another fool so why spend any energy. 

I'm tired of being treated like a robot.

advice:
-Continue the best in class strategic planning that has made us successful. 
-Continue our focus on developing excellent leaders. 
-Continue instilling customer experience in every decision we make. 
-Continue developing talent at all levels for future success. 

-We are losing too many talented and high potential employees at every level of the organization due to the following.  This is based on what has happened to me personally, as well as what I have observed occurring to others, at all levels. 

-Compensate deserving internal promotions (especially Exceeds and High Meets)  AT THE TIME OF THE PROMOTION the actual salary you'd pay an external hire.  The pay disparity between the rare internal increase approvals and external offers are offensive, kill morale, and cause us to lose top talent. In 8/10 cases your internal hire (Es and M+s) is going to have earned the external salary given his knowledge of our firm or specific expertise so it defies logic as to why we insist, in most cases, to compensate internal and external so differently. I love our company, have been relatively taken care of but am now at a point after several promotions where I am now almost forced to leave to be compensated accordingly. The more I am promoted the greater the disparity is growing. 
-Understand that promotions and merit increases for performance are two separate and distinct events. There are a very small amount of managers that see it this way and will fight for you to get it approved, and they do, but the vast majority believe if you're lucky enough to get an increase for a promotion, that it eliminates your ability to earn an end of year performance increase.  The lack of managers standing up and fighting for what is right in regard to compensation is mind boggling to me because having managed several hundred people myself, compensation approvals are based on the manager making a solid case for the employee having EARNED the compensation. In almost a decade I never had an increase denied after making a solid case, yet most mangers throw up their hands and act as though they are powerless. Very frustrating to those that have done compensation planning in previous roles. Too many weak managers.

cons: Very in-flexible in regards to pay if you're not above a certain level, i.e. executive level. At times too large for its own good - certain divisions had one set of rules while another was completely different.  No true bonus structure and reward system.

advice: Train management that it’s not okay to text your employees at 11 pm, weekends, and while they’re on vacation to work, especially when a report is t due for a month! Some managers need training that this is NOT OK.
pros: Compensation is decent, challenging work, you have opportunities to grow and move within the company.
cons: Healthcare benefits aren’t good. Like with any job, some managers will take advantage of you if they think you don’t know better. If a manager is asking you to work around the clock and never giving you time off, speak up!

advice: Listen to your employees before they check out mentally like most people, breakdown outdated processes that only create more friction for completing work, put some effort into career development by taking performance reviews seriously beyond 2 check-ins per year.
pros: Hours are mostly stable, benefits are ok
cons: Managers of all levels are not transparent and lack basic managerial skills, career development is non-existent (you'll have 2 conversations about it all year), finding information whether it be company policy or requirements for your job are difficult, most people hide behind processes to avoid work or responsibility, work from home policy varies by manager

summary: Not bad, but could be better
pros: PTO is good; you can carry over your days into the next year, but those days have to be used before the end of Q1. Internal mobility opportunities exist, but I found that this is more catered towards those in the front office position (i.e. email blasts, designated business resource groups). There is a lot to learn.
cons: Internal mobility with a pay bump is a hit or miss. If you are moving internally into a more demanding role, don't expect a pay bump UNLESS you have full support of your manager to vouch/argue on your behalf.

summary: At the right branch, you can be a super star
advice: Everything is micro managed at Chase. They track every single thing, which can feel like Big Brother is constantly down your throat. Individual employees don't feel like they can make a real impact because of all the corporate politics that take place.
pros: good benefits, opportunities for growth, ongoing training and development, they like to promote from within
cons: If you have a bad branch manager, it can be difficult to succeed. Your sales are dependent on your branch partners closing the deal for you, rude customers, no Kaiser, have to work most Saturdays

advice: Get retrained. Don’t pick employees based on personal relationships for new opportunities within the company . Start recognizing the real employees who have put in extra overtime and have good stats . They deserve a lot better .  Will say some managers were good and those were promoted to higher positions for a reason
pros: Great pay and benefits . A lot of room for overtime .
cons: Unprofessional management . They need to review managers and their duties. A lot of them were not qualified and they treat their employees based personal relationships , not their stats or numbers/ hard work.

advice: Never loose your vision.  It is one thing to be a good manager and manage people, but as Senior Management what makes you special and what makes you a leader is your vision.  If you want to retain truly passionate talent, the people working under you want to know that what they are doing is making a difference, and driving towards an ultimate goal. This is why people follow leaders, and merely work for managers.
pros: I felt that the position I was in offered a lot of scope in the sense that while I was working in my niche, I had visibility to other groups.  This visibility allowed me to better understand how my role fit into the overall organization.  People often get lost in the details of their particular role, however in order to be truly successful one must understand the bigger picture, and I felt that in this environment if you made the effort to learn more about other areas of the business, it knowledge was easily accessible.  In addition I was able to partake in several training events that were actually beneficial (since then I have been in plenty that were a waste my time).   I also found that the caliber of people I was working with was terrific, and everyone seemed to really have a lot of great experience that I was able to leverage.
cons: Work life balance can be very difficult, but it really depends on you as a person as well as the group you are in.  If you want to work in an elite area, you must be prepared to work harder and longer.  When I completed undergrad I had the energy and was ready for this commitment however I think that having not experienced the drain that this can be, I was not fully aware of what this commitment really meant.  Having a little more work life balance is important and can definitely be lost site of during the hustle at JPMorgan Chase.

jobTitle: Vice President Infrastructure Operations and Applications Support
summary: Good Company - Mid- Level Management Challenges
advice: Shake up middle management and hold them accountable for the vast resources being spent. They are moving too slow and are too ad hoc. Create better processes that will tap into the immense talent within the firm. Cut the dead weight, which there is a lot of.
pros: Excellent executive management team. Great benefits. Very stable firm.
cons: Weak mid-level management. Lots of silos. Need to get out of their own way so they can build better teams that can break down the silos and evolve the technology to match the rest of this world-class firm.

advice: Keep the momentum. The regression has forced us to cut corners and eliminate unnecessary tasks. Once we start rolling in some money again, I think we should continue spending like we're broke. The atmosphere is much more innovative!
pros: Employee Engagement, Networking, Break the walls down attitude, Cross-training and Mobility, Training, working with the best of the best, advance technologies
cons: Enormous Company that can be easy to get lost in a dark corner if your manager lacks leadership skills. IF you get stuck with a bad manager, everyone around them notices very quickly, so it won't last!

summary: Best financial institution in the country
advice: More employee feedback to identify and weed out the few (very few) bad executive managers.  Build time/expense in budgets for employee skills, relationship and systems training.  So glad the customer fees structure and process is being redesigned industry wide.  Customer education is the key.
pros: High level of accountability, action and ethics.  Performance wins and directly affects overall compensation.  Cross functional movement encouraged.  Continuous learning.
cons: Highly metric driven, very competitive and fast paced.  Shoot then aim.  Customer sometimes second.  Get it done, then tune and revise.

advice: Consider being a bit more competitive with salary, when bankers and tellers make the same, only difference is bonus potential which can fluctuate greatly even when you try hard to push sales, it makes you wonder why you aren’t doing the easier job of teller.
pros: The company overall is great in the sense they have tons of information and helpful employee programs accessible.
cons: The base is just not enough. The reasoning is potential for bonus but when bonus structures change and you no longer get paid for checking accounts, that puts a dent in your bonus capabilities.

summary: Overall good company to work for
advice: Be open to suggestions and willing to admit if a mistake is made. Disband the "cliques" within management that promote employees based on personal relationships and ignore feedback regarding the friends of management
pros: The Salary is competitive and there are numerous job opportunities in various cities. Potential for easy relocation. The company is perceived as leader in the industry with a strong and knowledgeable CEO
cons: It sometimes appears that rudeness rather than true ambition and hard are rewarded. Although there are numerous job opportunities, you have to "know" the right people to get an interview.

advice: This is a well-run company, so I would simply advise them to keep doing more of the same.  The project offices are very-well structured.  The upper management decides what projects to do and reviews them regularly at various levels of program management, so you have the backing you need on your projects.   If budget permits, it would be ideal if the project managers could work on fewer projects at a time.  The only reason I would rate culture and values at 4 instead of 5 is because the company is so big that there wasn't really any observable *company-wide* shared culture, at least in my opinion.  Each team or smaller unit, such as a business unit, however, had it's own organic "culture", shaped by it's individual leaders.
pros: (NOTE: I last worked here in 2009, but I could not select that in the dropdown.) Since the company was large and well-resourced, we rarely had budgeting issues on projects. Although teamwork, collaboration, communication, negotiation and diplomacy is required to get the maximum from your cross-functional team, generally, we always had enough people on our project teams to do the work. Most everyone was reasonable and good to work with. You must be a great problem-solver, be able to hunt down solutions across multiple business areas and be able to deal with lots of personalities, but this is simply required of all project managers.
cons: There are often long hours and late or early morning hours due to international teams balancing time zone constraints. Balancing this job as well as young children would be challenging but doable if you are highly organized, prioritize well and commit to a fit and healthy lifestyle so that you can work as fast as you can in order to leave each day with enough time to handle your "second job" at home.

advice: It is important to recognize good talent and ensure that hard work does not go unnoticed.
pros: Large organization that is financially sound and will be around for many years to come.  The amount of experience and exposure you get to various business processes are incomparable.
cons: Pay can be either average or below average compared to similar job responsibilities at other organizations and industry.  Easy to get lost in such a large organization, which takes a toll on losing good talent.  Too many senior leaders and not enough workers to actually get the work done.

summary: The job can be soul crushing, but the pay and benefits are nice
pros:
They have other benefits, but I only cared about these:
Health insurance benefits
401K contributions
Cheap Gym Membership
Good Pay for no college degree necessary
2019 they gave every employee a free turkey (Supposed to be yearly, but 2020 we all worked from home)
Fairly generous time off allowances (You can take Leave of Absences for Maternity, Bereavement, etc.)
They say that they drug test, but its randomly selected so you have a decently high chance of not being chosen
cons:
You're a debt collector; A lot of the calls will be pretty repetitive as you're just catching people up on their bills, but every once in a while, you'll get a really depressing call where they tell you their entire life story and they cry and stuff. You aren't really here to help them. You're supposed to negotiate and compromise with the company's interest at heart which made me feel a little dirty and heartless at times. You're basically a salesperson trying to sell "no debt" to a captive audience. On top of that, they try to create a positive, lighthearted environment which clashes really hard with the nature of the work at times, and it feels super cringe. Imagine listening to someone explain that they've been laid off and are having money issues while someone is blasting pop music and handing you candy. That literally happened to me once. I only really stayed as long as I have because of the pay and benefits

Standards can be a little hard to hit consistently. It feels like the luck of the draw. Your ability to sell to people without money will make or break you.

Typical customer service issues: demanding and entitled customers, idiots, high call volume at times, strict scheduling, team leaders can be unavailable, lazy, out of touch etc.

cons: Your experience working here is dependent on your direct manager (which is typical in most technology roles). If you are unlucky and get a manager that is like an overseer driving delivery like your team is a cog in a giant machine, you will be chewed up and spit out (burn out is real). If you get a REAL manager your experience will be amazing (speaking from experience).

pros:
amazing work environment, hard work and dedication.The hardest part of my job is ensuring that policies and procedures are followed on a daily basis in the handling of cash.

Training is given to ensure these policies and procedures are followed continuously and staff is updated with new and upcoming policies.
cons: Some managers are great, some are just awful. There is wide variety of management skills. Company is working toward improving their managers and they have a great management training program. advice: NO comment
pros: Chase is a great corporate company to work for. They offer great benefits (401k, health, dental, stocks) daycare discounts, phone provider discounts and the list could go on. They value their employees even though sometime you feel that they don't care because there are thousands of employees.
cons: Chase does offer a lot of career advancment however it's very difficult to get a response from a recruiter. You could e-mail , instant message, have your supervisor make contact with the recruiter but you will never HEAR anything. It's hard to get trained into a new position or crossed trained.

cons: weird competitive environment, mega office politics, sales pressure. overall just as exhausting as any other banking job. better than working at Wells Fargo and other large firms. Yet still will make you question why you chose banking in the first place. if you can handle the stress, go for it

advice: Management has been great! I have enjoyed all managers in my past 4 years, but when looking to progress within, I feel that managers will only do what is best for them and not best for the individual.
pros: Working with a great team. One Chase is truly a great opportunity to learn different divisions of the industry. Incentive plan is one of the best and if done correctly could easily double your salary.
cons: Base compensation is not as good as most other financial company’s. Can be difficult to move into a position you are wanting due to politics/personal relations.

summary: A smart organization, but one not without some significant inertia
advice: JPMorgan constantly emphasizes the importance of a nimble organization, and it continues to struggle with becoming one.  The bank works hard and fast on a particular project, without any real reconsideration of the approach.  If a manager recognizes a deficiency, and that deficiency is significant, the effort is abandoned and replaced with something else.  It is noteworthy that JPMorgan does even that, and doesn't just plod further into a poor decision; however, the bank should work to rebalance the projects as they progress, consistently re-tailoring them to the problem.
pros: As with most large banks, JPMorgan is very technology focused.  The company makes a concerted effort to consistently improve their existing technology solutions, and exhibits a healthy respect for the need for constant improvement.  As such, there are always many interesting problems to be solved, and JPMorgan definitely supports employees that are working towards those goals.  Additionally, broad common goals are obvious to everyone in the organization, and as a result there is generally good communication across divisions of the firm.
cons:
JPMorgan, like other banks, has a very rigid hierarchy, so its not uncommon to see vast - and unplanned - changes at low levels as the result of fundamental changes further up the ladder (hiring or firing at senior levels).  This is an effective way of bringing about change, but often times the resultant changes are poorly thought out or unnecessary.
  Within the technology side of the bank, everyone is more or less on the same page about roles, responsibilities, goals and requirements.  However, outside of the technology groups it becomes apparent that the rest of the bank views all technology costs as simple necessary expenses, and not capital outlays that could generate real revenue.  As a result, there is a significant that employees in technology groups are less respected than their business-side counterparts.

advice: Positive mobility needs to be encouraged and addressed to managers in their role for 10yrs+ to foster fresh thinking and new direction
pros: High talent. This company can attract a lot of new talent easily based on its industry reputation. If you have a fairly new manager 2-5years in their role, you will have a great learning and inclusive experience
cons: There are a lot of people/managers (Bear heritage) that stay in there role to long. They become micro managers and expect you to know what they know in 6months to a year. They are very bitter people to work with

pros: Hourly Pay - in some roles this can lead to significant overtime pay
cons:
