Each role is very specific, so there is little carry over to other professions. If you get a bad role, you are stuck there for 8 months and are growing less than other people in your career stage. 
- DO NOT do this program if back office roles do not interest you in the slightest bit

summary: Much more than just a prestigious name
advice: While it is important to get focus on getting work done, the benefits of career advice and mentoring would be helpful for an employee starting out.  Managers tend to get so busy with work that the new analysts and associates that join feel world's apart from their manager.  Usually, the analyst and associates do not want to disturb or waste the manager's time for career discussions, but this is extremely important since the manager has first hand experience with what it takes to rise the ranks.  Managers should make an effort to at least offer some assistance to the new employees.
pros: J.P.Morgan Chase has been recruiting top talent from all around the country.  One thing you will learn when working here is that the employees are down to earth and helpful, all working together to achieve a similar purpose.  The communication between upper management and the lowest level employees is commendable.  Compensation is top notch all across the company, from the front office I-banking to the Developers and Business Analysts in technology.  While the benefits and corporate perks are being cut down by our CEO, the money saved is going towards higher employee compensation and increased company stability.
cons: J.P.Morgan is a meritocracy, which is good except for the long hours and intense focus required to meet deliverables before deadlines.  Most of your conversations with colleagues will be work related and you will rarely see a group of people chatting by the watercooler.  As with any company that recruits from the best schools around the world, you will find it a major challenge to rise the ranks faster than your peers, as the requirements for each promotion are structured such that you should have a certain number of years of experience in the previous position.

summary: Great company to work for. but...
pros:
1. If you're lucky to work for the right people, the ball is in your court - it really just depends on you whether or not you will succeed
2. There are many wonderful professionals to interact with each day, it's not uncommon to have a conversation with the CEO in a random elevator ride
3. internal mobility opportunities 
4. diverse workplace
5. 401K matching contributions and other corp perks
6. Onsite amenities (Cafes, Starbucks etc)
cons:
1. there's a very fine line between a highly competitive and toxic work environment (there's a strong company-wide emphasis on leadership suggesting that everyone can and should strive to be one - this can lead to employees sabotaging one another's efforts and is often overlooked by higher management). 
2. It's difficult to get promoted although the company hosts events supposedly demystifying the process and makes it seem like it's so simple, it's all up to you, but it's not - it's still a mystery and it really comes down to who you know
2. long hours - when confronted about the demand of the work schedule and the challenge of toggling long hours with trying to raise a child while being a single mom, I was once told with a finger swinging in front of my face that "the job comes first kiddo". Back then, I was an hourly employee working 12-16 hour shifts and was told I can only report 8 hours for wage purposes. I wish I knew my rights better, but I was a new immigrant, single parent and my family's livelihood depended on this job.... so I thought. I'm sure many other people were exploited like I was. 
3. This company's general services department is plagued by incompetent people in management positions who have mastered doing very little, while appearing to have the hardest jobs on the planet. They have truly mastered corporate politics and are climbing the corporate ladder by exploiting their direct reports - having them do their duties and presenting them to the employee as an opportunity for growth (you get a call saying: you've been chosen and then you get inundated with extra work beyond your job scope for which the boss takes all the credit). I'm sure it's not like this in every department - I can only speak for what I have experienced. The incompetence at mid-level management is staggering.
4. Once a year there is an "anonymous employee survey" which isn't so anonymous after all. Somehow the boss always finds out who gave them the negative opinion and it's impossible to avoid repercussions. I've worked for a manager who wasn't afraid of a confrontation or criticism inviting the employees to come forth and speak to the manager directly about their issues so they can work on them together (a true leader), but I've also worked for years under a manager who didn't appreciate the criticism and held the employees responsible for their discontent. Let me just say - we learned very quickly that saying the truth never pays off - it was always the employees who were portrayed to be the problem and the ones who were penalized with additional work, so the manager could report the issue resolved. Employees who had the most to say were always the ones who got so much work thereafter, they no longer had any time to think about what just happened. It was obvious, but we all learned that it is how it is and no one can change it because the actor (read director) is so good at covering up their incompetence. I'm confident in saying many of us suffered PTSD from the way we were treated and some of us are still going through it - I'm sorry for them. It took me over 6 months to shake it off a bit. Definitely NOT "How We Do Business" which is the company's leading mantra.

summary: A mega-sized company with a lot of resources and well-meaning intentions
advice: Hiring trained job coaches with actual track records and effective methods to each function group or MD-led team may help upgrade the skillsets of managers and employees alike for the demands of the modern world faster than the current trajectory. JPMC is a good company. Best one in my personal past experiences. Like managers love to say on the Performance Reviews, there are always room for improvement. For individual contributors, managers of all levels and the company as a whole. "They" or "someone" will not get it done one day; because "they" and "someone" are us; each and every one of us.
pros:
- Potential of perceived prestige that comes with the employer name
- Global recognition of the company name and brand and its famous and publicly revered CEO
- Great brand image; great management by the PR and Legal teams
- Better diversity of employees than many other companies, with some planned efforts to become truly DEIB
- Company offers medical reimbursement accounts where employees could complete wellness activities to earn up to $800 per person in one's medical plan. The balance can be used to pay for eligible medical expenses, excluding dental and vision
- A lot of internal opportunities for the size of the company, the range of services and the fluidity in headcount
- Some monetary and work-hour investments to update different levels of internal and customer-facing technologies
- Generally polite coworkers within the firm, who would at least respond to greetings and smiles
- Many colleagues in a lot of countries and time zones; higher chances for individuals to find kindred spirits within the firm
- Relatively livable wages for back-office employees in the 601-604 range (aka. Analyst, Associate, VP (actually, Managers), ED)
- Have some data and metrics available for those who need to see tangible numbers that may or may not truly paint the full pictures
- New employees can setup contributions to their 401k from day 1, which comes effectively by the second paycheck at the latest
- Roughly 5% of the annual base pay for 401k match if one maxes out their annual 401k contribution to the annual IRS limit (for detailed verbiage, please contact HR or the hiring manager)
- 3-5% (depending on years of services) defined contribution to 401k in lieu of the original pension plan that phased out in 2018
- Some updated, modernized physical office buildings and space
- Increasingly more suburban office hubs and locations (helpful for people who want to live close to work but don't want to pay hyped-up city rents)
- Offers optional medical plan (two choices of insurance company), optional dental insurance, optional vision insurance, optional legal insurance, optional additional life insurance, etc. that all require payroll deductions. Most services employees selected and have to pay for partially also have not-so-low/not-so-affordable copays that may discourage usage
- Some managers are decent people who are definitely very capable with the hands-on work in their role and have the humanity to consider the perspectives of employees
- A lot of passive trainings through computer-based modules
- Some slightly more active training via in-person or virtual trainers/lecturers
- Short-Term Disability leave available for employees with needs and good doctor's notes
- A lot of people who volunteer their energy, additional hours and unpaid/uncompensated efforts into putting together webinars, panels, open discussions, in-person and visual events, etc. that help with DEIB efforts
- Great choices of emotionally uplifting music at town halls before the meetings officially start
- Have tech support members available for high-visibility meetings and events
- Most high-level managers and mid-level managers are eloquent, thoughtful and logical in the word choices and structures of their verbal and written messages
- Relatively less risk for not getting paid for your work since the company is so big and well-funded. One could expect steady income that does not change much over time.
- Have internal recognization message systems to help uplift people when monetary recognitions are not available or possible
- Efforts toward upgrading managers' and individual contributors' knowledge of reasons and ways to respect others and the right things to say; establish company-wide expectations
- Many managers seem extraordinary when compared with all the reports outside on toxic, micromanaging and incompetent managers; JPMC managers are very capable and effective with handling 3-jobs-worth of workloads all the time
- Phone apps that allows employees to check emails and handle less complex tasks at any time without needing access to an actual computer keyboard
- Some amount of fun at work, depending on one's capacity to join events
- Fast switch to work-from-home at the onset of the pandemic within 1 week
- Company offers 45 additional days to remain on the payroll after a layoff and provides job replacement training services via an outside supplier
cons:
- ***401k matching for a whole year does not get deposited into the employee's 401k until the following February. This means, a brand new employee does not get their first actual 401k match until up to 2.3 years after original start date
- ***Company kool-aid stresses the importance of mental health of everyone, except for those who have legitimately diagnosed mental health conditions that require consistent management by themselves and people involved and understanding and accommodations from most of whom they work with. Managers refer employees to HR. HR system dropdown options do not include anything related so that appropriate tickets cannot be opened
- 401k matching counter does not start for new employees until 1 full year of services
- CEO does not trust his people enough to let them work from home despite of the ongoing pandemic, firm's requirements for employees to get vaccinated and boosted, firm's statements of commitments to be responsible global citizen and dedicate huge money amounts to social causes such as climate change but not take stock of all the carbon footprint incurred from requiring employees to commute to office hubs
- Company believes in the importance of In-Person Engagement despite the fact that a good amount of teams are spread out across the globe
- CEO who chose to require (technically) everyone to return to the office simply because of occurrences where he cannot locate his direct reports and their respective admins when he needed to
- Managers generally would ask where employees were if the employees miss out on instant messages during work hours when they work remote; maybe employees should set up working desks in the restrooms at home as well
- Recruiters seem trained to relay the message that salary negotiations are quite impossible; may be different for people with highly-valued skills and experiences
- Messages don't usually match up with reality
- Expensive onsite cafe menus; $9-$25 range for cafeteria food that look and smell delicious but taste blend
- No budgets for former dressy year-end parties
- Tendencies to have early-morning, lunch-time and after-5pm meetings due to time zone differences for project team members
- No salary increases nor actual additional bonuses for many employees despite record-breaking earnings despite the pandemic, great exodus of employees and record-breaking compensations for the C-levels
- Management as a whole want employees to analyze, design and report on metrics but most information are on "need-to-know" basis that the individual contributors are not eligible to have access to
- Management as a whole talk about user experiences, but don't want individual contributors to reach out to the target users who are at the ED or MD levels since these users do not have time nor capacities to provide input about how they use or plan use the work products
- People talk about data and the need to communicate effectively but often don't put in their time investment to figure out the needed details to share to their audience/partners
- No pay increase nor additional benefits for the ones who make horizontal moves into internal roles; all recruiters will remind you that your pay is already at the max for the type of role you are going into
- Massive salary discrepancies between lines of businesses, functions, groups, teams and role titles
- Some cases of "simply going down the checklist"
- Employee Assistance Program exists but is not truly impactful nor helpful; most information in related systems/procedures are outdated with no efforts to keep current
- No customized training that fit the learning styles, schedules and roles of the employees
- Mangers ask for the employees to complete additional non-firm-wide-required-due-to-legal trainings but cannot afford to let the employees work on the training materials during normal business hours due to lack of manpower
- Unrealistic expectation of how much work and time employee can spend on work stuff in a calendar day, given the current limit of 24 hours a day per person
- Some legacy disconnects between different LOBs and levels of groups

summary: Looking elsewhere do to lack of current mobility internally.

cons: Large work force, stagnant/declining head count looming in the near future (similar across all large investment banks). Roll will most likely be very specialized within your line of business. summary: Decent Company; Just not for Software Engineers
advice: I’ve seen first-hand how hard it is to be an engineering manager here with so many layers of management so I really have no advice. So I feel like my only advice is either embrace the bureaucracy and just try to give your devs a consistent 40 hour weeks, or jump ship ASAP especially in Seattle.
pros:
I worked in the Seattle remote office and will be comparing it to other companies here, since even non-tech businesses here function as tech companies.

The base + bonus combo is pretty competitive for Seattle.

Work-life balance is pretty good.

It’s in a decent location downtown.

Most coworkers aren’t jerks despite being a huge company; generally a nice workforce.
cons:
So many meetings. Why does every meeting need 18 men in a room shouting at each other?

Diversity is good but remember JPMC is a global company so there will be culture clash. You know how somebody from Jersey and someone from California will probably have some miscommunication even though they’re both American? Well this will be amplified 10-fold when you’re at a global company. You will probably have a lot of remote meetings at random times with people across the globe. Moreover, there doesn’t seem to be a huge push for diversity and the majority of tech is the same majorities you seem to see at tech companies, and if you’re American of any race you’ll probably be in the minority. And remember, non-Americans haven’t confronted issues about race/ethnicity or as long as other countries, so prepare to hear some random tone-deaf remarks from immigrant coworkers (nothing mean per se, just tone-deaf).

The Seattle branch is facing the same issue that most non-Amazon companies face: every employee tends to be ex-Amazon and thus the new company becomes little Amazon. Recruiters love to reach out to Amazonians because they don’t know how the sausage is made, but those that are on the inside know they bring a certain Type-A culture and letting themselves be overworked. Moreover, recruiters assume Amazon experience == AWS experience, but really the non-Amazonians I’ve worked with had more hands-on AWS knowledge. 

It is still a top-down culture so there will be times when some random higher-up you’ve never met in person and is probably across the globe mandates an initiative with an arbitrary deadline.

Health/dental are overpriced. No benefits like orca card yet. Like a month of PTO depending on level.

Moreover, the dev environment is so locked down due to “security reasons”, which is fair. However, it means you’ll be using dated technology and if JPMC really cared about development experience, they’d spend some of that $9b quarterly profit to hire more security folk to help the developers get a modern experience to develop more business value. Instead, you’re between a rock and a hard place of getting arbitrary deadlines with so much red tape and so many meetings. Hard pass especially in Seattle where there are so many more fast-paced environments.

I’m all about company for a couple of years at least but it was extremely difficult to stay longer than a year at a company with so many meetings, so much red tape, so little development, and so bad for the resume, especially in Seattle where complacency is killer. Unless you’re hired for a very specific team and a very specific project that’ll perfectly align with your career goals, i would say don’t bother.

summary: Good company to be from, less interesting to work for
advice:
-VP-to-ED managers need to spend more time focusing on leadership & management and less time working as an individual contributor. Communicate to your team what your desired outcome is and what your expectations are and allow your team to rally behind you and accomplish the task/project.
-At the highest level, the firm needs to place a stronger emphasis on leadership within its management ranks. A one week class on leadership for new manager promotions is not enough to build a strong managerial corps. Managers should be evaluated on their subordinates professional development. If a subordinate is receiving the guidance, support, and autonomy from their manager and is growing in responsibility and performance, that should be a reflection of the manager as well as the subordinate. Good managers should be proud of their subordinates accomplishments and to promote them.
-When the world is past this pandemic, allow employees the ability to work from home at least a few days a week - especially if their team is dispersed in many different locations and not co-located together

It's possible to overcome, but a challenge to find the right hiring manager

summary: Smile and pretend you're not a used car salesman
advice: Consistency and integrity are often lacking. I know innovation is important, but there's a noticeable culture of change for change's sake. And please, keep your word. If a healthy workplace environment is really that valuable, stop overlooking bad behavior for the sake of short-term profit.
pros: Decent pay, great benefits, and a fairly easy job, overall. In other words, you can give 75% effort and coast fairly comfortably. Or, by working hard, you can see tremendous success and advance quite quickly. It's quite simple to gravitate toward the parts of the job you enjoy, or at least don't mind. If you hate cold-calling, you can easily focus on walk-in customers. If you hate dealing with people face-to-face, you can spend all day on the phone trying to schedule appointments and a half-decent manager will praise you for it. For a professional office environment, most of my former coworkers were remarkably relaxed and friendly. Work-life balance is fairly solid. Aside from days when I was asked to come in after a coworker called in sick, I never felt like I was on-the-clock after the branch closed.
cons:
Many years, raises were promised or hinted at and rarely materialized. For all the talk about customer service and taking care of clients, it's absolutely a pure sales job. Many bankers would gladly urge clients into financial products that weren't right for them because of a perverse commission incentive and pressure from upper management. You either adapt and start feigning enthusiasm for it around customers, or suffer the equivalent of a pay cut. There's always some new program or company initiative that gets pushed super hard for about 6 months, then vanishes without a word. Branches are perpetually understaffed. Not *terribly* but just enough that you're screwing coworkers out of their lunch break if you have to call in sick. 

The biggest con? A lack of accountability. If a banker is a top performer, sales-wise, they can basically get away with murder. I've known several who harassed customers, threw things at coworkers, or repeatedly violated internal controls. But, because they happened to land one or two multi-million dollar clients, management looked the other way for years.

I'm not saying it's like that everywhere or all the time. It's not. But... don't be surprised when you do see it happen.

• Name
* the above reasons is why JPMC is 2 stars instead of 1

• SEP is a joke. Not a bad first job for new grads if its your best offer. But it's a useless program to keep new grads docile and complacent as Analysts for 2.5 years. Nothing more. 
• A lot of the promotions, job titles, and hiring process are jokes and meaningless. It's banking titles applied to software work. Straight up, it doesn't work.
• COVID. How they handled COVID has been horrendous. Lack of leadership and follow through throughout the entire pandemic. From the top down they told us nothing for 1+ year.  We got told literally 10 different return to office plans within 1 quarter. The lack of leadership and transparency has been a huge turn off,  starting at the top. Jamie Dimon is extremely out of touch and it shows. If you want a flexible work schedule this company is not for you. One week they'll say one thing. The next week it'll be a complete reversal. summary: JPMorgan Chase Mostly Cons and a few Pros
pros: JPMorgan Chase offers great benefits. The health insurance and life insurance benefits are very good and the out of pocket expenses are very reasonable compared to other companies. They have a legal benefit that is very inexpensive and well worth it. It's nice to be able to have free checking and savings accounts for the whole family. I like the fact that the company is very ethnically diverse. The company always makes it a point to make sure that it's on the forefront of all the latest technology only for customer facing applications and systems.
cons:
*The company has grown too large and is out of control with too much red tape and bureaucracy. 
--It takes too long to get anything approved and there are too many manager approval levels involved. 
*Senior managers are involved with approving menial expenses instead of spending time on more important issues and concerns. 
*The company is top heavy with far too many directors, managing directors and executives, and there are far too few employees to actually take care of business and do real work. 
*JPMC does at least 3 rounds of layoffs each year, and each time they layoff more mid level and entry level employees that do the work.
--Consequently, those employees that are left to do the work end up doing the job of 3 - 4 people. 
*Also, it's very important to note, that when they do the 3 rounds of layoffs each year, they target workers that are 55 years and older. 
--So while JPMC is constantly bragging to the media and to their employees that they champion diversity and inclusion and that they don't practice discrimination of any kind, they are clearly and openly discriminating against workers that are 55 years or older. 
*Global Technology Infrastructure is the worst line of business to work for because the company treats GTI as an expense. 
--If you're going to work for JPMC, it's best to work for one of the other lines of business such as Chase Investment Bank, Asset Wealth Management, Commercial Bank or Mortgage Banking. 
*JPMC makes internal applications and systems for employees their lowest priority, and it makes it very difficult to get work done. 
--In addition, JPMC has gotten rid of most of the help desks where employees could talk to someone to get help.
--Unfortunately, if you are having issues with an application or tool that you need to get your work done, you will be relegated to opening a ticket through a clumsy automated system and it could be several days before anyone addresses your issue.

summary: Role isn't really what it used to be.. sadly wouldn't recommend

-Pretty high level of executions relative to pitches in the diversified NY team.

cons:
-The role originally was like a middle market leverage finance position with the day to day resembling a general leverage finance position.
-Over time senior management pushed more of the coverage side of the business and credit and treasury responsibilities onto the CCB analysts.
-Role became increasingly vague and began to resemble middle market commercial banking in the day to day, which is why I and many others left.
-Position is technically within the CB so many of the IBD initiatives do not technically apply. This was an issue with protected Saturdays (may have changed) and access to certain resources. Also they had different caps on bonuses which was more relevant at associate level and above.
-Would no longer recommend to a friend unless they are very passionate about treasury products.
-The role is becoming less IBD oriented. Huge exodus while I was there.

summary: Great place to start a career
advice: Figure out how to be more flexible when it comes to working remote. JPMC employees that have been at the firm for years and consistently demonstrate high levels of productivity should have the opportunity to go remote if their job can be done remote. Some people are ok with, and want to come into the office, but many want the increased flexibility and ability to go full remote. And figure out a strategy to bring employees that have been at the firm for years - up to the market rate. New hires, including interns - come in making more than seasoned professionals. This will continue to drive people out if not corrected. The lack of flexibility when it comes to competitive pay at the associate and VP level combined with lack of flexibility to work remote makes cybersecurity a lot less appealing from the perspective of an external candidate.  If JPMC cyber doesn't soften up on its no remote work policy - junior, mid-level, and senior-level analysts will continue to jump ship after gaining experience and go elsewhere for more money and full remote.
pros: Great place to start a career. Across the cybersecurity org there are some really great leaders, but also some really awful leaders. If you're lucky enough to have a great leader - life will be good, otherwise - not so much. JPMC offers great benefits overall. This includes 401k match, 20 vacation days (6 sick, 3 personal), paid holidays, tuition reimbursement. Cybersecurity has a decent training budget and always brings in the best cyber trainings.
cons: Leaders across the cybersecurity org are authorized to work full remote, but they don't allow middle managers and individual contributors to do so. The 'do as I say not as I do' is a bit ridiculous, especially after working years remote because of the pandemic and showing the job can be done. There's also a lot of office politics. Promotions more often than not seemed to be based on popularity and not on merit. And lastly, JPMC base salary / total comp isn't competitive at the associate and VP level anymore.

advice: For very senior management- of those likely never to see this, I would recommend NOT moving thousands of jobs yearly to lower paying regions domestically- or internationally. It is incredibly insulting, and when moved to offshore locations, downright unpatriotic. This is a topic that those on both "sides of (the political aisle) " can fully agree on (of those I worked with. I have been very happy working with people from abroad, many people I have worked with started in Indian locations, but then came over to the States. It has been a great learning situation- to learn from each other and to see what a small world it is, I have also found most people coming from abroad to have great attitudes, and really lovely. However, when full teams are wiped out at once, it was disheartening- especially when we know it is only to pay less money for work we had been diligent on.  It is a recipe for disaster for the States (invite people to come on visas on a path to citizenship- I have nothing against the actual people etc., as noted- I have had excellent experiences with people from the same regions- even and including the individuals I had to train - it was not their fault to want to have the roles- however, when I started to be asked about finding work at jpmc in New York, it made me think they may be underpaid for their region - which again, was disheartening). I took a star away for this reason- unfortunately, I know this goes way above the senior management in the regular office spaces- and up to the Jamie Dimon stratosphere for business planning across the lobs.
pros: Excellent benefits - best healthcare options available (though I am a firm believer that health care should not be tied to employment), I learned a tremendous amount while there too- training was decent. Management, depending on area can be great.
cons: Even in the best of areas- you will be working your tail off -likely- and often for more than 45 hours per week- if within the corporate offices (I have no idea what it is like in the branches- but worked in the Investment Bank and the Commercial Bank). Management has been wonderful- and less than wonderful, depending on team really. The negative, you can never feel too secure that there will not be a huge shake up beyond your little world, as the last few years I always felt as though I stepped over a ticking time bomb by not being part of an area that was being outsourced offshore. Ultimately, I was. I decided to leave the firm fully- although I was given ample time (luckily- about 8 mos) to prepare for the impending offshore move of our teams to India. The most insulting part was when my team had to virtually train our counterparts in India on our roles. At an Officer level, with many years at the Bank, I felt that was quite an insult to injury. However, I stayed professional, as did my colleagues, and nobody in the offshore team had a clue that they were actually replacing us.

Employees are not paid what they are worth.

summary: JP Morgan Technology -- The Experience Depends on your Role

pros: I am a business/systems analyst, and work in the Consumer & Community Bank ("CCB").  Technology has many functional organizations in different silos at JP Morgan, so this description might not be applicable elsewhere in the firm.  I honestly cannot provide universal reasons for why I like working in this community, but I do.  Every day is different -- entails a new challenge.  The organization is victim of the same politicking that is entrenched in any massive organization; but if you perform well and take necessary steps toward visibility, you can be noticed and, more importantly, rewarded.  Mobility is real -- upward and horizontally.  Compensation is fair -- in my experience, people earn what they deserve.  Management makes itself available, both professionally and personally.  The health benefits suit me very well -- although I do not require extraordinary medical or dental care, so enrolled accordingly in a plan that requires a low premium.
cons: Project administration -- the matrix environment -- is unnecessarily rigid and excessive.  It creates more work for the business stakeholders and analysts and adds time to projects that could be executed more quickly to the same degree of success.  This condition does not, however, prevent management's assigning unreasonable deadlines to projects, which would be difficult to meet even in a more agile environment.  The administration also comprises participants who do not have adequate subject matter expertise for the roles they are assigned.  This comment is not being directed to the participants themselves, but to the structure, which sets up these participants for failure or unpleasant project experiences.  Reorganizations occur frequently, which disrupts continuity and slows business initiatives.

advice:
Keep up the good work in innovative training tools!
Try to alleviate SME workloads to accommodate Training, at least for times before deliverables are due. Consider electing additional or replacement SMEs if original SMEs are too busy to participate.
The remote work is a giant 'plus' for those of us in the Consulting/Contracting world, so thank you for being flexible in that area.
pros:
JPMorgan offers professional service and expects the same back! Bring your A game and expect a great group of dedicated people. 
Project managers and Executives involved were all great to work with and did their best to help with the project.
For contractor positions pay is at level for experienced L&D and Tech professionals. 
Once you are in a position there is freedom to work remotely most of the time if you request it (at least in L&D where I was). The building I was assigned to in Chicago really didn't have the right spaces/tools to house me very often. Plus at least half of my team was in NYC, so it didn't matter that I worked at home most days. 
That said, be sure you show up looking as if you work at a bank on the days you need to be onsite!  Suits aren't necessary (only in NYC location) but Business Casual is a step above the usual definition.
Middle and upper management are committed to the Training solution, so they will commit resources when possible. Solutions can be complicated to achieve but a quality product results, which is a huge positive for everyone.
Management takes advice to be more innovative and will often buy into a new concept (eLearning tools, different ways of achieving a goal), making it a bit easier to work with than many companies of this size and structure.
cons:
As often happens, SMEs can be difficult to meet with due to emergencies and high workloads, so you may need to be creative at times to get information.
One project at JPM became a bit unwieldy, mainly because the client didn't understand training. If this happens, be sure to keep them informed about any items that start pulling the project out of scope! Be sure all bases are covered even if you end up going against your gut feeling. That way you have documented steps to remind them where their path clashed with L&D's advice.

 and HR doesn't care at all stating the managers are just being petty. advice:
Tell your people what you want, then help them to do it.  Trust your people.  Regain that family feeling we once had.  Can Christmas parties, activity clubs and blood drives affect the bottom line so very deeply?  Bind not the mouths of the kine that tread the grain.  

Not that any of that is imprtant - which is really my complaint; obviously it didn't help.  I don't so much fault Jamie Dimon for nipping at our perquisites and ultimately our jobs, but I do seem to recall a promise to take the stock price to $100 in two years.  Well, my options are still underwater.
pros: Great people work there, at least in my area (IT).  The right relationship really IS everything at Chase.  You can get a lot done going through channels, and sometimes more going through your own personal networks.  Much is given and much is expected.
cons:
Since the JPMorgan - Chase merger, and even more so since the JPMC-Bank One merger, I found the pressure growing.  Frills were trimmed and salaries were flat.  Perhaps it was my fault because my performance reviews did not seem to match my opinion of my job performance - a problem suffered by many, the more so as performance reviews were no big deal when I joined the bank.

Ultimately it seemed that we were desired to make bricks without straw.  For a while there was not much business to be done and frankly it iwas difficult to adjust - they wanted leadership, entrepreneurship, but I at least had no such background - what was I to do, open a microloans division?  They wanted us to find things to do.  Sadly for me this did not compute.

Finally they moved my entire division out of New York.  I was offered a position down South - but not a relocation package, and I was offered to 'fight for the management job' when the whole point of bringing me to the new location was, presumably, to leverage my experience.  And, given the comparative salary scales, I felt I would never get a raise without a promotion.  I decided that former Chase people did not have the confidence of the former Bank One-heavy management and took the package.

advice: First throw them out and start all over. Hire people that really have a passion for human development and let them gain experience before they get promoted, and I mean real experience, not "I have the gift of gab and I think I know how to be a mger". And change the structure to revolve around 2 things: Customers and Employees, and put a bigger emphasis on the latter, because the Co. aren't the walls and JPM logo, hint: its the Employees stupid.
pros: The Co. has bar none the best technology in the business. The most up-to date software out there along with security measures for customer's information protection. There is a lot of training access to materials to help you. It has benefits that are typical of any Fortune 500 Co. even though the health benefits for the retail side isn't all that great. The benefits include: 401k/Co. 5% yearly/match, ESPP 5% employee discount, etc.
cons:
I don't know even where to start, so lets start with the Career Choices: if you work in JPMorgan on the Retail side, you are screwed, to put it lightly. The Co. doesn't care for your future. You are STUCK in Retail for EVER. Management is useless and almost ALWAYS younger than you or close to your age. If you are a manager, that doesn't mean opportunity for you, but: Low Pay, Just "Winging" your career and not a solid foundation, because you cannot RUSH experience. What it means for JPMorgan is: Make a "Quick Buck" because they have very aggressive people, by “piles”, that just want to "move up" and JPMorgan can in the mean time pay them less as employees, with the promise to get promoted,, in other words, they will take advantage of that.
This is a recipe for disaster in your career. They have an incentive Plan called "PVCs" (Product Value Credits) that are based on a Monthly Plan, you have to meet the goals EVERY month, not quarterly like most financial sales positions in this level, but yes monthly! Your stress level is high because you are always thinking about PVCs. And I know some of you may be thinking: "Well you knew what you were getting into when you took the position". That is not entirely correct. Pre/Mid Jaime Dimon, CEO of JPM, these super aggressive goals didn't exist. The company is moving VERY swiftly to technology assisted based banking, which it should, but in the mean time the employees get no slack, the branches still open till 6pm, even though the rest of the "Big Banks" close at 4-5pm, they keep paying the lowest salaries, because they justify it by saying: "this is a performance based Co.", but they keep cutting the incentive plan sometimes every quarter, therefore reducing your ability to make more money. At the end there are 2 victims here: Clients, because there is less service, and employees, because there is less "walk-ins" and more "cold-calling"= more tough commission environment. Management, since they have an incentive to make their yearly goals have no idea how to be honest because the system is pit against your best interest and theirs, and the latter ALWAYS wins. The bankers and Mgers treat customer by importance of bank account size, in other words you are treated well based on how "big" your next bonus check could be. Horrible. This is how bad it is, when you leave, it's against Co. policy to not even give you a recommendation letter, regardless if you leave on good terms.
The employees satisfaction is abysmal, you cannot find people that say it is worth it to work in an environment like this that are being honest with themselves.   
If you want stability in your income, family time, and also, most importantly, peace of mind for your health, stay away.

summary: Great employees, great brand, lucky JP Morgan Chase
advice: Senior management compensation needs to include on a long and short term approach rather than just performance in the short term.  Stop compensating people for making a buck today if it costs the bank two dollars five years later.  Reward employees for doing the RIGHT thing.
pros:
Definitely the people.  There are so many good, talented, and knowledgeable employees found throughout the company, that it's easy to find a mentor or someone you can learn from.  
The size and breadth of the organization also allows for employees to transfer from one area to another in order to experience another side of the business.  I've had three such moves in my years here, which has allowed me to broaden my background.  
The compensation is reasonable for the work and geographic location.  In my experience WaMu certainly isn't a company that believes in paying its employees as little as it can get away with. They generally pay what your skills and experience are worth.
Generally speaking management is very supportive of a work/life balance and flexible schedules are possible if work isn't negatively affected.  This can vary from department to department and manager to manager though so shouldn't be taken as a given.
cons:
Besides senior management's over exposure into the world of sub prime mortgages, which led to WaMu's downfall? 
Inconsistent answers as far as benefits go is a large downside.  WaMu has outsourced many benefits and you can call and get three different answers on three different occasions and when you finally are in the middle of the scenario, a fourth answer is the one they go with.  
Getting IT help is a terrible ordeal.  Again, this is outsourced to India currently, so there's a language barrier first off.  As a remote VPN user, I have to call frequently for help, and the call center employees are ususally eventually able to help after, on average an hour.  Before outsourcing the exact same issues could be solved in under 10 minutes.  The remoteness doesn't allow for familiarity with how the networks are set up locally and any variances that are built in for specific businesses.  It's one of the most frustrating things about WaMu.
Come review time, management is told what the bell curve needs to look like, so there can only be x number of high performers within a group.  If you are lucky enough to have more star performers on your team, you have to adjust (fudge) your scores accordingly to fit the curve.  This isn't unusual in corporate america, but it's a downside.  Internal transfers/promotions are limited to a 15% salary increase, even if that means your pay is then below the salary range for the new position.  To get a meaningful salary increase you really have to leave and return to the company.

advice: Please....Please talk to the rank and file about the compensation. By rank and file I mean AVP and below. Chase is losing excellent talent!

cons: You will be evaluated by comparison to "the Chase Way". If your numbers don't match up in a negative way there is no way to advance. But if you benefit from being in the right place at the right time there is lots of recognition.

advice: Columbus is a major HUB for JPMC employees, and there are many talented lower and middle level managers who are overlooked when opportunities for advancement arise.  Management should seek opportunities to focus more on the identication, development and advancement of these talented individuals.
pros: Opportunities for new job roles; "do the right thing" culture; respected in the industry; complex environement with many opportunities to learn
cons: Siloed departments; difficulty receiving exposure to upper levels of management; lack of organizational focus on developing talented individuals at lower and mid-management level

summary: Chase is a great place to work if you know exactly where you want to be doing
advice: provide incentives to those who work hard.  know the strengths and weaknesses of your team.  build a better team.  care about your team.
pros:
unlimited resources
growth
mobility
huge company with lots of job opportunities if you know how to access them
training programs
cons:
company is too big, everything is compartmentalized, no one wants to do more than what their job specifies
people can stay under the radar for years and never be challenged to grow and be okay with that
lack of management

advice: I'm leaving because I don't feel like you've got my back.  We are posting consistent gains, and consistently underpaying our talent.  Those two go hand-in-hand and I finally put the two together.
pros: This is a stable environment ideal for someone with a family to support.  Do your job decently well and they won't let you go.
cons: Corporate automatons, are way too uptight, and slow to act.  What saves you guys is your inbound talent.  Unfortunately, they leave within 1-2 years because they don't like the culture.

summary: Excellent company to work, a LOT of days off and good co-workers.
advice: Keep up the good work and improve the training program. Define what’s top notch employees and focus on developing and retaining them.
pros: Good pay and full benefits for a call center. Time and a half pay for those who work on holidays, if not you earn a float day. Supervisors always willing to help and upper management has a firm open door policy.
cons: The training program needs a lot of improvement, specifically more enthusiastically trainers. Management is focus in quantity, more than quality.

advice: Give people options to move from a dept they feel uncomfortable in. Chase itself is great, in my 13 years there I never had an issue, when you have supervisors that are reported to human services by multiple people over several years, pay attention!
pros: Good benefits and outstanding vacation. Good opportunities for advancement.
cons: I was with the company for 13 years. The only reason I no longer work there is one manager, who has been reported to human services several times,  made a hostile work environment.

pros: Stable company. Better than average health 401K and pension. Challenging. Brand name goes a long way to getting you in the boardrooms of clients.
cons: Company's IT intranet security and structure goes to far into impeding basic business office functionality. Internal support system requiring a ticket are overly processed, documented  and formalized. One can wait 48-hours for support in any department.  Extreme high level management can miss the finer points to their proclamations. Not understanding the full impact (+ or -) of their decisions can and does adversely impact the welfare of workers.

summary: Did not support women in real estate
advice: Change the culture in global real estate to one that supports, values & retains women who  are ethical & seek to improve operations, & who have the courage & expertise to tackle tough issues, as opposed to letting them persist.
pros: benefits, size, financial performance, CEO
cons: Not women friendly in my dept. , all women were pushed out of dept. to support one manager threatened by their skills & new women were hired in their place, retained those who created risk & terminated those who wanted to mitigate it.

summary: Company lost its edge in career development and opportunity
advice: Employees will not stay with the firm without promotion and advancement opportunities in metropolitan city centers. The overall quality of the firm and our offerings will decline  with the reduced quality workforce and it will hurt our bottom line in the long run.
pros: Large organization increases opportunities to diversify work experience and work in new locations / functions
cons: Short-sided focus on cost reduction has led to backfilling positions with less experienced staff in lower cost locations and little opportunity for promotion or internal mobility.

summary: Women in IT Leadership - More talk than reality
advice: When associates say there are leaders who mistreat associates or create a culture that is counter-productive to diversity and inclusion, believe them. Take action. Remove that leader from being a people leader where they can cause the most damage.
pros: Good benefits and fairly good pay for IT associates.
cons: Still a boys club . Not very inclusive except for some high profile leaders as a way to demonstrate diversity. Women in IT Leadership is what they say they support but it is still a Boys Club except when forced.

advice:
- Improve Sales work systems
- Decrease the amount of stale leads due to misinformed referrals
- Pay more attention to the mental health of sales people, the job can definitely be stressful
pros:
- Sales role with consistent work and leads
- Role responsibilities take time to learn but with focus they can easily be mastered
- Work site is clean, professional, and lively.
cons:
- Work can be demanding during busy seasons
- Although it's a sales position, uncontrollable events do not always excuse poor results
- Working virtually is nice for the COVID-era, but very taxing.

advice: Create a job shadow and fast track program for successful bankers to gain experience in the area of finance that they see themselves in.
pros: Great systems and support for frontline workers, Clear expectations and training for how to be successful, bonus were paid monthly, benefits were in line with a major corp.
cons: the personal banker role was a glorified customer agent. Any clients who came in for a loan, investments, or business were immediately scheduled to meet with a specialized banker (via phone mostly) so the job experience was slightly lacking.

advice: Review the internal promotion process. You are losing talented people who deserve the VP title, while the only folks getting hired seem to be VPs and above.
pros: Lots of opportunity for internal mobility. Folks are encouraged to move to new roles.
cons: The 401K match is deposited once a year, right after the annual review. I find people leave each year. While there are opportunities for mobility, it is disruptive each year. It also seems it is harder to get promoted to next level and sometimes easier to leave to get the title and salary.

summary: Same as most big bank competitors
advice:
Improve communication from managers to employees.
More  flexible remote options.
pros:
The technology at JPM was very good. Always doing enhancements and introducing new tools. However could be overwhelming at first having to learn multiple systems. 
Benefits and vacation were probably as good or better than other big banks.
Co workers were friendly and always helpful.
cons:
Not a lot of management opportunity. Managers seemed to be content in their roles most staying there 10-15 years.
High turnover.
Directions from middle management were rarely clear especially when new procedures were introduced.

summary: Work here at your own cost!
advice: Management needs to have someone that can train people correctly and has the time and not having to train someone while having to do their own work and is concerned about their own production quota. Also need to make sure that instructions from clients are correct and precise and not so quick to write up the employee when instructions are not clear.
pros: Great co-workers to work with.
cons:
Management is HORRIBLE! 
They dont train people correctly
Machines do not work properly and they want you to somehow be able to keep up with production!

summary: Not a company for tech employees
advice:
Modernize job grades and titles
Match 401k in paychecks
pros:
Free on-site medical clinic is nice
Columbus McCoy center is awesome with plenty of food options.
cons:
Job grades need modernized; there are 2 levels of associate and then you become a VP. Trying to get promoted to VP is nearly impossible because it’s not about merit but how many executive directors you know. If you come from tech with levels like engineer 1-5 and principal engineer and the ability to easily get promoted then steer clear. 
Bonuses are under par from most other tech companies, my other employers had targets like 10-15% but at Chase they give you no idea; my bonuses were 7% and 9%. They only care about making bankers and brokers happy not the people keeping the systems working. 
Raises are very poor after 1 year I was not given a raise and told my 7% bonus was high which is why I started looking for new jobs, the next year I only got 2%.
401k matching is horrible, they do not match every pay check and will deposit the funds January the following year if you are still employed. 

No one takes responsibility for their products, if you have an issue with a system good luck trying to get support and it fixed. I had open tickets for bugs for 8 months that were never resolved. Most documentation is nonexistent or outdated.
I understand having to deal with risks and audits but the people managing risk are incompetent. They will say you need to fix this but tell you no information on how to or where to find resources. The whole SDLC risk team have the worst archaic system for getting an application from dev to prod, you have to paste screenshots in excel documents and post it to sharepoint. Every tollgate basically asks the same questions and you just end up copying and pasting from one worksheet to another.
I was told our team would hire new employees to help alleviate the team workload and over a year later they finally opened a couple contractor roles not even FTE as promised. By that time I was burnt out and already planning on leaving. 

Health benefits were great before changing MRA requirements, before you did some activities every quarter to get funds but last year they switched to making you wear a step counter and walk 7,500 steps 20 days a month. I don’t like wearing watches or things so I just decided to forfeit about $500.

summary: Lots of stuff to do but... Politics
advice: If you want to be known as a tech company, behave as one to your employees. So many people quit because of all the politics trying to please business, lack of pay, and many other reasons.  The only people that stay are those with families and even then that only applies if they don't feel they could get another job.
pros: Good benefits, lots of interesting projects.
cons: Significantly lower than average pay, devs are treated as second class citizens, very political, lots of unskilled contractors and offshore workers making you work overtime

summary: Terrible for your mental health but if you drink the koolaid you may like it for awhile
advice: This is a large cap company that can't really experience the endless growth of a smaller cap company with less market share. In order to maintain profits you have to cut staff size and slowly push more responsibilities onto less staff. I would say hire more people but then you'd have less profits. I'd say drastically increase employee pay as compensation for the genius business model, but of course you'd have less profits then too. I guess I have no advice things are working exactly the way you want them to.
pros: Bank hours, paid time off, okay benefits, 401k match up to 5%, some (extremely) minor employee discounts for banking products
cons:
I worked for Chase in two different roles over the course of 6 and a half years. I left the company incredibly dissatisfied. What I mainly want to convey is just how terrible the work environment is as described below. That's not to say that there's not plenty of other cons to include, believe me there are, but this is probably what had the biggest part in me leaving the company overall.

Branches are increasingly getting smaller forcing more and more work onto a smaller staff. You will be yelled at all day for the wait times. Tellers are now expected to do just about everything even though there are less tellers than ever. This obviously creates massive wait times for literally the simplest things. But of course, it's your job as an employee to convince clients that it's actually great and if they don't want to wait they should set an appointment which I'm sure you can guess the client always loves to hear. Rather than helping clients with traditional banker role tasks, bankers are expected to sit at their desks and make constant phone calls. The only time a banker isn't making a call is when they have an appointment. For the most part any employee who's not drinking the corporate koolaid finds this dynamic incredibly stressful to deal with on a day to day basis. 

The negative effects the branch environment has on mental health cannot be overstated. You will be stressed to the max if you're working in a branch these days.

advice: Too much tinkering with commission pay.  Pay consistently went down while production was similar or even increased.  This seems disengenious and definitely fosters poor sales habits from producers.
pros: Ample room for advancement across many different career directions.  (Was) Secure and steady employer.  Strong Benefits package offered.  Ample training provided.
cons: Weak pool of branch level management.  Didn't necessarily foster 'the right way to do it', but promoted those with good sales numbers by questionable tactics.  Banking gives you a little bit of the 'Office Space' type feeling.

summary: In a decade there, from incredible company with a unique culture - to massive beaurocracy, terrible reward for success.
advice:
Pay people based on their performance with explicit numbers  - avoid allowing metrics that can be subject to personal biases from managers. Replace mid-level management that's become too comfortable for too long in their fiefdoms - they're looking short-sightedly at their imminent retirement money, and have lost the vision for the future of the industry 'everything we do or say is right attitude etc'. 

Understand that 2008 is history and there are other firms hiring out there - you're getting too comfortable, failure to reward performers with no clarity on numbers when your competitors do means you'll only be left with the timid and the weak staffers that are too afraid to leave....

The beaurocracy is getting exponentially worse by the year, nothing can get done quickly or efficiently.
pros:
Huge name brand.... big balance sheet, strong derivative and alternative asset products.... great place for the resume.
That's it these days....
cons:
Terrible reward for success, team/region-based metrics with no formula (total black box), therefore subject to abuse for political biases. Metrics keep moving against you. You do not get paid for building a business over many years, each year you start from a scratch YoY metrics, no annuitized credit in your pay for past success plus huge sales pressure and expectation. Which is fine for any business in the industry - if they were to pay - If you do exactly the same job any number of other firms you would get paid at least double if not multiple times more, plus get paid for past year success.... also there's no clarity on how the money is cut-up, instead of relying on a perpetual annual disappointment, no matter how good your numbers are.... because politics and petty resentments can overrule your numbers.

The beaurocracy is unbelievably bad, the support is poor 'cheap', and the management in my division are incredibly weak, they get paid on margin growth, and that's clear from the anaemic pay. Healthcare costs go up double digits YoY.

I know this having now gone outside and seen quite how bad the reward structure is compared to others for the same pressure and success. The name remains great, but the reality is the products and support are often better elsewhere, management relies on telling staff that it's worse elsewhere and you basically owe them your pay deficit for using the name. I have no idea why someone would want to build a business over many years here versus several other houses.

advice: With the loss of the ABM and Managers now moving to Multi-site settings, Managers, LAOs and MODs should receive additional training as well as actually competitive pay raises. With the work load and responsibility $20/hour is not appealing and should be closer to what a supervisor makes of ~$28-$30
pros: Great place to build skills and connect with clients.
cons: Branch Management is a toss up especially now with them having to deal with more than 1 location at a time. This makes the brunt of the work left to the MOD or LAO

summary: Hard-working, smart people with some bureaucratic, big company headaches.
pros: There are some very thoughtful, intelligent, and capable people. Great networking opportunities. Because of the size of the firm, there is a lot of mobility within the firm.
cons: Because of the current regulatory environment, there is definitely a "CYA" compliance mentality. There are a lot of hoops to jump through just to get things done, all in an effort for the company to limit foul ups, losses, and bad press. This isn't different from other companies in the industry, but the bigger the company, the more the red tape.

advice: If they removed some of the old school managers, I think JP Morgan could be a good place to work.Working for a global entity can be interesting and challenging if done right, I was just stuck in a bad situation with management that thought saying "nobody goes home" every Friday was doing a great job.
pros: JP Morgan had some excellent employee benefits and compensation based on a 40 hour work week was fair. Some of the managers I worked with were smart, competent and fair.
cons: I worked for an immature management team. Simply too much uncompensated work, very poor work/life balance, ignorant, childish behavior from management at times. On call rotation was truly terrible and lack of appreciation from immediate management was very poor.

advice: Promote educated individuals in the respective fields. If the promotion is simply based on work performance then pay for college courses. Management in a large business should have general business knowledge, not just over payed paper pushers. Please figure out how grade work performance. Changing it every 6 months sets everyone up for failure.
pros: Large company that provides low grade opportunities across the US and world
cons: Horrible health care insurance and pretty bad benefits in general. Very difficult to move laterally to different LOB's. Upper management is not supportive to career growth. Get lost in the weeds.

summary: Great place for the long term
advice: Listen to your junior people. They are the future of the company that you hold so dear (and own stock in).
pros: Simply put it is the best bank on the street. A large network of professionals that are dedicated to being the best as well. A lot of room for growth and easy transition to other parts of the bank.
cons: Sometimes it is too big. The senior management live in bubble and at times don't really listen to the junior people. In addition, some of the promotions are not merit based.

summary: Too loyal for my own good!
advice: treat us as individuals, not by our standard ID numbers, provide encouragement and helpful suggestions, actions speak louder than words, not just "We will look into that."
pros: flexibility with hours and locations, coworkers who become like family, benefits, recgonition in other ways besides cash, team environment, creation of upper management positions to support me
cons: low salary, management made no move to keep me when I threatened to leave for another bank, did not make me feel needed or irreplacable, not much formal training, manager who "talks down" and doesn't do much encouraging

summary: Overall, I enjoy the opportunites and interactions with others at the company.
advice: I think the leadership is extremely talented and diverse. I would encourage the team to think about opportunites to offer employees exposure to other areas and managers.
pros: JP Morgan Chase's financial stability is solid. Senior managers ensure they communicate company performance and objectives in monthly meetings. There are many opportunites to attend training sessions to further your career.
cons: There are not many opportunities to interact with managers across departments or business lines. Mentoring opportunites with other areas and managers do not seem to be available.

summary: Nice people to work with but there are politics...
advice: Clear out the dead weight to bring in some fresh talent, that includes managers and employees.
pros: There are a lot of smart, fun people who work here. I was part of an acquisition/merger that went quickly and smoothly. JPMC are clearly experts at that! I enjoyed some of a great people I met and learned a lot while working there.
cons: It's a big of a 'boys club'. Lots of politics and high school behavior with managers and employees. The culture could use an update, but it's banking after all...

advice: stop micromanaging everything  - start helping some of these poeple instead of making up all of these rules to not be able to help them legitimately
pros: the pay scale, benefits, some of the managers are decent  -- it all depends on what site you are at
cons: they want blood  -- if you are in collections  you are to demand every penny now -- selll you posessions- your first born - get payday loans-  sell yourself on the street  - we want our money now !!!!

advice: Learn from your mistakes and surround yourself with people who tell you the truth ... and then resist the urge to run them off if you don't like what you're hearing.
pros: The vision was exciting at first and I was proud to be a part of WaMu. I was able to do some of my best work, with some very creative and bright people.
cons: Leadership--and by that I mean the C suite--got caught up in ego gratification and hubris. For the three to four years before the company went under it was all about the numbers.

summary: Good Place to work with some easily fixable issues
advice: Better to solve the current technology issues rather that promote new technologies
pros:
* Good People
* New technologies and Innovation
* 4-weeks vacation from day-1
* Great name to have in your work experience/resume
cons:
* Employees who have been in the company longer are trying to self-promote themselves
* Some groups have made is almost impossible to work with them due to process/paperwork
* Office politics in some groups in ridiculous
* Health Benefits plans have become more out-of-pocket costly over the last 2-3 years.
* Not much room for growth unless you know people higher up.

summary: Great place to start a career.
advice: Make sure that employees are utilized to their full extent. Some employees pay for the lack of focus displayed by lower quality employees.
pros: A great place to start a career when interested in joining the financial services industry. JPMC gives a good solid foundation for finance.
cons: It is a very large organization with a confusing hierarchy. The Investment Bank is undoubtedly the most important part of the bank, overshadowing other key parts. The large aspect of the organization also allows others to hide behind the mass hysteria of over 200,000 employees.

advice:
Don't be afraid to fire a problematic person. Who cares if they are meeting or exceeding their daily productive levels. If they are contributing to, or causing a problem, fire them. Don't pass the buck to another supervisor by transferring. Also, when hiring, choose people that are professional! Doing this in the first place will cut out many of the problems caused by hiring everyone under the sun. If they can't be bothered to dress appropriately or even tuck in their shirt and show a basic level of respect for authority, do not trust them with the biggest investment people will likely ever make! 
Pay attention to supervisors who play favorites. These people do not need to be in charge of anyone and allowing them to do so just creates a poor company culture.
pros: Fast paced environment; always something to be done; looks great on a resume; lots of potential for learning new aspects of the mortgage business; great benefits and perks; lots of potential for lateral moves and promotions; over time availability
cons:
The leadership at the supervisory (and above) is very spotty. In some departments you will have great higher-ups who actively get involved in the individual successes of their teams; while in others you have a culture of stagnation and disinterest in anything other than the bottom line. Having a supervisor who cares very little for your career growth makes it difficult to give all that you can.
Favoritism is also a large problem. I worked in two different departments and I have noticed that both of the supervisors for these departments will play favorites and rain praise and awards down onto the heads of their chosen few, allowing them to get away with many things that would get a lesser person fired or chewed out. This makes securing the team lead position is very problematic, because oftentimes those who are best for the job, but not the favorites, will get pushed to the sidelines during the application and interview process. 
Gossip and general sophomoric behavior runs rampant in throughout the location. It is especially prominent in areas in which there is very little direct supervision (my area). Employees will constantly be standing around and talking about a myriad of topics- many of them have no place in a professional environment, and despite the number of times I have brought it to the attention of management, the problems never get solved, and a band-aid of red tape gets applied for a few months. A prime example of sophomoric behavior is the constant presence of trash (empty drink bottles and candy wrappers) that get left behind by employees too lazy to pick one of the 14 trash bins located within the secure work area. This has prompted many halfhearted bans on food and drink within this area, yet, the problem never seems to get solved for more than a few months at a time.
All of these problems lead to a culture of disinterest in the very policies that attempt to guide the company in the correct direction. A prime and, to me, most telling example of this very disinterest is the recent case of an employee who for two years brought his cellphone into the secure area and took pictures of himself in the bathroom, then posted them to his facebook. We are not allowed to have anything that has a camera or could be used to store private customer information on our person when we enter the work-floor and especially not when we enter the file storage area. This is a security violation of the first order and is generally a fire-able offense simply because that person has now potentially exposed sensitive customer information to the world. The violator of this policy got a slap on the wrist from HR and is still walking around, doing very little work and most likely still taking selfies in the bathrooms.

advice: None, they're great. You've got to take responsibility to ask questions if you need help with anything.
pros:
-Easy Job with decent pay; 10% Shift Differential for more than 1/2 hours worked after 12:30pm and 15% differential for working Overnight
-Friendly Environment
-Great Training Program
-Ability for Lateral Movement and Growth; Managers really focus on your growth as an individual
-Overtime Always Available
-Great Benefits
-Company matches 3% for 401k
-The ONLY way to get promoted is to have EXCELLENT adherence
cons:
-Constantly Changing Rules & Regulations; difficult to stay informed
-Pressure In Statistics You Cannot Change but are responsible for upholding

advice:
Promote people based on merit.  
Don't implement processes before they are clearly defined and thought out.  People need direction and guidance.  They don't need a hastily slapped together application/process which is going to do nothing but confuse people and decrease efficiency in the work environment.
pros: Stable company in a tough economy.  Great benefits package, along with the ability to purchase stock at a 5% discount.
cons:
Poor long term strategy.
No advancement opportunities based on merit.
Bureaucratic environment with uneducated and unmotivated people.  
Plan on working here for ten plus years to get any advancement.

advice: Pick your managers better, hard working employees shouldn't be penalized for the horrible managers.
pros: I loved who I worked with, where I worked and what I did. I received a "promotion" after a year and a half of working there and was super excited. Average pay, learned a lot!
cons: The management at the new job was the worst I got fired after only working one month for being late. They considered me being sick and then coming in late the next day and getting sent home from being too sick as "excessive tardies".

advice: When promoting from within, please offer compensation that is consistent with the market.  Too often I see promotions in which the employ gets a 7-10% pay raise regardless of how big the advancement is.
pros: Great training and retirement benefits.  Overall a good company and great place to start your career.
cons: Compensation is pretty low. I've been with the company for 13 years and we were one of the highest paying banks when I started and now we're at the bottom.  Everyone that leaves the bank seems to find better compensation outside of the firm.

advice: Senior management needs to address the high turnover in the group.  This holds true particularly when the turnover is driven, not by the nature of the work, but by specific people in middle management.
pros: There is relatively flat structure so there is ample opportunity to learn from other groups including the FO.  The co-workers were a pleasure to work with, and internal mobility was excellent.
cons: The hours were very long no matter what group you are in.  The company is big so there is alot of red tape and inefficiency.

summary: Elitist mentality, long hours with stagnant income
advice: The "pay for performance culture" should actually include employees below the Executive Director level in the "pay" component. Invest in the infrastructure - too many manual and broken processes which cause client issues.
pros: not likely to have layoffs during down markets like other banks and asset managers. opportunity work in many locations but to advance you need to be in Manhattan
cons: Elitist mentality - if you didn't go to the right schools then you have very limited opportunities for advancement beyond a certain level. Executive management will work subordinates to death.

summary: Excellent career mobility and many opportunities to learn but corporate culture can be tough to negotiate
pros: Good benefits, decent work/life balance - at least by Wall St standards.  Inclusive behavior toward team members is highly encouraged.  Zero tolerance for any form of discriminatory behavior toward current or prospective coworkers.  Strong, consistent emphasis on employee career development and internal mobility.
cons: Corporate culture can be tough to negotiate, due to geographical and line-of-business inconsistencies, and skews toward being political.  Compensation may not be that great (compared to industry averages) for roles that do not generate revenue.

advice: Create customers for life rather than going after short term sales that can turn people off.
pros: You get a lot of experience and learn a lot about different sales techniques.  Chase has great products compared to other banks.
cons: You should understand going into this job that you are in retail sales.  This is not a high level professional position.  You are selling checking accounts and then up-selling additional products like credit cards and online banking.  You will be required to hit certain quotas.  It's like working at a cell phone store.

summary: Great place for experience, but need to jump ship to make the real money.
advice: You should not promote a place that encourages you to find another job within another company, rather than just fairly compensate your employee.  Chase is very stingy with salary and negotiation, they should actually calculate geographical averages rather than utilize the completely senseless means of calculating this number now.
pros: Bountiful amount of vacation, sick, personal and holiday time.  You almost get too many days off if there is such a thing.  Diverse environment and people, Chase is a melting pot for many, many cultures.  Certain departments will really take care of you in terms of raises and bonuses, however not all departments are that giving.  Chase also utilizes the latest technology which maximizes efficiency in the office.
cons: While Chase does have many notable upsides, their shortcomings unfortunately take the spotlight. Their toxic politics and unfair business practice make it a stressful place to work.  They would rather you quit and get more money from another company, and then match you a year later if you came back, rather than just give you a good raise that you deserve.  That is sad.  I started with the firm almost 8 years ago and I took home more money on my 1st day than what I make now.  They took wind that as an hourly employee, I made too much money in overtime.  I was then 'promoted' to a salary position which was pretty much my base salary, minus all of the OT.  I made 16k in OT one year, so imagine the significant pay cut I endured.  I then 'promoted' several other times as a lateral move and received no additional compensation other than a yearly 1% merit increase.  I finally did receive 1 raise as a result of a promotion, but out of 5 promotions they still fell very short of what's fair.   My work kept piling up, and then was approached about training to be a code programmer and taking on the job.  This is a very complex job and Chase paid quite a bit of money to train me and also promised a raise.  I did the job for over a year and had to apply within the company for another position just to actually get a raise and job title change.
