advice: Next time, don't take risks that put the company in line for failure and seizure by the goverment to be sold off.
pros: The location in DT Seattle was perfect, so close to metro and main attractions like Pike Place Market. Our team made coming to work a pleasure.
cons: There wasn't a whole bunch of great communication between teams in the bank. A lot of wasted technology was built but never used.

summary: Great company, Respected brand name,Good networking opportunities, and decent employee benifits.
advice: Reward and retain talent, encourage mobility.
pros: Good place to expand your network with various teams and will be a useful for future career advancement but nothing else. Large organization with typical structural issues and sometime you feel like you get lost.
cons: The downside is the room for growth is miminal and the salary increases are very low. keeep changing leadership at sr.level and low level of employee satisifaction.

summary: JP Morgan Chase transition employee in Seattle
advice: None.
pros: Colleagues in New Jersey and Ohio were supportive, responsive and a pleasure to work with.  They recognized hard work and extra effort and appreciate that issues could affect timing of deliverables.
cons: Lack of local opportunities within my area of expertise was discouraging after Chase completed my transition.  There was a discussion of prospective opportunities in New Jersey but I was not up to the move.

summary: Stay Away!! They are offshoring a ton of work to Mumbai!!
advice: Stop force ranking employees. Let actual managers rank employees not VP's setting in a conference room and deciding who is good and who is not good. After the rankings are established your review is written to your "ranking" is NOT acceptable!
pros: Offer full pay and benefits to anyone who is in the military that is called up to go to war.
cons: The place has really gone down hill! Quickly!! They are putting employees on written warning for being on the internet durning their lunch break in order to fire them! Don't go to work here! You will regret it!!!

advice: Management is outstanding. Workflow could be improved by streamlining the way in which approval is given for risk taking activities.
pros: Great opportunities for career advancement. Extensive resources available for professional development. Culture is very inclusive and welcoming, though still competitive.
cons: A very large organisation means that it can be difficult to see the direct result of the work that you do. Very structured and laboured approach to risk.

summary: a great place for a career
advice: Bring back the options for a Normal Health Insurance.
pros: There are opportunities everywhere, different LOB's different areas of expertice. If you don't like what you are doing move on to another area or role.  Great Comp and Benefits, although the new Health insurance is weak and not what i would ultimately want in my Medical plan.
cons: be ready for change, it is around every corner of the organization.

summary: The company in a nut shell
advice: Your screening process when it comes to internal employees is to stringent. You're loosing talent because your initial expectations are to high. No two jobs are similar, being that finance is all related you have to give some time (4 weeks) for an employee to get the hang of things.
pros: They are very flexible with my time (call outs, sick days, and vacation time.)
cons: Internal mobility lacks, Pay is low.

advice: The culture from merging so many companies for such a long time has created an uber political and bigoted environment. Fiefdoms and dog-eat-dog serve little purpose in getting the job done.
pros: There are many projects that provide interesting problem solving opportunities. But the tendency is to manage "up"and toady to management thus the information necessary to be successful is often kept from you.
cons: It is impossible for women to rise in JPMC. There are a handful of Female MD's and they are figure heads. Office Politics and gamesmanship lead the career path at JP Morgan not work well done. Very stressful arrogant place to work.

advice: Stop being so selfish, treat your employees better, stop wasting time scheduling pointless meetings, and stop forcing your employees to take the blame for your mistakes
pros: This job Pays pretty well and the work load is not heavy, nice vacation time, and the ability to work from home and travel is a plus
cons: Management is terrible, unreliable, does not back up their employees, play the blame game, do anything to make themselves not look bad

advice: Management is decent and caring. There is rarely any feeling of neglect or indifference to the employees. All make an effort to get to know their team.
pros: The salary is good. There are plenty of opportunities to move around. There is always work to do. People are always willing to help.
cons: The hours can get long. You will have to be on top of a number of things on a daily basis.

pros: Great benefits, great technology and access to the finest training tools. The company is always growing and trying to meet the needs of the always evolving banking world.
cons: The company can sometimes be very widget based and not always do what is right for the client. The priorities of the company can change on a quarterly basis and can be tough to follow, especially when what's right for the client should always come first.

summary: Think carefully about working for JPM
advice:
Get rid of the restrictions on the 2 year and 3 year programs. 
Allow employees to apply within all JPM after a year.
Dont waste the money spent on training by allowing employees to go external
pros:
Famous Company
Alot to learn
Decent compensation.
Industry leader
cons:
Company is too big, jobs are very focused and cannot see big picture
All sort of 2 year 3 year programs designed to restrict your ability to transfer internally

advice: Relax, the world will not end if you don't get everything done today.
pros: None.  Never work for a bank.  A friend told me this when we were acquired and I learned how right he was.
cons: Management is very knee jerk reaction.  Everything is a firedrill.  They treat you like garbage and on the first of the month for closing the month they have people there until after midnight sometimes...

advice: I really don't have any advise to management at JPMorgan Chase. It was a very nice place to work, and I loved the co-workers that I had.
pros: JPMorgan Chase is a Great place to work, depending on your senior managers, but that is typical with any job.
cons: I really don't have any complaints about JPMorgan Chase. It was a very nice place to work, and I loved the co-workers that I had.

summary: Great first job but get out while you can, hard to network out of Delaware once you've stayed too long
advice: To retain top talent you need to compensate them for their value.
pros: Great name on the resume, lots of opportunities to learn and network if you are motivated, very good job security
cons: Job satisfaction is minimal, easy to get caught in the cycle of the never ended "BAU" work, low salary, no overtime

advice: great company, but stop being cheap
pros: really good company that gives its employees the opportunity to take risks on projects and allow career growth. furthermore, the working environment of the debts that i've worked in were not too pretentious and serious. can have fun in the office and still get the job done.
cons: Employees brought up internally normally suffer from lower salaries vs their counterparts in other firms

advice: Don't go to colleges and pitch this as an alternative to the traditional investment banking -> HF/PE path. It's not. It's an operational business, where mobility outside of the firm is difficult.
pros: Good pay despite not that much work at all on the investor services side. Easy to slide by.
cons: As an associate in investor services, you can really only become valuable within the JPM machine.. it is difficult to translate elsewhere.

advice: In order to further enhance our customer service expirience we must learn to adapt to locations that cannot meet high balance requirments. Account types should be created based on the market. that is the only change i see Chase having to make
pros: The benefits are great, the compensation is great, the leadership is great
cons: No consideration to certain demographics as far as accounts that fit the financial needs of low to moderate income locations

summary: Chase is not a place for overall professional growth for entry level positions, unless come in with valuable experience.
advice: If you worked extremely hard, taken the steps to apply for other jobs within the organization, and presented yourself professionaly throughout that process and have not experienced "career growth" within 1.5 years, then it's time move on.
pros: Good place to start a career to gain experience in banking.
cons: Very easy to get in trapped in doing the same job and not experience professional growth.  It's up to you to build your career and depending on the situation, you're better off leaving and gaining additional experience elsewhere.

summary: My experience with JPMorgan Chase has been challenging and rewarding.
advice: Continue to share what company is doing to prepare for changes in requlatory enviroment and financial reform.
pros: Financial services industry leader.  Resources to help customers with all financial needs.  Focus on creating great employee and customer experience.  Leading market share in major markets.  Continuing to invest in technology and people.
cons: Changes in industry have forced company to eliminate and/or downsize programs/departments.

advice: Need to treat staff like humans.  I was told I was to nice to my team. Who always made every deadline and worked hard everyday.  Never ask your Manager to change information on a review to justify wanting people in there department to be reassigned.
pros: Overall company is great just not some departments.  Loved my co-workers and benefits.
cons: Senior management needs personal conduct training.  Treat all staff members the same.

advice: better training needs to be provided to new and existing employees
pros: Great Benefits, plenty of paid time off, flexible work schedule, awesome leave policy, friendly managment, open door policy, overall great place to work.
cons: lack of training, you have to be able to read a guide and pretty much train yourslef but they are very open to questions an concerns. I work in the Mortgage department and the workload is downsizing fast.

advice: Act like you care about the employees.
pros: It brought in a pay check. The best thing about this job is that you had weekends off. During high volumes, there may be extra hours available on weekends.
cons:
During low volumes people were asked to go home. It's a good place for students to work for extra cash but I don't see how people can support families with that kind of instability. 
You're a cog in a machine.

pros: Benefits and pay are fair and generally in alignment with the industry.  There are still a number of high quality people there.  The brand is still respected on the street and with clients.
cons: Has become cliquish--based on who you know, not what you know.  Constant change in strategy and management is disruptive and confusing.  Sadly, people are becoming quiet and reluctant to raise issues -- not good from a cultural perspective.

advice: The best branch managers work with their staff as a team and continuously coach them.
pros: Great training program will familiarize you with everything you need to know. You do not need a banking background prior to working for Chase in order to be successful. They will train you well.
cons: Branch managers can be hit or miss as far as how supportive they are your development and enabling your success.

summary: Great Company / Too Big To Be Recongnised
advice: Provide a mechanism for cross training in the technical / IT realm.  This go a long way to retain  your employees and keep them interested.
pros: The largest infrastructure you would EVER see in a lifetime!!!!  A diverse team.  Exposure to any relevant hardware imaginable.
cons: Because they are so large you have to specialize in one specific area.  There is no room for cross training.

advice: When you hire a new Loan Officer give them enough training to be able to go out to the Branch and hit above and beyond their goals!
pros: Decent pay, good benefits, consistently changing commission payout
cons: Regional manager just puts you in a branch, says they will give you training on their systems and be their to help you succeed at your job. Doesn't even show up or help you out, makes false promises.

advice: Senior senior leaders need to change the culture and actually execute on what they preach.
pros: working remote, close to public transportation, peers.
cons: silos, having to manage up, no motivation to innovate or change. salary is way below market. no job mobility (despite what they say, it doesn't exist. Recruiters treats internal employees the same as external employees). Not required to have onsite management, call me old school but managers need to be onsite.

advice: listen to your employees, they have their ears to the customer and hear every word.
pros: There are so many pros, but just to name a few,  Pay, Benefits, the people you work with and the people you work for. Its a great job, but you have to love what you do.
cons: you can get burned out if you let stress get you and keep you down, always remember its a business and that you shouldn't take it personal

advice: Be more interactive with your peers, instead of planning where will you have lunch... or what will you do on your weekends...
pros: Good to great benefits, Diversity was outstanding
cons: No advancement, unless you know someone internally... some positions can be available but you have to go thru the whole motion of applying, just to learn that someone else got it.. as the saying goes ... it's not what you know but who you know... Cannot keep up with the changes.... Some supervisors are as arrogant as they can come.... they seem geared to have you set up for failure if you're not liked... very discouraging...

advice: My direct managers for the most part have been fantastic. I have no real complaints. Its a great jumping off point, and if you are ambitious then you will know what you need to do.
pros: Great company training if you do not know the business.They are very knowledgeable and provide extensive information.
cons: If you are doing well and the department is struggling it is nearly impossible to move up because you become a commodity to the department.

summary: I would rather say "paper or plastic" than to work here...RUN..FAST
advice: Learn your jobs, and train employees instead of going to the bars during lunch
pros: Name on resume looks good
cons: Systems are old, (felt like I was in 1993) training is nonexistent, literally have to fight to learn job, high turnover, employees quit left and right with zero notice. Pay isn't great, morale is awful, health insurance is the worst available plans under cigna and united healthcare. The cons can go on for LIFE...Just run! If you take a job here make sure it's short term just so you have the name on your resume.

pros:
The pay is pretty good for midwest COL, but forcing employees to return to the office is causing the bank to absolutely hemorrhage talent.

?

NOT WORTH THE "GOOD" SALARY

advice: Create smaller internal organizations that are well funded.  It's far too big to effectively manage staff and provide rewards from the senior management level.
pros: Generally smart people, challenges (some good, some bad [see cons]).  Great environment to learn about managing through a large company.
cons: Extremely bureaucratic, difficult to stand out or execute on ideas.  Managing through a large company often means its slow to implement on great ideas effectively.

advice: Please check on your Branch Manager, not all are fair, doing the right thing for the employee, and annual performance reviewed were based on favoritism not actual work performed.
pros: Great benefits, high-tech software, prepare staffs well with proper training systems, promoted within.
cons: Chase does not seem to value the person to person interaction any longer. Adding Machines and letting go of their good employees. Some Manager played favoritism and not accurate on their performance review.

pros: Amazing WLB, and work with caring managers

advice: Stop playing favorites and treat everyone equally. Recognize the good and take proper action with the poor performers especially if they are in management.
pros: Great overtime if you are a non exempt employee. Good work/life balance. Opportunities to advance if you know the right people.
cons: Dealing with management who have no clue what they are doing. Hard workers do bit get properly recognized unless they are a a favorite.

summary: The experience at JP Morgan was great, great company to work for with excellent benefits.

pros: Company offers in house transfers, you have to be flexible to work for JP Morgan Chase.
cons: Sometimes your position may change so therefore you must be flexible.

pros: The company provides strong health benefits and retirement plans, along with somewhat mindful (albeit random) employee perks.

Great place for those who enjoy being challenged and  surpassing expectations

Provides the sense that one was  part of a small team even though WaMu was a fairly large corporation

Flexibility in how challenges are approached, how work is delivered
cons: It now no longer exists

summary: Pretty decent workplace, good benefits and reasonable office culture.

cons: I was in a support department, so there was essentially zero chance of advancement. Company was not supportive of growing into other areas. I may have stayed there if there had been more opportunity.

summary: Great company. You know where you stand with the organization.
advice: Management training is needed sometimes to know how to deal with people properly. Old school management does not work in todays environment. Value people.
pros: May opportunities to advance. Great compensation package. Great vacation time and PTO.
cons: Network type company. Who you know. A bit of less flexible around work hours.

advice: Need to start focusing on what really matters. Too much time spent checking the box on stuff instead of doing the work and making sure it is done right.

advice: I actually respect Jamie Dimon for what he has done to the company and survived through the meltdown, as well as how he fought his way back to Wal St.
pros:
Relatively competent yet down-to-earth people to work with. 
Promotes teamwork and diversity. 
Helps you find and move within the company, georgraphically and industry-wise.
cons:
Relatively lower salary base + bonus compared to its peers. 
Typical long hours, but perhaps not much recognition for junior employees.

advice: Be willing to spend time with the employees to obtain lending authority.  Sometimes it takes longer than the 90 days given to obtain it.  Good Employers are willing to help and train their employees to succeed- not just throw them out to do it on their own.
pros: Salary, challenged at work, learning new information
cons: Management not supportive, not helpful, not an open door policy.  Not willing to help get you up to speed and communicate updates to you.

advice: politics is the name of the game. Reputation is everything
pros: working at a global organization is a great opportunity to network and rub elbows with key members of the financial industry who can help develop your career.
cons: the saying at JPM is that the only constant is change. I average a new manager every 5 months which dampens salary and promotion. JPM is also incredibly cheap. Budget cuts are the norm.

advice: Leadership was out of touch with the inner workings of the company, they were all too concerned about the stock price and not the stability of the company. GREED!
pros: Great work life balance, ability to take time off as needed. Great benefits packages, IE Health, 401k medical, dental vision etc.
cons: Inability to have a definitive career path with the wall of the company. Managers were more concerned about their we;; being than ensuring eployees had a natural career progression

advice: Rein in the dilution of engineering talent in IT. Keep up the good work which has made J.P the best bank to work for.
pros: Considerate management and friendly colleagues. The bank has effectively encouraged a culture of healthy work-life balance and employees take pride in wearing the JP brand.
cons: Proliferation of program managers in IT with neither background nor interest in technology. Foolish obsession with hiring/retaining millennials - even at the cost of hardworking and more talented senior talent.

advice:
Improve on the career development program available to the employee.
The performance management central should be continued, cos it is a great idea.
pros: The employees are very friendly and the manager cared about my personal development. I had a lot of work to do and, I just wasn't sitting around.
cons: It is a very big company so it's easy to get lost in the crowd. One has to take responsibility or else will be kicked aside.

advice: Listen to employees! More importantly, don't just shuffle people around when a position opens up; start promoting within to those that have demonstrated the necessary skills to suceed
pros: Great co-workers and nice benefits.

advice: More management training to acknowledge hard work & successful employees. Regular employee development/mentoring to provide positive consistent growth.
pros:
Ability to be sponsored for FINRA licensing & to be paid to study 8 hours per day while you complete the program.

Ability to advance into new careers/fields of interest
cons: Be prepared for a lateral move i.e. a painstaking approval process for any salary increase when you are promoted with little chance to be paid fair market value for your position

advice: Do what's right and clients and employees benefit.  Keep the natives happy and the firm will become more profitable.
pros: Good benefits, 401k, and free checking for employees
cons: The company has moral issues.  There are many, many, many articles about JP Morgan in Forbes and the New York Times.  Simply do a web search.  It is ALL about sales and increasing revenue at any cost.  That's not ethical.

jobTitle: IT Support Role Level I and II

advice: Give employees an opportunity to be certified and work hard and reward them for working hard and you will retain the best but failure to do so and you will get the bare minimum performance until they quit and find an employer who will.

cons: Modern day slavery, very little pay, expect 24 hours from you in an 8 hour day, too much politics and lies from the top of management on down, no reward for hard work all year especialy if you are in an IT support role level 1, 2, and 3

summary: Good company for learning and advancement
advice: The initial onboarding of employees should be more structured including traiing of critical background into the environment for which an employee is working.

cons: Not a 9 to 5 environment. Be prepared to work long hours to be very successful.

advice: i do not believe that an employees career development should lie solely in the hands of management. we control our own paths within the company telling me otherwise is why i no longer work for them. pros: staff is very supportive of your current role within the company.
cons: Senior management only cares about covering their own tails.

cons: Of course with any large corporation, imagination and personality is discouraged and you will deal with the hierarchical structure.  Very vanilla culture.

summary: Working with J.P Morgan was a great experience. I learned things about loans to buy properties.

summary: Terrible technology stack, terrible leadership and a tragically awful work-life balance
advice:
Fix the work life balance.  Turnover was so high because you treated your developers so poorly.  The great ones all left and you were left with the ones who couldn't find something better.  

You have to break the cycle or you will never be an employer of choice, just an employer of last resort.
pros: Compensation was good.  I had four weeks of vacation and then a few personal days and a week of sick time on top of that starting right away from day one.  Base pay was average for the local banks, but a bit above average for the area.  I did not stay long enough to receive a bonus.
cons:
Terrible technology stack, terrible leadership, and a tragically awful work-life balance.  You will carry a pager, work weekends, late nights and early mornings.  My team was also Agile, but in name only.  The focus was project based timelines rather than product based change management. 

I was on a team of 12 (way too large for Scrum or Agile) and we had 3 teams and one of the Scrum teams was closer to 20.  Yet with nearly 50 employees, we only had 8 full timers.  As a full time employee, when the project slips because it can't adapt to change, all the pressure will fall on the handful of full time employees and you will be ground down with long hours and weekend shifts supporting a project built by contractors.  

JP Morgan is a fine place to work if you can get into a small, noncritical project.  But if you get pulled into any new development, you will be stretched way beyond industry norms working with the cheapest contracting labor.  While the pay was good, my wife got pregnant and with such an awful work life balance I had to leave.  If you have young kids that you want to spend time with, do NOT come here.

Culturally, senior leadership felt very strongly that it was best to be second and to follow the industry leaders because it was much cheaper than taking risks and inventing something novel outright.  Senior leadership had several townhalls/meetings expounding upon this ideal.  The problem with this approach was after somebody succeeded with a specific project JP Morgan would have to run twice as fast as the original inventor in order to launch fast enough to garner any significant market share.  As such, any new development projects were already way behind schedule and had overtly unrealistic expectations causing pretty widespread burnout among full time employees.  

As a final aside, this shop is 95% Indian males within the Wilmington development groups.  JP Morgan has a much, MUCH higher proportion of Indians than the surrounding employers.  It was not a problem, but the complete lack of diversity was a bit surprising for a fortune 500 company.

summary: RUN as fast and as far as you can from this place
advice: Treat your call center employees with some respect. Don't pretend like the PTO you offer up is really a benefit when you don't have much availability to actually use it.  Don't give us an in house doctor and then punish us if we have to go to that doctor because we're genuinely sick. Don't treat us like we're criminals because we get sick or have to go to the bathroom or go to get water to stay hydrated.  At Chase we are all definitely guilty until proven innocent and even then we're still punished.
pros: The benefits are good, IF you get to use them.  There is literally nothing else good about this company.
cons:
The company doesn't care about their employees. They allow abusive calls and are very restricting. You can't even use the bathroom unless your on your break. 

Start treating your employees like humans. We have family we want to spend the holidays with. We get emotional, verbally and mentally abused by the customers and we have to suck it up. You don't need to be open 24/7, 365 days a year. Give people a chance to spend the holidays with their families. 

Chained to a desk for 8 hours every day. You get a 30 min lunch and 2/ 15 min breaks, literally from the second you log off your phone till the second you log back on and are available to take calls.  That means you honestly get about 6 minutes of break and maybe 15 minutes to eat lunch and be sitting down and ready to log back in and be taking calls.  Forget about going to the bathroom during the day.  Micro managed to death.  No job safety whatsoever even if you are doing a fantastic job. Then there are the call center call audits where they spend d 10 minutes telling you how you've failed every little detail of the call.  Not one word of praise or encouragement, only beaten down because you either talked too long and didn't dispatch a customer quick enough, or you failed one or more of the oh so precious Chase procedures that change almost daily.  The metrics are pretty much impossible to reach, and you will absolutely be beaten up daily if you're not reaching those 3 minute max call times and ready to jump on the next call the very next second.  There's even a metric to measure your ability to account for every second of your shift. The pressure is intense and you know you're being failed at every turn, even if you did the right thing and genuinely took care of the customer. 

Give call center employees an extra 20 minutes for bathroom breaks throughout the day. We're not camels and it actually causes severe health issues to hold it for 6 to 8 hours every single day. Let people calm down for a few minutes after a rough call, or go to the in house Dr without making them use vacation time, AND when that happens, we get an occurrence for a non scheduled vacation time. They go on about having an in house doctor, but you get punished if you have to go see that doctor during your shift. They write you up for it AND they steal your PTO, AND they nick you for the unscheduled absence. 

Training is a joke. You get told how to do this or that in training and then when you're in the next phase of getting to your permanent position you're told contradicting procedures, and then even more contradictory information comes along every day. They intentionally keep changing procedures so you're always off balance and they can then give you a bad review and keep you at the low, low, low salary that you're barely surviving on. 

The pay is so embarrassingly low that it's barely enough to make ends meet. Chase is the definition of living paycheck to paycheck. 

They start you out with three weeks of vacation, but you'll never get to actually use it and of course you lose any unused at the end of the year. Work every holiday unless you have seniority and take the small allotments of available holidays so every other unlucky employee has to be chained to their desk while their families are at home where they should be, celebrating without you.

advice: Way too much to list here

Onsite Starbucks 
Tasty cafeteria food
cons:
Worst experience I've had out of 3 of the largest financial services firms. Management is incompetent and micromanages, if you think of that guy who who is all about face time and says yes to whatever his boss asks of him only to burden the team, this will be who your manager is. They are where they are because they were too stupid to see the writing on the wall and go elsewhere. These are not people who you want to have any influence on your career or your day to day work. 

Environment is chaos. Everything is urgent, everything was needed yesterday, even though it was asked for today. Training is extremely poor due to high turnover (at least on my team.) You'll be handed an SOP that is outdated or incomplete, yet your manager will swear by it and then berate you when you can't use it.  Your apology for his mistake is that you have to update it ASAP. If you are lucky, you might not be berated by the colleague who was supposed to train you but did a terrible job because he/she is also working on another team. Btw, the open roles on your team will be back 
filled in Poland.

So many roles and regions were consolidated into your role that you will need access to 20+ systems to do your job on a daily basis. And btw, you'll have to submit your own access requests because your team either doesn't have time or doesn't remember how to do it because there are so many. You'll then have to hound the IT teams about granting it because they are incredibly under resourced. 

Colleagues are grumpy, overworked, overwhelmed, several people on my team taking days off due to stress. Huge number of people heading to the health center on a daily basis due to emotional breakdowns because they can no longer take the abuse, intense micromanaging, and overall negative work environment. 

It's not worth your stress or time. Focus on other companies.

From there once that group had the opportunity I was pushed onto yet another middle office team (where I was above the title team manager and had to report to someone else until this person was promoted). I the short time I was at JPMorgan (just over 3 years) I had 8 different managers.
Training is non existent, you are given links to soft copies of manuals that describe the roles and responsibilities (these "manuals" are out of date and often have numerous updates located in places other then the manual itself with no guidance on where the links to the information is located (read that to be hidden - the company website is horrible to navigate).
When you have questions/issues (human resources/technology) there is no number to call (you don't have an assigned HR person) and everything is submitted via electronic "tickets" that often can take several days to get a response (in one case my computer crashed and it took 2 1/2 days before there was a response from the technology team - I just sat there and read a book or played games on my phone (Some of the tickets I raised were never completed after 3 years. Teams would pass the problem around until no one else was left to handle it and they would mark it resolved even though nothing was fixed). The technology is junk,  most so over engineered that it doesn't work with other systems and most of the time is developed with no input from the team that uses it or any consideration to how it is going to work (or in most cases not work) with the existing processes that are in place. All of the available web browsers were so out of date that most did not support the functions required to complete your work.
The last group I worked in had no synergy between the teams, in fact management had set up the matrix reports for individual performance that adversarial relationship dominated the work place and left everyone in terrible state of mind (the group I was in got so fed up with management inability to fix the problems over 65% left for external or internal positions in 6 months and no one was replaced - adding that much more stress to everyones lives).
Business units are so walled off from one another that policies/procedures are put in place that do not work with any other groups and then it is a mad scramble to find workarounds that correct the problems. Also policies and procedures are changed more often then underwear.
To sum it up a terrible place to work, so bad that I would only recommend it to someone that I hated and never to someone I liked.

summary: Working in the Real Estate & Facilities Department was a disappointing experience
advice: People and Real Estate are some of your greatest assets. I would expect one of the largest banks in the world to be a more well oiled machine. The person who was our leader was not leading. He would point fingers and intimidate. The moral was low. End users would abuse or try to abuse me and other Project Managers. I understood their frustration, but it should not be tolerated.
pros: Nice office space, great location in NYC. There were some really nice, knowledgeable people that I worked with. Salary and benefits were good.
cons:
1.) The position I was being hired for was nothing like what was described during my interview. The size of the projects were smaller and dollar value was well below what I was told prior to being hired. It felt like I took five steps back career-wise. 
2.) I sat down on numerous occasions with my immediate supervisor, to discuss the "gap" between his understanding and my understanding of the position I was hired for. I was appalled by his attitude. When I pressed him on certain points, he later confessed that I was not the first person to have these issues. He had heard it before.... I also found the person (thru LinkedIn) who held this position prior to me, and she quit because of the same issues. Nothing was going to change. 
3.) Many of my immediate co-workers were miserable. They hated their job and hated the work. Some were former Bear-Stern Facilities people and felt grateful to have a job. This made for a very low moral work environment.
4.) There were several employees that I had to work with that were lazy, lied and withheld important information that was needed to keep the projects moving forward. I would ask for the information in-person, during meetings and as an email as a follow up. Once I would copy our supervisor, along with his boss, these employees would somehow "remember" the information and provide it. 
5.) I found many of the people I worked with were uneducated and lacked the basic understanding of construction, furniture or how to plan a facilities move. They worked their way up in the company but did not have a clue because they were not trained. Conversations had to be dumbed down constantly. Often I stopped to explain whatever it was that my co-worker didn't understand, and I would wonder what else they needed to know so I was not surprised at any point in the process.  
6.) There were a few people I worked with that were "loud talkers". There were small conference rooms available for conference calls or calls that could be made on speaker phone. Why these few felt it was okay to hear their entire conversation, I will never understand. 
7.) Somehow the end users felt it was okay to complain and send nasty emails to me directly, about how it was not acceptable that their new workstation was smaller than their old workstation because they worked at the company for x number of years / or that their job title required a larger workstation. I felt like a punching bag.... I would remind these people that the cubicle size was determined by the higher ups and not me. 
8.) The IT people were impossible to deal with. They could not commit to a date to move equipment... even something as small as a fax machine. So it became impossible to schedule the movers and the furniture people until the IT people could provide a time and date. IT somehow did not have to work with others. 
9.) The vendors were all very nice and very patient. It was hard to not provide them what they needed in a timely manner. It was even harder each week to hear my immediate supervisor to remind us all in the weekly meeting, that "we hand out the lollipops, so they (the vendors) can wait." 
10.) We had a department that took care of all of the artwork thru-out all of the office spaces. I sent out many emails to this department giving them the location of the artwork, the day and time period that this artwork needed to be moved. I also provided them with two names of contacts for people who worked on the floor in question. I copied everyone on these emails so everyone had the same information. On the day the artwork was to be moved, the art movers went to the wrong floor and started taking artwork down off the office walls in occupied areas. I was in meetings in another state, no where near this office space and was bombarded by phone calls / texts / emails. Anyone who would have taken a half a second to look at the information that was provided would have seen that the art movers were on the wrong floor. But instead... they called my boss. They told him that I made a HUGE mistake. He calls me up ranting and raving. And when I forward to him the emails he has been copied on, he does not apologize for his behavior. 

In conclusion: I was at this job for three miserable months. If the economy would have been better, I would have quit after two weeks. I was not a good fit for this position and the department was not a good fit for me. I am sure there are some great departments to work in, but I did not find any.

advice:
Unless you want to see a mass exodus of your employees, these problems 
need to be fixed.  Morale in the branches is at an all time low. Give

base salary should too. Value your employees, move long term employees 
up in the company
pros: Good benefits, strong brand name, decent health care plan, good branch systems and technology and good training
cons:
Company has completely neglected its employees over the past 2 years.  
In 5 years, I have not received a raise despite having stellar reviews 
every single year.  Staffing has seriously been cut in half over the 
past year which leaves double the workload for the remaining staff.  I 
have personally been asked to act as "manager on duty" several times 
over the past 2 years.  A position that requires more responsibility 
but with less pay.  Yes, LESS pay, because the time you are spending 
performing management tasks reduces the amount of time you could be 
earning incentive pay through sales.  In the past year the company 
demoted a huge number of higher level positions including assistant branch 
mgrs who have been with the company for 30 plus yrs.  Also District 
mgmt position has been eliminated.  Base pay is $39,500(same as it was 
when I started 5 yrs ago) In some parts of the country that's not bad, 
but in Long Island NY, that is embarrassing. The equivalent position at 
Bank of America down the street is $60,000 for a licensed  banker.  
Upper management will tell you that the base is so low because the 
incentive plan is so good.  What they don't tell you is that only the 
top 5% of bankers really do great numbers in terms of incentive.  And I 
will say, that for the top 1%, Chase gives the opportunity to do great! 
  But for everyone else, the struggle is real!  I'm at about the top 20% 
of all bankers and only made about $17k in commissions.  That's still 
below the Starting Base Salary at Bank of America.  Opportunity for 
advancement is a joke.  They make false promises, put you on 
development plans that amount to nothing and place no value in the time 
that you've spent with the organization. The company recently settled a 
class action law suit over things like not properly paying overtime, 
requiring employees to wear company apparel but not paying for it, and 
breaking laws in accordance with Sick Time.  They are still making the 
same mistakes.  They changed the sick time policy so that employees can 
not "officially" get written up for being sick.  But they reduced staff 
so much, that if you do  call in sick, you hurt all your co-workers, 
and are socially ridiculed upon returning. Calling out sick is NOT a 
viable option most of the time!

summary: Great benefits but terrible advancement for current employees
advice:
The hiring of candidates for all more desirable  positions above the operations level really needs to be evaluated.  There is way too much preference being given to personal relationships when candidates are chosen for positions.  There are many current employees  that put forth a lot of effort both at work and outside by also furthering their education just to get into a higher positions and no one there will even consider them because they don't chat you up or befriend you.  It's really demoralizing to the quality employees that really care and want to better their careers and lives.  You are going to continue losing the good, quality employees  if you don't give the internal people in "low" positions a chance to better themselves.  
This office has become well known in the company as being terrible for advancement and monetary rewarding of dedicated employees for doing a good job.  The only ones that can change that are senior managers, by demonstrating and encouraging middle managers to hire fairly and ensuring all managers are receiving proper management/leadership training.  There is a huge difference between a manager/supervisor and a leader.  It's unfortunate that you do not have very many leaders in this office.
pros: They truly have great benefits; 401K, employee stock, PTO and health insurance.
cons:
The biggest negative is that this specific location has the worst advancement opportunities for current employees .  They are the ones that come in every day work hard, take on extra hours, always help, are the most knowledgable and the ones that consistently get the job done.   The internal individuals that get ahead here are the ones that choose to play into the corporate politics game, are not very knowledgeable and spend large portions of their day getting in good with higher ups in order to get hired for a better position.  This all has created a very cliquey atmosphere between operations and other departments that are considered higher than operations.  Another important bit of info, external candidates especially those that have personal relationships with managers in the company are much more likely to get hired for desirable open positions even if they are under-qualified &/or lack experience.  
 Half of the management & supervisors are also some of the worst I've had at the company.  Not every employee eager for power should have a manager or supervisor title, there is a lot to be said for hiring real leaders as your managers versus 'yes people' that are unqualified & dishonest to their reporting employees.  
It's really disappointing to me because I know first hand not all JPMC locations are like this.  I previously worked at other locations that really helped their employees advance and continue their career growth, which is actually the JPMorgan way.  This location does not follow that.

summary: Great from the outside, terrible from the inside
advice: None. You're too big to fail, so continue looking after yourselves. I'll join JP again when I'm 55 and continue your legacy by screwing all the lowly employees and collecting my fat paycheck. But before that, I'll keep innovating and building new products to challenge the industry.
pros:
Pays slightly more than the market rate.

Jamie Dimon and his executives are actually very smart people. The high-level MDs are also smart individuals. The low-level, the mid-level MDs and most EDs are... wow, I'm being very polite when saying that they're not the smartest.
cons:
The minuscule difference in pay is not worth you'll experience there. No employer cares about how many blue-chip company names you have on your resume -- today's employers care about what you've done, whether you were at JP or a small startup.  

Most of the people at JP are a bunch on misfits -- people who have been there for decades pushing the same button every day; all they want is a paycheck. At almost every town-hall meeting, they keep saying how they're investing in technology, yet, they keep using mainframe systems from the 1980s (I am not kidding -- their backend systems are literally mainframe from the 80s). 

If you're an ambitious, new-ideas and innovation driven person, this is not the place for you. This company is so big and so many people want a slice of the pie, that nothing ever gets done. Too many MDs have built their small empires and they want to keep it that way.

Promotions and big bonuses only go to those that keep agreeing and never challenge their managers. If you have an idea to improve the business, keep it to yourself -- you only follow what your manager tells you to do. 

If you're 55 years old and you're looking for a place to retire, or all you care about is your 8-6 job and a steady paycheck, then you'e in luck, you've found your perfect company. 

I know all this because I was an Executive Director -- I ran an entire department, but resigned because I couldn't waste my life away pushing the same button for the next 30 years.

summary: Worst job I've ever had, by far and I've had many
advice: Burn the rotten structure to the ground and start over
pros: Um... they used some cool technologies I guess
cons:
I would rather work at McDonald's that come back here. Every minute of every day I was worried I would be fired. I saw countless people quit or get fired. Early on people were fired left and right, but when people quit like crazy they found they wouldn't have anyone left to manage at this rate.

The organization I joined was an automation testing organization, testing their various apps and website. Despite over a month of background checks, and that they knew I was coming, I (a Software Engineer!!) never got a laptop ordered. Several weeks in, I finally got one when a coworker was fired. I waited 3-4 weeks for my badge to let me in, until then I would beg several people via text to let me in. I didn't even have a consistent place to sit for several weeks, again until the forementioned employee was fired.

I was hired as a contract employee, and long before I had received my laptop or had any of the necessary software installed, management was already demanding to know why I hadn't completed all the tasks assigned to me.

There is nonexistent planning. Requirements gathering, estimating, etc nonexistent. They are always asking you to complete impossible tasks in a matter of a week or even a few hours, tasks that should be given months or even years to complete. If you don't manage the impossible over and over again, they ask you to work weekends pro bono, making implied threats to your employment status. It is always YOUR fault and not theirs that the impossible wasn't done. Their is nonexistent coordination between the project managers, scrum masters, managers, etc. They all operate independently. The people in charge of the madness only interact with you in the form of threats, yelling, and making demands.

They run things by fear, brow beating, yelling, and intimidation. As people were dropping like flies they finally started to get an inkling that maybe the way they run things needs a tweak, but things were still an unmitigated disaster.

It's a huge company and I don't pretend to know whether the rest of the company is run like this, but the organization I worked in was worse than can possibly be imagined.

That said, my immediate manager Sergey Tuchinsky was a swell guy and several of my coworkers were great people. Everyone above him were some of the worst people I've ever encountered.

summary: They protect themselves with an arbitration agreement
advice: Going to the media when you think employees are not producing at the same level as they were before the global pandemic happened, issimply bad form.  Other companies can make work from home work,why can’t you?  If your help desk has to just close because of so many systems issues, maybe the reason for the production issues is not lazy employees that the CEO creeps on in insta,but your crappy systems.  Before offering something as absurd as scheduling an apppintment with an ATM to make a withdrawal, fix your outdated systems so employees can provide a good customer experience!
pros: Secure company, can move departments fairly easily for low level employees. Great if you like the idea of selling your soul.
cons: Where to start...they have a binding arbitration agreement so most employees have no option to take them to court, even for egregious violations. They have a new “virtual ID badge” that requires you to have a smartphone (that you supply and pay for) so you can get into the building, it also requires you to allow them to track your location, ALWAYS. They constantly force people to work off the clock, even though they already were taken to court for this, you have to log in and get your systems up and running, and only after everything is up and running can you log in, so that is all unpaid time. The systems are extremely outdated, many of them date all the way back to “BankOne”, believe it or not! The CEO goes to the media to complain that the employees are not producing enough in the middle of a pandemic, which puts massive pressure on every level of management on down to freak out about production. Communication in the company is laughable, nobody knows what is going on. They play games and do these experiments with things like your family’s health insurance, and you have nothing you can do about it. The pressure to smile and pretend that everything is GREAT, even though it is not, is insane, but if you don’t play along then you are the problem. Managers are elevated to the level of their incompetency and then left there to rot, and nobody trains anyone in anything so when someone that knows how to do something leaves, that knowledge leaves with them and everyone that is left has to just guess and assume and hope for the best. Bureaucracy is mind numbing and soul crushing. The hardest part of the job is trying to get the systems to work, keeping the access to the systems you need to be able to work, trying to figure out how to use these outdated systems, and keep the customers from figuring out how poorly everything works and the massive security failures that happen constantly. The place is soul crushing, I strongly recommend to find anyplace else first.

They finally hired a new manager and the first thing he did was write half the team up including myself. He fabricated many stories within the first week. jobTitle: Mortgage Banking Credit Underwriter Program Underwriter
summary: Mortgage Banking Credit Underwriter Program- Phoenix, AZ
advice:
Culture and structure of the entire Mortgage Banking division require complete overhaul. Just Google the reviews on Chase Mortgage and that will tell you everything about how terrible this business is. The business is totally rotten and dysfunctional internally, and this translates into abysmal customer satisfaction scores. 

A business where people are most concerned about keeping their salary and getting more weeks of vacation will not give any employee a satisfaction of working there.
pros:
Pros are ability to do NOTHING for weeks and management would not say a word. 90% of people in my department would be doing nothing for 8 hours a day and management would not say a thing. Sitting in your cube and looking at the Amazon, Ebay, shoe sales, concerts or anything else to make your day better was the SOP. 

Benefits and pay are good. Everyone out of 60 people who worked in my department was there because of cash. The SOP saying was: "I am here because nobody else would pay me the money I am making here for doing this kind of work". You had senior people who benefited from past pay adjustments and were making $100k+ for basically data entry work. Yes you make the money, but you are brain dead for 5 days out of the week. Your co-workers have no ambition and only come to work for that pay check, nobody is even trying to move up or out.

Work life balance is good, hence why the job is appealing to older people with families. Work schedule is pretty flexible and people can come and go as they please.
cons:
Where do I start?

1) Abysmal training.
2) Non-existent possibility to move up or out of the department. Underwriting is the apex of the mortgage organization, and you skills are extremely specific. So moving up or out is nearly impossible.
3) Toxic and lifeless office environment. It is a basic cube farm, with no new ideas. You have your "checklist", "excel calculators" and that is it. You enter data and do that 1000 times over every day. 
4) Lack of transferable skills. Once you get into underwriting, that becomes your skill. It is an extremely narrow field, so after a few years of doing the job you are basically stuck. To move out, you have to start at the bottom again.

advice: Talk to your employees more. Give advice and help them become a better leader. Join team meetings more so you know what's going on. Give resources to your employees. And not to make this message so long because there is just too much advice that management needs to here. To be a leader you need to care about your employees and do everything in your power to help them become a better employer and to do that you need to interact with them more and actually care about their future and help them succeed. cons:
Like I said in the pros:

I read a quote once how a great leader needs to genuinely care about the success of their team and it sad to say many mangers don't look out for their employees and give them the resources to grow. But please do note that's not all the managers at chase. With pay, they don't look at the market value so their pay is poor. Every year they just give a few thousand raise and bonus even though you did amazing. It's impossible to negotiate your pay with them also. Lastly, with when you are either joining chase or switching roles internally come prepared to ask lots of questions on what your day to day will be so you can be in a role you will be happy with. pros: decent pay for anyone with little to no education and substantial work history

I worked 80 hours prior to my departure thinking I would get my normal check, and only received $300. Then you ask me to pay you $250 a week later. At the call center level, too much emphasis is placed on your "scorecard". It is to the point that we were told we could only have one bathroom break a day, anything else was seen as excessive. There is little to no upward mobility at this level yet they are eager to give much more responsibility. End of the year raises will not eclipse $3. They also hold you hostage in your position for one calendar year before you are eligible to even apply for other positions within the company. This job pays well for college students looking for something that isn't retail. Although, you will have to fight for the ability to get part-time hours. This is not something that is easily granted based off of your request. The position is highly stressful, you're asked to close customer accounts on behalf of the bank. Imagine the response of the customer when you tell them you cannot provide a reason why. Strongly consider how much you need the $15 an hour before you apply for this job. You will work every single holiday with the exception of Christmas and possibly New Years Day. You are not eligible to even change your shift for the first six months of the position so any students or people with children heed this. The training is sub-par, pedestrian at best. You really do not learn how to perform the job until you reach the floor. Be wary of who you befriend because it is a gossip-laden environment, managers play favorites. It is pretty akin to prison meets high-school with the politics of the company and leniency given to employees. This place did not deserve my two weeks notice. Glad I am on to bigger and better.
